text:
This is a free preview of the upcoming Africa EVs Weekly Digest, part of the new CGSP Intelligence service.

Nobody wants to hear that their car has been recalled.

In the global energy transition, recall-driven safety concerns about EVs have proven a significant hurdle to EV adoption. In Global South countries, manufacturing defects raise further concerns about limited vehicle maintenance ecosystems.

While a recall is manageable for buyers who buy from dealerships, second-hand owners may not be as lucky—especially if the vehicles are not under warranty.

This is important because in many African countries, second-hand vehicles are a common choice due to their affordability. This week, BYD announced that it is recalling 183,211 Qin and Tang series vehicles produced between 2014 and 2022 due to a defect in a batch of brake pedal stopper pads, while another Chinese EV maker, Nio, is recalling some 686 of its Firefly-brand electric vehicles (EVs) over a steering system component manufacturing defect.

This recall news should create an urgency for localized EV solution centers to promptly address any issues that arise. Otherwise, African countries could become a dumping ground for technology that could quickly become obsolete.

Recalls aside, Chinese automakers continue to set up assembly lines in different African countries across various transport modes, from two-wheelers to heavy moving machinery. Kenya, Rwanda, Ghana, and South Africa remain the main hubs for these activities.

Still, exploration of more vehicle assembly and battery projects continues across the continent, with companies like BYD and Chery seeking to increase their vehicle-building capacity outside China.

Overseas, at the just-concluded 23rd China-ASEAN Expo (CAEXPO) in Nanning City, Guangxi, Chinese companies have been signing agreements with vehicle and component manufacturing stakeholders not only from Africa but also from Malaysia to Vietnam and Laos as they seek to grow their footprint beyond China, which has hit vehicle saturation amid declining car sales at home.

In South America, more Chinese vehicle investment is heading to Brazil as Chinese EVs increasingly gain ground in the region’s ride-hailing market.

Still, after-sales services and manufacturing development are likely to play key roles in the competitiveness of Chinese firms in the Global South during a key period when they face steep competition with one another.

This week in the Chinese EV scene:

Rwanda Edges Closer to Establishing a Chery EV Assembly Plant

The Rwanda Cabinet approved a strategic investment agreement under which Chinese automaker Chery will establish a local EV assembly plant. The approval on Friday, September 18, 2026, marks a formal step toward implementing the project.

Why This Matters: As a landlocked country, Rwanda’s move could become a template for how African countries without ocean access (key to easy imports) build sustainable EV businesses. Additionally, it could lead countries in the region to finally coalesce around a sustainable EV ecosystem, where interdependence creates more value.

BYD Mulling EV Assembly, Battery Projects in DR Congo

Chinese electric vehicle manufacturer BYD could build a vehicle assembly and battery projects in the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) if the exploratory stages proof the investment feasible. The company is looking at opportunities in the country’s growing electric mobility and energy sectors with discussions between BYD and the National Investment Promotion Agency (ANAPI) examining possible projects covering electric buses, local EV assembly, battery manufacturing and energy storage.

Why This Matters: If this goes through, BYD’s move could become one of the most strategic moves since the DRC supplies 70% of the world’s cobalt, a critical mineral for battery manufacturing. It could also become a catalyst for the DRC to refine its resources.

Ghana Inaugurates Phase Three of Chinese Vehicle Assembly Plant

Ghana’s Chinese-owned Zonda Tec has expanded its vehicle assembly capabilities by commissioning its third assembly plant. The new facility will support the local assembly of vehicles from Chinese automotive brands, including Great Wall Motor (GWM) and Chery.

Why This Matters: With the Chinese vehicle market reaching saturation, markets outside China are becoming more attractive as companies look for new ways to expand. In addition to bringing more Chinese vehicles into the African market, investments like Zonda’s will catalyze growth across Ghana and its intermediary markets.

Chinese Expo Showcases Electric Tuktuks Targeting African Markets

Chinese manufacturers showcased electric three-wheeler tuktuks aimed at international markets, especially in Africa and Southeast Asia, during the 23rd CAEXPO, and among the exhibitors was Guangxi Yuchai Special Purpose Vehicle Co., which displayed an electric three-wheeler with a 260 km range on a full charge. Other companies like Henan Fengshou New Energy Vehicle Group had four electric three-wheeler models on display.

Why This Matters: Two- and three-wheelers are the fastest-electrifying segment in East Africa and in Southeast Asia. Range has been the main challenge, but longer-range vehicles could accelerate the transition as more drivers feel less anxious about how far their batteries can go.

SAIC-GM-Wuling partners with Tan Chong to Manufacture EV Batteries in Malaysia

Malaysia’s Tan Chong Motor has signed an agreement with Chinese EV maker SAIC-GM-Wuling to explore the feasibility of EV battery packs and components manufacturing in Malaysia. The scope also includes recycling, reuse, and disposal of dead EV batteries.

Why This Matters: Chinese EV battery tech is increasingly expanding beyond the country, closely following vehicle trends and shifting potential markets. This expansion opens the door for other countries to benefit from skills and technology transfer, which could help build local ecosystems.

Dongfeng Signs Agreement with Vietnamese Partner

Chinese vehicle manufacturer Dongfeng Motor Group’s subsidiary Dongfeng Liuzhou Motor showcased its new EV and hybrid lineup and signed a cooperation agreement with a Vietnamese partner to jointly build a commercial vehicle knock-down kit factory.

The vehicles on display during the just-concluded 23rd China-ASEAN Expo included the Forthing Star Sea V9 hybrid camper, the Star Sea V6, the Chenglong H7 hydrogen fuel tractor, the Chenglong Yiwei 5 pure electric tractor, and the Chenglong Yiwei 2 intelligent pure electric light truck.

Why This Matters: Growing investment in manufacturing by Chinese automakers’ subsidiaries highlights the multi-pronged approaches they are taking- including selling fully built units of both electric and combustion engine vehicles as well as local assembly at different KD levels- to enter new markets and segments, expanding their reach and offerings.

SHACMAN X5000e Electric Heavy Truck Debuts in Laos

China’s heavy-duty truck manufacturer SHACMAN has introduced its X5000e in Laos. The X5000e supports dual-gun fast charging and battery-swapping capabilities and can handle complex road conditions. To simplify ownership, the company has also integrated a “purchase + finance + insurance + maintenance” solution that enables low down payment installments, battery risk assessment, an extended warranty, and rapid replacement in case of accidents.

Why This Matters: SHACMAN also plans to work with local partners to build a dedicated parts-center warehouse, train service engineers, provide 24-hour rescue, and coordinate charging piles. This approach offers assurance for buyers, which could help accelerate adoption in Laos’ logistics sector.

Chinese EVs Gain Ground in South America’s Ride-Hailing Market

Brazil’s Chinese-owned mobility platform 99, which offers ride-hailing vehicles and is operated by Chinese DiDi Chuxing, has partnered with car rental company Movida to give drivers access to lower-cost rental electric vehicles. The deal expands DiDi’s role in Brazil’s shift toward electric mobility, where 99 has more than 60 million active users and over 1 million drivers. While DiDi operates mixed fleets, it has been promoting the deployment of China-made EVs in Brazil.

Why This Matters: When Chinese businesses do business with one another in other countries, it can accelerate EV adoption, but it could also cause disquiet if localization isn’t supported. Also, if the operations become monopolistic, they may lead to fierce competition and even end up in court, as is currently happening with DiDi and Brazil’s dominant food-delivery platform, iFood, which is owned by a Dutch investment group.

In Context:

As the spread of Chinese EV technology across the Global South accelerates, the recalls by BYD and Nio show that market expansion also requires the infrastructure and expertise to keep those vehicles running throughout their life cycle. This is particularly important in African markets where second-hand vehicles are common, because without localized parts, diagnostics, trained technicians, and reliable after-sales support, technological expansion could leave buyers with vehicles that are difficult or costly to maintain once warranties expire. SHACMAN’s approach in Laos could help stakeholders elsewhere to offer comprehensive packages that “incentivize” adoption.

The Takeaway:

The emerging assembly and service projects matter not only for expanding Chinese EV access, but for determining whether Chinese technology becomes a foundation for durable local automotive ecosystems or simply another stream of vehicles flowing into markets without enough capacity to support them.

description:

Asked by Surge if other White House advisers shared his view, he added that Trump “wants to see reduced pressure on diesel prices.
We’re open to any idea that’ll lower diesel prices.’” Wright’s comments show what a big difference a year makes.

text:
With help from Sara Schonhardt and Zack Colman in the U.S., Johanna Sahlberg in Germany, Zia Weise in Belgium, Nicolas Camut in France, Charlie Cooper in the United Kingdom, Mike Blanchfield in Canada, and Brian Dabbs in Singapore.

Surge Preview

Energy Secretary Chris Wright campaigns against his boss’s potential diesel export ban at Climate Week.

The U.K.'s climate minister says nice things about data centers.

See the sentence that PM Mark Carney removed from his speech at Climate Week.

WHO’S WRIGHT ON DIESEL?: A crack in the White House’s energy policies revealed itself at Climate Week.

Energy Secretary Chris Wright used a series of appearances at the New York event Wednesday to forcefully argue against a ban on diesel exports — a position that’s potentially at odds with his boss.

Wright’s comments came as diesel prices have soared to around $6.50 a gallon, leading to a real time debate within the White House about how to confront voter angst over spiraling cost of living expenses. President Donald Trump pledged Tuesday to make a decision “fast, one way or the other” over curtailing diesel exports to other countries.

The White House is preparing a plan to halt diesel shipments abroad for 90 days, POLITICO reported moments ago.

“The blunt tool of banning diesel exports definitely doesn’t work,” Wright said in an event hosted by the Economist.

The public display of tension showed the mounting political pressure within the administration to alleviate high energy prices ahead of midterm elections that could remove Republicans from power in Congress.

Asked by Surge if other White House advisers shared his view, he added that Trump “wants to see reduced pressure on diesel prices. So we’re constantly talking about ways to do it. Politicians, senators, House members are constantly calling for a diesel export ban as they have for a long time. The president’s saying, ‘I hear you. We’re open to any idea that’ll lower diesel prices.’”

Wright’s comments show what a big difference a year makes. When the Energy secretary appeared at Climate Week last year, he used the occasion to question climate science and criticize countries for greening their economies.

This year, those culture war comments were drowned out by questions on energy prices.

The moderators of panels hosted by the Economist and the Wall Street Journal pressed Wright for information on the export ban, oil shipments flowing through the Strait of Hormuz and crude inventories in the U.S. Strategic Petroleum Reserve.

Wright blamed Ukrainian attacks on Russian refineries and California refinery closures for making the fuel more expensive. He said environmental regulations had made it impossible for the U.S. to build more refineries, but expressed hope a new one could be built in Texas.

Wright made the case for Washington working with oil companies and refineries to rebuild American diesel inventories, but stressed the effort should be voluntary.

“You’ll hear more from us in the coming days on this,” he added.

High diesel prices touch a nerve politically because they push up transportation and food costs. Trump, for example, has been hearing pleas from farm state senators to keep U.S. diesel at home.

But analysts say the higher costs owe to market factors and military conflicts.

“The diesel shortage has many fathers,” Kevin Book, the managing director of ClearView Energy Partners, told Surge. “Stocks were tightening on Ukrainian strikes before the Middle East disruption, and even if the California closings most directly affected the Golden State, lost capacity is lost capacity. But it is also a matter of throughput: Hormuz impairments and damage from Iranian reprisals which shuttered previously operable facilities tightened supply balances.”

Wright acknowledged that high prices are a hard problem to solve. When the Wall Street Journal asked him how long Americans would give the administration to fix the price crunch, Wright conceded, “I don’t know. That’s up to Americans.”

He argued the nuclear threats posed by Iran are “existential” and justify the temporary spike in prices.

“We’re making a trade-off that politically again is not a winner. I think it’s the right thing to do for America and Americans in the long run,” Wright told the Journal. “This conflict will pass, and you will see energy prices go down.”

WELCOME TO SURGE: I’m Ben Storrow, your lead author. Reach out with tips and ideas at bstorrow@politico.com.

Power Players

TALKING SHOP: Surge spoke to Katie White, the U.K.’s climate minister, about the COP31 goal of electrifying 35% of global energy consumption by 2035.

Is that an achievable goal?

In the U.K., we’ve very much been driven by our national interest in terms of electrification. We’ve got quite a long way to go in terms of meeting that 35 by 35 target, so it will be an ambitious target, but I think the focus on moving towards a more practical area and also threading together energy and climate is really helpful right now.

Electricity demand is surging. How will you address that?

We built quite a lot of kit in the U.K., so what we want to do is use it, and we want to use it really effectively. Now, first of all, we need to get it docked into the grid. We’re also investing in a grid upgrade, and we’re then looking at how to use the grid most effectively.

But actually, electric vehicles — the vehicle-to-grid shift, so that we can use the electric batteries to help the grid — are going to be helpful. Data centers could play a helpful role. I mean, if we get them connected to the grid and we use those data centers and that AI to manage the grid most effectively, that can be helpful.

Are you thinking about requiring data centers to use renewable energy?

My job is to support the transition towards a clean energy system. We can do that with data centers in the best way. They could be an asset. It could also be adding to our needs in a way that might not be effective. There is a lot of discussion going on in the U.K. at the moment, both within government and outside government. We are listening and we’re trying to figure out what’s the best way to do that to meet the AI growth opportunity within our carbon budgets, as well as say there’s this whole electrification opportunity which could do both.

How do you explain the benefits of electrification to consumers?

So when our new prime minister came in, one of the first things he did was take VAT off electricity. That is to meet people where they’re at now to try and give them some breathing space and reduce the pressure of the bills, but also to look at that longer-term trend that we know electrification is going to be good for communities. It’s also going to be good for businesses. So we are looking at how we do that.

But I think people know. I don’t think they need me to tell them that anybody there in the U.K. who has an EV, has had a lot cheaper driving experience than those who have had petrol and diesel cars over the summer. They’ve seen prices go through the roof. So, I think actually, quite often that talks. —Sara Schonhardt

QUOTABLE: Arizona Sen. Ruben Gallego, a Democrat, was asked at Climate Week how Congress should regulate data centers. Here’s what he said:

“I think it’s important that we do upgrade our grid. But I think those hyperscalers and the companies that are involved in getting the net benefit right now of AI are going to have to pay a big portion in terms of paying for that, because the general public right now does not see a benefit to AI, yet. And if we tell them that we’re going to go and tax them more to actually upgrade our grid in order for us to actually make sure we have a strong AI economy, we’re going to get pushback.” — Sara Schonhardt

REDACTED: Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney — the former United Nations special envoy on climate action and finance — wasn’t in the mood Wednesday to dwell on the threat of climate change during an appearance at the U.N.

Check against delivery: In the prepared text of a speech Carney gave at an event on improving the monitoring of the world’s oceans, Carney skipped over this line and left it on the cutting room floor: “We are living through the consequences of a world that, collectively, hasn’t taken climate change seriously enough.”

Context: Since becoming PM a year and a half ago, Carney has faced criticism for rolling back climate change policies of his predecessor, former Prime Minister Justin Trudeau. So much so that Trudeau’s former environment minister, Steven Guilbeault, quit Carney’s Cabinet earlier this year. He also skipped last year’s U.N. COP climate conference in Brazil after attending in previous years before becoming prime minister.

Today: Carney pledged a five-year CA$82 million Canadian commitment to the European Union’s OceanEye observation program.

“The ocean is warming. The Arctic Ocean is warming at four times the global average. We know the ice there is thinning. We can see the water’s opening, but we recognize our picture is incomplete,” Carney said as he announced the new funding. “We can’t protect what we can’t see. We can’t manage what we don’t understand.” — Mike Blanchfield

Driving the (global!) day

BUZZ THRILL: Electricity could meet 33% of global energy consumption by 2035, falling just shy of a 35% goal proposed by the hosts of this year’s U.N. climate talks, according to the International Energy Agency.

That’s based on current technologies and if energy prices return to where they were before the Iran war. Electricity currently accounts for 23% of total energy consumption, the IEA said.

Climate context: Faster electrification could cut climate-warming pollution 40% by 2035, in line with international climate targets, the report says. It could also slash costs of fossil fuel imports by $400 billion, removing 18 million barrels of oil per day from global markets.

But really?: Getting there won’t be easy. It would require greater investments in grids and clean energy generation, and more diversified supply chains, the IEA said. — Sara Schonhardt

TSCHÜSS TO FOSSIL FUELS: German Environment Minister Carsten Schneider presented a national road map for phasing out fossil fuels by 2045 on Wednesday at the U.N. General Assembly.. The 22-page plan was obtained by POLITICO ahead of its official release.

“Overall, the federal government will work to decarbonize the country’s power plant fleet in line with its climate targets by 2045 at the latest,” the document says. The phase-out includes all energy, not just electricity generation.

A big but: The road map does not contain new policy measures. However, it bundles the government’s existing efforts in the first comprehensive German document to lay out the country’s path away from fossil fuels.

The road map reaffirms Germany’s commitment to domestic and international climate targets. The EU’s 2050 net-zero target in particular came under scrutiny after Schneider questioned it at CERAWeek in Houston in March.

More context: Germany is the third country to present a road map for phasing out fossil fuels, following France and the Netherlands. Berlin hopes to inspire other countries in the process.

“Our roadmap is meant to send an international signal. I am sure that many more countries will follow,” Schneider said in a press release. — Johanna Sahlberg

FREEDOM GAS? A push by U.S. energy companies to deepen their influence in the Western Balkans is fueling EU concerns that the region could end up hooked on American fossil fuels — just as it attempts to reach clean energy targets.

The stakes: Albania, Kosovo, and Bosnia and Herzegovina have all signaled interest in buying up large volumes of liquefied natural gas from the U.S. or building infrastructure to support inflows. The countries say gas is needed as a transitional fuel as they reduce both Russian imports and coal consumption and switch to renewables. Both are key prongs of their EU membership bids.

Road bloc: EU officials say the plan could complicate the Balkan nations’ push to join the bloc. They question whether the projects being touted are feasible given that these countries currently have little to no domestic gas demand — meaning that flooding these markets with the fuel risks locking them into long-term gas addictions rather than helping them diversify.

“The countries ... in their wider aspiration to join the EU, have taken commitments to decarbonize, to set out the path and keep to this, to phase out basically fossil fuels,” András Hujber, who fronts the EU executive’s energy diplomacy in the Western Balkans, told a forum in Vienna in response to question from POLITICO. — Ben Munster

Our open tabs

PULLED PERK: Maryland Gov. Wes Moore (D) on Wednesday called for repealing his state’s data center tax incentives, joining a wave of state officials moving to crack down on the industry ahead of the November midterm elections, reports Adam Aton.

CHINA’S ENERGY LEVERAGE: The Iran war has strengthened China’s leverage in global energy markets, giving the country little incentive to yield to Trump’s demands during Chinese President Xi Jinping‘s visit this week, write Scott Waldman and Ben Lefebvre. While the war has spiked global prices for energy and created a political albatross around the neck of the U.S. Republican Party, it has enabled China to export its clean energy technologies and present itself as a more stable geopolitical partner.

That’s all for today. Thanks for reading!

title: Heinrich Introduces Legislation to Supports Investments to Build a More Resilient, Reliable Grid
description:
The Grid Resiliency Tax Credit Act would provide a 10-year tax credit.
The Grid Resiliency Tax Credit would support investments in new transmission projects, modifications to existing transmission projects, interconnection, subcomponents, and grid-enhancing technologies.
As electric cooperatives make the investments necessary to achieve these goals, having access to the transmission investment tax credit is crucial to reducing costs for consumers.
“The Navajo Transitional Energy Company (NTEC) supports Senator Martin Heinrich’s legislation establishing a 30% investment tax credit for qualifying transmission infrastructure.
An Investment Tax Credit is one of the best vehicles to bring key investors and developers to the table to grow our grid.
text:
The bill creates an investment tax credit to boost construction of significant transmission projects across the nation, could create 1 million jobs & help cut electricity costs by 0ver $27 billion annually

WASHINGTON – Today,U.S. Senator Martin Heinrich (D-N.M.), Ranking Member of the U.S. Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee, introduced the Grid Resiliency Tax Credit Act, legislation to incentivize the construction of new electric transmission infrastructure to help meet growing electricity demand, strengthen the grid, and lower costs for customers.

The Grid Resiliency Tax Credit Act will provide a targeted 30% investment tax credit (ITC) to support investments in large-scale transmission projects and grid-enhancing technologies that help to provide consumers with low-cost, reliable electricity.

At a time when energy costs are already through the roof, Americans need solutions that can bring down the cost of electricity while making sure our grid can keep up with growing demand. According to an analysis by ACORE and Grid Strategies, a 30% investment tax credit for transmission projects would create more than 1 million new American jobs building and maintaining transmission projects. Transmission expansion could save American families and businesses up to $27.7 billion per year on their residential electricity bills, according to Grid Strategies and Americans for a Clean Energy Grid (ACEG).

“As our energy demand increases, we need to improve our grid infrastructure and invest in building more transmission lines that deliver on the promise of reliable, affordable, and clean power,” said Heinrich. “At a time when families are already facing sky-high energy costs, we need to make sure our investments in the grid actually help bring those costs down. My Grid Resiliency Tax Credit Act will do just that by incentivizing private investors to put their capital behind building critical energy infrastructure projects, creating long-term certainty, starting from planning to the construction of transmission projects.”

The Grid Resiliency Tax Credit Act could be applied for the following investments:

Large significant transmission lines and line upgrades that cross certain geographic jurisdictions or are at least 100 miles which are:

At least 500 MW in capacity

At least 345 kV AC or 200 kV DC in voltage

Generator-tie lines and network upgrades to connect additional electricity supply and storage to the grid.

Innovative technologies such as advanced transmission conductors and grid-enhancing technologies.

The Grid Resiliency Tax Credit Act would provide a 10-year tax credit. Starting in 2026, all qualifying transmission projects that are placed in service would qualify for the credit and any qualifying project that starts construction before December 31, 2036, could claim the credit. The Grid Resiliency Tax Credit would support investments in new transmission projects, modifications to existing transmission projects, interconnection, subcomponents, and grid-enhancing technologies.

The Grid Resiliency Tax Credit Act is endorsed by the National Rural Electric Cooperative (NRECA), Berkshire Hathaway Energy, the American Public Power Association (APPA), the International Brotherhood of Electrical Workers (IBEW), the Edison Electric Institute (EEI), Oceti Sakowin Power Authority (OSPA), Navajo Transitional Energy Company (NTEC), the National Electrical Manufacturers Association (NEMA), SouthWestern Power Group, Pattern Energy, ACORE, Americans for a Clean Energy Grid (ACEG), and the Natural Resources Defense Council (NRDC).

“Investing in transmission infrastructure is critically important to meet soaring electricity demand and maintain a reliable grid. As electric cooperatives make the investments necessary to achieve these goals, having access to the transmission investment tax credit is crucial to reducing costs for consumers. We appreciate Sen. Heinrich’s leadership on this issue and his commitment to ensuring that all Americans reap the benefits of this critical federal resource,” said Jim Matheson, CEO of the NationalRural Electric Cooperative Association (NRECA).

“We applaud Sen. Heinrich’s reintroduction of the Grid Resiliency Tax Credit Act, which would leverage private capital to build the new transmission capacity needed to meet today’s surging electricity demand. If enacted into law, the Grid Resiliency Tax Credit Act would unleash historic grid infrastructure investment, enhance system security and reliability, and help keep electricity prices affordable for the customers we serve,” said Patrick Reiten, Senior Vice President of Berkshire Hathaway Energy.

“Customers nationwide are facing rising electricity costs, including increasing transmission costs, which are reflected in monthly bills. Senator Heinrich’s bill would help address that challenge by reducing transmission investment expenses, including for public power utilities, which would access the credit’s benefits through elective pay. This allows community-owned, not-for-profit public power utilities to receive the full investment incentive, keeping benefits local, supporting grid reliability, and reducing customers’ transmission rates,” said Scott Corwin, President and CEO of the American Public Power Association (APPA).

“IBEW members proudly build, operate, and maintain our nation’s bulk electric grid, and Sen. Heinrich’s proposed tax credit will spur the massive transmission buildout that our country urgently needs. This bill will catalyze private investment to create thousands of good-paying jobs for the lineworkers who build these projects while improving reliability and lowering costs for consumers, and the IBEW looks forward to working with Congress to pass this important legislation,” said Kenneth Cooper, International President of the International Brotherhood of Electrical Workers (IBEW).

“Across the Great Plains, Tribal lands hold some of the strongest renewable energy potential in the country, but inadequate transmission capacity remains one of the biggest barriers to bringing that power to market. The Oceti Sakowin Power Authority strongly supports the Resiliency Tax Credit Act, and we thank Senator Heinrich for his efforts to accelerate investment in the high-voltage transmission infrastructure our country urgently needs. Expanding transmission is fundamental to unlocking Tribal clean energy resources, advancing energy sovereignty, meeting America’s growing energy needs, and creating lasting economic opportunity for Tribal communities,” said Lyle Jack, Chairman of the Board of Directors of the Oceti Sakowin Power Authority (OSPA), a Tribal utility authority owned by seven Sioux Tribes in South Dakota.

“The Navajo Transitional Energy Company (NTEC) supports Senator Martin Heinrich’s legislation establishing a 30% investment tax credit for qualifying transmission infrastructure. Expanding the nation’s transmission system is essential. Rising demand, mounting reliability pressures, and long interconnection queues all point to the same conclusion: America needs more wires, substations, and switchyards, and it needs them soon. By taking a technology-neutral approach, the bill focuses on the infrastructure itself rather than any generation resource. That is the right frame. Every customer and every resource depend on a stronger grid,”said Vern Lund, CEO of the Navajo Transitional Energy Company (NTEC).

“America’s electric grid is under mounting strain from record demand growth, and the tools to relieve that strain — including grid-enhancing technologies like advanced conductors — already exist and are ready for deployment. What’s needed now is a policy framework that makes building them easier,” said Will Hupman, SVP of Government Affairs of the National Electrical Manufacturers Association (NEMA). “Sen. Heinrich’s Grid Resiliency Tax Credit Act does exactly that, offering an investment tax credit for qualified, regionally significant electric power transmission or generator-tie lines that meet rigorous performance standards for capacity, efficiency, and resilience. By providing an incentive to deploy high-performing transmission technology rather than just new poles and wires, Senator Heinrich’s legislation will help deliver the faster capacity expansion our economy needs.”

“Our country cannot meet our ever-growing energy needs without more modern transmission. But the patient capital required to work through the approval process, and then the high cost of construction, limits who is willing to take on necessary and large transmission projects. An Investment Tax Credit is one of the best vehicles to bring key investors and developers to the table to grow our grid. We deeply thank Senator Heinrich for his continued dedication and work to this end and are so appreciative for how much he prioritizes smart, needed transmission policy,” said Darryl Sockwell, General Manager of SouthWestern Power Group.

“A stable policy environment is key to unlocking investment in American energy infrastructure to strengthen grid reliability, support economic growth, and deliver affordable energy to communities across the country. Meeting growing energy demand requires significant investment in transmission, which serves to both improve reliability and provide the backbone to efficiently utilize both existing and new generation assets. Senator Heinrich’s Grid Resiliency Tax Credit Act recognizes the critical role transmission plays in advancing these priorities,” said Hunter Armistead, CEO of Pattern Energy.

“We need to add enough electricity supply to our grid by 2030 to power New York City 15 times over. That pace of growth is unlike anything we’ve seen, and this bill is a constructive step toward preparing our grid to affordably and reliably deliver that power,” said Ray Long, President and CEO of ACORE. “We at ACORE look forward to working across the aisles of Congress to deliver bipartisan solutions to grid modernization, permitting reform, and energy security.”

“This bill supports smart investments to help us build the grid that Americans deserve,” said Grace Henley, tax attorney at the Natural Resources Defense Council. “We need a resilient grid for the 21st century that delivers affordable, clean, and reliable energy across the nation.”

A fact sheet of the bill is here.

The full text of the bill is here.

This Congress, as Ranking Member of the U.S. Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee, Heinrich has introduced multiple bills aimed at strengthening our electrical grid and lowering energy costs for families.

Last month, Heinrich introduced the GRID Savings Act, legislation that aims to ensure that the biggest new electricity users play by the same basic rules that have applied to new power plants for two decades, while increasing transparency, protecting grid reliability, and making sure that families and businesses aren’t left paying for infrastructure that only serves new, high-demand customers. Last week, Heinrich took to the Senate floor to encourage his colleagues to put the GRID Savings Act up for a vote, however, Senate Republicans blocked the effort.

In July, Heinrich introduced the Grid Connection and Congestion Management Act, which would require grid operators to establish a fast-track process for connecting new energy projects to the electric grid, reducing delays and easing congestion.

text:
Gov. Josh Stein buckled his seatbelt Wednesday and sailed into the Lee County skies inside an electric plane no louder than a toy drone — a symbolic flight launched as North Carolina opens a new era of high-tech aviation.

By climbing into the cockpit, Stein became the first governor anywhere to ride an electric aircraft, part of a pilot program that will soon see “air taxis” flying across the state, some of them autonomous, some taking off vertically.

“Awesome,” said Stein, stepping out. “How many G’s did we pull?

“I’ll check the log,” said Kyle Clark, the pilot and CEO of Beta Technologies. “Maybe about 2.”

“I think it was 10,” Stein joked.

North Carolina and a handful of other states have been chosen for an FAA-backed program that will create a network of “air taxis” connecting hospitals, underused airports and rural residents of the state.

The idea is to use developing aviation technology to send aircraft that are both more nimble and inexpensive to get critical medical supplies into the state’s rural corners, especially during hurricanes or forest fires that conventional planes might not navigate.

“Too many people don’t have access to an emergency room in a short drive,” Stein told a crowd of several hundred at Raleigh Executive Jetport outside Sanford, “and that’s to say nothing of the specialty medicine.”

Joby Aviation, one of the state’s industry partners, traveled 121 nautical miles from Manteo to Raleigh last week in the first-ever autonomous flight, meaning the plane largely flew itself with no input from the safety pilot onboard.

Between Joby and Beta Technologies, the state has already seen roughly 30 of these experimental flights in the last week, and in the pilot program lasting until 2029, will one day evolve to carrying patients along with medical supplies.

State officials noted that North Carolina has 3.4 million people living in rural areas — second-highest in the country. This complicates care for patients needing unique surgeries offered far away or time-sensitive medicines and donated organs.

“We want more health care in rural areas,” said Debra Farrington, deputy secretary of NC Health and Human Services. “We must reduce the degree geography influences access and outcomes.”

Planes capable of traveling where roads are damaged by hurricanes and floods will allow for critical relief supplies to arrive quickly. NC Department of Transportation Secretary Daniel Johnson asked the crowd to imagine if relief supplies could have been delivered by air taxis during and after Hurricane Helene, easily passing over flooded highways and blocked rural roads.

“These air taxis will play a vital role in areas where minutes can mean the difference between life and death,” he said.

NCDOT assembled a team to carry out the program so the FAA can study data and make informed decisions about rules for air taxis in the future, including aircraft manufacturers Joby and Beta, operators Causey Aviation and Metro Aviation and health systems WakeMed and UNC Health. UPS Flight Forward, a subsidiary of the ubiquitous shipping company, will help with logistics.

“This is an exciting day for North Carolina,” Stein said. “Today we are cementing North Carolina’s aviation legacy ... North Carolina is first in flight, and we are the future of flight.”

title: What the climate movement can learn from organized labor | Waging Nonviolence
authors: Emma Jacobs, Kevon Paynter, Raphael Mimoun, Sarah Freeman-Woolpert, Erin Blondeau, Eileen Flanagan, Scot Nakagawa, T.P. Mishra, Saba Chaudhry, Mark Engler
description:
The coalition’s demands don’t yet include climate, but the climate movement can still organize with them to learn nonparticipation tactics and build solidarity toward a broad base that sees climate, anti-authoritarianism and affordability as one united fight.
The coalition includes many climate groups, like Climate Defenders, Extinction Rebellion, the Climate Museum, the Sunrise Movement, and more.
None of this is to suggest that the climate movement should stop organizing for local climate policies.
Noncooperation has been underleveraged in the climate movement, and we now have a chance to learn the tactic from organized labor while expanding our base.
Broad coalitions are being built to oppose the authoritarian takeover, but the climate movement has found itself on the periphery.
text:
Climate activists engaged in nonviolent direct action are used to the rinse and repeat of arrest: handcuffs, short trip to jail, a misdemeanor charge and then release to friends for a post-action pizza dinner. Show up at court a few weeks later for a brief arraignment and wait for the case to be dismissed. Low drama.

That’s changed under Trump. From the Declare Emergency activists charged with felonies (for applying washable paint to the protective case around a Degas sculpture) to the Extinction Rebellion activists under investigation by an FBI terrorism task force (for undisclosed reasons), activists can no longer depend on walking away unscathed from direct actions. Multiple states have passed anti-protest laws since Trump was elected, increasing penalties imposed on activists. Grassroots action has a higher cost now.

Simultaneously, with the gutting of the Inflation Reduction Act and its attendant tax credits for clean energy investment, the federal path to climate action is blocked. And local wins, while important, cannot surmount the incredible rollbacks happening at the federal level, as Sunrise Movement Executive Director Aru Shiney-Ajay recently pointed out.

Indeed, the U.S. climate movement is in deep trouble. If all that weren’t enough, the climate crisis is no longer top of mind for many on the left, especially with the rising authoritarian threat and the focus on affordability. With civil disobedience demanding greater risk, traditional policy advocacy for climate action at the federal level closed off and public attention turned elsewhere, what tactics do we in the climate movement have left?

What’s left is deep engagement with the labor movement — its members and its tactics.

Organized labor has a broad base, a track record of major wins and the power to shut down the economy. And make no mistake: Economic leverage is a necessary ingredient in the struggle to bring down companies as profitable as those in the fossil fuel industry.

Climate activists have relied heavily on tactics of protest and persuasion (see Gene Sharp’s categories), underinvesting in tactics of economic noncooperation. While the environmental movement has a history of consumer boycotts, there have been fewer instances of work stoppages or rent strikes. The climate groups that do engage in symbolic work and school stoppages (most famously, Fridays for the Future), have mostly been confined to students and are largely to make a political statement rather than a strategic attempt to gain concrete concessions from a specific target.

Strategically aligning workers with a rapid energy transition not only broadens the coalition needed to win durable policy victories, but builds power with a movement versed in strikes, walkouts, slowdowns and other forms of economic disruption. (Not to mention a bevy of tools like community benefit agreements and co-enforcement to promote follow-through on corporate environmental promises.)

Labor-climate alliances go back decades (see Blue Green Alliance, Climate Jobs National Resource Center and Labor Network for Sustainability), and unions have long advocated for a just transition that supports workers employed in polluting industries. But in the current political environment, we need these relationships to be stronger than ever.

One major opportunity for the climate movement is the May Day Strong coalition, which brings labor and community groups together to organize mass strikes and make big demands for systemic change. The coalition’s demands don’t yet include climate, but the climate movement can still organize with them to learn nonparticipation tactics and build solidarity toward a broad base that sees climate, anti-authoritarianism and affordability as one united fight.

Lessons from labor

Think about the situation at your job. Workplaces are pretty authoritarian: the leader doesn’t care much for the input of the people on the shop floor, and what the leader says goes. If someone gets hurt, let the government step in to help them. As unions teach us, for a group of workers to extract real concessions from a profit-maximizing boss requires building enough power among workers to shut the workplace down (or at least threaten to do so).

The same dynamic is true of the fossil fuel regime and the general public. The fact is that fossil fuel companies operate with little accountability to the public they endanger through their greed, harming the many for the enrichment of the few. By thinking of them as essentially authoritarian, we can focus on how to weaken their pillars of support so as to bring about their collapse (per Gene Sharp). In the face of fossil fuel oligarchs who operate without checks and balances, a worker-inclusive climate movement capable of strategic noncooperation offers the most viable path to transformative change in the current political landscape.

Pillars to target might include shareholders, frontline workers, the regulatory landscape, physical infrastructure and institutional investors. Some of this can be done in direct partnership with unions and workers (which I’ll explore more in another piece). Concentrating on a specific choke point like port logistics or oil refining can paralyze supply chains, amplifying our impact. Sectoral strikes within these industries are also powerful, making building common cause with their workers paramount. Strikes by public-sector workers like teachers also carry a heavy punch (though they are only legal in about a dozen states and typically only when a contract has expired).

Identifying the demand, as well as the target, is key to such acts of noncooperation. Strikes targeting companies can include demands for corporate investment in public infrastructure, on-the-job retraining, environmental audits or electrification of the supply chain. Strikes by municipal workers can include demands to divest pensions from fossil fuel companies, electrify public transit, retrofit publicly owned properties, pass heat safety mandates or clarify protocols for workers responding to climate disasters. Some of this is already happening through existing climate-labor alliances. Winning more campaigns like these would weaken the fossil fuel regime’s pillars of support by targeting the physical infrastructure, financial systems and legal regulations that enable it to continue wrecking the planet.

In addition to weakening the pillars of support, other indicators of a campaign’s success include increasing popular engagement and enhancing the capacity of the movement to escalate further (by bringing in more organizers, developing replicable tactics, etc.). The tactic of economic noncooperation can deliver all three.

But if we are serious about making a real dent in emissions, we need to target the federal government. The fossil fuel industry is so profitable and so powerful that it will likely require a major policy intervention to curb its rapacious behavior. The Inflation Reduction Act was a step in the right direction, but our movement was unprepared to exert the leverage needed to protect it from an unfriendly administration. That kind of leverage comes from bringing the economy to a standstill.

Almost all of us are workers (and customers, renters, borrowers, etc.), and all of us rely on a functioning planet to live. So what would happen if we simultaneously stopped? Didn’t show up at work for a few days, and didn’t buy anything? This would take massive preparation and coordination of course, but the impact would grind the economy to a halt. No bus drivers, no teachers, no bank tellers, nothing being built or sold. This is what is known as a social strike –— a mass action by an entire population.

Carbon emissions might briefly drop, but the impact of a strike reaches beyond a single day. The United Auto Workers’ use of the “rolling strike” to win big concessions from the nation’s three largest automakers shows the power a movement wields when it can credibly threaten to strike anywhere, at any time, in enormous numbers. Just as runaway capitalism caused the climate crisis, it has also constructed an economy that would be hobbled by mass work stoppages and consumer boycotts.

This is a tall order, to be sure. Even the labor movement’s use of work stoppages has declined over the past 40 to 50 years due to national policy change, employer opposition campaigns, the collapse of union membership and deindustrialization. But recent years have seen an upsurge of interest in unions, increased organizing and heightened class consciousness — suggesting a renewed opening for organizing workers and showcasing their power.

Previous Coverage

The People’s Climate March was a convergence of stories

And the climate movement has turned out en masse in the past; by some estimates, the 2014 People’s Climate March turned out 400,000 people. Imagine the number that will turn out after a historic El Niño cycle and four years of federal incompetence. Now imagine if that number of people — rather than flying to New York City and marching — all stayed home for a week. No shopping, no selling, no driving, no working.

Social strikes are rare and tough to pull off, but we saw a stirring example of their power in Minnesota this year. Roughly 25 percent of voters in the state either participated in the day-long strike or had a loved one who did.

For community members and workers across industries to participate in a nationwide social strike would take years of organizing. That’s why we need to start planning now.

The power of relationships

To engage broader swaths of the population, we need to build a bigger tent. Here the labor movement provides valuable wisdom. A helpful distinction that organizers often make is between our base and our allies. Our base shares our values but not necessarily every demand, while our allies share a specific demand but not necessarily all our values.

The climate movement’s base is made up of environmental activists, while our allies come from a wide variety of backgrounds including faith communities, student groups, human rights activists, lawyers, Indigenous groups, politicians, scientists, renewable energy companies and more. Anyone may have kids in public schools that are struggling with rising utility costs; they may rent an apartment in a complex with crumbling infrastructure; they may be part of a religious community that emphasizes responsibility for creation; they may be active with a political party that values outdoor recreation and fiscal responsibility.

These identities and memberships are valuable when we recognize that we do not need to agree on every issue in order to share some common self-interest and cooperate on a specific campaign. What enables us to continue to take coordinated action with our allies is a commitment to continued relationship building rather than shutting each other down for divergencies in viewpoints. Here climate can take a page from Saul Alinsky, who advocated for sidestepping ideological landmines and focusing on concrete issues that make a difference to real peoples’ lives.

In the current political climate, organizing based on shared self-interest is the only way forward. Families are struggling to pay the bills, and calls to deprioritize climate messaging in favor of an affordability frame are mounting. (Even Democrats are engaged in “climate hushing.”) We need a coalition broad enough to fight for both a living wage and a livable planet. Relational organizing based in self-interest is the way to build that. In his book “People, Power, Change: Organizing for Democratic Renewal,” Marshall Ganz explains that “relationships grow out of the realization of mutual benefit, the creation of shared value, and the commitment to a shared future.” Organizing to save our planet checks all three boxes.

In a labor campaign, relational organizing relies on the identification of organic leaders, training the leaders to recruit other workers, the workers agreeing on issues and then engaging in increasingly challenging structure tests — smaller actions that build organization and faith in each other. The bonds built between the workers through these tests are the basis for future organizing. In her book “No Shortcuts: Organizing for Power in the New Gilded Age,” Jane McAlevey spoke to the interaction between risky actions and building strong relationships. “[F]or workers to win substantial gains, the strike weapon is essential. … Transformational experiences come through high-risk collective action,” she wrote. Those transformational experiences tighten the bonds holding the group together and facilitate political education.

Previous Coverage

The data center fight is going global

Relationship building is also important for climate groups. Organizations like the Sunrise Movement or Fridays for the Future rely heavily on peer-to-peer organizing and one-on-one conversations. Incoming activists are given real responsibilities and opportunities to guide campaigns. And campaigns against specific pipelines or other pieces of fossil fuel infrastructure tap into preexisting community networks (like neighborhood groups, Indigenous communities and faith congregations), growing stronger by building alignment around a common demand.

What the climate movement needs now is to expand those networks to include communities that we may not see as natural partners. These diverse coalitions are prominent in local struggles against data centers that engage disparate groups such as farmers, parents, IT professionals, local businesses, sports clubs and more. We need to make sure they include workers across sectors, too.

The fulcrum

The ramp-up to May Day 2028 offers a prime opportunity for the climate movement to build powerful relationships with labor groups, while at the same time engaging in structure tests toward a social strike making climate demands upon the federal government.

After the United Auto Workers, or UAW, won their successful September 2023 sit-down strike (winning wage increases, job security and the inclusion of electric vehicle plants into existing contracts), they began building for more. The union called for locals across different sectors and unions to strategically align their contracts to expire on April 30, 2028, so workers can strike on May Day, the international worker’s day (rather than run the risk of an unauthorized “wildcat” strike). When different unions align their contracts in this way, they have more leverage than if one union acted alone. The May Day 2028 demands are not yet set, and the UAW’s goal is broad: “to create a crisis for the billionaire class to win more for all of us.”

Given low union density, even 2028 contract alignments by the UAW (and possibly the American Federation of Teachers and other unions) would have limited impact without community support. Even if some workers couldn’t walk off the job in a general strike (such as those covered by a current contract, precariously employed or unable to afford taking time off), they could still participate by not buying anything, calling in sick, engaging in a slowdown, working to rule, showing up to picket lines or rallies while off work, supporting striking workers with donations or sharing strike demands on social media.

That’s the idea behind May Day Strong — a labor-community coalition that deploys economic noncooperation to demand taxing the rich, protecting the vote, reining in ICE and expanding democracy. May Day Strong explicitly organizes community members who do not belong to unions, thereby building a broader community-labor coalition. On May Day 2026, they coordinated one of the most widespread May 1 actions in U.S. history. Right now, they’re focused on solidarity schools and local actions, like support for an Indiana community that lost power during a series of storms due to the local utility company’s alleged malfeasance. Ultimately, they are ramping up to a nationwide action on May Day 2028.

The coalition includes many climate groups, like Climate Defenders, Extinction Rebellion, the Climate Museum, the Sunrise Movement, and more. But the coalition’s affordability agenda contains not a single mention of climate change. Given the presence of climate organizations in the coalition, that could change, depending on the power that climate-focused coalition members bring to the table.

Regardless, May Day Strong represents an opportunity for the climate movement to engage in deep relationship building, both with union and nonunion workers, and to build strike-ready capacity. It offers a chance for the climate movement to stand in solidarity with unions and with working people, in a show of good faith. If the climate movement shows up for organized labor in 2028 — and the year and a half of organizing that precedes it — strong relationships will be built.

That means participating in structure tests so the strike muscle is strong and practiced when the time comes to use it. Climate activists should commit to deeper engagement with May Day Strong, attending trainings, turning out for May Day and Labor Day actions and advocating for the inclusion of climate demands in the platform. Climate activists should also show up for workers anywhere they are on the picket line, finding common cause against the billionaire elite who threaten us all.

None of this is to suggest that the climate movement should stop organizing for local climate policies. Local decarbonization and climate resiliency remain key battlegrounds. But in the face of overt hostility to national climate policies that encourage job growth while protecting our planet, we must also expand our tactics.

Noncooperation has been underleveraged in the climate movement, and we now have a chance to learn the tactic from organized labor while expanding our base. The time is ripe for these efforts. Broad coalitions are being built to oppose the authoritarian takeover, but the climate movement has found itself on the periphery. Despite the urgency of threats to our democracy, we cannot overlook the escalating threat to our planet. Engaging more deeply with May Day Strong allows the climate movement to drive home how the pillaging of our planet goes hand in hand with efforts to squash dissent and dismantle democracy. The climate movement cannot afford to wait until other threats are resolved. When the next “natural” disaster inevitably comes, the climate movement needs to be strike ready.

Where we go from here

By using May Day 2028 as a structure test, the climate movement can build capacity for a later date of climate noncooperation. Possible demands might include asking the president to declare a climate emergency or pass an executive order reinstating certain Inflation Reduction Act provisions. The important thing is to make a clear demand that can feasibly be granted by the specific target; in Minnesota, it was simple: “ICE out.”

Significantly, this tactic could be effective regardless of the party in power. The concepts of the pillars of support and Erica Chenoweth’s rule of 3.5 percent (the principle that movements have historically succeeded when they engage 3.5 percent of the population in sustained nonviolent action), both come from the literature on civil resistance to authoritarianism, so they do not depend on a functioning democracy. Furthermore, both parties rely on the economy functioning normally and would face significant public pressure if essential workers like teachers and janitors stayed home. Economic noncooperation — including, but not limited to strikes — has the benefit of being legal (for workers not covered by a contract with a no-strike clause). And if the climate movement keeps showing up for our allies in labor, we signal to all presidential candidates in 2028 that we will not be hushed.

Even in this time of movement winter, climate activists don’t have the luxury of despair. With heightened danger from climate chaos and increased political hostility towards climate activists, the stakes have never been higher for our movement and our planet.

But there is opportunity here, too.

text:
All 22 electric vehicles in a new BCAA and CAA road test completed a 230-kilometre Ontario route without stopping to charge, but the results showed significant differences in energy efficiency, charging performance and cost.

The 2026 BCAA & CAA EV Circuit Road Test took the vehicles from Blue Mountain to Vaughan across city streets, rural roads and highways. Even the vehicle with the shortest advertised range completed the route without charging, while the group used an average of just 40 per cent of available battery charge.

“For many of today’s EVs, the question is becoming less about whether you can complete a trip and more about how efficiently you can make it, where you will charge, how long charging will take, and what it will cost,” said Shawn Pettipas, BCAA’s Director of Corporate Purpose, in a statement.

Those factors varied considerably. Energy consumption ranged from 11.43 kilowatt-hours per 100 kilometres to 28.91 kWh/100 km. BCAA said the EVs used the energy equivalent of approximately two litres of gasoline per 100 kilometres, compared with roughly eight to 10 litres for the average Canadian passenger vehicle.

Lowest energy consumption (kWh/100 km)

Highest energy consumption (kWh/100 km)

Charging performance also showed a wide spread. During a standardized 15-minute session at a public Tesla charger, vehicles added an average of 110 kilometres of displayed range, while individual results ranged from 58 to 178 kilometres. Nearly two-thirds added at least 100 kilometres.

Most kilometres gained in a 15-minute charging session

Least kilometres gained in a 15-minute charging session

Costs varied as well. Based on the test’s charging session, the Tesla Model 3 recorded the lowest cost per 100 kilometres at $7.28, followed by the Model Y at $8.23. Tesla vehicles received preferred pricing at the Tesla charger used for the test. The GMC Hummer EV SUV had the highest cost at $24.39 per 100 kilometres.

Lowest cost per 100 kms

For dealers, the results provide another way to discuss EVs with shoppers beyond advertised range. Charging speed, efficiency and expected charging habits can create materially different ownership experiences even when vehicles can comfortably complete the same trip.

text:
Projects to Generate Over $3.7 Billion in Private Investment, Create More Than 1,000 Jobs

The New York State Energy Research and Development Authority (NYSERDA) today announced awards for eight new bulk energy storage projects and 13 large-scale renewable energy projects. Combined, these projects are expected to provide 1.7 gigawatts (GW) of new large-scale energy resources, create more than 1,000 family-supporting jobs and generate over $3.7 billion in private investment. This reinforces New York’s commitment to the development of locally-produced clean energy, energy storage, grid resiliency and economic development.

NYSERDA President and CEO Doreen M. Harris said, “These newly-contracted large-scale energy projects not only further the growth of clean energy and more than double the utility-scale energy storage that exists currently statewide – but they contribute to New York’s comprehensive, all of the above energy strategy. This will help reduce costs for New York ratepayers while continuing to improve the reliability of our state’s grid.”

These newly contracted awards are the result of NYSERDA’S first Bulk Energy Storage solicitation and its 2025 Tier 1 Renewable Energy Standard solicitation. By producing and storing clean energy, these projects will provide public health benefits from reduced exposure to harmful pollutants and are expected to provide over $127 million in economic benefits to disadvantaged communities , as defined by the Climate Justice Working Group.

New York’s First Bulk Energy Storage Awards

Once operational, the eight contracted bulk energy storage projects will add 950 megawatts (MW) of new energy storage capacity. The projects represent a diverse portfolio ranging geographically from New York City and Long Island to Hudson Valley and Western New York. They were selected through a competitive process that included bid proposals from 46 projects totaling approximately 6 GW of capacity. The eight contracted projects range in duration from four to eight hours and will provide critical reliability benefits to the state’s electric grid. The awarded energy storage projects include:

Western New York

Lighthouse Energy Storage, Chautauqua County

Zenobe Burns, Allegany County

Finger Lakes

Eastwater Energy Storage, Monroe County

Hudson Valley

KCE NY 5, Ulster County

New York City

Blue Spruce Storage, Bronx County

Palladium Storage, Bronx County

Long Island

Holtsville Energy Storage, Suffolk County

KCE NY 37, Suffolk County

Payments under these contracts will not commence until projects have begun commercial operation, after having obtained all required permits and local approvals. All projects are expected to be placed in-service by the end of 2030 as required by the 2024 Public Service Commission’s Energy Storage Order.

The contracted projects will use lithium-ion technology and, as with all NYSERDA-supported energy storage projects, are contractually required to meet the new storage safety codes that became effective January 1, 2026, and reflect the work and recommendations of the New York State Inter-Agency Fire Safety Working Group – convened by Governor Hochul. These safety codes, which are among the most robust in the nation, ensure that first responders have the necessary training, facilities are sited safely, and that all sites have comprehensive emergency response plans.

NYSERDA will issue the second annual Bulk Energy Storage Request for Proposals by year-end to continue progress toward procuring 3 GW of bulk energy storage over three solicitations.

2025 Land-Based Renewable Energy Solicitation Awards

The 13 contracted large-scale land-based renewable energy projects will total more than 719 MW of renewable capacity – enough to power over 230,000 New York homes annually, once completed. Awarded projects include land-based wind, hydroelectric and solar:

Capital Region

Flint Mine Solar, Greene County

Hecate Energy Greene 1, Greene County

Hecate Energy Greene 2, Greene County

Spier Falls, Saratoga County

Central New York

High Dam Hydroelectric Facility, Oswego County

Finger Lakes

Wethersfield Windpark, Wyoming County

North Country

Chateaugay Windpark, Franklin County

Diamond Island Hydroelectric Facility, Jefferson County

Ellenburg Windpark in Clinton County and Franklin County

Greens Corners Solar Park, Jefferson County

Rich Road Solar Energy Center, St. Lawrence County

Theresa Hydroelectric Project, Jefferson County

Southern Tier

Canisteo Wind Energy Center, Steuben County

The payments under the contracted projects will only begin once projects are constructed and begin delivering renewable energy to New York after obtaining all required permits and approvals. Several projects have already commenced construction activities. All projects are expected to be operational by 2030.

These projects will add to New York's robust portfolio of large-scale renewable energy projects, now comprised of 95 solar, land-based wind, hydroelectric and offshore wind projects currently operating or under development that are expected to deliver approximately 10.5 GW of clean power to the grid - enough to power over 4.6 million New York homes. Of these projects, over 3.2 GW of capacity are under construction, which, once completed, will add to the 36 operational projects currently delivering 2.7 GW of clean energy to the grid – now supplying enough clean energy to power nearly 2 million New York homes.

The State will continue to emphasize engagements with the projects’ host communities. NYSERDA offers resources and no-cost technical assistance to help local governments understand how to manage responsible clean energy development in their communities, including step-by-step instructions and tools to guide the coordination of new clean energy projects, permitting processes, property taxes, siting, zoning, and more.

Public Service Commission Chair Rory Christian said, “Opening the door to more renewable and storage projects shows the intersection of clean energy and economic growth to lower costs, pollution, and channel more energy resources to the electric grid. These projects will bring more power to communities across New York State while driving local investment and benefits to underserved communities.”

New York State Department of Environmental Conservation Commissioner Amanda Lefton said, “Governor Hochul is committed to reducing costs for New Yorkers while also advancing climate action, despite challenges and rollbacks from the federal government. These projects announced today by NYSERDA will help New York reduce reliance on fossil fuels, help ensure that the state has the energy it needs year-round to support the grid, and create good jobs in the clean energy economy.”

New York State Department of Labor Commissioner Roberta Reardon said, “New York’s transition to a clean energy future is a powerful engine for economic growth and job creation. These exciting new projects will not only enhance our state’s renewable energy production but will also offer New Yorkers a direct pathway into the growing green economy. By investing in both our clean energy infrastructure and our workforce training programs, we are ensuring that New York’s workers are fully equipped to lead the nation in climate action and sustainable innovation."

State Fire Administrator James Cable said, “As New York State invests in our clean energy future, protecting our first responders and the communities they serve is our highest priority. Thanks to the work done by our New York State Inter-Agency Fire Safety Working Group, these new energy storage projects will meet the highest safety standards. The Office of Fire Prevention and Control will continue to provide the support and training to fire services across the state to make sure they have the resources they need to keep their communities safe."

State Senator Kevin Parker said, “New York is building an energy future that is cleaner, stronger, and more reliable. These investments in renewable energy and storage mean good-paying jobs, stronger communities, and a more resilient grid. But our work must always come back to one priority: making sure New Yorkers, not just the energy system, benefit from this transition. Clean energy must be reliable, affordable, and deliver real value to the people who pay the bills.”

New York State AFL-CIO President Mario Cilento said, “Today’s announcement is yet another step toward achieving New York’s clean energy goals. We applaud Governor Hochul and NYSERDA for continuing to deliver for New York workers by ensuring these projects will create and maintain family-sustaining careers while providing New York residents and businesses the energy we need to thrive. We look forward to continuing our work together to ensure New York remains a leader in clean energy and good union jobs.”

Building and Construction Trades Council of Greater New York President Gary LaBarbera said, “As New York continues to pursue clean energy development, we must ensure that, in addition to improving our grid resiliency, these projects are creating family-sustaining union careers for hardworking people. As our energy program continues to grow, we applaud NYSERDA for ensuring these initiatives provide pathways to the middle class and improve the lives of all New Yorkers.”

NY-Best Executive Director William Acker said, “New York just took a major step toward the affordable, reliable grid our state needs. NY-BEST applauds Governor Hochul and NYSERDA for this important milestone in the state's first bulk energy storage procurement. These projects will strengthen the grid, lower costs, and help meet New York's growing electricity demand.”

Alliance for the Clean Energy New York Executive Director Marguerite Wells said, "The more renewables New York builds, the more insulated New York's ratepayers are from the global volatility and price shocks that have detrimental effects on our pocketbooks. Thank you to Gov. Hochul and the entire NYSERDA team for continuing to put New Yorkers first and advancing these long-term solutions that will benefit all."

New York League of Conservation Voters President Julie Tighe said, “Kudos to Governor Hochul for advancing major new clean energy infrastructure while Washington action is driving up energy costs. It's time to deliver on projects that will help us get off the fossil fuel roller coaster that’s choking our air and our wallets and that's what today's announcement will do. These gigawatts of new large-scale renewable energy projects are an important step toward more stable energy prices, better air quality, and good union jobs for New Yorkers. NYLCV congratulates NYSERDA on this important progress, for making sure projects will be cheaper by capturing dwindling federal tax incentives, and we thank Governor Hochul for her commitment to a clean energy future.”

Citizens Campaign for the Environment Executive Director Adrienne Esposito said, “Our energy demand continues to grow necessitating the need for large-scale renewable energy and energy storage projects to play an essential role in meeting this demand. Clean energy projects are rapidly scalable, are cost competitive, have lower operating costs and immensely reduced emissions. They will help insulate New Yorkers from the volatile geopolitical circumstances that are wreaking havoc to our energy costs and our economy. These projects will provide power for a safer, more affordable energy future. That’s a win for all New Yorkers! We commend NYSERDA President Doreen Harris for her leadership in advancing clean, renewable energy across the state.”

Natural Resources Defense Council NY Utility Regulatory Director, Climate and Energy, Chris Casey said, "New York needs to keep adding a diverse mix of clean energy resources to help replace its aging fossil fleet, meet growing electricity demand, and keep energy costs in check. The renewable energy and storage projects announced today will strengthen the grid, reduce exposure to volatile fossil fuel prices, and help deliver a cleaner and more affordable electricity system for New Yorkers."

Advanced Energy United Senior Vice President of Advocacy Amisha Rai said, “This announcement couldn’t come at a better time, and we’re glad to see the Hochul administration showing leadership on energy issues. Bringing new renewable energy and storage projects online means more homegrown power, more flexibility for the grid, and more investment in communities across the state. New York is showing other states that we can build the reliable, local energy resources we need, and build them quickly.”

New York City Environmental Justice Alliance Senior Energy Planner Daniel Chu said, "Renewable energy paired with energy storage is the most critical infrastructure to retire and replace the aging and dirty fossil fuel peaker plants. These awards will reduce pollution and improve service delivery in low-income communities of color, which have borne the brunt of energy pollution and been subjected to more frequent blackouts for the past few decades. We thank NYSERDA for their work and hope for continued expansion of bulk energy storage and large-scale renewable energy projects like this toward New York State's zero-emissions grid by 2040 mandate."

CHARGE Agenda

The Clean, Highly Affordable, Reliable Grid Expansion (CHARGE) agenda is a comprehensive plan to keep the lights on and costs down for New Yorkers while achieving a reliable, zero-emission grid. The five-pronged strategy focuses on driving down consumer costs, holding energy companies accountable, building clean energy at scale, modernizing the state's aging grid, and growing a clean economy with family-sustaining jobs. Through bold initiatives like the Ratepayer Protection Plan, historic transmission buildouts, and a new 8.4-gigawatt "Nuclear Backbone," the CHARGE agenda ensures an affordable, resilient, and self-sufficient energy future that prioritizes everyday ratepayers while building a cleaner, more sustainable New York.

text:
NEW YORK CITY – As Illinois marks five years this month since the passage of the landmark Climate and Equitable Jobs Act (CEJA), Governor JB Pritzker this week joined national and global leaders in New York City to highlight the state’s progress toward a cleaner, more reliable, and more affordable energy future.

Throughout his time at Climate Week, the Governor participated in meetings and events focused on advancing climate action and growing a clean energy economy. At a time when the Trump Administration has pulled back on climate regulation and clean energy investments, the Governor highlighted how Illinois is continuing to pursue a bold climate agenda, including expanding clean energy, creating economic opportunity, and protecting consumers as energy demand continues to grow.

“Five years ago, the Climate and Equitable Jobs Act set the standard for building a clean energy future that creates jobs, strengthens communities, and puts consumers first,” said Governor JB Pritzker. “While the Trump Administration is hindering the national clean energy movement, Illinois continues to pursue an aggressive carbon-free energy plan. I am proud to join leaders from across the country and world to showcase Illinois’ continued progress – from our growth in solar and wind to our nation-leading nuclear fleet. We are demonstrating what is possible when states invest in innovative solutions to some of the biggest climate challenges. Illinois is leading the way, and we are only getting started.”

Building the Clean Energy Economy in Illinois

In 2021, Governor Pritzker signed the Climate and Equitable Jobs Act into law, putting Illinois on the path to 100% carbon-free power by 2050. Since then, Illinois has set the national standard in clean energy equity, building a renewable energy economy by creating jobs, training a highly skilled workforce to fill them, and putting money back in the pockets of working families.

In the five years since CEJA was enacted, Illinois has passed significant milestones, including:

Building on CEJA Through CRGA

In addition to marking the five-year anniversary of CEJA, Governor Pritzker also highlighted how Illinois is expanding on that work through the Clean and Reliable Grid Affordability Act (CRGA).

Signed earlier this year, CRGA expands energy generation and storage, strengthens energy efficiency programs, and ensures the state can meet future energy demands. The law establishes a target of 3 GW of battery storage by 2030 and provides new tools to reduce electricity use during periods of peak demand when energy is most expensive. Together these provisions are expected to save Illinois consumers $13 billion over the next two decades. ​

CEJA is an investment in Illinois’ workforce, our communities, and our future – and the state is already seeing returns. As Climate Week NYC comes to a close, Governor Pritzker remains committed to helping Illinois build a more reliable, affordable, and sustainable future.

Together, CEJA and CRGA demonstrate how Illinois is creating jobs, strengthening reliability, protecting consumers, and building a more competitive clean energy economy.
