text:
Timeline: Impacted Communities Against Wood Pellets

The Industry Grows Quickly in NC

In 2011, Enviva opened its first wood pellet production facility in Ahoskie, NC. From 2011-2019, Enviva built and expanded four wood pellet facilities in NC. North Carolina became the largest producer of wood pellets in the nation.

Opposition Also Grows

North Carolinians mobilized to oppose the expanding industry. In 2019, Enviva underwent production expansions at three of their NC facilities. This was at the Northampton, Sampson, and Richmond County facilities.

Each facility had a public hearing. The hearings were about the expanded production and new air pollution controls. There was major organizing with big turnouts at the public hearings. But the Department of Environmental Quality (NC DEQ) granted Enviva the expansion permits.

In 2020, Active Energy Renewable Power planned to build a facility in Lumberton, NC. The local community organized with other impacted communities. They created the Impacted Communities Against Wood Pellets coalition. The ICAWP was victorious in stopping the AERP facility.

The Movement for Just Policies and the Next Generation

ICAWP continues to work toward policies and regulations. Ones that protect people and forests. The coalition is building legislative allies. It’s pushing for stronger pollution controls. Coalition leaders are nurturing the next generation to carry on this important work.

text:
Support CleanTechnica's work through a Substack subscription, on Patreon, or on Stripe. Help us produce all of the high-quality, original content we publish week after week despite the challenges of content-scraping AI, antisocial media, inflation, and other hurdles.

Vehicle electrification fans cried bitter tears earlier this month, when the startup Autonomy announced that it has added gasmobiles to its lineup of subscription service cars. The company’s EV journey is not over yet, though. Earlier today the company announced that it has also added the popular Volkswagen ID.4 to its roster.

A New Subscription Service For EVs

Drivers in the US routinely lease cars instead of buying them, but leases typically come with long term commitments, considerable paperwork, and credit restrictions.

Autonomy offers a more easily accessible alternative to leasing, in the form of month-to-month subscription plans. Flexibility and accessibility are the key selling points, though a subscription plan could also be more economical than leasing or renting, depending on the driver’s situation (check out the options here).

Autonomy’s founders are self-described auto retail, finance, and insurance “disruptors” Scott Painter and Georg Bauer, known for their NextCar venture among other transportation-related endeavors. In 2021, NextCar acquired the Autonomy brand and related assets from its former owner, Micro Focus (for the record, before Micro Focus entered the picture, Autonomy came under the Hewlett-Packard corporate umbrella).

“The acquisition of Autonomy includes the primary global domain, Autonomy.com, along with a family of country and subdomain extensions as well as trademark applications, goodwill, and related brand IP,” Autonomy explains of itself.

“Going to market with a compelling brand that people can relate to in tandem with a magical product and consumer experience creates a moat for any business and is the foundation for scaling this business profitably,” Painter added in a press statement dated November 4, 2021.

Bauer also chipped in his two cents. “The ability to immediately become a global brand through our acquisition of an IP brand library that is inclusive of assets in over a dozen countries is an incredibly valuable strategic asset,” he said.

Thousands Of EVs

Things started off with a bang. Autonomy initially offered select subscriptions for the Tesla Model 3 and Model Y, then quickly announced plans for scale-up. “The electric vehicle subscription company — the biggest in the USA — has ordered 23,000 electric vehicles from 17 different automakers in order to expand and diversify its subscription fleet,” CleanTechnica reported in August of 2022.

That same month Autonomy also hooked up with the leading car dealer AutoNation. Although Autonomy provides an all-online experience at the subscription end, someone has to take care of the hardware, and AutoNation provided it with A-list backup. “As Autonomy’s ‘Dealer of Record,’ AutoNation will support Autonomy’s planned acquisition, over the next 12–18 months of up to 20,000 electric vehicles from automakers that produce the most sought-after electric vehicles,” CleanTechnica reported.

Specifically, the partnership tasked AutoNation with vehicle preparation and delivery services for subscribers, alongside ongoing maintenance, repair, and reconditioning services for the Autonomy EV fleet.

Autonomy Adds Gasmobiles

Anyways, that was the plan. It made sense in 2022, but just one year later it almost fell to pieces, partly on account of the EV price war launched by Tesla CEO. The price cuts devalued vehicle fleets in one fell swoop. Hertz was most notably wounded, having once pledged to acquire 100,000 Teslas though eventually falling far short of that goal, and Autonomy also came in for its share of the fallout.

Autonomy has stayed afloat despite the setback, with part of the business plan involving a diversion into the ICE (internal combustion engine) field, announced on September 9. The timing is rather curious, considering that US President Donald Trump’s war in Iran has sent gas prices through the roof. Still, many US drivers prefer the security of a gas tank, however much it costs to fill up.

“The expanded lineup includes a range of gas-powered Ford vehicles including the Mustang, Ranger, F-150, Bronco Sport, Escape and Explorer,” Autonomy explains, adding that the move “signifies an important evolution of Autonomy’s product offering, which was previously exclusively focused on electric vehicles.”

“Our customers are telling us they want more choice and expanding the lineup enables us to serve a broader range of drivers. While EVs remain a key part of our business, adding gas-powered vehicles gives customers more options to choose what works best for their lifestyle and needs,” explains Autonomy CEO Fred Weick, who was evidently informed by his longtime, senior level activities at Mercedes-Benz and Daimler. Weick joined Autonomy as CEO earlier this year.

At present, the ICE lineup is only available for subscribers in California, with the in-state dealer Galpin Motors supporting the hardware pipeline. Near-term plans include partnerships with other dealers to support Autonomy services in Arizona, Florida, Texas, New York, North Carolina and Washington.

More EVs For Autonomy

The detour into gasmobiles could be a temporary blip on Autonomy’s screen if the war in Iran continues to spin out of control. In the meantime, the company’s EV fleet is still rolling.

In the September 9 announcement Autonomy also emphasized that it will “continue to expand its vehicle portfolio in response to customer demand and opportunities with automotive manufacturers and dealer partners.” Sure enough, the company followed through earlier today, announcing that the ID.4 has joined the lineup.

“The ID.4 vehicles join Autonomy’s fleet that already includes a wide variety of electric vehicles (EVs) including Tesla Model 3, Ford Mustang Mach-E, BMW i4, Hyundai Ioniq 5 and Chevrolet Equinox EV,” Autonomy explained, while also reminding everyone that the options include newly ICE vehicles, namely, the Ford Mustang, Ranger, F-150, Bronco Sport, Escape and Explorer.

Autonomy also took the opportunity to refresh everyone’s memory about its future plans. “The expansion follows the recent appointment of longtime Mercedes-Benz executive Fred Weick as Autonomy CEO,” Autonomy stated.

“Weick, who brings more than 30 years of global automotive, fleet management and financial services experience, is leading Autonomy’s next stage of growth as the company expands its vehicle offerings and partnerships with automakers and dealers,” the startup added.

Readers, what do you think? The gasmobile angle aside, Autonomy subscriptions can make access to an EV easier for anyone with a credit card and the ability to navigate online transactions. The system could help EV drivers stick with a zero emission ride when they move or relocate for short periods, including students and military among others. It could also help EV-curious drivers get over the hump with a relatively short-term commitment to the electric experience, ideally followed by purchasing an EV of their own.

The two canceled New York projects alone were expected to bring a more than $16 billion investment to New York and create more than 2,800 new jobs in the state.

text:
Gov. Kathy Hochul and New York Attorney General Letitia James on Tuesday announced that New York is leading seven other attorneys general in suing to block two illegal deals by the Trump administration that would hand energy companies $1.4 billion in taxpayer dollars in exchange for canceling four critical offshore wind projects. In the two lawsuits, one challenging a deal with Bluepoint Wind and the other challenging one with Invenergy, Attorney General James and the coalition argue that the deals unlawfully misuse taxpayer dollars and sabotage states' ability to meet growing energy demands. Filed during climate week, the lawsuits ask the court to stop the deals, which kill critical wind projects just to bankroll fossil fuel plants elsewhere in the country.

"The Trump administration’s unlawful pay-to-not-play scheme to pressure companies to forego planned offshore wind projects in America is an outrageous abuse of taxpayer dollars that hurts our ability to meet our energy needs, reduce emissions, create good paying jobs, and help secure American energy independence," Governor Hochul. "Working with Attorney General James and the seven other AGs who filed this lawsuit, we will continue to fight back against the unending war against clean energy being waged by this President and his Republican allies to ensure a healthier and cleaner future that allows us to keep the lights on and costs down here in New York.”

Since the beginning of the president's second term, his administration has continually attempted to stop offshore wind development. The President himself has stated that his "goal is not to let any windmill be built," and his interior secretary promised that "under this administration, there is not a future for offshore wind." After Attorney General James and other attorneys general secured repeated court wins striking down the federal government's efforts to eliminate wind development, the administration pivoted to a new strategy: paying off companies to abandon their wind energy projects.

"Americans are facing increasing energy costs because this administration would rather pay off energy companies than let us build the new power sources we need," said Attorney General James. "These illegal backroom deals take money that should have gone toward lowering New Yorkers’ bills and hand it to fossil fuel projects in other states, all while our energy demand continues to grow. At a moment when every available resource should go to keeping the lights on and prices down, this administration is choosing corruption over communities. We will fight until these unlawful deals are struck down."

The first lawsuit challenges the U.S. Department of the Interior's (DOI) deal with Bluepoint Wind, which canceled the company's lease off the coast of New York and, in exchange, paid Bluepoint $765 million from the Judgment Fund, a taxpayer-funded account reserved for legitimate legal settlements. Now, instead of building the offshore wind farm New York was counting on, Bluepoint will use the money to build a liquefied natural gas facility and has committed not to pursue future offshore wind developments in the United States.

In the second lawsuit, the attorneys general are challenging DOI's deal with Invenergy, which canceled three offshore wind leases, including one off the coast of New York, and paid the company $653 million from the same fund. Under the deal, Invenergy will not build a single wind turbine. Instead, it will redirect the $653 million to natural gas plants in Indiana, Wisconsin, Iowa, Kansas and Missouri and geothermal projects in the western United States, none of which will deliver a single watt of power to New York.

The two canceled New York projects alone were expected to bring a more than $16 billion investment to New York and create more than 2,800 new jobs in the state. The canceled projects would have connected directly to New York City's electric grid, providing a new source of electricity at a time when the state anticipates significant growth in demand. Combined with the other two Invenergy leases, the canceled projects were expected to generate over eight gigawatts of electricity, enough to power more than four million homes.

The cancellations come as New York's own energy planners project electricity demand will grow 8 percent by 2030 and 24 percent by 2040, driven in part by economic development and new large loads such as data centers. At the same time, aging fossil fuel generators are approaching retirement, making new sources of power essential to meeting growing demand and maintaining grid reliability. If the administration deprives the Northeast of new energy generation while demand continues to outpace supply, electricity scarcity and grid congestion will worsen, which could increase energy costs for consumers.

The lawsuits assert that the administration is unlawfully using taxpayer dollars to advance the president's policy preference for oil and gas development. The agreements do not resolve any actual or imminent litigation, meaning the administration has no legal basis to pay these companies hundreds of millions of dollars from the Judgment Fund, which Congress established solely to pay legitimate legal claims against the government.

Hochul, James and the coalition argue that the deals violate the Administrative Procedure Act, the National Environmental Policy Act, the Outer Continental Shelf Lands Act, the Judgment Fund Act and other federal spending laws. They are asking the courts to declare the agreements unlawful, void the lease cancellations, and block the administration from taking any further action to carry out the deals.

Joining Attorney General James in filing both lawsuits are the attorneys general of Connecticut, Delaware, Maine, Massachusetts, New Jersey, Rhode Island and Vermont. California is filing a separate, concurrent lawsuit challenging a deal between Invenergy and the administration to cancel a lease off its coast.

title: How a TESI Internship Opened Doors in Energy and Policy
description:
At TECO, I worked with the Emergency Management team on projects that connected technology, energy infrastructure, and environmental resilience.
TESI had taught me to look at environmental and energy issues from multiple perspectives, which helped me better understand how those issues translate into real-world utility operations.
This summer also reinforced my interest in the policy side of the energy industry.
I am now seeing many of the issues I researched at TESI discussed at the federal level, including energy affordability, clean energy, environmental protection, and infrastructure.
Coming to D.C. without a political science background was intimidating at first, but my experience at TESI gave me a foundation for understanding and communicating about policy issues.
text:
When I first joined the Thompson Earth Systems Institute (TESI) at the Florida Museum of Natural History, I did not expect the experience to lead me into both the energy industry and federal policy. Looking back, the skills I developed at TESI have shaped nearly every step of my career so far, from my summer internship with TECO Peoples Gas to my current role as a Legislative Intern for Representative Kathy Castor in Washington, D.C.

As an Environmental Leaders Intern, I learned how to take complex scientific research and turn it into information that people could actually understand and use. I researched scientific literature, environmental datasets, and historical sources to create educational publications for broad audiences. One of my most valuable projects was a guide to proposed Florida legislation related to energy, agriculture, and land-use planning and development. Researching legislation required me to understand technical issues, identify their potential impacts, and communicate those ideas clearly without losing the important details.

That experience became especially valuable when I began my internship with TECO Peoples Gas. At TECO, I worked with the Emergency Management team on projects that connected technology, energy infrastructure, and environmental resilience. I developed an Emergency Preparedness Dashboard in Power BI and created a Situation Reporting system using Power Apps, cloud-based databases, and Power BI. I also had opportunities to participate in environmental audits, visit solar sites, and see utility operations firsthand. TESI had taught me to look at environmental and energy issues from multiple perspectives, which helped me better understand how those issues translate into real-world utility operations.

This summer also reinforced my interest in the policy side of the energy industry. That interest brought me to Washington, D.C., where I am currently working as a Legislative and Communications Intern for Congresswoman Kathy Castor, a member of the House Energy and Commerce Committee and Ranking Member of its Energy Subcommittee. I am now seeing many of the issues I researched at TESI discussed at the federal level, including energy affordability, clean energy, environmental protection, and infrastructure.

Coming to D.C. without a political science background was intimidating at first, but my experience at TESI gave me a foundation for understanding and communicating about policy issues. It taught me that environmental work does not always happen in a laboratory or field setting. Sometimes it happens through a publication, a dashboard, a legislative briefing, or a conversation with a constituent.

TESI helped me discover that my interest in the environment extends beyond science itself. I want to understand how science, technology, energy, and policy can work together to solve problems, and the opportunities I have had at TECO and in Congress have allowed me to continue building on that foundation.

text:
MAST-P opens access to manufacturers in all 83 counties seeking to strengthen operations and pursue opportunities in aerospace, defense, electric vehicles and advanced energy

TROY, Mich., Sept. 23, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Small manufacturers across Michigan can now access no-cost business support through the Michigan Auto Supplier Transition Program (MAST-P), following an expansion of program eligibility from six counties to all 83 counties in the state.

Previously, eligible companies were required to be located in Oakland, Wayne, Macomb, St. Clair, Lapeer or Kent counties. The expanded eligibility opens the program to qualifying manufacturers throughout Michigan, to help small manufacturers strengthen their businesses, prepare for growth and diversify into new industries.

The MAST-P program is designed to help very small manufacturers with fewer than 10 employees who are connected to the internal combustion engine supply chain pursue opportunities beyond traditional automotive manufacturing. Participating companies can receive support as they evaluate and prepare to enter adjacent and growing industries including aerospace, defense, electric vehicles and advanced energy.

Companies accepted into MAST-P receive access to a coordinated network of partners, providing tailored support including:

Technical and industry assistance to strengthen operations and evaluate new market opportunities

Accounting and financial guidance to improve financial management, pricing, profitability and capital readiness

Legal support to identify potential risks and compliance needs

Capital preparation and connections to help companies pursue lending, investment and other funding opportunities

MAST-P is funded through the federal State Small Business Credit Initiative Investing in America Small Business Opportunity Program (SSBCI SBOP) and administered by MEDC on behalf of the Michigan Strategic Fund. The three-year initiative provides more than $9 million in funding to support small manufacturers as they adapt to changes across Michigan's automotive and advanced manufacturing economy.

Michigan manufacturers can learn more about the program, its qualifying criteria and apply by visiting automationalley.com/mast-p/.

About MAST-P

The Michigan Auto Supplier Transition Program (MAST-P) is a collaborative initiative led by the Michigan Economic Development Corporation in partnership with Automation Alley, Michigan Manufacturers Association, the Michigan Manufacturing Technology Center, the Michigan Minority Supplier Development Council and the University of Michigan Economic Growth Institute. The program supports very small Michigan suppliers as they transition to emerging manufacturing opportunities such as electric vehicle production, advanced aerial mobility and defense through coordinated technical assistance, financial guidance and education.

This project is supported, in whole or in part, by federal award number SSBCI-21034-0001 awarded to the Michigan Strategic Fund by the U.S. Department of the Treasury.

The Michigan Economic Development Corporation is the state's marketing arm and lead advocate for business development, job awareness and community development with the focus on growing Michigan's economy. For more information on the MEDC and our initiatives, visit www.MichiganBusiness.org. For Pure Michigan® tourism information, your trip begins at www.michigan.org. Join the conversation on: Facebook, Instagram, LinkedIn, and Threads.

Automation Alley is a nonprofit technology business association and Digital Transformation Insight Center focused on driving the growth and success of businesses in Michigan and beyond through innovation and automation. With a global outlook and a regional focus, we foster a vibrant community of innovators, entrepreneurs and business leaders through opportunities for collaboration and learning. text:
Despite the growth in renewable energy adoption, misinformation and disinformation about these technologies persist. That prompted the Sabin Center for Climate Change Law at Columbia University to release a report debunking 38 false claims about solar, wind, electric vehicles, and battery storage.

Notably for farmers and rural areas, this report highlights the multitude of ways in which solar energy will be beneficial to these communities. Agrivoltaics, for example, has been shown to enhance agricultural production and can increase the economic value of the average farm by over 30%. Additionally, farmland could be used more efficiently, as tens of millions of acres of farmland are currently being used to produce corn ethanol. Utility-scale solar produces approximately 31 times more energy than corn-ethanol crops.

The report continues to disprove notions that solar energy is harmful to the environment and biodiversity. Through careful implementation of solar development, negative impacts on biodiversity can be mitigated, and in some instances, can produce benefits to local biodiversity. Furthermore, there is a surplus of evidence showing that the lifecycle emissions of solar energy generation are far lower than fossil fuel generation.

text:
Cuts to U.S. federal incentives for carbon capture projects and an uncertain regulatory environment going forward have prompted some start-ups to move from solely capturing and storing carbon dioxide to selling it to oil companies to help them boost oil recovery.

Carbon management engineering company Spiritus, for example, has recently signed preliminary agreements with three U.S. oil and gas producers to sell them the captured CO2 for enhanced oil recovery (EOR).

The injection of CO2 into reservoirs could help unlock an additional 70 million barrels of oil from wells in Texas, the Rockies, and the Midwest, the CEO of Spiritus, Charles Cadieu, told Bloomberg in an interview published on Wednesday.

“The removal market is challenged right now,” Cadieu told Bloomberg, adding that “The pull is just great in the EOR space and that’s part of what it is to be a company: to go where the commercial traction is.”

After an initial momentum of carbon capture technologies, including the still not-matured direct air capture, the economic and commercial feasibility of projects has worsened amid insufficient government support and high costs.

In the U.S., the Trump Administration removed many projects from funding and the biggest buyers of carbon credits, such as the tech giants, have scaled back carbon credit purchases as they pursue investments in AI development.

The challenging market for carbon removal has led some businesses to fold while others, including Spiritus, have pivoted to providing CO2 to boost oil recovery at U.S. producers.

A University of Houston report from last month found that as many as

137 billion barrels of U.S. oil are technically recoverable using carbon dioxide-enhanced oil recovery (EOR). Texas and the U.S. Gulf Coast contain more than half of the U.S. oil resources considered technically favorable for this technology, according to the University of Houston white paper.

“Injected CO2 works to revitalize mature oil fields by reducing oil viscosity, improving sweep efficiency and restoring reservoir pressure, resulting in incremental oil production beyond primary and secondary recovery,” the report reads.

“CO2-EOR also supports permanent carbon storage and by virtue of this will produce uniquely low-carbon intensity oil for global markets.”

text:
WASHINGTON, D.C. — U.S. Transportation Secretary Sean P. Duffy celebrated North Carolina’s first demonstration flight of its next-generation aircraft under USDOT’s Advanced Air Mobility Integration Pilot Program. North Carolina is the fifth location to launch under the Department’s initiative, following Texas earlier this month.

Under Secretary Duffy, USDOT has created one of the largest real-world environments for testing electric vertical takeoff and landing aircraft (eVTOLs), autonomous planes, and drone technology.

The first-of-its-kind testing initiative has the potential to create jobs, connect communities, and strengthen American leadership in aviation. Data from the pilot projects will be used by the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) to develop new regulations that safely enable this futuristic technology at scale.

“Under President Trump, we are unlocking the future of flight, one test flight at a time,” said U.S. Transportation Secretary Sean P. Duffy. “More than 120 years after the Wright Brothers took to the skies at Kitty Hawk, North Carolina is again leading the charge to transform how Americans move. Thanks to these tests, we are closer than ever to welcoming next-generation aircraft into our skies.”

Joby Aviation, BETA Technologies and the North Carolina Department of Transportation are collaborating to test regional flight and medical transport capabilities between small local airports and a major hub. Last week, Joby’s remotely piloted J208 flew from Dare County Regional Airport (MQI) to Raleigh-Durham International Airport, while BETA’s electric ALIA aircraft completed multiple test flights between Raleigh Executive Jetport, Pitt-Greenville Airport and MQI.

“Integrating these new aircraft into our airspace is an exciting step, and these demonstrations in North Carolina help ensure we do it safely,” said FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford. “We’re taking the data and lessons learned to build a system that connects communities and creates more opportunities for jobs and essential services.”

“Rooted in our legacy as the First in Flight state, North Carolina is committed to shaping the future of aviation. Through eLIFT-NC, we’re exploring emerging technologies that can expand access, strengthen connections to rural communities and create new ways to move people and goods across our state,” said North Carolina Secretary of Transportation Daniel Johnson.

“It is fitting that the next generation of aviation technology will be taking to the skies in North Carolina. Today’s milestone shows how our state, private industry, and federal government can partner to unleash the power of American innovation, and I am grateful that advanced air mobility technologies can join the list of storied aircraft the Old North State has helped foster,” said North Carolina Senator Ted Budd.

“Aviation was born in Kitty Hawk, NC thanks to the determination and heroic efforts of the Wright Brothers. It is only fitting that the next generation of aircraft such as eVTOLs, autonomous planes and drones are tested in the birthplace of flight. Thank you to President Trump and Secretary Duffy for their leadership in the next frontier of aviation and for utilizing the legendary conditions of the Outer Banks to test this incredible technology,” said North Carolina Congressman Greg Murphy, M.D.

"120 years ago, North Carolina led the world in innovation when the Wright Brothers took flight for the first time. Today, North Carolina is once again leading the way in the next generation of aviation technology. I'm excited to see the new possibilities eVTOL aircraft will unlock for the American people, from connecting our small towns to major hubs to creating new jobs right here at home. I'm thankful to Secretary Duffy for his leadership in advancing the future of travel for all Americans,” said North Carolina Congressman Brad Knott.

“Over the past week, our aircraft flew more than 16 medical and disaster response missions between Raleigh Executive Jetport, Pitt-Greenville and Dare County Regional Airport,” said BETA Technologies Founder & CEO Kyle Clark. “We carried a field medical station and supplies along a route that connects the Research Triangle to North Carolina's coast, overcoming the distance that often prevents the movement of critical supplies, specialists and care in the times they are needed most. The FAA and U.S. DOT designed the eIPP to gather the data that will govern this industry, NC DOT brought these partners together to put e-LIFT to work under that framework, and Metro Aviation has flown every mission with us. Together, we are staging the future of routine medical and disaster response service across North Carolina.”

"From the first powered flight at Kitty Hawk to NCDOT's eLIFT-NC initiative today, North Carolina has always been where aviation's next chapter gets written. By conducting real-world flight operations here, we are showing how autonomous technology can support regional economies, lower transit costs, and bring the benefits of modern flight directly to communities that need it most," said Joby Aviation Chief Product Officer Eric Allison.

The North Carolina Department of Transportation and other eIPP participants are planning additional test flights throughout the rest of the year.

Additional Information:

In March, Secretary Duffy unveiled the eIPP program to begin testing advanced air mobility vehicles and their real-world applications. The eight selected projects span 28 states and partner with leading aircraft manufacturers, operators, and state partners, including:

Urban air taxi services

Regional passenger transportation (including short Takeoff and Landing aircraft)

Cargo and logistics networks

Emergency medical response operations

Autonomous flight technologies

Offshore and energy-sector transportation

The eIPP is a first-of-its-kind initiative outlined in President Trump’s Unleashing Drone Dominance Executive Order. It creates one of the nation’s largest real-world testing environments for next-generation aircraft with the potential to create jobs, connect communities, and strengthen American leadership in aviation.

text:
New Mexico Sen. Martin Heinrich introduced September 23 a bill to establish an investment tax credit for installation of regionally significant electric power transmission lines.

The act, called the Grid Resiliency Tax Credit Act, is meant to address the problem of aging infrastructure and help expand the power grid.

According to the wording of the bill, electric power transmission investments will:

improve resilience and lower costs by enabling access to diverse generation resources across the country;

increase the electric grid’s ability to weather storms and wildfire by enabling access to financial support for grid resilience measures;

promote economic benefits and create new jobs in communities across the country; and

enhance electric grid reliability.

Qualifying transmission lines would receive credits for an amount equal to 30% of the investment for such taxable year with respect to any qualified electric power transmission line of the taxpayer.

Qualifying property shall include: any conductors or cables, towers, insulators, reactors, capacitors, circuit breakers, static VAR compensators, static synchronous compensators, power converters, transformers, synchronous condensers, braking resistors, and any other property which is part of a substation, converter station, or switchyard, and ‘‘any property which increases the capacity, efficiency, reliability, resilience, or safety of a qualified electric power transmission line.”

The act would cover any transmission line with a capacity of not less than 500 MW and transmits power across a state boundary or between transmission planning regions. The act has a voltage requirement of not less than 345 kV in alternating current or direct current voltage of not less than 200 kV.

According to the National Electrical Manufacturers Association (NEMA), electricity demand is expected to increase by as much as 55% by 2050, making this bill well-timed.

“We need to deploy technologies that squeeze as much capacity as possible out of the existing grid while we continue the work of adding new generation, transmission, and distribution resources. The DOE's own Transmission Needs Study has flagged the same urgency,” said NEMA Sr. Director of Government Relations, Peter Ferrell.

"Senator Heinrich's bill gets that. It recognizes that increasing transmission capability doesn't have to mean building new poles and wires from scratch. A lot of it can come from strategic upgrades to what's already in the ground, like swapping in advanced conductors on existing corridors. That's not only faster, it's also reliably cheaper, and it means households and businesses aren't waiting years for entirely new infrastructure,” Ferrell said.

text:
The U.S. solar industry is entering a new phase. Solar installations continue to expand, but the market is also undergoing a major shift in where panels and components are manufactured.

After years of relying heavily on overseas supply chains, the U.S. has attracted billions of dollars into domestic solar factories. New manufacturing capacity is emerging across the country, while developers continue to build large amounts of solar power despite changing tax incentives, trade rules, and permitting challenges.

New research shows just how large that manufacturing push has become.

Cumulative U.S. solar photovoltaic manufacturing capital expenditure is expected to reach $12.2 billion by the end of 2026 since the Inflation Reduction Act (IRA) was introduced in 2022, according to analysis from Terawatt PV Research reported by pv magazine. That figure represents more than half of all U.S. solar manufacturing investment since 2001.

At the same time, the latest US Solar Market Insight Q3 2026 report from Wood Mackenzie and the Solar Energy Industries Association (SEIA) shows that the domestic solar market continues to operate at a substantial scale, with a large pipeline supporting demand for locally manufactured equipment.

U.S. Solar Manufacturing Investment Surges

The scale of recent investment stands out against the industry’s earlier history.

According to Terawatt PV Research, U.S. solar manufacturing capex exceeded $2.5 billion annually from 2023 onward. Spending reached a record $4.14 billion in 2024, with more than 60% coming from First Solar and Qcells.

First Solar’s spending included new manufacturing facilities in Alabama and Louisiana, while Qcells expanded its vertically integrated manufacturing operations in Georgia.

From Factory Investment to Actual Solar Production

The investment is also changing the structure of the domestic supply chain. The research firm tracks spending across buildings and infrastructure, new production equipment, and maintenance or upgrades.

Buildings and infrastructure accounted for roughly 60% of U.S. solar manufacturing capex between 2023 and 2026

It highlights how much capital has gone into establishing physical production facilities rather than simply upgrading existing lines.

This distinction is important because manufacturing announcements do not automatically translate into production.

A factory can have several gigawatts of announced capacity while still operating well below that level during its initial ramp-up. Terawatt’s analysis therefore looks at effective capacity, actual production, and capacity-conversion rates alongside capital spending.

The research found that conversion rates can range from just 15%-20% during early ramp-up to 70%-80% at some established manufacturing facilities.

READ MORE: The Ultimate Guide to Solar Energy: Everything You Need to Know in 2026 and Beyond

U.S. Solar Manufacturing Buildout Tops 75 GW as Cell Capacity Surges

According to recent SEIA and Wood Mackenzie data, U.S. operational module manufacturing capacity reached 75.3 GW, with another 14.4 GW under construction. Domestic solar cell manufacturing is also expanding, with 10.6 GW of operational capacity and 19.1 GW under construction.

That upstream growth could gradually reduce one of the biggest weaknesses in the domestic solar supply chain: the gap between module assembly and production of cells and other components.

Texas Emerges as a Solar Manufacturing Hub

The new manufacturing investment is also creating regional clusters.

Texas has emerged as the leading U.S. state for solar module production in 2026, according to Terawatt PV Research. Companies including Canadian Solar, Sirius/Elin, Imperial Star, SEG Solar, T1 Energy, TOYO/Abalance, and Waaree Energies are contributing to the state’s growing manufacturing base.

The Southeast has become another important manufacturing region, particularly across Louisiana, Florida, the Carolinas, Georgia, and Alabama.

This geographic shift could become increasingly important for developers and suppliers as the U.S. solar industry places greater emphasis on domestic sourcing and supply-chain security.

The expansion also extends beyond modules.

READ MORE: Google Backs One of America’s Largest Solar Projects to Power AI and Cut Emissions

Solar Demand Keeps the Factories Busy

Manufacturing investment would have less value without strong domestic demand.

The Wood Mackenzie and SEIA Q3 2026 outlook shows that the U.S. installed 11.4 GWdc of solar capacity in Q2 2026, a 45% increase from the same quarter in 2025 and a 43% increase from Q1.

Utility-scale projects accounted for nearly 10 GWdc, up 61% year over year.

Developers accelerated construction partly because of deadlines associated with federal clean-energy tax credits.

Wood Mackenzie estimates that more than 200 GWdc of utility-scale solar projects sit within the safe-harbored pipeline, providing significant near-term demand visibility.

The residential market presents a different picture. Wood Mackenzie expects U.S. residential solar installations to decline 23% in 2026 following the expiration of the federal residential 25D tax credit.

Utility-scale solar therefore remains an important source of demand as the industry moves through the policy transition.

EIA Data: U.S. Solar Capacity in 2026

EIA’s latest short term energy outlook revealed U.S. solar capacity to reach 181 GW and provide 8% of U.S. electricity generation in 2026

Its latest capacity data also shows how quickly new solar projects are being added. Developers plan to bring 43.4 GW of new utility-scale solar capacity online in 2026, a 60% increase from the 27.2 GW added in 2025, if all planned projects are completed.

Texas accounts for about 40% of the planned 2026 utility-scale solar additions.

The growth comes as U.S. electricity demand also rises. EIA expects electricity sales to reach 4,135 billion kWh in 2026, nearly 2% above 2025, with data centers and manufacturing contributing to higher commercial and industrial demand.

Can the Market Nearly Double by 2031?

Despite the policy and trade changes, Wood Mackenzie expects the broader U.S. solar market to maintain a substantial buildout.

The research firm forecasts annual U.S. solar installations to average around 44 GWdc through 2031, with cumulative solar capacity exceeding 545 GWdc by 2031.

The longer-term trajectory is even higher, projecting cumulative U.S. solar deployment to reach 769 GW by 2036.

However, the path will not be straightforward.

Permitting delays, interconnection constraints, changing trade policies, and the transition away from existing federal tax incentives could affect the pace of future installations. Wood Mackenzie estimates that permitting delays currently affect about 30% of the early-stage utility-scale pipeline.

Trade policy is also reshaping the economics of domestic manufacturing. New tariffs and minimum import prices are increasing pressure on the supply chain while potentially improving the economics of fully integrated U.S. production.

A New Phase for U.S. Solar Manufacturing

The $12.2 billion investment shows that U.S. solar manufacturing has moved beyond factory announcements. Capital is now going into buildings, equipment, and production capacity.

The next test is how quickly these factories can ramp up and compete as costs, technology, and trade rules change.

For investors, manufacturers, and developers, the focus is shifting from announced capacity to operating factories, actual output, and cost competitiveness. The U.S. solar manufacturing story is increasingly about production and capital already moving through the supply chain.

title: Pacific Power to charge new Oregon data centers for all costs associated with growing energy need
description:
Oregon’s second largest investor-owned electric utility could soon directly assign the costs of new energy projects and infrastructure needed for data centers to data center operators.
Data centers would also pay for any upgrades that are needed to serve them, even if those same upgrades benefit other customer classes.
Pacific Power’s data center customers are mostly large facilities in more rural parts of the state.
Pacific Power’s plan applies to future data centers, while PGE’s applies to future and existing data centers.
Pacific Power will need to address costs associated with its current data center customers and their demands next spring.
text:
Oregon’s second largest investor-owned electric utility could soon directly assign the costs of new energy projects and infrastructure needed for data centers to data center operators.

Pacific Power last week agreed to the deal following months of negotiations with staff of the Oregon Public Utility Commission, the watchdog Citizens’ Utility Board and a handful of environmental and community advocacy groups.

The Citizens’ Utility Board in a news release Tuesday called the agreement “the strongest from a for-profit electric utility yet” under Oregon’s new POWER Act, which mandates the state’s monopoly electric utilities create a separate rate class for data centers to ensure other customers aren’t subsidizing the massive energy demand from the server farms.

Both Pacific Power and the state’s largest electric utility, Portland General Electric, have raised customer rates 50% since 2020, while most customer classes became more energy efficient, and data centers grew to make up nearly one-quarter of all retail electricity sales statewide.

The three-member Public Utility Commission is expected to approve Pacific Power’s deal on Nov. 13, according to Charlotte Shuff, a spokesperson for the Citizens’ Utility Board. Shuff expects the Data Center Coalition, an industry group representing the tech companies, will attempt to appeal.

The coalition also appealed a recent PGE proposal to assign costs based not on how much each rate class is driving “peak demand” on the system, which is moments when usage is at its highest point. The state utility commission rejected the appeal, but the citizens’ board expects the coalition will bring the case to the Oregon Court of Appeals.

While Pacific Power’s plan assigns costs based on who is driving overall demand, PGE’s plan assigns costs based on how much each customer class is growing and adding to the system’s highest demand periods.

After the state’s Public Utility Commission approved PGE’s proposal in July, the company announced rates for data centers would increase by nearly 30% while residential payers would see their bills decline slightly.

Pacific Power goes further

Pacific Power’s proposal goes further than PGE’s by requiring new data centers that receive electricity from Pacific Power to cover the costs for all new energy generation and storage projects needed to power them, including new power plants and batteries, even if those additions also benefit other customers. Data centers would also pay for any upgrades that are needed to serve them, even if those same upgrades benefit other customer classes.

Data centers would be responsible for the cost of all wires and poles built for them to receive distributed power, and all costs related to energy purchased on the market from other companies to power them. If a 100 megawatt transmission line is needed to serve a 50 megawatt data center as well as other residential and industrial customers, the data center would pay for 50% of the transmission line, directly corresponding with its overall demand, according to the citizens’ board.

New transmission lines can cost several million dollars per mile to build, and the West is in need of more than 12,000 miles of new transmission according to one recent estimate.

Shuff said Pacific Power’s proposal came a long way in recent months and “to their credit they (Pacific Power) worked really hard to get to this. We’re really pleased with where we landed,” she said.

The utility serves more than 650,000 Oregon customers, and has seen energy demand grow by 8% between 2013 and 2023 due to data centers, according to a Sightline Institute analysis of U.S. Energy Information Administration data.

PGE is the state’s largest electric utility, serving 930,000 customers, and has absorbed the most data center load growth of any private utility in the state during the last decade, according to that analysis.

PGE’s system of charging customers based not on overall demand growth but “peak demand growth” is driven in part by the fact that they serve a higher number of small data centers in densely populated counties, according to Bob Jenks, executive director of the Citizens’ Utilities Board. Pacific Power’s data center customers are mostly large facilities in more rural parts of the state.

It’s easier to make the case that building a new transmission line in Washington County could benefit all customer classes, who are all using more air conditioning in the summer, he explained, “whereas if you build a data center in Madras, it’s pretty clear whether or not new energy investments and infrastructure costs associated with that are for the data center or not,” Jenks said.

Drew Hanson, a PGE spokesperson, reiterated in an email the different challenges the two utilities face.

“(Pacific Power’s) service area is larger and more spread out, so a single data center may require infrastructure built specifically for that customer, such as a new transmission line, substation, or power resource. In those cases, costs can be tied more directly to the customer creating the need,” he said.

Pacific Power’s plan applies to future data centers, while PGE’s applies to future and existing data centers. Pacific Power will need to address costs associated with its current data center customers and their demands next spring. The company has just a handful of data center customers at present “but dozens want to get onto their system, and some of them are massive,” Jenks said.

title: Holding company for clean energy contractors in Philadelphia aims to turn workers into owners
description:
Burgheiser said creating high-quality, dignified jobs must go beyond the future benefits of employee ownership.
Because of their recession-resistant recurring revenue, such businesses have become one of the hottest targets for private equity investors.
But where most such roll-ups end in a resale to the next PE buyer, Bergheiser’s end-goal is employee ownership.
That case is winning over a growing number of retiring business owners choosing employee ownership over a sale to private equity.
With three years of experience, according to Bergheiser, workers can easily earn a six-figure annual income with overtime.
text:
The workers installing your heat pump or EV charger could one day own a piece of the company doing the work.

That’s the thesis powering Celsius Companies, a new Philadelphia-area holding company that already owns two companies and is looking to acquire more small HVAC, electrical and other clean energy contractors in order to scale them up and transition 100% ownership to employees.

The family office Spring Point Partners is backing Celsius as a model that combines “entrepreneurship through acquisition,” or ETA, strategy with a planned employee stock ownership plan, or ESOP, to give ownership to workers. The ESOP would hold shares in Celsius, the holding company, which in turn owns the operating companies in the portfolio.

“The bottom line of this is, how do you create wealth for the folks who are doing the work?” says Matt Bergheiser, who founded Celsius this year after 16 years running University City District, which fosters workforce and economic development near the University of Pennsylvania, Drexel University and the Children’s Hospital of Philadelphia, with financial backing from those institutions.

In that job, Bergheiser says “he got the bug” for workforce development and building scalable programs to move frontline workers into stable, well-paying jobs. “I think that workers, especially blue-collar workers, should own a part of the value they’re creating for an enterprise,” he told ImpactAlpha.

What’s now Celsius began as Bergheiser’s own search fund. He used a mix of private debt, seller financing and equity to acquire two southern New Jersey contractors whose owners were approaching retirement. D&L Custom Services is an HVAC contractor that specializes in residential and commercial geothermal heating and cooling for net-zero constructions, and installs heat pumps. Ten minutes down the road in Camden, Spotlight Energy Solutions is an electrical contractor that now gets roughly of its revenue from EV charger installations and whole-home electrification.

Under Bergheiser’s ownership, Spotlight has since taken over electrical work D&L used to outsource. The two companies share a customer base in Philadelphia, New Jersey and Delaware.

Bergheiser’s promise to keep the businesses locally rooted and do well by their employees drew in the previous owners of D&L and Spotlight, who were put off by the approach of private equity buyers. The undisclosed equity investment from Spring Point will help sustain the holdco, acquire more businesses and form the ESOP, which brings substantial tax benefits. Burgheiser said creating high-quality, dignified jobs must go beyond the future benefits of employee ownership.

“I went in with both companies and instantly we created insurance plans which didn’t exist. We created or improved 401k plans, which didn’t exist,” he adds. “We created pathways to promotions. And now we’re working on the ESOP model.” Celsius will also have a profit-sharing plan that pays workers small bonuses.

Workers at ESOP-owned companies had median retirement account balances of $80,500 in 2023, more than double the $30,000 held by comparable non-ESOP workers, according to research by the National Center for Employee Ownership, or NCEO.

Frontline workers

The clean energy transition depends on a growing supply of electricians, HVAC technicians and installers. Yet those same workers rarely gain a stake in the businesses their labor is building.

HVAC and electrical contractors are prime candidates for employee ownership as a wave of trade-business owners nears retirement, often with no clear succession plan. Because of their recession-resistant recurring revenue, such businesses have become one of the hottest targets for private equity investors.

“Both HVAC and electrical, particularly HVAC, are prime targets for private equity acquisition,” Bergheiser says. Private equity’s share of HVAC M&A deals has surged from roughly 8% in 2023 to over 50% by mid-2026, as they consolidate small, independent contractors into large national portfolios.

Celsius is competing for the same deals, but with a twist. The holding company looks to acquire small operators, modernize their back offices and build regional scale. But where most such roll-ups end in a resale to the next PE buyer, Bergheiser’s end-goal is employee ownership.

In Celsius’ model, he says, “You’re not selling to a private equity where they’re going to absorb you into something that’s called something else.”

By implementing shared ownership at the holdco level, Bergheiser aims to build lasting wealth for Celsius’ workforce, help the portfolio grow faster and more profitably, and keep the businesses anchored in the communities they serve.

That case is winning over a growing number of retiring business owners choosing employee ownership over a sale to private equity. Even some PE firms are starting to share at least some of their gains at their portfolio companies with workers.

Bergheiser sees an opportunity to build a diverse workforce to meet the shortage of skilled workers the energy transition demands. He is launching an apprenticeship program to attract underrepresented talent and grow the workforce.

“We openly talk with [workers] about, ‘Hey, you’re an HVAC technician, you’re an electrician, but you’re also on the front lines of this climate change problem,’” he says. “We want to present them as businesses that are about modernizing facilities and future-proofing facilities and making them energy efficient. We think that’s our calling.”

At D&L and Spotlight, entry-level workers start with an average wage of $28 an hour. With three years of experience, according to Bergheiser, workers can easily earn a six-figure annual income with overtime.

“Our companies, it’s largely young men working at them. I think they’ve got to be given an opportunity and a path to feel like they’re part of something that’s bigger than themselves,” he says. “And an ownership stake is key to that.”

Employee-owned firms also see lower turnover rates, higher productivity and greater resilience during downturns than comparable companies. In an industry already short of skilled trades workers, these fundamentals may matter as much as the wealth building.

The owners of D&L and Spotlight, both in their mid to late 60s, have stayed on well past the six-month consulting and transition period typical of an acquisition. They were drawn by the chance to help build the employee benefits and shared ownership plans they’d long wanted for their employees.

“D&L’s owner rolled over a little bit of equity and has stayed, and is essentially my general manager,” Bergheiser says. “Spotlight’s owner has stayed in kind of a sales role.”

Wealth building

With Spring Point’s backing, Bergheiser plans to build a portfolio of a half-dozen businesses over the next five years. The goal is for those companies to generate $30 million to $35 million in combined annual revenue, employing 150 to 175 people, and for all them to be employee-owners.

“Spring Point’s investment will help us scale our vision of centering frontline workers in the clean energy transition, enabling skilled tradesmen and women to share ownership in one of the largest wealth-building opportunities of the next quarter-century,” Bergheiser said in a statement.

Spring Point has become a minority owner of Celsius and expects to recoup its capital from the sale of its stake to the ESOP. That eventual distribution also responds to a concern of investors with the holding company structure, which otherwise has appeal as a permanent capital vehicle that doesn’t require quick exits from well-operating companies.

Other holding companies under development include New York-based Nine Dean, anchored by the Ford Foundation, which is creating a holdco around a “quality jobs” thesis, but without a specific worker-ownership focus. Baltimore-based Obran, a self-described “worker-owned cooperative conglomerate,” has acquired more than a half-dozen companies in healthcare and logistics. Denver-based Ownershift buys small HVAC, plumbing, home services and other companies and transitions them to employee ownership, via employee-ownership trusts at the company, rather than the holding company, level

“We view employee ownership as a critical level towards more equitable wealth building,” says Sprint Point’s Norbert Cichon. Spring Point, the family office of Philly’s Berwind family, has also backed Apis & Heritage Capital Partners, a Washington, DC-based private credit firm that offers mezzanine financing for employee-led buyouts, particularly among companies with large representations of low-income workers of color.

Both D&L and Spotlight have been rolled up into the Celsius holdco. The two dozen workers at the two companies will become the holdco’s first employee-owners through the ESOP. Bergheiser suggests that ownership at the holdco level is a risk mitigation strategy for the employee-owners, especially in a situation where “there’s a business that’s lagging behind performance-wise with others,” he says.

Celsius is targeting trades businesses that can speed clean energy deployment and energy efficiency in residential, commercial and light industrial buildings, including high efficiency HVAC applications, electric vehicle infrastructure build-out and solar panel installation.

“I’m running an HVAC business, electrical business with zero technical expertise in those areas,” Burgheiser says. “I know how to market, I know how to sell, I know how to piece together deals and hire good talent.

“But they are the ones who are going to create the value in this enterprise.”

title: LSU's DeepFire Team Wins XPRIZE Wildfire Award for AI That Sees Fires Coming
description:
Today, the team received a $100,000 Special Recognition award at the XPRIZE Wildfire awards ceremony at the New York City Fire Museum.
The team, DeepFire, is led by Supratik Mukhopadhyay, professor in the Department of Environmental Sciences in LSU’s College of the Coast & Environment and a faculty member in the LSU Center for Computation & Technology.
DeepFire is an AI-based platform that can detect wildfires early, before they become destructive, and was recognized by XPRIZE for demonstrating its operational capability.
About XPRIZE Wildfire XPRIZE Wildfire is a four-year, $11 million competition to develop technologies that rapidly and accurately detect, understand and respond to wildfires.
Its co-title sponsors are the Gordon and Betty Moore Foundation and Pacific Gas and Electric Company; the Space-Based Wildfire Detection & Intelligence track is presented and co-designed by the Minderoo Foundation.
text:
Out of more than 300 teams worldwide, LSU’s team became one of eight finalists in a four-year, $11 million global competition to end destructive wildfires. Today, the team received a $100,000 Special Recognition award at the XPRIZE Wildfire awards ceremony at the New York City Fire Museum.

The team, DeepFire, is led by Supratik Mukhopadhyay, professor in the Department of Environmental Sciences in LSU’s College of the Coast & Environment and a faculty member in the LSU Center for Computation & Technology. It competed in the Space-Based Wildfire Detection & Intelligence track, where a system has as little as 60 seconds to detect every fire across a landscape larger than many countries and 10 minutes to report them to decision-makers on the ground with the fewest false alarms.

DeepFire is an AI-based platform that can detect wildfires early, before they become destructive, and was recognized by XPRIZE for demonstrating its operational capability. The team won one of five awards totaling $1.05 million in the space-based detection track.

“These teams pushed the boundaries of what is possible today, demonstrating meaningful advances in wildfire detection and response while helping identify where continued innovation is needed to move these technologies toward real-world deployment at scale,” said Andrea Santy, XPRIZE Wildfire executive program director.

“This is a great example of how LSU’s unified research enterprise brings together the best minds from across our campuses to solve problems that matter to Louisiana and the world,” LSU Chancellor Jim Dalton said. “Recognition on this stage tells the country what we already know: LSU is poised to reach its goal of becoming a top 50 research institution through meaningful innovation and excellence.”

DeepFire is three AI models working as one. A prediction model digests years of fire history, real-time weather, lightning forecasts, land cover and vegetation to map where fire is most likely to break out in the days and weeks ahead. Those risk maps tell a detection model where to look, focusing satellite feeds on the highest-risk ground so it can spot a fire while it is still small enough to stop. A third model forecasts how a fire, once found, will spread. Traditional wildfire forecasting is roughly 70% accurate, while DeepFire is above 90%. Wiring the three models into a single loop, DeepFire stands out from other systems that react only once a fire is already burning. DeepFire has been licensed from LSU by Firemark AI, a startup based in Calgary, Canada, which plans to commercially deploy the system.

“Wildfires take lives, homes, forests and entire local economies,” Mukhopadhyay said. What DeepFire gives fire managers is the thing that matters most in their work, and that is time. Catch a fire early and you can put crews where they will count, instead of chasing one that is already past stopping. But a warning only helps if it is almost never wrong.”

The final XPRIZE round put that claim to the test. Teams had to find fires in real time over New South Wales, Australia, where the 2019–20 bushfires killed 33 people and burned tens of millions of acres. Across the test days during the final, 96 percent of the fires DeepFire reported were independently confirmed, and the 10 alerts the platform was most confident in each day were confirmed every time.

Mukhopadhyay leads the DeepFire team alongside Thomas Douthat, associate professor of environmental science; Rubayet Bin Mostaviz, research assistant professor with the LSU AgCenter and LaHouse; and Saiful Sajol, a graduate research assistant in environmental sciences and doctoral student in computer science.

Students did much of the building. Dylan Wichman, a Stamps Scholar from wildfire-prone Montana who graduated in computer science in 2023, led work on the prediction model, an idea he first explored in a high school science fair project. He also developed the space-based detection system in collaboration with Sajol.

“This award belongs to a team, and above all to our students,” Mukhopadhyay said. “We have been building this technology at LSU since 2019, and the XPRIZE gave us the chance to prove it in the real world against the best systems on Earth. The problems we work on here, for Louisiana’s forests, its coast and its communities, are the same problems the whole world is facing.”

Along the way in the Wildfire XPRIZE competition that started in 2023, DeepFire earned a spot among 20 teams in 2024, chosen from more than 300 worldwide. It won a $50,000 Milestone Award for its data analytics in 2025, and a place among eight finalists judged live this year. LSU honored the team in February through its We Build Teams That Win recognition program.

About XPRIZE Wildfire

XPRIZE Wildfire is a four-year, $11 million competition to develop technologies that rapidly and accurately detect, understand and respond to wildfires. It awarded $3.5 million across its two tracks in September 2026. Its co-title sponsors are the Gordon and Betty Moore Foundation and Pacific Gas and Electric Company; the Space-Based Wildfire Detection & Intelligence track is presented and co-designed by the Minderoo Foundation. Lockheed Martin sponsored the Accurate Detection Intelligence Bonus Prize, and supporting sponsors include the Conrad N. Hilton Foundation, Costa Navarino, American Family Insurance, Fairfax Financial and the Roddenberry Foundation.

text:
The Trump administration unlawfully rescinded a $250 million grant program for solar energy for the largest county in Texas, a federal judge ruled.

The Environmental Protection Agency failed to convince the US District Court for the District of Columbia that claims brought by Harris County, Texas, were solely contractual and belonged in claims court, according to an opinion issued Tuesday.

Judge Tanya S. Chutkan ruled the EPA violated the Administrative Procedure Act by issuing guidance to rescind all $7 billion appropriated Solar for All funds, as last year’s spending bill only instructs the agency to rescind unobligated funds.

“By rescinding only unobligated balances available to carry out, Congress impliedly declined to rescind obligated ones, meaning the provision left funds already obligated to grant recipients undisturbed,” the opinion said.

Chutkan vacated the termination decision but stopped short of ordering the EPA to restore Harris County’s grant, which is set to fund solar panel installation in low-income and disadvantaged communities. The EPA said the Solar for All funds will remain in a Treasury account until 2031, and while the Trump administration has shown hostility to greenhouse gas reduction programs, “it does not show that the agency would defy a judgment of this court,” the opinion said.

This is the latest court ruling to strike down EPA guidance that led to the cancellation of a climate program, as the Rhode Island AFL-CIO also won its case to scrap the Solar for All cancellation language last week, and several courts have ruled the agency failed to review the terms of each grant.

Harris County is represented by Foley Hoag LLP.

text:
Chemours, a chemical company that’s notorious for leaking toxic “forever chemicals” into the Cape Fear River, is still discharging PFAS at higher than allowed levels, the company’s own water sampling data reveals.

The Southern Environmental Law Center says the ongoing discharges violate a 2019 agreement that Chemours struck with North Carolina’s Department of Environmental Quality. That agreement required the company to reduce chemical discharges into rivers, groundwater and air.

“We demand that N.C. DEQ use its authority to hold Chemours accountable and force the company to protect people’s health and the environment,” said Kemp Burdette, head of the Cape Fear River Watch, in a Wednesday press release. “If the state fails to protect its citizens, and chooses to protect Chemours instead, we’ll go back to court.”

PFAS, also known as “forever chemicals,” are a family of human-made chemicals that do not break down easily, and can remain in the environment for thousands of years. Over time, PFAS exposure can cause higher rates of cancer, lower fertility rates, and can weaken the immune system.

Chemours knowingly dumped PFAS from its Fayetteville plant into the Cape Fear River for decades and was aware of its harmful health impacts for humans, The Wilmington Star-News revealed in 2017. Since then, North Carolina authorities have pursued litigation against the company, hoping to make it pay for the damage to drinking water systems across the state.

In a letter sent to Chemours and DEQ officials on Wednesday, attorneys from the SELC said publicly available results from PFAS testing showed Chemours has still not met several goals from the 2019 consent order with DEQ.

For example, Chemours agreed to reduce the amount of PFAS that was reaching certain groundwater wells by 93% compared to the first year of testing. Testing data compiled by Geosyntec, a consulting group, shows that one of the groundwater wells only detected a 37% decrease in PFAS between 2019 and the first three months of 2026.

Geosyntec also found earlier this year that Chemours was discharging PFAS into Willis Creek, a tributary of the Cape Fear River, at about half the levels of the discharges from before 2019. Chemours’ agreement with the state required it to reduce these discharges by at least 75%.

“Today, contaminated groundwater discharging to Willis Creek is the leading source of PFAS entering the Cape Fear River from the Fayetteville Works facility,” Wednesday’s letter from the SELC reads.

While Geosyntec’s quarterly reports have shown that Chemours was meeting many terms of the consent order in previous years, its report from early 2026 shows PFAS discharges far above the allowable limits in several locations.

SELC’s letter also asserts that Chemours hasn’t reduced air emissions of GenX, another type of PFAS, by 93% as required in the consent order. Testing data from 2024 shows that Chemours had reduced GenX emissions on average by only 54.5%.

The letter comes just weeks after North Carolina leaders announced a new settlement with Chemours, in which the chemical company and two others will pay a total of $590 million in remediation costs to local authorities in the Cape Fear River basin. As part of that settlement, DEQ officials agreed to go over the 2019 consent order and identify which parts of it Chemours is still not compliant with.

“The coming months will show whether DEQ is willing to fully enforce the Consent Order against Chemours,” said Jean Zhuang, senior attorney for the Southern Environmental Law Center.

Officials from DEQ and Chemours did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

text:
Summit Charging is a “full-service EV charging station developer and operator” that was founded in 2026. The company currently holds NEVI grant awards for eight sites in Washington DC, Texas and California, representing 40 DC fast chargers and 56 charging ports, and is simultaneously developing four self-funded sites in California, and planning five additional sites in New York and Pennsylvania.

EV charging system manufacturer BTC Power has announced its role as a key technology partner with Summit Charging. The two companies have worked together on the technical specifications, Build America, Buy America (BABA) documentation, and site economics behind Summit’s expanding charging network.

Each Summit Charging location is planned to feature at least eight DC fast charging ports supporting both CCS and NACS connectors, along with restrooms and other customer amenities.

BTC Power says its support has helped Summit build stronger business cases for its NEVI applications. BTC Power’s All-In-One DC fast charging platform (available in 180 kW, 240 kW and 320 kW configurations) allows Summit to match charger output to the specific power requirements, traffic patterns and economics of each location. The companies are incorporating Battery Energy Storage Systems (BESS) into site designs to help manage peak power demand and reduce demand-charge exposure.

“Summit Charging is demonstrating what is possible when you combine the right locations with the right charging technology and business model,” said Seung June Oh, Chief Revenue Officer at BTC Power. “They are identifying locations where people already park, shop, work and travel, and developing those locations into public EV charging destinations. We have been developing and deploying public EV charging technology in the US since 2012, and we understand the equipment, site requirements and operating challenges that come with building a reliable charging network.”

Rather than evaluating sites solely by traditional gas station or travel center criteria, Summit assesses each potential location individually, weighing parking, traffic, accessibility, electrical capacity, nearby competition, customer demographics and utility infrastructure before selecting equipment and configuration.

“BTC Power is more than a charger supplier to us. They understand what it takes to turn a location into a viable charging station—from equipment selection and technical requirements to the economics of the project,” said Bruce Lee, founder and President, Summit Charging. “Our experience shows that EV charging can be built in many different types of locations. If a business has the right parking, traffic, and customer demand, there may be an opportunity to add EV charging and create a new revenue stream. Having a technology partner with the experience and product range of BTC Power gives us the flexibility to develop each site based on what that location actually needs.”

ETS is the first total battery solution provider in Echion's partner network, and it will cover production line design, cell assembly equipment and Korea-based cell design R&D for XNO.

Under the MOU, Echion will use ETS as a contract manufacturer for demonstration cells and product design iteration. For customers that want XNO cells, ETS will allocate part of its capacity in Chungju to customize cells to cylindrical, pouch and prismatic form factors. It also offers full turnkey cell design and manufacturing.

ETS is headquartered in Seoul and has additional locations in Chungju and Detroit.

Echion developed XNO for industrial applications such as mining, rail, maritime and data centers, and the company says it outperforms mainstream lithium-ion batteries on performance and durability. Niobium-based batteries are often considered a higher-performing alternative to lithium titanate (LTO) batteries in the premium category of fast-charging batteries with long cycle lives, according to the release. Like LTO anodes, niobium-based anodes operate at a higher voltage than graphite, which reduces the risk of lithium plating during fast charging.

ETS aims to demonstrate XNO-based batteries with up to 50,000 cycles and charge rates as high as 10C.

"We're confident that XNO batteries manufactured by the experts at ETS, on their well-trusted equipment, will give those customers seeking to produce their own XNO batteries the charging speed and cycle life they need to run their businesses," said Jean de La Verpilliere, Echion's CEO.

text:
Expanded capabilities support businesses pursuing investments across energy, manufacturing, emissions reduction, and emerging technologies

HOUSTON, TX / ACCESS Newswire / September 23, 2026 / ABGi USA has added carbon capture and clean fuel production tax credit services to its growing portfolio of energy incentives, extending support to businesses undertaking a wider range of energy and decarbonization projects.

The additions include the Carbon Oxide Sequestration Credit, Section 45Q, and the Clean Fuel Production Credit, Section 45Z. Together with ABGi USA's existing capabilities in clean energy investment, advanced manufacturing, and clean hydrogen incentives, the expanded portfolio allows the firm to support projects across multiple stages of the energy transition.

Section 45Q provides performance-based tax credits for qualifying facilities that capture and store carbon oxides rather than releasing them into the atmosphere. Depending on applicable requirements, qualifying projects may generate credits for up to 12 years after a facility is placed in service.

Section 45Z supports qualifying production of low-carbon fuels, including biofuels and sustainable aviation fuel, with potential credit value tied to verified lifecycle emissions.

These additions build on ABGi USA's broader energy incentive capabilities, which also include investment tax credits for qualifying clean energy technologies under Sections 48 and 48E, production-based incentives for qualifying domestic manufacturers under Section 45X, and credits for low-emission hydrogen production under Section 45V.

The value of these incentives can vary significantly depending on the type of project. Some may help reduce the effective cost of a capital investment, while others are tied to production, emissions performance, or qualifying activity over multiple years.

For businesses evaluating new facilities, energy infrastructure, manufacturing expansion, carbon reduction initiatives, hydrogen production, or cleaner fuel technologies, understanding which incentives may apply can help provide a more complete view of project economics and potential value.

"As energy projects become increasingly complex, businesses need to understand how federal incentives can support their investments. Expanding into carbon capture and clean fuel incentives allows us to help clients identify more opportunities and maximize the value of projects they are already pursuing," said Kris Huffman, Associate Director, Strategic Incentives & Capital Solutions.
