title: Climate disasters are growing. So are cuts to programs that prepare for them - Seymour Tribune
description:
As such disasters intensify, international climate adaptation and disaster preparedness aid programs have been slashed, leaving countries facing billions of dollars in avoidable damage and dwindling recovery funds.
Covering Afghanistan, Bangladesh, Myanmar, Nepal and Pakistan, the program used satellites and geospatial analysis for disaster risk reduction, water resources and land cover.
Cuts to programs like SERVIR-HKH will have cascading effects for years, said Neha Rai, a climate finance expert at ICIMOD.
Rai likened the cuts to climate programs to abruptly halting funds for cancer research, which needs years of sustained research for success.
“Climate risk is also a generational challenge,” said Rai.
text:
KATHMANDU, Nepal (AP) — Sitting on the floor of a makeshift shelter for survivors of Nepal’s deadly recent floods, Tenzin Dolma Ghale said she had nothing left but the clothes she was wearing. Her entire village and members of her family were washed away by the surge of water and debris that killed over 1,450 people and left more than 6,000 missing.

After speaking, she waved a hand and looked at the ground. “It’s all finished,” she said.

Ghale is among millions of people living with the deadly consequences of climate-related disasters. As such disasters intensify, international climate adaptation and disaster preparedness aid programs have been slashed, leaving countries facing billions of dollars in avoidable damage and dwindling recovery funds.

“The reality is that we need trillions of dollars every year, but developed countries have not met their obligation,” said Harjeet Singh, founding director of New Delhi-based Satat Sampada Climate Foundation.

Aid cuts weaken disaster monitoring in the Himalayas

The Trump administration’s abrupt cuts to U.S. foreign aid in 2025 eliminated or sharply curtailed programs serving millions of people worldwide, with devastating consequences for many communities. Reductions by other major donor countries deepened the funding crisis.

Among the programs shut was SERVIR-Hindu Kush Himalaya, a joint initiative of the U.S. Agency for International Development, NASA and the Kathmandu-based International Centre for Integrated Mountain Development, or ICIMOD.

Covering Afghanistan, Bangladesh, Myanmar, Nepal and Pakistan, the program used satellites and geospatial analysis for disaster risk reduction, water resources and land cover. It facilitated flood risk services, collaboration with the Nepal Red Cross Society on risk communication and more than 170 public data sets on glaciers, disasters and vulnerability.

Glacial and disaster preparedness experts praised the organization for its extensive research, cross-border coordination and support of local disaster reduction measures.

Before losing its funding due to USAID cuts, the program addressed mounting risks in a region where climate change has caused rapid glacier melt, shifting monsoons and increasingly frequent floods, landslides and glacial lake outburst floods, or GLOFs. Those changes endangered food, water and energy security for nearly 2 billion people living in or downstream of the region, according to ICIMOD.

Himalayan glaciers are losing mass 65% faster than they were a decade ago, according to a new report by global consultancy Systemiq, produced with ICIMOD. Yet only around 0.1% of the Himalaya’s estimated 40,000 glaciers are currently monitored in detail and on a sustained basis, the report said.

When funding for SERVIR-HKH ended, so did programs that monitored landslide forecasting, daily flooding, training programs and regional collaboration between countries.

With the program’s loss, millions now face a heightened risk of GLOFs, which can release millions of cubic meters of water and debris in just a few hours.

In northern Pakistan, melting glaciers have created 3,044 glacial lakes, with over 30 identified as likely to result in such floods in areas where over 7 million people live, according to the United Nations Development Program.

Afghanistan also faces an increased threat of GLOFs, according to research published by the University of Lausanne in Switzerland.

In India — which was not part of the SERVIR-HKH program but borders all of the countries that were and is also home to over half the Himalayas — over 130 high-altitude lakes are at risk of flooding.

South Asia is already experiencing deadly climate-related disasters. The 2022 Pakistan floods killed more than 1,700 people and caused an estimated $40 billion in damage. Flooding in Nepal in 2025 killed nine people and caused millions of dollars in damage. Cloudbursts, landslides, flash floods and extreme rainfall have wreaked havoc in the Indian Himalayas, resulting in the death of over 12,000 people and damage exceeding billions of dollars in the last 15 years.

The region suffered economic losses of at least $7 billion in 2025 due to climate-driven extreme weather, according to the Emergency Events Database maintained by the University of Louvain, Belgium. This database itself is at risk of being shut down as a result of USAID funding cuts.

In a statement to The Associated Press, the U.S. State Department said that the U.S. supports Nepal’s flood warning capacity through programs with the World Meteorological Organization and National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration. The department noted that SERVIR-HKH ended in January 2025 but that its tools remain active through ICIMOD.

The impact extends beyond communities hit directly. The Himalayan region is vital to national economies, with agriculture, industry, tourism and domestic use all dependent upon it.

Cuts to programs like SERVIR-HKH will have cascading effects for years, said Neha Rai, a climate finance expert at ICIMOD.

Rai likened the cuts to climate programs to abruptly halting funds for cancer research, which needs years of sustained research for success.

“Climate risk is also a generational challenge,” said Rai. “You need long-term observations, expertise, you need institutions that cannot simply be switched off and on as short-term priorities.”

Rai said cuts to cross-border programs have also impacted information sharing between governments, scientists and organizations across the region — a critical function in a region where what happens upstream directly affects countries downstream.

Climate finance shrinks as vulnerable countries face rising debt

These cuts are part of a larger trend. According to the Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development, official development assistance from its Development Assistance Committee members, which includes the U.S., fell 23% in 2025 — the largest annual contraction on record. Traditionally large donors such as the United Kingdom, Germany, France, Japan and Canada have also announced massive reductions, reallocating funds to defense and other domestic priorities.

Global South countries spend approximately 225 times more in debt repayments than what they receive in grant-based climate finance, according to a recent report by the advocacy group, ActionAid International.

“There is a toxic relationship, in fact, between the climate crisis and the debt crisis,” said Teresa Andersen of ActionAid International.

She said countries take loans to recover from climate impacts but then cut investments in clean energy and preparations for future climate-related extreme weather to repay the loans.

The money being provided isn’t nearly enough, and climate often isn’t prioritized, said Richard Sherman, a board member of the Fund for Responding to Loss and Damage, an international climate finance mechanism to assist developing countries vulnerable to the adverse effects of climate change.

“There’s plenty of money if it goes to certain priorities, but for climate change right now, we’re witnessing a severe depreciation of the importance to act and make systems more resilient,” he said.

While disaster recovery funds still exist, they’re also losing funding and aren’t equipped to handle the expected increase in disasters, he said.

“We’re not expecting developed countries to act as an ATM,” said Sherman. “But supporting vulnerable countries, helping them adapt and become more resilient means they’re less likely to suffer the kind of impacts we have right now.”

___

Arasu reported from Bengaluru, India.

title: Indiana advocates win solar suit, reopen door for $130 million program - IndyStar
description:
Solar energy groups in Indiana are among the victors in a legal battle to bring back federal funding to help electric customers save money on their bills.
The program, which former President Joe Biden's EPA created in 2024, would have brought more than $130 million to Indiana to help low-income Hoosiers cut their utility bills by funding community solar projects.
“EPA is taking action to end this program for good,” EPA Administrator Lee Zeldin said, announcing his intent to close the program.

“Since the Solar for All program was terminated last year, we've seen electric bills continue to go up,” Schalk said.
text:
Solar energy groups in Indiana are among the victors in a legal battle to bring back federal funding to help electric customers save money on their bills.

A U.S. district judge ruled Sept. 18 that the U.S. EPA unlawfully terminated the federal Solar for All program last year. The program, which former President Joe Biden's EPA created in 2024, would have brought more than $130 million to Indiana to help low-income Hoosiers cut their utility bills by funding community solar projects.

The EPA lacks authority to stop the program’s funding, Judge Mary McElroy wrote in her decision in the U.S. District Court for the District of Rhode Island. About six plaintiffs joined the suit, including Indiana's Black Sun Light Sustainability.

In the decision, McElroy wrote that Congress clearly intended for the EPA “to administer the already obligated [Solar for All] grants.”

The EPA in August 2025 announced it was stopping the $7 billion program, which was administered through the Greenhouse Gas Reduction Fund, a program President Donald Trump repealed on July 4, 2025.

“EPA is taking action to end this program for good,” EPA Administrator Lee Zeldin said, announcing his intent to close the program. “We are committed to the rule of law and being a good steward of taxpayer dollars."

But McElroy, whom Trump appointed in 2019, ruled against the agency.

Groups like Solar United Neighbors, which works in multiple states, helped lead the charge against the funding withdrawal, said Indiana Program Director Zach Schalk. SUN organizes communities and helps them obtain solar powered infrastructure.

“I'm thrilled that we won,” Schalk said. “We obviously believe Solar for All is a transformative program that will help tens of thousands of Hoosiers, and hundreds of thousands of folks around the country, save money on their electric bills and increase resilience in communities and decrease harmful pollution.”

Indiana groups celebrate solar victory

Black Sun Light, a plaintiff on the case, had been one of the Indiana groups leading the charge to assist Hoosiers. The group is an environmental justice organization focused on clean energy equity within Indiana.

The EPA must reopen the program immediately, Denise Abdul-Rahman, executive director and founder of Black Sun Light Sustainability, said.

“They broke the law,” Abdul-Rahman said. “This judge and court held them accountable.”

The Solar for All program is a game changer for historically marginalized communities, Abdul-Rahman wrote in a statement. The program would fund resilience centers that could assist people experiencing extending outages – as happened last month in northwest Indiana – by providing them with a place to get power or store their medicines in a refrigerator.

The money meant for Indiana was split into two programs that would bring solar access to Hoosiers. The larger program, comprising $117 million, was for statewide funding. The cities of Indianapolis and Fort Wayne would have split the remaining $15 million.

“This is a big win for us, and we’ve been committed to fighting for what we think is right,” Schalk said.

SUN, Black Sun Light Sustainability and other Indiana organizations have kept working this past year deploying solar around the state, Schalk said, but this court order breathes life into the yearslong plan the groups put together under Solar for All to expand access.

“Since the Solar for All program was terminated last year, we've seen electric bills continue to go up,” Schalk said. “We've seen significant storm related power outages and other events that just make the energy system more relevant than ever, especially for folks who are looking at budgets and trying to be mindful of their pocketbooks.”

The EPA, in 2025, pointed to the so-called One Big Beautiful Bill Act as justification for withholding the $7 billion from Solar for All, senior attorney Nick Torrey with the Southern Environmental Law Center told IndyStar. The court, however, said that the act did not support shuttering the program.

"The court clarified Congress wanted this to continue, and EPA can only act when they're authorized by Congress," Torrey said. "So what they did here was unlawful because they were acting without authorization."

Questions about Indiana's renewable energy? Ask IndyStar's environmental reporting team.

Karl Schneider is an IndyStar environment reporter. You can reach him at karl.schneider@indystar.com. Follow him on BlueSky or Twitter @karlstartswithk

text:
At this time last year, electric vehicle buyers in the United States were rushing to take advantage of the final weeks of the federal government's popular $7,500 tax credit for plug-in models that was set to expire at the end of September 2025.

That tax credit, which was first adopted during former President George W. Bush's administration in 2008 to help spur EV adoption, was eliminated on Sept. 30, 2025, by a law that was passed by Republicans in Congress and signed by President Donald Trump.

EV sales have been closely watched since then, as both supporters and detractors sought to understand how much demand for plug-in cars there would be without any government support. In recent months, in a bid to replace some of the lost federal support, state leaders in California stepped in to offer $3,750 in instant EV rebates to first time buyers in their state, which accounts for about a quarter of the nation's EV market.

According to Cox Automotive, U.S. EV sales were down nearly 24% in the first half of 2026, which is the most recent data available, compared to the first half of 2025, when the $7,500 federal tax credit was still available. But the group said EV sales in the second quarter of 2026 were up more than 14% over the first quarter of the year as rising gas prices pushed shoppers toward more fuel-efficient models.

With that in mind, the USA TODAY Cars Team took a look at where the U.S. EV market stands one year after Trump killed the federal tax credits and what shoppers can expect moving forward.

What happened after the federal EV tax credit went away?

Several of the most popular electric car models experienced steep sales drops in the fourth quarter of 2025, after setting records in the third quarter as car buyers rushed to take advantage of the $7,500 federal tax credit before it expired at the end of September 2025.

Here's how some of the top selling U.S. EVs fared in the third quarter of 2025 compared to the fourth quarter of that year, which was the first since Trump pulled the plug on the federal tax credit:

Tesla Model 3 and Model Y | Q3 2025: 481,166 | Q4 2025: 406,585

Ford Mustang Mach-E | Q3 2025: 20,177 | Q4 2025: 9,658

Hyundai Ioniq 5 | Q3 2025: 8,408 | Q4 2025: 2,279

Honda Prologue | Q3 2025: 20,236 | Q4 2025: 2,641

Volkwagen ID.4 | Q3 2025: 4,518 | Q4 2025: 248

As the auto industry moved forward into 2026, several automakers responded to Trump's decision to eliminate the U.S. EV tax credit by announcing plans to pull the plug on low-selling electric models.

Ford announced plans to transition its F-150 Lightning pickup from a fully electric vehicle to a hybrid car type known as an Extended Range Electric Vehicle, or EREV.

Meanwhile, Honda axed three of the three electric models that it planned to build and sell in the United States. The Japanese automaker announced in a March 12 statement that it ended its plans to produce the electric Honda 0 SUV, Honda 0 Saloon and Acura RS.

Lamborghini also abandoned plans to develop fully electric cars by the end of the decade in favor of building more hybrids. The Italian automaker, a subsidiary of Volkswagen, confirmed to USA TODAY that they are not following the plan to build battery electric cars by 2030 because of weakening demand in the United States.

Also, Tesla is planning to end production of its Model S luxury electric sedan and Model X luxury electric SUV in the spring in favor of building robots, company CEO Elon Musk told investors on Tesla's January earnings call.

Where does the US EV industry stand now?

Early signs pointed to continued increases in EV interest as summer turns the fall. Cox said carmakers sold an estimated 78,895 electric cars in August, which the group said was up 2.5% from July but, as expected, was down 46.9% from August 2025. By contrast, hybrid sales were forecasted to increase by approximately 9% in the first half of 2026.

"August brought further evidence of a steadily maturing electric vehicle (EV) market," Stephanie Valdez Streaty, Cox Automotive's director of Industry Insights, said.

"New and used EV sales increased from July, inventory levels moved closer to (hybrids) and growing off-lease returns continued to expand used EV availability," she continued. "At the same time, lower-priced models gained share in the new market, helping narrow the price gap between EVs and (hybrid) vehicles."

California started its "MyFirstEV" rebate program in August, and 13 major automakers confirmed plans to participate in California's new $3,500 instant rebate program for new EV buyers in the state. California accounted for nearly 20% of all U.S. EV sales in the first half of 2026, according to the Alliance for Automotive Innovation, which lobbies in Washington for most major carmakers.

New polling from the Zero Emission Transportation Association, which lobbies for EV-friendly policies in Washington, shows willingness to consider EVs may be more closely tied to age than partisan affiliation, which was the assumption in the early days of the second Trump administration.

ZETA's poll showed 75% of Americans under 35 say they are likely to purchase or lease an EV within five years, compared to just 23% of adults over 65 who said they would consider buying a plug-in model soon. By comparison, ZETA said 57% of Democrats and 45% of Republicans. The group said the 52% spread on the age comparison dwarfs the 12% spread on the partisanship question, showing age is a better predictor of openness to EV adoption now than politics.

"What this data shows us is that EVs are the cars of today and of the future," Corey Cantor, research director at ZETA said in a statement. "Even if they don't own one now, many people see themselves driving EVs within the next five years. Consumers want industry and policy choices that will make that ownership easier to attain, not harder."

Keith Laing is an automotive reporter on the National Trending Desk at USA TODAY. Contact Keith at klaing@usatodayco.com.

text:
This article is based on an official investor relations (IR) press release from the company. See references for the source.

Entergy New Orleans today joined leaders from the U.S. Department of Energy to break ground on a grid-hardening project that will upgrade 94 distribution poles serving the Leonidas area and directly benefit more than 1,900 customers. Making the grid stronger means customers will experience fewer, shorter outages.

Entergy New Orleans President and CEO Deanna Rodriguez stood with Katie Jereza, the Assistant Secretary for the U.S. Department of Energy's Office of Electricity, and Louisiana Department of Conservation and Energy Secretary Dustin Davidson to kick off the new project — which will make the grid stronger and more reliable, reducing day to day outages.

The project is funded in part by a $2.05 million grant awarded this spring by the U.S. Department of Energy.

"This federally funded grant will save our customers money by helping pay down the cost of large infrastructure projects, and it will make our community safer. A stronger grid helps us stand up to stronger, faster storms," said Rodriguez. "Securing the support of the Department of Energy was critical in making this project possible and continuing our work to make the grid stronger."

"Faster recovery starts before a storm hits by having poles that meet today's wind standards and less vegetation putting power lines at risk," said Katie Jereza, Assistant Secretary for the U.S. Department of Energy's Office of Electricity. "This investment will directly benefit the more than 1,900 families and businesses in New Orleans and result in fewer disruptions by keeping critical infrastructure operating when the community needs it most, continuing to advance President Trump's agenda to deliver affordable, reliable, and secure electricity for Americans nationwide. By reducing damage and downtime, this project is projected to avoid $7.4 million in outage-related and restoration costs over the next 50 years."

The Entergy grant is one of 13 projects throughout the state that the Louisiana Department of Conservation and Energy selected to receive Grid Resilience Grants funded by U.S. Department of Energy, ranging from grid modernization to vegetation management.

"The resilience of our power grid is a critical and constant priority for Louisiana, given our proximity to the Gulf of America and its tropical systems and our location in a part of the country where high temperatures fuel strong storms on land," Davidson said. "We are working to find ways to establish a power grid that is reliable in the face of wind and flooding events, and resilient enough to be restored quickly afterwards, focusing on communities where the need is greatest."

The work beginning today will replace approximately 94 distribution poles and harden approximately 1.6 miles of the distribution network. In addition, Entergy New Orleans will implement a targeted vegetation management program in the project area to trim back trees and foliage that could impact service wires.

Entergy New Orleans is committed to strengthening the electric grid, investing in resilient infrastructure and preparing year-round to provide safe, reliable service for customers across the city.

Currently, Entergy New Orleans is midway through a grid-hardening initiative with upgrades being made in every district to make our grid stronger and to make the community we serve more safe.

text:
As the energy and climate world gathers for Climate Week NYC, many of the conversations will come back to AI data centers. Policymakers and businesses are navigating an unprecedented new era of rising energy demand – driven by data centers, electrification, and manufacturing – as well as affordability challenges and growing community backlash.

The vast majority of Americans are concerned about how data centers could impact electricity prices, water supply, and grid reliability, according to recent polling. These concerns are why local communities blocked or delayed 45 data center projects across the U.S. between just April and June this year.

Demand for solutions to address the challenges of the AI data center buildout is hitting a critical point. States that set strong, consistent rules now will shape this build-out for the benefit of communities and give businesses the certainty they need to invest.

This moment is also an opportunity to address existing weaknesses in the energy system. Most of America’s grid is decades old and could need $1.4 trillion in upgrades over the next few years, with the costs passed on to consumers. Policymakers must shape a cleaner, more efficient system that keeps bills affordable, keeps us economically competitive, strengthens national security, and protects communities from pollution.

The encouraging news is that we’re starting to see governors and state legislators meeting the moment with commonsense policies to ensure data centers are powered by affordable clean energy and limit impacts on water supplies and communities.

I want to celebrate four examples of state policymakers acting, with support from Ceres and businesses across the economy, on sustainable data centers. They reflect many of the principles laid out in Ceres’ reports and policy work on data centers this year, and they should be models for policymakers around the country. More must be done by states to provide consistent and enforceable standards that guide the industry towards a sustainable future.

California

Gov. Gavin Newsom this week signed a suite of data center bills from the state legislature into law, including an important measure supported by Ceres to guide data center permitting.

SB 887 will create a faster review pathway for projects that meet high standards on grid costs, clean energy, water efficiency, demand response, and community benefits. That includes an enforceable community benefits agreement. The overall package also includes many of the principles for sustainable data centers that Ceres laid out in a letter to Newsom earlier this month.

California now has a clear path to powering data centers with clean energy and ensuring that they do not threaten the state’s water supply.

Pennsylvania

Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro signed an executive order last month spelling out requirements in the state permitting process for data center developers to be transparent about their impacts, include communities in the development process, pay costs for the electric infrastructure they will need, and meet water conservation requirements.

The governor's order will empower communities to share the benefits of nearby projects if they choose to host them and ensure that new electricity demand is met with affordable, clean energy.

Virginia

The data center capital of the world is now a national leader in data center sustainability, thanks to an executive order this month from Gov. Abigail Spanberger. The order lays out a framework to incentivize clean energy, limit polluting backup generation on-site at data centers, improve energy efficiency, and limit water use.

It will bring benefits to the entire energy system and, as demand grows, maximize use of the cheapest sources of energy: Solar, wind, and storage. That will also help all businesses – outside of hyperscalers and data center developers – reap the benefits of cheaper energy and a more efficient power grid.

Ceres will be advocating in Virginia in the coming months, as legislators in the General Assembly look to write many aspects of the governor’s order into state law.

Massachusetts

In Massachusetts, Gov. Maura Healey signed an executive order this month requiring local approval of data centers and moving the state towards a “bring your own clean energy” model for development.

Healey has long acknowledged AI’s potential economic benefits, and her order shows that smart policy can make this buildout a win for the power grid, the environment, and the communities that want to host data centers.

Looking ahead

Policymakers increasingly recognize that when built and operated sustainably, and powered by clean energy, data centers can contribute to local economies and put downward pressure on electricity prices by helping pay for grid upgrades. They are also reckoning with water impacts, which can come both from the data centers themselves and from the generation that powers them.

But there is still much more to come when state legislatures meet again next year. Ceres will continue to focus on commonsense sustainability guardrails for data centers to protect communities, as well as broader solutions to modernize the power grid, limit costs, and deploy clean energy more widely.

There is a window now for policymakers to get this right. Without state leadership, communities will be left to navigate data center development on their own with few guardrails and limited transparency.

text:
On September 14, 2026, the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) finalized a significant rollback of federal greenhouse gas (GHG) requirements for fossil-fuel-fired power plants, repealing most of the Carbon Pollution Standards adopted by the Biden Administration in 2024.1 At the same time, EPA issued a supplemental proposal that would go further and eliminate the remaining GHG emission standards applicable to fossil-fuel-fired electric generating units (EGUs) under Section 111 of the Clean Air Act (CAA).2

EPA’s final rule repeals three principal components of the 2024 Carbon Pollution Standards. First, EPA repealed the emission guidelines for existing fossil-fuel-fired steam generating units, including requirements for certain coal-fired units based on 90 percent carbon capture and sequestration storage (CCS) or 40 percent natural gas co-firing. Second, EPA repealed CCS-based standards applicable to coal-fired steam generating units undergoing a large modification. Third, EPA repealed the Phase 2 CCS-based standards for new base-load stationary combustion turbines, which would have required compliance with a standard based on 90 percent CCS beginning in 2032. No replacement standards were issued.

EPA concluded that 90 percent CCS is not adequately demonstrated for these sources, that the necessary capture, pipeline, and sequestration infrastructure is unlikely to be deployed at sufficient scale by the applicable compliance deadlines, and that the associated costs are unreasonable. EPA also reversed its position on natural gas co-firing, interpreting West Virginia v. EPA3 to prohibit requiring coal-fired units to shift a substantial portion of their fuel use to natural gas because, in EPA’s view, such a requirement constitutes impermissible generation shifting.

The final rule does not, however, eliminate every GHG standard applicable to fossil-fuel-fired power plants. EPA left in place certain efficiency-based standards for new combustion turbines and stated that highly efficient generation remains an appropriate best system of emission reduction (BSER) for new base-load combustion turbines.

EPA’s supplemental proposal would go substantially further. EPA is proposing that CAA Section 111 does not authorize the Agency to regulate power-plant emissions in response to global climate-change concerns. If finalized, the proposal would rescind EPA’s prior findings supporting regulation of power-sector GHG emissions and repeal all remaining GHG standards for fossil-fuel-fired EGUs under Section 111, including standards that were not affected by the final partial repeal. EPA published the supplemental proposal on September 17, 2026, and comments are due November 2, 2026.

The proposal follows EPA’s February 2026 rescission of the 2009 GHG Endangerment Finding applicable to motor vehicles under CAA Section 202. EPA is now applying a similar statutory interpretation to Section 111, proposing that global climate-change concerns do not satisfy the statutory prerequisite that emissions contribute significantly to air pollution which may reasonably be anticipated to endanger public health or welfare.

Shortly after EPA issued these rules, environmental and public-health organizations, including the American Lung Association, Environmental Defense Fund, and Natural Resources Defense Council, petitioned the D.C. Circuit for review of EPA’s final partial repeal.4 The challengers contend, among other things, that the 2024 standards were consistent with West Virginia v. EPA because they relied on pollution-control measures that could be applied at individual power plants rather than the system-wide generation shifting addressed by the Supreme Court in that case.

Given these initial challenges, companies should keep in mind that a reversal of some or all of the rules is possible. EPA recognized few reliance interests at stake, citing the effective date of 2032 and the lack of comments on this issue. Nevertheless, companies that do have reliance interests, should document their decision making. Additionally, the rollback does not affect independent state requirements or cap-and-trade programs.

CATL announced plans for its second European battery plant in Debrecen in August 2022.

text:
CATL has officially begun trial production at its newly built battery cell factory in Debrecen, Hungary, marking a major milestone for the company’s European manufacturing expansion.

The trial run started on September 22, 2026, after CATL completed all the required conditions and obtained the necessary permits to begin operations. The initial trial production covers the first two cell manufacturing lines at the facility.

The purpose of the trial phase is to set up, optimize and validate the factory’s production equipment and manufacturing processes before series production begins.

CATL said it will continue working closely with the Hungarian government and local authorities throughout the trial period, with particular attention to environmental protection, employee health and workplace safety.

CATL announced plans for its second European battery plant in Debrecen in August 2022. The facility was designed to strengthen the company’s position in Europe’s automotive and electric mobility supply chain while allowing it to better serve major European automakers.

Construction of the first cell manufacturing building began in summer 2023. By spring 2026, the building had been equipped with what CATL describes as advanced manufacturing technology.

The company received the facility’s occupancy permit in August 2026 and subsequently completed the remaining requirements associated with its Integrated Pollution Prevention and Control (IPPC) permit.

Those steps cleared the way for trial operations to begin on September 22.

Before the occupancy permit was issued, the Hajdú-Bihar County Government Office carried out regular inspections at CATL’s facilities. The inspections followed earlier concerns raised during the permitting process. According to the authorities, CATL had addressed the deficiencies previously identified.

Once fully operational, the Debrecen facility is expected to become CATL’s largest manufacturing site outside China, with planned annual battery cell production capacity of 100 GWh.

The factory is strategically located within Hungary’s growing automotive manufacturing network. Several major automakers have established significant electric vehicle production capacity in the country, creating increasing demand for locally produced batteries.

CATL says the Debrecen plant uses flexible production lines designed to accommodate the requirements of its automotive customers.

The company has already been producing battery modules at the Debrecen site since autumn 2024. CATL says the facility has produced approximately 537,000 battery modules to date.

The transition to cell production represents the next major stage in the development of the Hungarian factory and could further integrate CATL into Europe’s rapidly expanding EV battery supply chain.

CATL says environmental protection, employee health and workplace safety will remain key priorities during the trial production phase.

The company plans to closely monitor health, safety and environmental factors throughout the initial operations and proactively submit the results to the relevant authorities.

CATL also said it remains committed to transparency and welcomes inspections by government and regulatory authorities at the Debrecen site.

The start of trial production represents an important step toward full-scale battery cell manufacturing in Hungary. For CATL, the Debrecen facility is intended to strengthen its European production footprint, while for Hungary it further expands the country’s role in the continent’s electric vehicle and battery manufacturing ecosystem.

text:
By Ju-min Park

NINGBO, China, Sept 23 (Reuters) – China’s Geely responded to the challenge posed by rival BYD on Wednesday with a system that can charge an EV in just ​four minutes, the industry’s fastest speed.

Geely also introduced a ‌next-generation electric vehicle battery and an upgraded Galaxy E5 pure-electric SUV as it seeks to revive sales in China, where EV sales declined for 11 consecutive months through August.

China’s EV market has moved into a battle over technology, with ‌automakers ​competing on intelligent driving systems, range and ⁠ultra-fast charging capabilities to attract ⁠buyers.

Supported by a 2.2-megawatt charging infrastructure and a high-rate battery capacity, Geely said its new setup can charge a vehicle from 10% to 70% in 4.5 minutes, and from 10% to 97% ​in 8 minutes and 40 seconds under normal ambient temperatures.

“Current charging speeds are already approaching the physical limit, and the marginal ⁠gains from pursuing even faster speeds ⁠in the future will become increasingly small,” Geely executive ​Zhang Dewang told Reuters at the launch event.

To ensure stability and ​safety under such high power, Geely is deploying AI across ‌cloud and on-vehicle systems.

It uses cloud-based twin simulations paired with deep-learning models deployed directly on the EV to monitor battery health, manage thermal control, and predict potential hazards.

The new technology is Geely’s direct response ⁠to aggressive moves by rivals such as BYD, which have invested heavily in flash-charging and megawatt-level charging networks to ease range anxiety and win ⁠customers.

Earlier this year, ‌BYD unveiled a new generation flash-charging system that ⁠can charge a battery from 10% to 97% ​in nine ‌minutes. It plans to build 90,000 stations by ​2028, Deutsche ⁠Bank has said, citing a meeting with BYD’s management.

Geely’s Zhang said the broader charging ecosystem would in the future resemble traditional gasoline stations with diverse brands, adding that multi-party infrastructure development will accelerate the global rollout of fast-charging networks.

(Reporting by Ju-min Park; Editing by Miyoung Kim ​and Alexander Smith)

By David Shepardson WASHINGTON, Sept 23 (Reuters) – A US judge on Tuesday dismissed an antitrust lawsuit in which Michigan accused four major oil companies of colluding to forestall competition in renewable energy, ​including electric vehicles, a decision in line with prior rulings ‌in similar cases.

WASHINGTON, Sept 23 (Reuters) – A US judge on Tuesday dismissed an antitrust lawsuit in which Michigan accused four major oil companies of colluding to forestall competition in renewable energy, ​including electric vehicles, a decision in line with prior rulings ‌in similar cases.

US District Judge Jane Beckering in Grand Rapids rejected the lawsuit filed in January by Michigan Attorney General Dana Nessel, a Democrat, against BP, Chevron, Exxon, Shell and the American Petroleum Institute.

The judge said antitrust laws protect against none ‌of the ​injuries for which Michigan sought a remedy, ⁠except for energy overcharges.

The complaint said the companies sought to “restrain the emergence of electric ​vehicles and renewable primary energy technologies in the United States.”

Other judges have rejected similar climate lawsuits including in Delaware, Maryland, New Jersey, ⁠New York, Pennsylvania, Puerto Rico and South ⁠Carolina.

A spokesman for Nessel said she disagreed with the ​ruling and was considering the state’s options.

A spokesman for Nessel did not immediately comment.

A lawyer for Chevron, Ted Boutrous, said the decision adds “to the growing list of federal and state courts that have ⁠dismissed climate lawsuits.”

Michigan’s suit said in the 1970s, Exxon developed the first hybrid gas-electric vehicle technologies but never marketed it and cited Exxon’s internal research ⁠in 1979 that “predicted that ‌renewable energy would increasingly become a competitive threat ⁠to fossil fuels.”

text:
The Trump administration made several consequential announcements this past week, from rescinding environmental protections to supposedly banning several news agencies from the White House.

The United States Environmental Protection Agency (EPA), which sets national regulations to protect the environment and public health, announced on Monday, Sept. 14, that it will remove regulations on greenhouse gas emissions from power plants. These polluting gases, emitted when power plants burn coal and gas, contribute heavily to global warming, intensify extreme weather events and harm public health.

At Monday’s meeting with the G-20 energy ministers, EPA administrator Lee Zeldin announced plans to repeal most of the Biden administration’s greenhouse gas requirements for U.S. power plants. Zeldin also proposed to repeal all other greenhouse gas regulations for the power sector. According to the EPA, repealing the remaining standards would save $370 million in direct compliance costs, while saving families and businesses billions of dollars by lowering transportation, heating, utility and manufacturing costs. However, experts warn the rollback could potentially result in an additional 5.8 billion metric tons of carbon dioxide emissions by 2050, leading to billions of dollars in health damages from pollution-driven disease, according to the Los Angeles Times.

Zeldin justified the EPA’s decisions

“For over 15 years, the Obama and Biden administrations implemented a war on coal to destroy reliable and affordable energy,” Zeldin said. “The Trump Administration has come in to protect American energy and to make sure you can afford to keep the lights on.”

Earlier this year, the EPA also eliminated greenhouse gas standards for car tailpipes and loosened restrictions on planet-warming chemicals used in appliances. Most significantly, the EPA repealed the scientific determination that grants the agency legal authority to determine climate regulations.

If courts accept the EPA’s argument that greenhouse gases from power plants do not endanger human health or the environment, the agency may be blocked from restoring environmental protections under future administrations.

“GHG emissions from power plants have no material impact on global climate change,” The EPA said in its recent statement on the repeal of the 2024 power plant regulations. “In fact, if all carbon dioxides were eliminated tomorrow, there would be no meaningful climate impact.”

Additionally, on Friday, Sept. 18, Trump announced that he has banned the news agencies CNN, Politico and MS NOW from the White House, claiming there has been continuous “fake news” reporting from the outlets.

“Media outlets shouldn’t be able to constantly write or report FICTION and LIES when they’re covering the President of the United States, the Trump Administration or the United States of America,” Trump said in his Truth Social post announcing the ban. Trump also wrote that there would be “other Fake News Media Outlets to follow.”

It is not entirely clear how such a ban would be applied, as legal experts, journalist groups, and citizens alike insist it would be unconstitutional under the First Amendment, and journalists from the cited news outlets were still seen on Friday doing their usual work on the White House grounds. Both Politico and CNN have vowed to defend their First Amendment rights, with CNN stating they would challenge the ban in court.

Trump’s recent efforts to restrict news coverage follow his extensive history of clashing with the press. There have been many reports of the Trump administration attempting to intimidate and control news outlets, including filing defamation lawsuits and decreasing reporting access to government sites. He has also called for the firing of late-night talk show hosts, including Jimmy Fallon and Jimmy Kimmel, who have mocked or spoken out against him. Trump has most notably clashed with CNN reporters, frequently launching verbal attacks at CNN’s chief White House correspondent, Kaitlan Collins, chiding her for “not smiling” and, most recently, calling her a “very dumb and unhappy Fake News CNN reporter” on social media last Tuesday.

Recent developments from the White House have drawn attention to the current administration’s policies and direction as the country approaches the halfway point of Trump’s second presidency.

description:
(TestMiles) – Tesla has pushed the entry price of its electric sedan below $39,000, including its destination and order fees.
Tesla reaches the lower price with simpler interior materials, fewer speakers and less acoustic glass.
The $5,500 decision The Premium Long Range Rear-Wheel Drive is Tesla’s strongest all-round Model 3 on paper.
Other automakers now use the North American Charging Standard connector and can access many Superchargers, but Tesla still controls the most integrated version of the experience.
The Standard deserves consideration from buyers who can charge at home, like Tesla’s software-led approach and prefer a lower purchase price to extra cabin equipment.
text:
(TestMiles) – Tesla has pushed the entry price of its electric sedan below $39,000, including its destination and order fees. It did not create a smaller car to get there. It took the familiar Model 3 and began removing things.

The 2026 Model 3 Standard costs $38,630 before taxes, registration and options. Tesla lists 321 miles of estimated range, rear-wheel drive and a zero-to-60-mph time of 5.8 seconds. Those numbers make it a proper long-range electric car rather than a joyless bargain model.

The compromise becomes clear when it is parked beside the $44,130 Premium Long Range Rear-Wheel Drive. That version adds 42 miles of estimated range and restores comfort, audio and cabin features deleted from the Standard. The decision is therefore less about whether the cheaper Tesla works and more about whether living with less is worth saving $5,500.

This is a vehicle analysis based on Tesla’s current U.S. information and government and insurance-industry sources. Test Miles has not road-tested this configuration, so no firsthand driving, charging or range results are presented.

The missing features are the ones owners touch

The Standard retains the Model 3’s central touchscreen, route planning, phone-based access, over-the-air updates and access to Tesla’s Supercharger network. It also has a conventional turn-signal stalk, a small item that became newsworthy only because Tesla previously decided drivers should indicate with steering-wheel buttons.

Tesla reaches the lower price with simpler interior materials, fewer speakers and less acoustic glass. The Standard also gives up ventilated front seats, heated rear seats and some rear-cabin conveniences included with the Premium version.

None of those omissions stops a commute. They can change how the car feels every day. Heated rear seats matter in Minnesota. Ventilated front seats matter in Phoenix. Better sound insulation matters almost everywhere that has a freeway.

The Standard will make the most sense as a one- or two-person commuter. Families and owners planning to keep the car for many years should calculate the saving across the full ownership period rather than celebrating the lower order-page number for five minutes.

The $5,500 decision

The Premium Long Range Rear-Wheel Drive is Tesla’s strongest all-round Model 3 on paper. Its estimated 363-mile range is the highest in the current lineup, while its claimed 4.9-second run to 60 mph is considerably quicker than most family sedans need to be.

The $5,500 difference equals roughly $92 a month when spread across 60 months before interest, taxes or a down payment. That is real money. It is also a useful way to judge the upgrade. Buyers should ask whether the additional range and restored equipment are worth about three dollars a day.

Someone who charges at home, drives a predictable route and rarely uses the back seat may reasonably choose the Standard. A frequent highway traveler has a stronger case for the Premium. The extra 42 miles will not appear in every real journey, but it creates more flexibility when cold weather, speed, elevation or a detour cuts into the official estimate.

Tesla also sells all-wheel-drive and Performance versions. They add traction and startling acceleration, but neither is necessary to make the Model 3 useful transportation. America has survived for generations without every trip to the supermarket taking less than three seconds to reach 60 mph.

Charging may matter more than range

The ownership argument for a Model 3 is not merely the number printed beside its battery icon. Tesla’s greater advantage is the relationship among the car, its navigation system, the Tesla app and the Supercharger network.

The route planner can select charging stops, estimate the battery level at arrival and prepare the battery for faster charging. Billing normally happens through the owner’s account after the cable is connected. Other automakers now use the North American Charging Standard connector and can access many Superchargers, but Tesla still controls the most integrated version of the experience.

Home charging remains the practical dividing line. An owner who plugs in overnight can leave most mornings with the desired charge. A driver dependent on public stations must price the electricity, travel to the charger and wait. In some areas, public fast charging can erase much of the operating-cost advantage over an efficient hybrid.

Tesla says charging performance and driving range vary with vehicle configuration, charger type, battery temperature, state of charge, weather, speed and elevation. A peak charging figure is not a speed the battery maintains from empty to full. Road trips normally work best as a series of shorter stops rather than one heroic wait for 100 percent.

One screen, no smartphone projection

The Model 3 places the speedometer, navigation, climate settings and most vehicle controls on its central touchscreen. Some owners learn the system quickly and enjoy the uncluttered cabin. Others wonder why adjusting a mirror should feel like opening a spreadsheet.

Apple CarPlay and Android Auto are not offered from the factory. Tesla uses its own navigation, media services, voice functions and phone app. That integration helps the car plan charging, but it reduces the driver’s choice.

A serious buyer should spend time operating the exact car before ordering. Set a destination, change the temperature, adjust a mirror and find the wipers. The interface is not decoration. It is the car’s operating philosophy.

Tesla markets Full Self-Driving (Supervised), but the driver remains responsible for watching the road and intervening. It is driver assistance, not permission to text, sleep or relocate to the back seat. “Supervised” is the most important word in the product’s name.

Safety results are good in places, mixed in others

The Insurance Institute for Highway Safety applies its 2025 Model 3 testing to 2026 models. It rated the car Good in small-overlap front and updated side crashworthiness tests. The updated moderate-overlap test received an Acceptable rating, with a Marginal chest-injury measure for the rear passenger.

IIHS rated the standard vehicle-to-vehicle and pedestrian front-crash-prevention systems Good. Headlights and child-seat-anchor ease of use were Acceptable. The seat-belt reminder received a Marginal rating because the front audible warning did not last long enough under IIHS criteria.

Those results are more useful than saying the car is simply safe or unsafe. Buyers should also check the specific vehicle identification number for open recalls through the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration because equipment, software and recall eligibility can vary by build date.

The market has caught up

The Model 3 no longer competes with an empty parking space. Hyundai’s Ioniq 6 offers rapid charging and a more conventional driver interface. The Polestar 2 uses a Google-based system and provides a different cabin experience. BMW’s i4 is more expensive but feels familiar to buyers moving from a traditional luxury sedan.

A lightly used Model 3 can also compete with a new one. Tesla’s price and equipment changes have created substantial variation in the used market, so shoppers must verify the exact battery, hardware, remaining warranty and accident history rather than trusting the model name alone.

The Standard deserves consideration from buyers who can charge at home, like Tesla’s software-led approach and prefer a lower purchase price to extra cabin equipment. The Premium Long Range Rear-Wheel Drive is the more complete car for regular passengers and long trips.

Tesla has made the Model 3 cheaper without making it inadequate. It has also priced the better-equipped version close enough to keep whispering from the next box on the order screen.

Geely’s Zhang said the broader charging ecosystem would in the future resemble traditional gasoline stations with diverse brands, adding that multi-party infrastructure development will accelerate the global rollout of fast-charging networks.

text:
Chennai: The Centre and states have committed over Rs 1.25 lakh crore to incentivise the use of electric vehicles, finds Niti Aayog. By 2025-26, EV penetration in India reached 8.25% and 2.5 million vehicles were registered during 2025-26 alone - a growth of 25% over the previous financial year.

The Centre has committed more than Rs 90,000 crore, spread across several ministries and multiple fiscal years, towards public investment in demand incentives, charging infrastructure, bus electrification, manufacturing support and research.

This comprises Rs 24,000 crore across the FAME-I, FAME-II and PM E-DRIVE schemes; Rs 20,000 crore as central assistance through PM-eBus Sewa; Rs 44,000 crore for the PLIs on the National Programme on Advanced Chemistry Cell Battery Storage and on the Automobile and Auto Component Industry in India; Rs 3,435.33 crore for the PM-eBus Sewa Payment Security Mechanism; and Rs 1,150 crore for e-mobility-related research and development (R&D).

Besides the central subsidies, States and UTs have committed Rs 37,613 crore under PM-eBus Sewa for public transport electrification, layered their own EV purchase incentives onto the central FAME and PM E-DRIVE support, exempted EVs from road taxes and registration fees, eased commercial permit requirements, and backed charging infrastructure through fiscal and regulatory measures. Many have also offered capital subsidies, concessional land and tax exemptions to attract EV and battery manufacturing investments to their regions.

By 2025-26, EV penetration in India reached 8.25%, up from 0.5% in 2018. By 2025-26, more than 8.7 million EVs were running on Indian roads, and close to 2.5 million were registered during 2025-26 alone, a rise of about 25% over the previous financial year. Two-wheelers accounted for most of this volume at 1.3 million units, followed by passenger three-wheelers, while passenger cars held a modest and rising share of the total vehicles.

Commercial goods vehicles saw the sharpest growth across the electric light, medium and heavy-duty segments, where penetration climbed from 0.6% in 2024 to 1.4% in 2025. However, adoption of e-buses, which stood at 8.75% in 2021 has moderated to 6.4% by 2025.

The number of public charging stations touched 29,000 by June 2025. Vehicle assembly has scaled quickly, and localisation of the component supply chain is also deepening, although the development of domestic cell manufacturing has progressed slowly. Startups are working at the technical frontier on cell chemistries suited to Indian ambient temperatures, motor and power-electronics design, battery management systems, swapping networks and financing models for commercial fleets.

The commission approved $611,862 through North Dakota’s Renewable Energy Program during its latest round of funding.

Grant recipients are required to provide matching private funds.

This morning on Fox Business, NAM President and CEO Jay Timmons spoke with host Cheryl Casone, underscoring manufacturers’ optimism—but warned that persistent headwinds demand action from policymakers now, including passage of long-overdue permitting reform.

The big picture: “You’ve got the highest optimism rate or outlook … in four years,” Timmons said, but manufacturers are still facing “headwinds,” including high energy costs due to the war with Iran and “additional costs because of tariff policy.”

“The good news is … that we were able to get that tax reform of 2017 renewed in 2025. It was rocket fuel, as the president said at our board meeting in 2017, for the manufacturing economy. And renewing it has … given that push of optimism to manufacturers,” he added.

However, “We have to deal with these other issues. There’s no question about that because the most important thing is obviously to reduce the cost of doing business here in the United States so that we’re more competitive.”

Why permitting reform matters: After noting the Environmental Protection Agency’s progress on regulatory reform, including in rolling back the power plant rule, Timmons emphasized that “if we’re going to actually see real progress, we have to have permitting reform because [outdated permitting laws cost] about $8 billion for manufacturers [per year].”

“We’re very, very optimistic about the path forward on permitting reform,” he continued. “For one of the first times I can ever remember, we’ve got a bipartisan consensus with [Sens. Shelley Moore Capito (R-WV), Sheldon Whitehouse (D-RI), Mike Lee (R-UT) and Martin Heinrich (D-NM)] working around the clock to get this done. And my hope is we’re going to see some really good news this week on that, and then we’re going to be looking to the House to expeditiously get that over the line … as well.”

The importance of certainty: “When we have certainty, manufacturers can plan for the future,” Timmons said. “They can make investment decisions. They can make hiring decisions. They can plan for wage growth for their workers to make us the strongest manufacturing economy in the world.”

Manufacturers need this certainty in many areas, Timmons continued—in permitting, in trade policy and in workforce development, so they know they will have sufficient workers for the future.

Setting national policy: “Permitting is going to be important at the federal level to try to pull together the patchwork of laws and regulations in the states, but we also need help from states and localities,” Timmons pointed out.

“They have to expedite their processes as well. Many states are getting that right. I look at Arizona. I look at my home state of Ohio and others who figure that out. Virginia, where I’ve worked for many years, they understand it, [as well as] North Carolina and others, but some other states are not getting the message.”

“And unfortunately, they’re probably going to be the ones that don’t benefit from that manufacturing investment. When you have a process that encourages investment, encourages manufacturers to hire people in the communities, that’s where manufacturers are going to invest.”

The last word: “Eighty percent of manufacturers say that if they get this law passed, they’re willing to invest and they’re willing to hire,” Timmons concluded. “And that’s what Sens. Capito, Whitehouse, Lee and Heinrich all understand.”

“That’s why we’re so excited. I mean, you’ve got two Democrats, two Republicans, they’re working on this. I think we can get it done.”

title: With federal funding windfall, X-energy advances small nuclear reactor - Canary Media
description:
The federal government has thrown its weight into reviving America’s long-stagnant nuclear industry, and X-energy’s first-of-a-kind reactor project is among the biggest beneficiaries so far.
X-energy’s Seadrift project now enjoys a level of federal funding that rivals any other advanced nuclear development in the nation.
Nuclear energy has struggled in recent decades in America, but surging energy demand and a desire by some states and companies to secure carbon-free electricity have revitalized the industry.
Blown deadlines and blown budgets have dogged the industry, and in 2023 contributed to the dissolution of the first small-modular reactor project with an NRC-approved design.
It’s inevitable that the first commercial advanced nuclear reactors will be more expensive to deploy than more mature power-generation technologies — and costlier than the next iterations of those same reactors.
text:
The federal government has thrown its weight into reviving America’s long-stagnant nuclear industry, and X-energy’s first-of-a-kind reactor project is among the biggest beneficiaries so far.

The U.S. Department of Energy last month said it would award $1 billion to X-energy, an Amazon-backed advanced nuclear startup working to bring four novel 80-megawatt electric reactors online at a Dow Chemical facility in Seadrift, Texas, in the early 2030s.

The award nearly doubles the federal government’s commitment to X-energy, following a $1.2 billion investment in early 2021. Both tranches were structured as 50-50 cost-sharing agreements under the DOE’s Advanced Reactor Demonstration Program, launched in 2020 to commercialize next-generation nuclear technologies.

X-energy’s Seadrift project now enjoys a level of federal funding that rivals any other advanced nuclear development in the nation. The Bill Gates–backed TerraPower’s commercial demonstration project in Wyoming, which broke ground earlier this year, has also been awarded up to $2 billion in cost-sharing funds through the ARDP.

The X-energy project does not yet have a license from the Nuclear Regulatory Commission, though it received a key environmental approval in May and expects the regulator to green-light reactor construction in early 2027. Only TerraPower and the Google-backed startup Kairos Power currently have NRC construction permits.

Nuclear energy has struggled in recent decades in America, but surging energy demand and a desire by some states and companies to secure carbon-free electricity have revitalized the industry. Tens of billions of dollars in public and private funding are now flowing into a crop of startups looking to build advanced reactors — as well as efforts to restart or build new large-scale reactors like the 96 America already has.

For the nuclear renaissance to truly arrive, however, these new projects need to be completed on a reasonable timeline and at a reasonable cost. Blown deadlines and blown budgets have dogged the industry, and in 2023 contributed to the dissolution of the first small-modular reactor project with an NRC-approved design.

In early 2023, before it had fully engaged with Dow or selected Seadrift for its commercial debut, X-energy estimated the cost of completing the full ARDP scope between $4.75 billion and $5.75 billion.

X-energy has not publicly updated its cost estimates since then, though the federal funding of up to $2.1 billion implies at least $4.2 billion will be spent on the project. In securities filings this year, however, it said that it faces the same broad inflationary and trade-related pressures that have pushed up costs for natural gas, renewables, and other types of energy infrastructure.

CEO J. Clay Sell told investors and stock analysts on an Aug. 13 earnings call that he expected the government to contribute more funding as needed.

“I’m confident to the extent more dollars will be required, they will be provided by our partners at the Department of Energy and Commerce,” he said. ​“We’ll see where the number ends up.”

Andrew Kleiman, an energy transition research analyst with Wood Mackenzie, said there’s no indication yet that X-energy’s final project costs will be substantially higher than its 2023 estimate.

As of June 30, the DOE had reimbursed X-energy for about $546 million in spending under the ARDP agreement.

The agreement covers the design and licensing of the Xe-100, its standard plant; design, licensing, and construction of TX-1, its first commercial fuel-fabrication facility near Oak Ridge National Laboratory in Tennessee; and construction of its first commercial plant at Dow’s Texas site. The company remains on track to open TX-1 in the first half of 2028, it said last month.

Unlike conventional reactors, which use water to control the nuclear reaction and transfer heat for power generation, high-temperature gas reactors like the Xe-100 use graphite to control the reaction and helium or another inert gas to transfer heat. The Xe-100 also uses a special type of uranium-based fuel, called TRISO, that is expensive but designed to withstand the superhot conditions in the reactor core.

The Xe-100’s high operating temperatures and stability make it ideal for providing both heat and power to industrial operations like Dow’s Seadrift petrochemical plant. If built, the Seadrift reactors will replace Dow’s aging steam and power generation assets, reducing the facility’s annual greenhouse gas emissions by approximately 440,000 metric tons.

The chemicals giant is expected to make a final investment decision on the project in 2028 at the earliest.

“Dow’s partnership with X-energy is not purely financially motivated,” Kleiman said in an email, pointing out that the firm aims to reduce its annual emissions by 5 million metric tons from 2020 levels by 2030. Backing out of the project and instead using fossil-fueled alternatives ​“would require the company to take a step backward in reaching its sustainability goals.”

X-energy’s original ARDP partner was Energy Northwest, a Washington electric utility. In 2023, it backed out of the arrangement as Dow stepped up.

“As an at-cost developer and provider of electricity to public power utilities, Energy Northwest does not have the significant development capital on hand to initiate this project without a committed off-taker, compared to a company such as Dow,” it said at the time.

Energy Northwest eventually found that offtaker in Amazon, which is bankrolling up to 12 Xe-100s at a central Washington site controlled by the utility. That project is at an earlier stage of development than Seadrift.

In total, X-energy’s commitments with Dow, Amazon, and the United Kingdom–based energy company Centrica call for as many as 144 Xe-100 reactors built worldwide, the company said in a securities filing last month.

X-energy’s current cost estimates cover the Seadrift project and the company’s TX-1 fuel facility, making it hard to know exactly how much one reactor would cost and at what price it could deliver power.

Estimates are more readily available for other advanced reactor designs. Wood Mackenzie expects the Tennessee Valley Authority and GE Vernova Hitachi to spend more than $14,000 per kilowatt to bring a 300-MW electric BWRX-300 reactor online in Tennessee early next decade, Kleiman said. (The federal government is chipping in for that project, too, and the NRC is ​“approaching a decision” on the development.)

Wind and solar developers spent well under $2,000 per kilowatt to bring utility-scale projects online in 2022, according to the U.S. Energy Information Administration, though their costs have risen in recent years.

X-energy’s initial reactor is likely to be more expensive than the BWRX-300. The Xe-100’s underlying high-temperature gas technology has limited operational history and relies on costly TRISO fuel, whereas the BWRX-300 is ​“an evolution of GE’s conventional [reactor], which makes up one-third of operating U.S. nuclear fleet and utilizes conventional fuel which is already licensed, produced at scale and has an established supply chain,” Kleiman said.

Ontario Power Generation is expected to bring the world’s first BWRX-300 online in 2030.

It’s inevitable that the first commercial advanced nuclear reactors will be more expensive to deploy than more mature power-generation technologies — and costlier than the next iterations of those same reactors.

That’s why Judi Greenwald, president and CEO of the Nuclear Innovation Alliance, said the best way to drive down the cost of nuclear development is to build more of the same design. The second AP-1000 reactor at Georgia Power’s Plant Vogtle cost about 30% less than the first, she noted.

“There is a huge difference between these early-mover projects and what’s going to happen when we get to ​‘nth-of-a-kind.’… It’s expected that early-mover projects are going to have higher costs,” she said.

text:
Biomass power generation is playing an increasingly important role in the global energy transition. By converting organic materials into heat and electricity, biomass plants offer a renewable alternative to fossil fuels – and, unlike solar or wind, they can provide stable, baseload power around the clock. As a result, they are now a mainstream renewable energy source in Europe, Asia-Pacific, and North America.

As countries seek to improve energy security, reduce their reliance on fossil fuels and meet climate targets, investment in biomass power generation continues to grow.

The sector is evolving rapidly. New developments include higher-efficiency combustion systems, greater use of artificial intelligence (AI) for predictive maintenance, increasing digitalization of plant operations, and growing interest in bioenergy with carbon capture and storage (BECCS). BECCS has attracted significant attention because it offers the potential to generate electricity while removing carbon dioxide from the atmosphere, creating so-called carbon-negative energy generation.

However, growth comes with challenges. Biomass facilities combine the fire and explosion hazards of fuel handling with the mechanical complexity of power generation, with additional risks related to feedstock handling, combustible dust, sustainability requirements, emissions management, supply chain dependencies and increasingly sophisticated digital systems. The sector is also facing greater regulatory scrutiny regarding sourcing practices, carbon accounting and environmental performance.

For risk managers and insurers, effective engagement with biomass facilities requires understanding both the operational realities of power generation and the unique characteristics of biomass as a fuel source.

Early involvement in project design, robust loss prevention measures and specialized insurance products – such as feedstock supply insurance for example – can help manage exposures while supporting the sector’s continued growth.

As the energy transition accelerates, biomass will remain an important part of the renewable mix. Managing its risks effectively will be essential to realizing its potential.

text:
This story was originally published by Inside Climate News and is reproduced here as part of the Climate Desk collaboration.

A federal judge has declared that the Trump administration unlawfully terminated $7 billion in grant funding for clean energy programs in disadvantaged communities.

The Solar for All (SFA) program, established during the Biden administration as part of the Inflation Reduction Act, provided dozens of grants for states, municipalities, tribes and nonprofits designed to reduce electric bills, create jobs, and address the greenhouse gas emissions warming the global climate.

The Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) canceled the program after President Donald Trump’s inauguration in 2025. The Conservation Law Foundation, Southern Environmental Law Center, Lawyers for Good Government, and Lawyers’ Committee for Rhode Island sued in the US District Court for the District of Rhode Island on behalf of workers, businesses, nonprofits, and individuals harmed by the withdrawal of funding.

“Congress’s clear intent was that EPA continue to administer the already obligated SFA grants,” Judge Mary S. McElroy, a Trump appointee, wrote in her ruling, issued Friday. “Defendants acted contrary to this intent, and with no other statutory authority, when they terminated the SFA program.”

The ruling means the EPA will have to release the funding, said Nick Torrey, senior attorney at the Southern Environmental Law Center.

“We have seen this administration try to resist and appeal and fight,” Torrey said. “They don’t have any excuse for sitting on this money anymore. They have to get this money out.”

The EPA argued the court lacked jurisdiction over the plaintiffs’ claims and that the claims were meritless. The federal agency told Inside Climate News it is “reviewing the decision and considering options for appeal.”

The EPA awarded the grants in 2024 and said at the time the program would save families $350 million a year on electricity bills and support 200,000 jobs and workforce training opportunities. Among the recipients was a coalition of nonprofits in Florida, which received $156.1 million to create new and expand existing solar programs for low-income communities in the state.

The program was canceled before much of the funding could reach communities, according to the groups involved in the litigation. In 2025 Congress approved the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, which repealed unobligated funding aimed at greenhouse gas emissions. The groups argued the program’s termination was unlawful because the funding was already obligated.

The lawsuit was filed on behalf not of grant recipients but what the litigation described as “downstream beneficiaries.” Among them were solar companies that invested in personnel and equipment based on funding awarded to the states of Georgia and Pennsylvania, a labor union that helped develop an implementation plan in Rhode Island, and a nonprofit that received a sub-award from a grant to the state of Indiana.

Grant recipients filed two subsequent lawsuits against the EPA. State grant recipients also filed challenges in the Court of Federal Claims.
