title: New Harvard Database Provides Policy Insights Into Climate Disclosures
description:
As the United States backtracks on federal climate commitments, many companies are reassessing their ambitious net-zero targets and other climate commitments.
The Corporate Climate Targets Database — produced by the Salata Institute at Harvard University’s Corporate Climate Targets Project — is the most comprehensive effort to date to track corporate commitments and their implementation across Russell 3000 companies.
It will be important to understand the effect of these policy shifts on corporate climate commitments.
The database will fill a gap by providing interested parties with more complete information on corporate climate commitments.
The database also incorporates state clean energy and climate policies to help users analyze how state policies affect corporate climate ambition.
text:
As the United States backtracks on federal climate commitments, many companies are reassessing their ambitious net-zero targets and other climate commitments. The current administration has begun to systematically dismantle federal climate regulations and undercut states’ emission reduction and disclosure policies. Some companies are walking away from their climate commitments, no longer publicizing information about targets or progress toward them, or weakening their emissions reduction goals. We need better data to understand how companies are responding to this shifting landscape and to design future policies that drive emissions reductions and enable robust corporate climate disclosures.

The Corporate Climate Targets Database — produced by the Salata Institute at Harvard University’s Corporate Climate Targets Project — is the most comprehensive effort to date to track corporate commitments and their implementation across Russell 3000 companies. This dataset and online tool cover climate targets and emissions trends over the past 25 years. It draws from primary sources such as annual reports, 10-K filings, and sustainability reports. This information provides transparent data to investors, advocates, companies, and others, helping them assess the value of corporate targets and consider their efficacy against alternative approaches to driving emission reductions. Users can also assess how shifting regulatory regimes, including federal and state disclosure efforts and state renewable energy mandates, affect net-zero commitments and emissions reductions.

Climate-Related Risk Disclosure Policies

Disclosure policies that require companies to publicly share information about their greenhouse gas emissions, climate-related risks, and other information allow stakeholders to better understand a company’s emissions profile and climate strategies. Many companies are beginning to disclose their greenhouse gas emissions and climate risks and impacts under mandatory reporting regimes, notably in California and the European Union. Other U.S. states are also considering these types of disclosure requirements. As a result, there is a shift from primarily voluntary disclosure to required public disclosure of company emissions and climate risks in some jurisdictions. Lessons from these policies can inform future federal disclosure requirements, with the goal of driving investment in sustained emissions reductions.

In California, hundreds of companies have reported on their climate-related risk despite a court ruling that paused the new requirement’s enforceability. The reporting companies include a mix of private and public companies across a range of sectors, including technology, health care, real estate, consumer goods, and hospitality. While many of these companies have been disclosing climate risk voluntarily for some time even without the legislation, California’s new requirements appear to be inducing a surge of first-time reporters. The data show that over half of the reporting companies — many of them private or smaller U.S.-based companies — are disclosing their climate risks publicly for the first time.

At the same time, the federal government is expected to cease emissions reporting programs, which will limit the data available to track emissions and make informed decisions. The Trump administration has proposed to end the Greenhouse Gas Reporting program, which requires companies in many high-emitting sectors to report their emissions annually. The SEC has initiated its rescission of Biden-era climate-related risk disclosure requirements, which had not taken effect because of litigation, but with which some companies were preparing to comply. The loss of federal data will result in a patchwork of information as companies report different content in different jurisdictions using different formats, leaving investors and advocates with inconsistent and piecemeal data on corporate climate risks and impacts. The information environment is deteriorating just as the federal government is rescinding federal greenhouse gas reduction rules for major emitting sectors, including vehicles and power plants. It will be important to understand the effect of these policy shifts on corporate climate commitments.

The database will fill a gap by providing interested parties with more complete information on corporate climate commitments. We hope it will help researchers design meaningful disclosure policies that achieve emissions reductions while avoiding unintended consequences, like chilling compliance in the face of litigation risk. The database also incorporates state clean energy and climate policies to help users analyze how state policies affect corporate climate ambition. This state-level data can help shed light on the extent to which certain policies shape corporate behavior and enable researchers to explore this interaction between state policy and corporate decision-making. In the long term, however, federal disclosure requirements will need to fill this information-forcing role.

Looking Ahead

That proposal drew roughly 220,000 public comments during its 45-day comment period, which closed on January 5, 2026.
On September 9, 2026, the Agencies published a Supplemental Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (“SNPRM”) in the Federal Register, offering narrower alternative definitions for the terms that anchored their November 2025 proposal.
For wetland “mosaics,” only the portion of the wetland that is actually indistinguishable from the jurisdictional water would be jurisdictional, not the wetland complex as a whole.

text:
In our February 2026 article, WOTUS 2025/2026: The Regulatory Pendulum Swings Again as Agencies Propose New Definitions, we described the Environmental Protection Agency’s (“EPA”) and U.S. Army Corps of Engineers’ (“USACE”) (together, the “Agencies”) November 20, 2025 proposal.

The proposal would codify, for the first time in regulatory text, the twin pillars of the Supreme Court’s Sackett v. Environmental Protection Agency (“Sackett”), 598 U.S. 651 (2023), decision for what qualifies as “waters of the United States” (“WOTUS”) under the Clean Water Act: “relatively permanent” waters and “continuous surface connection” wetlands. That proposal drew roughly 220,000 public comments during its 45-day comment period, which closed on January 5, 2026.

Rather than proceed directly to a final rule, the Agencies went back to the drafting table. On September 9, 2026, the Agencies published a Supplemental Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (“SNPRM”) in the Federal Register, offering narrower alternative definitions for the terms that anchored their November 2025 proposal. The SNPRM does not withdraw or replace the original proposal; it supplements two discrete pieces of it and asks for additional public comment on those pieces alone. Comments on the SNPRM are due October 9, 2026.

The supplemental options include:

Perennial Flow as the New Baseline for “Relatively Permanent”

Narrowing “Continuous Surface Connection” to Require Perennial Surface Water in Wetlands

Possible Elimination of “Adjacent” and “Abutting”

Defined, Time-Limited Treatment of Drought and Seasonal Dry Spells

Narrowing “Relatively Permanent.”

The November 2025 proposal defined “relatively permanent” waters as those “standing or continuously flowing year-round or at least during the wet season” — a formulation that, as we noted in February, was intended to exclude ephemeral streams while still capturing many seasonal ones. Commenters pushed back hard on “wet season” as unworkable and legally unmoored from Sackett and the Rapanos v. United States, 547 U.S. 715 (2006) plurality opinion. In response, the SNPRM offers a stricter alternative: a water would be “relatively permanent” only if it is perennial, defined as having standing or continuously flowing water every day of the year under ordinary conditions. The Agencies propose two narrow exceptions to that year-round requirement: (1) anomalous events, such as drought or an unusual dry spell, which would not defeat jurisdiction if the interruption does not persist for more than five consecutive years (a period tied to the USACE’s five-year jurisdictional determination cycle); and (2) non-anomalous events, such as low tide or a regularly recurring dry spell, which would not defeat jurisdiction if the interruption lasts no more than a single 30-day period in any given year. The Agencies acknowledge that many intermittent streams treated as “relatively permanent” under the amended 2023 Rule would not meet this stricter standard.

Tightening “Continuous Surface Connection.”

The November 2025 proposal defined “continuous surface connection” as a wetland, lake, or pond that abuts a jurisdictional water and has surface water connecting to it at least during the wet season. The SNPRM’s supplemental option abandons the wet-season touching/abutting test for a perennial-connection standard: a continuous surface connection would exist only where a wetland has perennial surface water continuously connected to the jurisdictional water, such that it is difficult to tell where the jurisdictional water ends and the wetland begins. The same temporary-interruption allowances (drought, low tide, seasonal dry spells) described above for “relatively permanent” would apply to “continuous surface connection” as well. For wetland “mosaics,” only the portion of the wetland that is actually indistinguishable from the jurisdictional water would be jurisdictional, not the wetland complex as a whole.

Separately, the Agencies are soliciting comment on whether “adjacent” and “abutting” should be eliminated from the WOTUS definition entirely, on the theory that Sackett’s “indistinguishability” test already subsumes adjacency as a freestanding concept. Under this approach, the regulatory text would provide that wetlands are jurisdictional when “surface water in a wetland is continuously connected with the surface water in the jurisdictional water such that it is difficult to determine where the jurisdictional water ends and the wetland begins.” This text dispenses with any separate touching requirement in exchange for a pure hydrologic-connection inquiry. The Agencies expect that many wetlands currently treated as jurisdictional “adjacent wetlands” would not satisfy either version of this narrower standard, since most wetlands lack perennial surface water.

What the SNPRM Does Not Touch.

Practitioners should note what remains unchanged. The SNPRM does not revisit the November 2025 proposal’s treatment of traditional navigable waters, impoundments, the definition of “tributary,” or the exclusions for waste treatment systems, prior converted cropland, ditches, or the newly proposed groundwater exclusion. Nor does it disturb the proposed removal of “interstate waters” as a standalone jurisdictional category. Those portions of the original proposal remain under review based on the comments already received, and the Agencies have signaled they intend to finalize a single rule addressing both the November 2025 proposal and the SNPRM’s supplemental options together.

Practical Takeaways

If finalized, either alternative in the SNPRM would shrink the scope of federally jurisdictional tributaries and wetlands well below both the current baseline in the amended 2023 Rule and the November 2025 proposal itself, with the most pronounced effects on intermittent streams and non-perennial wetlands in arid and seasonally dry regions. Landowners, developers, and agricultural operators who calibrated Clean Water Act Section 404 permitting strategies around the November 2025 proposal should revisit those assumptions, particularly for projects involving intermittent drainages or wetlands lacking year-round surface water. Because the SNPRM leaves the bulk of the November 2025 proposal intact, this is best understood as a targeted recalibration rather than a fresh start, but it continues to move in one direction: narrower federal jurisdiction.

Given the short 30-day comment window closing October 9, 2026, stakeholders with an interest in the ultimate scope of “relatively permanent” and “continuous surface connection” should not wait for a final rule to weigh in. As with each prior swing of the WOTUS pendulum, informed and timely comments remain the most effective way to shape the final outcome rather than after-the-fact litigation.

title: Cities as Climate Labs: Inside the U20 Summit | The Nation
authors: Lara-Nour Walton, Mark Kaplan, David Futrelle, Ilana Cohen, Jake Werner, David Broder, The Nation, Mychal Denzel Smith, www.thenation.com
description:
From intensified rains and flash flooding in New York City to fatally hot temperatures in Paris, cities are often on the front lines of climate change.
The Summit, organized by C40 Cities and United Cities and Local Governments, brought together mayors and senior leaders from more than 30 cities to discuss the pressing and deeply interconnected challenges of climate change, migration, and housing.
In cities, climate change ceases to be a global phenomenon and becomes a firsthand experience.” As cities undertake these bold climate initiatives, the U20 Communique ratified at the Summit asks national government leaders to support them.
A commitment to climate action means a commitment to climate justice, and addressing climate change as an integral part of migration and housing strategy.
“Climate action isn’t [just] something we’re going to talk about at COP,” said Aki-Sawyerr, referencing the upcoming annual UN Climate Change Conference, where key international climate negotiations take place.
text:
Amid tumultuous global politics and pervasive climate catastrophe, mayors from around the world have a clear message: Cities are taking up the mantle of climate action and international cooperation, regardless of whether their national governments choose to do so.

From intensified rains and flash flooding in New York City to fatally hot temperatures in Paris, cities are often on the front lines of climate change. In recognition that metropolitan areas are both uniquely vulnerable to these impacts and crucial laboratories for innovative solutions, climate was a core theme at the 2026 Urban 20 Summit (U20) cohosted by Los Angeles and New York City from September 19 to 21.

The Summit, organized by C40 Cities and United Cities and Local Governments, brought together mayors and senior leaders from more than 30 cities to discuss the pressing and deeply interconnected challenges of climate change, migration, and housing. The Summit occurred on the heels of High-Level Week at the United Nations and Climate Week NYC, both of which will see national governments discuss the future of climate action in a world already surpassing the 1.5-degree warming limit enshrined in the Paris Agreement.

With the shadow of these upcoming national government dialogues looming, mayors and city leaders made clear that climate action remains a priority for local leaders, and that tackling the climate crisis cannot be done in isolation from other interconnected social issues or without international cooperation.

Their unity and commitment represented a sharp contrast to the nationalist, xenophobic, and anti-science rhetoric of a surging far-right politics. Under the right-wing Trump administration, the US has withdrawn for the second time from the leading global climate treaty, the Paris Agreement, and undertaken a seismic environmental deregulation. Climate skepticism has also become a staple of right-wing parties in the United Kingdom and Europe. Meanwhile, New Zealand recently passed a law shielding fossil fuel polluters and the government from climate liability.

Yet, in a powerful display of global solidarity, the Summit made clear that many cities are working to move in the opposite direction. “Climate change does not stop at our borders, which makes collaboration all the more important, and as the mayors…said, we are more powerful when we work together,” Louise Yeung, chief climate officer of New York City, told attendees.

In the spirit of collaboration, mayors shared their experiences of piloting programs to mitigate and adapt to wide-ranging climate impacts. These solutions ranged from helping communities establish decentralized, renewable energy systems in Amsterdam to electrifying buses in Jakarta to expanding tree canopy and public-private sector electric vehicle partnerships in Miami. “Cities learning from each other is going to be more important…[as] climate change is accelerating,” said Eileen Higgins, mayor of Miami.

While national governments have significant tools at their disposal to reduce emissions, “they don’t transform a street, renovate a building, or plant a tree,” said Emmanual Grégoire, mayor of Paris. “Cities are where climate policies become a tangible reality for residents. In cities, climate change ceases to be a global phenomenon and becomes a firsthand experience.”

As cities undertake these bold climate initiatives, the U20 Communique ratified at the Summit asks national government leaders to support them. It calls for the G20 to support cities with climate finance, include them in national road maps for climate resilience and just energy transitions, integrate climate action with housing and economic development, give cities access to critical environmental and public health data, and strengthen public trust in climate science and communication.

“More and more, [people] experience [government] through the heat wave that keeps them up at night and the storm that floods their street,” said New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani. “That is why mayors from around the world came to New York to say that cities need the power and resources to protect and deliver for the people we serve.”

The Summit and the Communique also highlighted the importance of equity in the climate conversation. As Grégoire and Jan van Zanen, mayor of The Hague, noted, climate change impacts often reveal and exacerbate underlying inequalities in cities. A commitment to climate action means a commitment to climate justice, and addressing climate change as an integral part of migration and housing strategy. Mayor Yvonne Aki-Sawyerr of Freetown spoke of creating good green jobs for young people in the sanitation sector, while Mayor Roberto Gualtieri of Rome emphasized the importance of requirements for housing that included green design features.

The Summit further affirmed that many cities maintain their support for multilateral institutions, which have been central to global climate action, at a moment when these institutions, as New York City mayor’s chief of staff Elle Bisgaard-Church remarked, are “under duress.” The UN, for instance, faces a significant liquidity crisis, and the international rule of law is being tested by multiple wars in the Middle East and Europe. Several UN representatives spoke at the Summit about the importance of making space for cities at the organization and municipalities’ value in implementing climate policy and Sustainable Development Goals on the ground.

Simultaneously, mayors and city leaders made clear that their climate action would not only rely on traditional multilateral processes. “Climate action isn’t [just] something we’re going to talk about at COP,” said Aki-Sawyerr, referencing the upcoming annual UN Climate Change Conference, where key international climate negotiations take place. “It’s something we’re going to be doing everyday.”

title: From Utility to Lifestyle: How Electric Mobility Is Expanding the Role of Specialized Vehicles
description:
The Evolution of Specialized Vehicles Specialized vehicles have always been shaped by their surroundings.
From Utility to Lifestyle One of the most interesting developments is the shift from purely functional specialized vehicles toward lifestyle-oriented models.
A Broader Electric Mobility Market The emergence of lifestyle-oriented EVs does not mean conventional electric cars are becoming less important.
The Evolution of Specialized Vehicles Specialized vehicles have always been shaped by their surroundings.
A Broader Electric Mobility Market The emergence of lifestyle-oriented EVs does not mean conventional electric cars are becoming less important.
text:
The electric vehicle market is often discussed through the lens of familiar categories: electric sedans replacing gasoline cars, electric SUVs replacing conventional SUVs, and electric trucks entering commercial fleets.

But the transition to electric mobility is not limited to replacing vehicles that already exist.

It is also changing how people think about vehicles built for specific purposes.

Golf carts, neighborhood vehicles, utility carts, recreational vehicles, and other specialized forms of transportation have been around for decades. Their purpose has traditionally been clear: move people or equipment over relatively short distances in environments where a conventional car may not be necessary.

Electric power is giving many of these established vehicle categories new possibilities.

Instead of viewing specialized vehicles simply as alternatives to conventional automobiles, consumers and businesses are increasingly treating them as part of a broader mobility ecosystem. A vehicle can be designed for a resort, a private community, a golf destination, a coastal town, a campus, or recreational use without trying to replicate everything a conventional car can do.

That distinction is more relevant as electric mobility expands.

The Evolution of Specialized Vehicles

Specialized vehicles have always been shaped by their surroundings.

A golf cart does not need to perform like a highway vehicle. A utility vehicle used around a large property does not necessarily need the capabilities of a family SUV. A vehicle used inside a private community may prioritize maneuverability and accessibility over acceleration and long-distance range.

The rise of electric power makes these applications even more practical in certain settings.

Electric drivetrains are well suited to many short-distance applications because they provide quiet operation, straightforward charging, and zero tailpipe emissions. For businesses managing transportation across a defined property or community, the ability to match a vehicle to the environment can be more useful than having capabilities that may rarely be used.

This is creating a more diverse mobility market.

From Utility to Lifestyle

One of the most interesting developments is the shift from purely functional specialized vehicles toward lifestyle-oriented models.

The purpose of a vehicle can influence how it is designed, but it can also influence how people feel about using it.

A vehicle used around a beach community, for example, can become part of the character of that destination. The same applies to resorts, country clubs, private communities, and other environments where transportation is closely connected to leisure.

This is where specialized vehicles can move beyond utility.

They can become part of the experience.

Moke America: A Specialized Vehicle With a Long History

Moke America provides an interesting example of this evolution because the Moke itself was never simply a conventional passenger car.

The original Moke was developed in Britain as a lightweight military vehicle in the late 1950s and early 1960s. Its military role was short-lived, but its open-air design found a very different audience. It became associated with beaches, islands, celebrities, and leisure destinations, eventually developing a cultural identity far removed from its original purpose.

That history makes the Moke particularly relevant to the changing role of specialized vehicles.

Moke America brought the concept into the electric era rather than attempting to turn it into another conventional automobile. The company says its current U.S. vehicle retains the recognizable open-air design while incorporating modern electric technology and updated engineering. As of September 2025, its newer street-legal model reaches speeds of up to 45 MPH and offers up to 80 miles of range with its lithium battery.

The result is an electric lifestyle vehicle that occupies a different position from a conventional sedan or SUV.

Why the Application Matters

The significance of vehicles such as the Moke is less about replacing every conventional car and more about demonstrating that electric mobility can serve very different purposes.

A buyer looking for an electric beach vehicle may have a different set of priorities from someone shopping for an electric family SUV. A resort operator may care about guest experience and property mobility. A private community may value local transportation that fits its environment. A golf destination may have entirely different requirements again.

These are distinct applications, and they create room for specialized vehicles.

Moke America's current vehicle, for example, is positioned for environments such as coastal communities, resort towns, golf communities, and private neighborhoods. Its open-air configuration and distinctive design make the vehicle part of the setting rather than something designed to disappear into it.

That creates a different value proposition from simply owning another electric car.

Customization Becomes Part of the Product

Specialized mobility can also change the relationship between the vehicle and its owner.

Traditional automobiles tend to offer customization within a relatively standardized format. Lifestyle-oriented vehicles can place greater emphasis on appearance and personalization because design is part of the reason customers choose them.

Moke America offers multiple exterior colors, seating options, tops, wheels, and accessories, allowing buyers to configure the vehicle around their preferences.

This is commercially significant because personalization can turn a functional purchase into a lifestyle purchase.

The vehicle becomes an expression of where and how the owner intends to use it.

A Broader Electric Mobility Market

The emergence of lifestyle-oriented EVs does not mean conventional electric cars are becoming less important. Instead, it points to a larger and more segmented market.

Electric mobility can support vehicles designed for commuting, delivery, commercial operations, recreation, neighborhood transportation, tourism, and specialized environments. Some of these categories have existed for generations. What is changing is the technology available to them and the range of applications they can serve.

For manufacturers, this creates opportunities to focus on specific use cases rather than designing every vehicle for the broadest possible market.

For consumers, it means the question may increasingly shift from "Which electric car should I buy?" to "Which type of electric vehicle actually fits the way I live and move?"

That is an important distinction.

The next phase of electric mobility may not be defined solely by how quickly conventional cars become electric. It may also be defined by how many different types of vehicles can be rethought, refined, and repositioned around electric technology.

Moke America offers one example of that evolution. A vehicle that began with a practical military purpose eventually became a symbol of leisure and open-air driving, and today continues that identity through an electric platform.

The story of specialized electric vehicles, therefore, is not really about replacing the automobile.

It is about recognizing that mobility has never been one-size-fits-all, and electric technology is giving more vehicle categories the opportunity to serve their purpose in new ways.

title: Could abandoned mines house Pennsylvania's unwanted data centers?
authors: Jessica Klein, Inside Climate News, Jessica Klein, Inside Climate News, Taylor Sisk, KFF Health News, Audrey Carleton, Capital & Main
description:
Pennsylvania has the most abandoned coal mines in the country, totaling around 5,586 sites across the state.
Building data centers on abandoned mine lands would provide an alternative to destroying farmlands or local forests, instead making use of already unwanted acreage.
His research suggests that it’s a proposition worth pursuing—at least compared to building data centers in people’s non-polluted backyards.
Typically in the 40s or low 50s degrees Fahrenheit, mine pool temperatures are theoretically low enough to cool data centers.
That could include proximity to roads and the electricity grid, which can be repurposed for data centers.
text:
This article originally appeared on Inside Climate News, a nonprofit, non-partisan news organization that covers climate, energy and the environment.

Almost nobody wants a data center for a neighbor. Residents fear noise and air pollution, excessive energy and water use and the loss of open land. In Pennsylvania, a hot spot for new data centers, researchers see an opportunity to solve some of these issues by taking advantage of a much older environmental hazard: abandoned coal mines.

Pennsylvania has the most abandoned coal mines in the country, totaling around 5,586 sites across the state. The state reports it would take roughly $5 billion to reclaim these polluted and sometimes dangerous areas, which have contaminated thousands of miles of waterways and are linked to underground fires, subsidence and sinkholes. At the same time, local opposition to data centers is growing.

Building data centers on abandoned mine lands would provide an alternative to destroying farmlands or local forests, instead making use of already unwanted acreage. Underground mine pools could cool data centers without relying on outside water sources. And companies could help shoulder cleanup costs of existing contamination. The idea is appealing enough that federal researchers investigated it in 2023, concluding that abandoned mine lands offer “land, power infrastructure, and mine water cooling” to data center developers, particularly in a place like Pennsylvania.

“If the data centers can demonstrate that they can clean up, treat the acid water and help restore their local environment, the local people are more likely to accept such development proposals,” says Zhongyang He, a researcher in Penn State’s Department of Energy and Mineral Engineering who’s been examining possible data center development on abandoned mine lands in the state. His research suggests that it’s a proposition worth pursuing—at least compared to building data centers in people’s non-polluted backyards. But could it actually work at scale? Or would Pennsylvania end up replacing one intractable environmental problem with another?

An opportunity for reuse

There’s already some proof of concept in western Pennsylvania, where a former mine has housed a data center since 2013. The site of an old limestone mine, Iron Mountain’s West Pennsylvania data center in Boyers sits 220 feet below ground, a 330,000-square-foot facility on a 315-acre campus that doesn’t bring in any outside water. Instead, the data center cools through a closed-loop system that relies on the 53-degree water in a 100-acre, underground lake (not a mine pool, but a comparable concept).

“We are using what the miners had left behind,” said Iron Mountain’s senior director of energy and sustainability, Chris Pennington. Boreholes, dug in mines to reach deep water or minerals, provide infrastructure for internet access, and data center clients appreciate the security of storing their information deep underground. Though the facility regularly recycles its lake water, Iron Mountain brings in some refrigeration to supplement the system.

Former coal mine sites in Western Pennsylvania slated to become data centers include the former Robena Mine in Greene County, which members of the county’s Planning Commission voted in favor of late last year and would use water from a nearby river that it would convert into steam. Another proposed data center at the former Consol coal mine in Washington County, owned by natural gas company CNX Resources, would use nearby natural gas reserves and “remediated mine gas,” per the Pittsburgh Business Times.

There’s precedent outside of Pennsylvania, too. In West Virginia, Energy DELTA Lab’s 450-acre Data Center Ridge boasts access to almost “10 billion gallons of underground water” for cooling at a former mine site. In Italy, an active dolomite mine is home to a data center located 328 feet underground, cooled by the surrounding rock and chilly air.

Typically in the 40s or low 50s degrees Fahrenheit, mine pool temperatures are theoretically low enough to cool data centers. Mechanical cooling accounts for around 40 percent of an average data center’s energy consumption, and medium-sized data centers can consume around 100 million gallons of water per year. Penn State researcher He and his colleagues found that of the 5,586 abandoned mine sites they analyzed in Pennsylvania, 160 had mine pools large enough to accommodate data centers (there are currently at least 100 data centers proposed in Pennsylvania).

He’s research team landed on other advantages in addition to natural cooling, like “legacy infrastructure,” he said. That could include proximity to roads and the electricity grid, which can be repurposed for data centers. Transmission lines powered large equipment at former mines, and some of that infrastructure remains. “That does not mean that…the line transmission capacity is enough for data centers,” He said, but it does mean relevant permits could be in place.

Both Penn State and the Eastern Pennsylvania Coalition for Abandoned Mine Reclamation have assessed a former mine in northeastern Pennsylvania called Morea as a possible data center site. It harbors an estimated 7 billion gallons of underground water via a nearby creek that was routed underground when the mine was active. It still has an electric transmission line, “sufficient for utility-scale solar or a large industrial facility, and expensive and slow to replicate,” per the coalition’s report.

That report also acknowledges the ongoing economic burdens carried by communities that once produced coal. In Mahanoy Township, home to the Morea site, the coalition notes a 20.3 percent poverty rate (compared to 11.6 percent statewide)—a commonality across former Pennsylvania mining regions. A study published in Nature in 2024 notes that people living in areas of Pennsylvania exposed to mine drainage had incomes 30 percent lower than people in unaffected areas.

Data center development could help with that. The federal report brings up the thousands of job opportunities that could materialize from abandoned coal mine restoration, which increase with data center builds. A June study by the research project Resilient Energy Economies found that communities in Pennsylvania with some restoration of mine drainage-contaminated waterways experienced more population growth than areas without. Restoration attracts skilled workers, which can in turn increase commerce.

Choosing the lesser evil

If abandoned mine lands proved a hospitable home for data centers, possible sites could be found across the U.S., from West Virginia, Ohio and Kentucky to Western states like Wyoming.

But before new development could begin, companies would need to contend with the many kinds of pollution left behind by decades of mining, from acid mine drainage in streams to coal ash piles.

Today, you can observe this mess all over Pennsylvania. In Luzerne County, streams run orange with iron from abandoned mine drainage, emitting the sulfuric stench of rotten eggs and deterring the local trout. Piles of anthracite coal tower over fields that abut residents’ backyards, their formations almost resembling peaks in the Grand Canyon, only inky black. Ash pillars of burnt coal erode into the streams below when it rains, bringing toxic discharge.

Nearby, however, where you’d once find dead frogs flipped underside-up from the drainage, wildflowers buzz with bees and butterflies, water striders float on clear streams and foxes traverse fields of sprouting grass (albeit with pools of anthracite coal still looming in the background).

These environmental changes came partly due to the Surface Mining Control and Reclamation Act, which Congress enacted in 1977 and established a trust fund to reclaim and restore abandoned mine lands. Since 1980, Pennsylvania reports receiving more than $2 billion for this effort, and the state’s Department of Environmental Protection still offers reclamation grants to counties, municipalities and certain nonprofits.

Environmental groups like the Eastern Pennsylvania Coalition for Abandoned Mine Reclamation then do much of the on-the-ground work in the region, assessing sites and taking steps to restore the area’s natural ecosystem.

Fish have returned to clean, cold waters near sites where waste coal piles have been dismantled in favor of planted trees, said Bobby Hughes, the coalition’s founder, when showing ICN around some former mine lands in late August. “The plants are starting to grow back—a native wildflower mix,” he said, which attracts pollinators. He pointed out one spot where coal piles have been reduced and shaped to redirect mine drainage from the homes just yards away, creating a big, open field between backyards. That space might be used for the public to enjoy long-term, or ultimately house some kind of development. But for now, it’s much more pleasant for residents to traverse than piles of mining residue.

Hughes also pointed out some corporate developments on former mine lands, including an Amazon distribution center, and the reclamation happening at those sites, like developers putting down seed and carving out drainage systems. Hughes and his team have planted trees nearby.

In the rapidly expanding data center landscape, where to build can come down to the lesser of multiple evils. Building on mine lands “kind of beats taking down natural forest land,” said Hughes. That doesn’t mean it would be easy.

Hughes knows what would need to happen before developers even begin to build a new data center. Those underground mine pools that offer such promising natural cooling? “The majority of them are not mapped accurately,” he said, which would not only present structural challenges to engineers, but would also require investigation to figure out where their tainted discharge ends up (not to mention ongoing monitoring).

When mine pool water heats up from data center use, ideally in “closed loop” systems that mean the same water gets reused instead of siphoning water from nearby communities, that could spur chemical reactions. “If that happens, you could get an increased metal load into extremes [the area] hasn’t seen before,” Hughes said, “and that could lead to problems…[like] fish kills downstream.”

The unknown consequences of using mine pools for closed-loop cooling systems begs further study. Not only could the changing chemistry prove damaging to the surrounding environment, but long-term use could also raise water temperatures to the point that the mine pools cease to offer effective cooling systems.

To those who insist the mine pools are large enough to accommodate small temperature changes without issue, Hughes has a challenge: “Prove that to me,” he said. “If the mine water temperature changes slowly over time, you may not see something until after the change is already inverted from cold to warm.”

Then there’s the local wildlife. Hughes said builders would have to complete bat surveys and look at the Pennsylvania Natural Diversity Inventory to ensure their builds don’t disturb threatened plants and animals.

Builders may not love the idea of building on old mines, either. Despite the subterranean lake’s cooling “advantage” at Iron Mountain, Pennington said building underground was no simple feat. “I don’t think anybody would go through the work and expense of putting a data center below ground just to take advantage of a natural cool environment down there,” he said. (Iron Mountain’s Boyers site had been used for years as a storage facility before it housed the data center.) Workers also have to monitor the lake’s temperature and water level “constantly,” he added, even though there’s no concern about chemical drainage, unlike in former coal mines, which would require even more intensive observation.

Infrastructure at old coal mines isn’t a given. Not all the mine lands Hughes works on in eastern Pennsylvania have power infrastructure ready to go. “In our assessment report for solar, we found that most of the areas that we’re looking at…the grid infrastructure isn’t there,” he said.

Matt Prusak, a former executive at several data center companies and current chief business officer at data center systems manufacturer Giga Energy, says building on former mine lands has come up as developers seek out novel, viable sites, but the power issue remains. “The mine can solve land and sometimes cooling,” Prusak says. “However, it does not solve the grid… The bottleneck is typically in megawatts, not acreage.”

Local skepticism endures

Walking past fuzzy mullein and saplings growing on former mine land, Hughes emphasized that his organization’s work lies in assessments of these sites to determine the next steps for reclamation. “It’s not for me to decide if I think mine lands are the right locations” for data centers, he said. Where he lives, just outside the areas that used to house coal mines, his community is shoring up their zoning ordinances to keep data centers out.

Heading north toward Hughes’ office on windy Pine Run Road, white signs with bold, red letters make a familiar demand every few miles, peeking out between roadside shrubs: “NO DATA CENTERS.”

In Archbald, about 30 miles north of Hughes’ office, the promise of treating polluted former mine lands for iron, aluminum, sulfuric acid and other heavy metals before any construction takes place isn’t enough to appease residents who fear data centers will destroy their communities, nor is the potential use of mine pools for cooling the site’s high water needs (up to 3.3 million gallons per day in the hot Pennsylvania summers). The proposed 500-acre Wildcat Ridge Data Center campus has met fierce local resistance.

At a hearing about the project earlier this year, County Commissioner Bill Gaughan spoke out against the proposal with a nod to the long history of coal mining and pollution in the region. “I am not anti-technology, and I’m not anti-progress. I don’t think anybody is, but I am absolutely opposed to sacrifice zones, which I think this is what we’re becoming,” he said. “I am opposed to a future where communities like Archbald are once again told ‘trust us, be patient, it will be worth it in the end.’ We have heard that before. Coal was supposed to be worth it. It wasn’t.”

text:
Cirba Solutions, General Motors (GM), and their partners have completed a closed-loop EV battery recycling pilot designed to return recovered critical minerals from end-of-life batteries to the manufacturing process.

The programme involved processing used GM EV battery packs and recovering materials including nickel, cobalt, and manganese for use in new battery cells.

As part of the collaboration, Cirba Solutions disassembled and processed end-of-life GM EV battery packs at its lithium-ion recycling and recovery facility in Ohio.

The batteries were processed into Black Mass, a concentrated intermediate material containing critical minerals recovered through the shredding and processing of lithium-ion batteries.

The programme has resulted in the production of GM EV batteries using cathode active material (CAM) containing 100% recycled nickel, cobalt, and manganese.

The recycled materials were further refined into new CAM before being used to manufacture battery cells through Ultium Cells, the joint venture between GM and LG Energy Solution.

Speaking on the landmark EV battery recycling initiative, David Klanecky, President and CEO of Cirba Solutions, said: “Battery recycling is an important, intersecting component across the battery supply chain, and this programme effectively demonstrates the value that recycling end-of-life batteries brings to creating a closed-loop supply of critical minerals.

“The global battery supply chain is an interconnected network of innovative and collaborative organisations – and engaging in partnerships like this with GM shows us how this work can truly strengthen our supply chains, manufacturing, global competitiveness and national security.”

From battery waste to new cells

Recovering critical minerals is only the first stage of EV battery recycling.

Materials such as nickel, cobalt, and manganese can influence battery performance, meaning recycled materials must meet the same standards as virgin minerals before they can be used in new EV cells.

To achieve this, the partners further refined the Black Mass produced by Cirba Solutions.

The process showed that recovered minerals could be processed into CAM that met battery-manufacturing requirements, with the resulting CAM made entirely from recycled materials.

Ultium Cells then used the recycled CAM to produce new EV battery cells. GM manufacturing teams subsequently assembled the cells into battery modules and packs at GM’s Factory ZERO and Spring Hill assembly centres.

The first EVs powered by battery cells containing the recycled CAM have now rolled off the production line and are heading to consumers.

Melissa Flaherty, Director of Sustainable EV Battery Ecosystem at GM, added: “This pilot shows that the value of an EV battery can extend well beyond its first life, and that strong partnerships across the battery ecosystem are essential to building a more circular, resilient future for battery technology.”

Scaling closed-loop EV battery recycling

The project comes as the number of batteries reaching the end of their useful lives is expected to grow.

Nearly 14 million EV batteries are projected to reach end-of-life globally by 2040, while annual global demand for lithium-ion batteries is expected to reach approximately 4.2 to 6.8 terawatt-hours over the next decade.

This creates a growing role for EV battery recycling, allowing critical minerals recovered from used batteries to return to the supply chain and be used in new products.

The Cirba Solutions and GM programme also highlights the potential for domestic processing capabilities to support closed-loop models across other battery applications, including energy storage systems, data centres and consumer devices.

Recovering and reusing critical minerals could help support lower-cost batteries over time, reduce reliance on newly mined materials, advance manufacturing and strengthen supply chain resilience.

text:
Clean Energy Supply Senior Lead - Energy and Sustainable Business Program

This is a hybrid position which requires 8 days per month in the office. You will be based in our office in WRI Indonesia, Jakarta. Existing work authorization is required at the time of application submission as WRI is unable to sponsor any visa work sponsorship for this position.

Program Overview

The Energy and Sustainable Business (ESB) program works to accelerate Indonesia’s transition toward a low-carbon economy while supporting continued economic development. In support of Indonesia’s net-zero emissions and energy transition goals, we work across both the demand and supply sides of the energy system: helping businesses reduce emissions and access cleaner energy, while also advancing the broader conditions needed to accelerate renewable energy deployment. In collaboration with industries and industrial parks, business associations, key ministries, PLN, financial institutions, and other partners, we provide technical assistance and capacity building to businesses, support policy and regulatory improvements that enable greater renewable energy integration into the grid, and help strengthen the investment ecosystem needed for renewable energy projects to scale. Combining policy and technical expertise with WRI’s convening power, the program seeks to bring together government, businesses, utilities, investors, and other stakeholders to translate Indonesia’s energy transition ambitions into concrete action, investment, and measurable emissions reductions.

The Clean Energy Supply (CES) is an intervention pillar under the ESB program aiming to ensure the availability and affordability of clean energy supply for all. It discuss key topics that are essential to enable a progressive energy regime, infrastructure, and business ecosystem supportive to more development of renewable energy across the country. Research topics include grid flexibility, green power procurement, integrated resources planning, renewable energy sources, and grid financing.

On green power procurement, we established the Clean Energy Investment Accelerator (CEIA) in 2017 as an innovative public-private partnership initiative that advances policy and financing frameworks to meet the clean energy needs of commercial and industrial energy consumers. We believe that as the largest energy consumer group, the commercial and industrial sector could use their buying power to drive energy transition through policy advocacy, business model and technology adoption. CEIA has led to our partnership with PLN since 2019 in diversifying green power procurement options to increase companies’ accessibility to credible renewable energy sources. The establishment of Renewable Energy Certificate (REC) by the end of 2019, followed by Green Energy as A Service in 2024 have marked important milestones in our efforts in briding companies’ aspiration with national priority. We continuously provide recommendation to improve green power products that will adjust to customers’ variety needs of clean energy, as well as the more robust international standards (e.g. GHG Protocol) and trade policies (e.g. CBAM). In support to 100 GWp solar PV plan by the government, the program is looking into diversifying more business model applicable to solar PV + BESS procurement where businesses can participate and achieve their RE targets.

On grid flexibility, we initiated a research on transport electrification impact to the Jakarta grid and how it will influence the future transport electrification planning in the city. We collaborate with the Cities Program to collect data, engage key stakeholders such as PLN and Transjakarta, and coordinate with the WRI Polsky Energy Center team to formulate global research on this topic. On integrated resources planning (IRP), we aim for national and subnational actors to be able to produce and use reliable and credible energy demand projections, which then enable more synchronized, adaptive, and reciprocal power planning in Indonesia. This will be done through increasing the availability of high-quality energy demand data, strengthening the modelling capacity of subnational government, and building a better coordination mechanism between key institutions to incorporate more accurate energy data. We collaborate with WRI India who has done successful intervention in several states in India.

We believe these interventions will play key roles in transforming the energy system and market. By making clean energy solutions more accessible and affordable for all, WRI Indonesia aims to increase Indonesia industry’s competitiveness in the market through greener operations and products which ultimately significantly contribute to Indonesia emissions reduction.

WRI Indonesia believe that sustainable development highlights the need for integrated approaches to finding solutions that are aligned with the challenge of achieving economic, social and environmental goals that are often interlinked. This can be daunting task, as the interlinkages are complex and context specific and depend, inter alia, on the issues under consideration, the geographic and temporal scales, sector of the industry, and the existing technologies. Therefore, the ESB program works across disciplines with the cities team, climate team and the ocean to combine low carbon technology systems, quantitative models, and other policy-making decision tools to achieve and support key national initiatives in Indonesia such as the acceleration of the achievement of national renewable energy targets and net zero ambition.

Job Highlight

The Clean Energy Supply Senior Lead will play a leading role in shaping and strengthening the program intervention and research agenda of WRI Indonesia’s ESB’s clean energy pillar, contributing to the overarching WRI’s energy pillar’s goals and impact targets. The role will provide strategic and technical leadership accross a range of clean energy supply topic, including green power procurement, grid flexibility, integrated resources planning, solar PV and BESS, energy tariff, transport and power integration.

On day-to-day basis, the role will report directly to the Senior Manager for Energy and Sustainable Business while working closely with Clean Energy Demand and the ESB research team to strategize research priorities and workplan, identify research gaps and opportunities, coordinate the team’s research execution, engage with keystakeholders, and ensure the timely delivery of high-quality research outputs in line with WRI standards. Furthermore, the role will coordinate with WRI’s Polsky Energy Center and other WRI country offices to strengthen research collaboration and knowledge exchange on clean energy supply.

This position will be based in Jakarta with office-flex working arrangement and the possibility of doing travel. In support of WRI's DEI commitment, you are responsible for actively participating in these collaborative efforts by integrating equity into your work, our workplace, and the organizational culture.

What You Will Do

Research & Development

Provide direction and strategic insights to the development of CES pillar project interventions and research

Lead and facilitate policy and technical studies to produce policy recommendation or technical guideline in the field of (but not limited to) corporate renewable energy procurement, energy transition for industrial decarbonization, integrated resource planning, energy tariff, grid flexibility and storage.

Oversee CES research quality and alignment across topics in the WRI’s energy and sustainable business portfolio

Co-develop technical analyses on green power procurement to provide insights/technical assistance to utility/corporates and relevant ministries

Lead and oversee coordination with subject matter experts (e.g. consultants/experts, universities, governments, research institutions) to produce research products

Lead strategic discussions relevant to the advancement of WRI’s CES research excellence and portfolio expansion, and its alignment to the broader WRI Energy and Sustainable Business Program

Regularly coordinate with WRI Polsky Energy Center’s CES Pillar Lead to provide update and maintain support from global or other international offices.

Contribute to develop WRI Indonesia’s communication product such as blogpost and brief writings to advance the impact of Energy and Sustainability Business initiatives in coordination with Communications team.

Projects Management and Engagement

Work with project leads to oversee the overall implementation and budget spending of CES projects and ensure its achievement according to donor requirements and WRI Indonesia standard

Provide day-to-day leadership to the CES team, including assignment of responsibilities, performance monitoring, coaching, coordination, and problem-solving.

Monitor CES research results and impacts by working collaboratively with WRI’s monitoring and evaluation, and communication team

Oversee external experts, consultants, and service providers supporting the CES activities.

Contribute in proposal writing and reporting to donors

Serve as the senior representative of the ESB program in engagements with donors, government institutions, PLN, financial institutions, investors, developers, corporate stakeholders, and other partners.

Develop and maintain strategic collaboration and partnerships that can strengthen CES interventions and project implementation

What You Will Need

Bachelor’s Degree in Energy Economics, Economics, Energy System, Natural Resources Management or related field of study. Master’s degree is preferred.

Minimum 6 (six) years of experience working in the issue of renewable energy, power systems, energy transition, or other closely related field.

Proven in-depth knowledge of renewable energy and power sector issues, with experience in areas such as renewable energy procurement, power system planning, grid flexibility, energy storage, energy markets and tariffs, or industrial energy transition.

Demonstrated experience in designing and overseeing robust, transparent, and reproducible data collection and analysis processes, with appropriate consideration of impact to people, nature, and climate, and clear documentation accessible to relevant team members and reviewers

Strong ability to formulate research questions, select appropriate research approaches, and lead literature reviews and evidence synthesis to generate robust and relevant findings

Ability to communicate research approaches and findings effectively to both technical and non-technical audience, and to integrate research with engagement and communications activities to translate evidence into clear and actionable insights and achieve intended outcomes.

Strong ability to work independently and collaboratively, manage competing priorities, and maintain effective coordination and positive working relationship with team member and external counterparts.

Strong organizational and time management skills, with the ability to adapt to changing priorities, manage multiple assignments and deadlines, and deliver high-quality work product.

Business proficiency in Bahasa Indonesia and English

Ability and willingness to travel as assigned.

Legally able to work in Indonesia

Contract Arrangement

Full-time with fixed-term employment agreement for 6 (six) months with a possibility of extension up to 31 December 2027 subject to individual performance, project needs, and budget availability.

How to Apply:

Please submit a resume with a cover letter by 6 October 2026. You must apply through the WRI Careers portal to be considered. We may close for applications sooner if we receive a high volume of applications from qualified candidates

Must have authorization to work in Indonesia to be eligible for this position

Final candidates might be required to take a certain test and/or to produce/share writing samples when needed.

What we offer:

Salary that is commensurate with experience and skills

Competitive and comprehensive benefit package

Access to the WRI global network with the opportunity to exchange with and learn from passionate colleagues working at the cutting edge of their fields.

A workplace that strives to put diversity and inclusion at the heart of our work

The opportunity to join and get involved in different working groups and affinity groups to shape the future of WRI

Commitment to hybrid working model with flexible working hours

About Us:

World Resources Institute works to improve people’s lives, protect and restore nature and stabilize the climate. As an independent research organization, we leverage our data, expertise and global reach to influence policy and catalyze change across systems like food, land and water; energy; and cities. Our 2,000+ staff work on the ground in more than a dozen focus countries and with partners in over 50 nations.

Our mission and values:

WRI’s mission is to move human society to live in ways that protect Earth’s environment and its capacity to provide for the needs and aspirations of current and future generations.

Our values are shared ideals that bind us together: Independence, Integrity, Impact, Partnership, and Care.

Our culture:

WRI is committed to advancing gender and social equity for human well-being in our mission including equal opportunities in employment. All qualified applicants will receive consideration for employment without regard to race, ethnicity, religion, sex, national origin, age, caste, marital status, sexual orientation, gender identity and expression, disability, or protected Veteran status.

Our Human Resources Team carefully reviews all applications.

text:
India is producing more green energy - but wasting a lot of it

On a hot July afternoon this year, electricity generated from renewable energy briefly met over half of India's peak power demand - only the second time this happened. The first instance was around the same period a year ago.

While it was only briefly that power generated from solar, wind, hydro and nuclear sources collectively outstripped coal-based output, it was a milestone moment reflecting the astonishing growth of non-fossil fuels to the country's electricity mix over the last decade.

"It showed that renewable energy is no longer a marginal source sitting at the edge of the power system," Sumant Sinha, CEO of ReNew Power, one of India's largest Nasdaq-listed clean energy companies, told the BBC.

To be sure, coal-based power plants still continue to generate 70% of India's electricity on average because they run on a higher load factor, or for more hours than solar or wind. Yet, the country's push for clean energy appears to have reached a crucial inflection point.

A decade ago India's installed renewable energy capacity was barely 4GW. It now makes up 300GW or 54% of its total 552GW installed capacity - a target that's been achieved five years ahead of schedule.

For a nation long seen as the poster child for dirty coal dependence, this rapid transition points to a remarkable achievement in decarbonising its grid.

Yet, the gains are tempered by some serious challenges.

Foremost among them is a shortage of grid capacity. The renewables' build out has significantly outpaced transmission infrastructure, a point of major concern for policymakers.

"In the first quarter of 2026, transmission constraints accounted for nearly two-thirds of all renewable energy curtailment at 300 gigawatt-hours (GWh)," according to Ember, a global energy think-tank.

Put simply, that means a bulk of the clean energy that was produced in India was wasted because the country's transmission lines have been dogged by missed targets, with one out of four inter-state projects facing delays of over a year.

The difficulty lies in matching the speed of generation projects with the grid build-out, says Sinha.

"Generation projects can be constructed in 18-24 months… Transmission can take much longer because they involve right-of-way, land acquisition, approvals and coordination across many agencies. It is an execution issue that becomes more important as the system gets larger," he adds.

Vibhuti Garg of the Institute for Energy Economics and Financial Analysis also blames "poor planning" for the problem.

The grid was able to absorb new capacity as long as India was generating 10-15GW annually, she told the BBC. But that pace has dramatically increased, reaching a record 51GW last year, and the infrastructure is no longer able to cope.

The concentration of renewables projects in the north-western states of Gujarat and Rajasthan has also compounded the challenge of evacuating power in the face of such grid shortages.

Analysts at Ember now believe this growing mismatch between fast-moving generation projects and slower-moving transmission infrastructure, is the "most critical operational risk to the country's 2030 target of 500 gigawatts (GW) of non-fossil electricity".

A quick solution to addressing this gap would have been to build battery storage systems at renewable pooling stations to integrate the power into the grid.

"Had that been the case, India could have stored the energy and used it during evening hours rather than wasting it," says Garg.

But storage capacity has not grown because of a huge jump in the price of batteries, raw material shortages due to the war in the Middle East and a fall in the value of the Indian currency which has jacked up financing costs for Indian companies.

"Many storage projects that were meant to come up fell through as a result," Garg adds.

Yet, finance isn't a constraint merely for storage projects but an industry wide problem.

While ample global capital is available for green transition across the developed world, getting access to it remains a persistent struggle for Indian clean energy companies, despite the strides that the country has made in its renewables commitments.

Estimates suggest the country will require $400-$500bn to meet its 500GW renewables target by 2030. But currently, around 83% of India's finance for climate mitigation is sourced domestically, according to the government's economic survey. While the Paris Agreement clearly mandated developed countries to provide financial resources to the tune of $100bn annually up to 2025 to developing countries for their climate action, that money has been hard to get.

"Emerging and developing economies outside China receive only around 15% of global clean-energy investment, despite accounting for roughly two-thirds of the world's population," says Sinha.

According to him, while India does not necessarily need developed countries to finance its entire transition, help is needed in the form of cheaper loans, guarantees and protection against currency losses so that private investors are encouraged to put in more money into the space.

Plugging these critical gaps in finance, transmission infrastructure and storage will be critical given this transition is under way at a pivotal moment, say experts.

India is the world's third largest emitter of greenhouse gases and facing a sharp rise in electricity demand, which has grown at a compounded rate of over 7% every year. It is expected to further accelerate with the expansion of industries like data centres and chip manufacturing.

The International Energy Agency predicts India's electricity demand will increase by 80% by 2035, the sharpest jump among emerging economies. It also credits the country's robust expansion of its renewables as a major contributor for slowing emissions in the developed world this year, even as energy related CO2 emissions rose more strongly in advanced economies for the first time since the 1990s.

title: Fort Worth weighs data center growth as residents raise concerns - TCU 360
description:
There are currently four data center developments operating in Fort Worth: Meta Fort Worth Data Center, QTS Data Centers, TierPoint and Centersquare Data Centers.
Electricity is one of the most important elements of a data center because it is the only thing that allows it to operate.
On Sept. 8, Krause held a town hall for residents to speak about their concerns surrounding the growth of data centers.
The Fort Worth Data Center and Infrastructure Commission (DCIC) is expected to report its recommendations to the city council on Nov. 3.
A public hearing on the proposed moratorium is scheduled for 6 p.m. Nov. 10 at Fort Worth City Hall.
text:
The city of Fort Worth is taking a closer look at the development of data centers as concerns grow over how they might affect neighborhoods, local land and water.

On Aug. 11, the city began considering a 90-day moratorium on the construction of new data centers while they study and prepare for possible regulations.

The demand for supporting artificial intelligence and cloud storage has been rising over the past months. North Texas has attracted new investors because of its large amounts of developable land and strong fiber-optic infrastructure.

There are currently four data center developments operating in Fort Worth: Meta Fort Worth Data Center, QTS Data Centers, TierPoint and Centersquare Data Centers. One additional facility is under construction, and four more are proposed within the city.

While these facilities are becoming more common, many people do not know what a data center is or why it requires so much land, water, and electricity.

Data centers are large buildings filled with computers that serve, store, process, and send information. They support everyday services such as cloud storage, video streaming, social media and artificial intelligence.

Those servers operate continuously and generate large amounts of heat, requiring extensive cooling systems to prevent overheating. Many large centers use water-based cooling systems as they can efficiently remove heat in highly dense systems.

Depending on their size and cooling system, data centers can use hundreds of thousands to several million gallons of water per day. According to the Environmental and Energy Study Institute (EESI), large facilities use up to 5 million gallons daily. That is equivalent to the daily water use of a 30,000-person town.

Electricity is one of the most important elements of a data center because it is the only thing that allows it to operate. A 20-megawatt data center uses 480,000 kilowatt-hours of electricity a day. According to U.S. Energy Information Administration household-use data, that is enough electricity to power 16,550 average U.S. homes for one day.

Data center development can also require large amounts of land. The average land transaction reached about 224 acres in 2024, according to Cushman & Wakefield. The price per acre reached an average of $244,000, although costs vary significantly depending on location and access to electricity and fiber optics.

Those demands have become a growing concern for some North Texas residents.

A fifth major project, Circle T, is proposed nearby in Westlake and has faced opposition from nearby residents. Some Keller residents have raised concerns about how close the development would be to their homes.

Tarrant County Commissioner Matt Krause said he asked residents whether measures such as supplying separate energy and water and reducing noise would ease their concerns.

“They still did not want one of these centers 506 feet from their residential neighborhood,” Krause said.

On Sept. 8, Krause held a town hall for residents to speak about their concerns surrounding the growth of data centers.

“It turned out to be really good, really good attendance,” Krause said.

Many residents expressed that they were not opposed to the construction but did not want these facilities near their homes and could possibly negatively impact their quality of life.

“Everybody said, ‘We understand the need for them. We understand why we have to have them. but there has to be some kind of guardrails put into place for these things,’” said Krause.

The Fort Worth Data Center and Infrastructure Commission (DCIC) is expected to report its recommendations to the city council on Nov. 3. A public hearing on the proposed moratorium is scheduled for 6 p.m. Nov. 10 at Fort Worth City Hall.

Krause encouraged residents on both sides of the issue to contact their elected officials.

“Go to your elected officials and make your voice heard,” Krause said. “Because at the end of the day, elected officials work for you. You don’t work for them and they need to hear from you on these important topics.”

text:
By David Shepardson

WASHINGTON, Sept 22 (Reuters) – A US judge on Tuesday dismissed an antitrust lawsuit in which Michigan accused four major oil companies of colluding to forestall competition in renewable energy, including electric vehicles, a decision in line with prior rulings in similar cases.

US District Judge Jane Beckering in Grand Rapids rejected the lawsuit filed in January by Michigan Attorney General Dana Nessel, a Democrat, against BP, Chevron, Exxon, Shell and the American Petroleum Institute.

The judge said antitrust laws protect against none of the injuries for which Michigan sought a remedy, except for energy overcharges.

“The distance is too great between the alleged conspiracy and Michigan’s and its residents’ overcharges to find that the conspiracy proximately caused the overcharges,” Beckering said.

The complaint said the companies sought to “restrain the emergence of electric vehicles and renewable primary energy technologies in the United States.”

Other judges have rejected similar climate lawsuits including in Delaware, Maryland, New Jersey, New York, Pennsylvania, Puerto Rico and South Carolina.

A lawyer for Chevron previously called Michigan’s lawsuit “baseless as demonstrated by multiple related court dismissals.”

Chevron and the other companies have been fighting for years against lawsuits by state and local governments seeking to hold them responsible for climate change, many of which remain pending.

The Trump administration has taken a series of actions to make it easier for automakers to avoid building electric vehicles and make them more expensive for consumers to buy, reversing Biden administration policies.

(Reporting by David Shepardson; Editing by Cynthia Osterman)
