text:
NEWARK, N.J. – September 22, 2026 — PSE&G's energy efficiency programs are helping participating customers save energy and manage costs while also generating broader economic benefits across New Jersey, according to a new economic impact analysis conducted by E Source.

Commissioned by PSE&G, the analysis found that every $1 invested in the utility’s energy efficiency program generated $2.85 in economic output. Projects completed in 2025 generated more than $1.15 billion in total economic output. The analysis also found approximately $467 million in associated wages and $164 million in local, state and federal tax revenue across New Jersey.

The findings build on the measurable benefits PSE&G's energy efficiency programs are already delivering for residential and business customers. In July, PSE&G highlighted the bill savings impact of the programs for participating customers, including helping them save over $1 billion while reducing energy use and better managing energy costs.

This new analysis looks beyond those direct customer benefits to provide a broader view of how energy efficiency investments contribute to New Jersey's economy.

"Energy efficiency starts with delivering real value for our customers," said Lauren Thomas, vice-president, PSE&G Clean Energy Solutions – Customer Solutions. "These findings show that the value of the programs extends beyond bill savings to support economic activity across New Jersey, creating benefits for businesses, workers and communities throughout the state."

The analysis focused on PSE&G Clean Energy Future-Energy Efficiency II projects completed during calendar year 2025. Approximately $404.5 million in portfolio investment was modeled, representing approximately 60,000 participating customers and 75,000 projects.

Nearly half of the $1.15 billion in economic output came from the direct impact of program investments and customer projects. The remaining value came through supply-chain activity and household spending associated with wages and energy bill savings, showing how program investments generate additional economic activity statewide.

2025 Economic Impact

E Source’s analysis found that PSE&G energy efficiency projects completed in 2025 generated:

$2.85 in economic output for every $1 invested

More than $1.15 billion in total economic output

Approximately 4,737 jobs supported

11.7 jobs supported for every $1 million invested

Approximately $467 million in related wages

Approximately $164 million in related local, state and federal tax revenue

PSE&G commissioned E Source to conduct the study using IMPLAN, an industry-standard economic modeling framework that incorporates New Jersey-specific economic relationships. The analysis examined economic activity associated with program expenditures, participant investments and energy savings, including direct, supply-chain and household-spending impacts.

To learn more about PSE&G's energy efficiency programs and view the economic impact study, visit pseg.com/ImpactHub.

(TestMiles) – Volvo’s updated XC60 and XC90 plug-in hybrids promise up to 78 and 73 electric miles, extending the brand’s bridge toward full EVs.
That phrase has been used frequently across the industry, but nearly 80 miles of claimed electric range gives it considerably more substance.
Volvo says that is more than twice the electric range of the existing plug-in-hybrid versions.
Driving speed, temperature, terrain, climate-control use, vehicle configuration and driving behavior can all affect actual electric range.

text:
(TestMiles) – Volvo’s updated XC60 and XC90 plug-in hybrids promise up to 78 and 73 electric miles, extending the brand’s bridge toward full EVs.

Volvo is making a larger bet on plug-in hybrids at the same time the auto industry is wrestling with a complicated question: How quickly are American drivers actually ready to abandon gasoline?

The Swedish automaker has unveiled new long-range plug-in-hybrid versions of its XC60 and XC90 SUVs, claiming preliminary electric driving ranges of up to 78 miles for the XC60 and 73 miles for the larger XC90. If those figures hold through final certification, Volvo says they will be the longest electric ranges offered by any plug-in hybrids in the American market.

That is more than a routine powertrain update. It pushes the plug-in hybrid much closer to functioning as an electric vehicle for ordinary daily driving while preserving a gasoline engine for longer journeys.

For Volvo, the vehicles also carry unusual strategic importance. The XC60 is the company’s best-selling model of all time, while the XC90 has served for years as a flagship for Volvo’s safety, design and premium aspirations. Rather than moving those nameplates directly from combustion engines to fully electric propulsion, Volvo is expanding the middle ground.

The company describes the two SUVs as a bridge to full electrification. That phrase has been used frequently across the industry, but nearly 80 miles of claimed electric range gives it considerably more substance.

A Plug-In Hybrid That Can Cover a Real Commute

Most plug-in hybrids have historically offered enough electric range for local errands and shorter commutes, but many owners eventually encounter the gasoline engine during ordinary daily use.

Volvo’s new numbers alter that equation.

The new XC60 can travel as far as 78 miles on electricity under preliminary EPA-based testing, according to Volvo, while the XC90 is rated at up to 73 miles. Volvo says that is more than twice the electric range of the existing plug-in-hybrid versions.

The improvement comes from a larger battery integrated into the floor along with a more powerful electric motor. The gasoline engine remains available when the battery’s usable charge has been depleted or when additional propulsion is required.

That combination is the central argument for a long-range PHEV. A driver who charges regularly may be able to complete a large share of weekly driving without starting the gasoline engine, yet can still make a long interstate trip without planning around public charging stops.

EPA range figures are standardized estimates rather than promises. Driving speed, temperature, terrain, climate-control use, vehicle configuration and driving behavior can all affect actual electric range. Volvo itself notes that its announced figures are preliminary.

Still, the magnitude matters. Even if real-world conditions reduce the number, a plug-in hybrid beginning with more than 70 miles of rated electric capability creates a much larger electric buffer than one beginning with 25, 30 or 40 miles.

It also exposes one of the important conditions behind successful PHEV ownership: charging. A buyer who plugs the vehicle in regularly can use the electric system as intended. Someone who rarely charges is carrying the weight and cost of two propulsion systems while surrendering much of the reason for buying the vehicle in the first place.

The XC60 Gets More Than a Battery Upgrade

Volvo has used the powertrain update to make wider changes to the XC60 rather than simply installing a larger battery.

The exterior receives a revised front and rear design, including an updated grille, front bumper, hood, front fenders and wheels. Volvo has also reworked its familiar “Thor’s Hammer” LED headlight signature and revised the rear lamps, tailgate and bumper.

The changes preserve the restrained Scandinavian visual identity that has become familiar across Volvo’s lineup rather than attempting a wholesale design reset.

Inside, the XC60 gets a redesigned dashboard and door panels, new wood trim and available Cardamom ventilated Nappa leather. Volvo says upgraded interior lighting is intended to reinforce the quieter, more subdued character of the cabin.

Technology takes a larger role as well.

An 11.2-inch center display runs Volvo Car UX, the company’s latest infotainment interface. Google Gemini is being integrated as an in-car assistant, allowing drivers to use more conversational language for tasks that can include route planning, finding stops and handling messages.

That development may be more important than simply enlarging a screen. Automakers increasingly have to determine whether voice-based artificial intelligence can reduce the amount of visual interaction drivers need with touchscreen interfaces. The useful test will be whether Gemini can reliably complete common tasks without requiring drivers to learn exact phrases or dive back into menus.

Volvo also says the XC60 receives updated sensing hardware using radar, cameras and other sensors to support its driver-assistance and active-safety systems.

Those functions include automatic emergency braking and steering interventions intended to help avoid or mitigate collisions, along with lane-change assistance and a 360-degree camera with a three-dimensional view.

The company also describes a system capable of warning occupants about an approaching cyclist before a door is opened.

None of those systems eliminates the driver’s responsibility. Driver-assistance technology can expand the amount of information available to the person behind the wheel, but it remains assistance rather than autonomous driving.

XC90 Keeps the Familiar Formula

The XC90 follows a different path because Volvo has already made recent changes to its large three-row SUV.

Instead of receiving the XC60’s more extensive redesign, the long-range XC90 builds on its existing family-oriented formula while adding the dramatically increased electric capability.

The seven-seat SUV remains positioned above the XC60 and continues to emphasize space, materials, comfort and safety.

Its electric range of up to 73 miles is five miles short of the XC60 figure but significant for a large premium SUV that retains a gasoline engine.

That may make the XC90 especially interesting for families whose normal weekday use consists of school runs, commuting and local activities but who also use the same vehicle for vacations and long-distance travel.

An owner with access to reliable home charging could theoretically treat many ordinary trips as electric journeys without committing the household’s primary family vehicle to an entirely battery-electric powertrain.

Volvo says the XC90 also receives Google Gemini and retains available features including its Bowers & Wilkins premium sound system.

The vehicle remains one of the company’s most important products symbolically as well as commercially. The modern XC90 was central to Volvo’s move further into the premium market, and its design language influenced much of the lineup that followed.

Now Volvo is asking that same nameplate to play a second transitional role: helping customers move from combustion power toward electrification without requiring them to make the entire jump at once.

Why Volvo Is Extending the Middle Ground

The automotive industry’s transition toward battery-electric vehicles has become less linear than many companies once projected.

Consumers have shown strong interest in electrified vehicles, but charging access, purchase prices, trip planning, home circumstances and regional differences continue to shape what type of powertrain works for individual households.

A long-range plug-in hybrid tries to solve several of those problems simultaneously.

It offers an electric drivetrain for the trips that make up much of everyday driving while retaining liquid fuel for situations in which charging may be inconvenient or unavailable. That is particularly relevant for buyers who want an electric experience but remain uneasy about making their only vehicle fully electric.

There are compromises.

A PHEV carries a battery, electric motor, gasoline engine, fuel system and associated hardware. That makes it mechanically more complicated than a pure EV and potentially heavier than a conventional hybrid. Its environmental and operating-cost benefits also depend heavily on how consistently it is charged.

The strongest use case is therefore quite specific: an owner with dependable access to charging whose ordinary driving fits comfortably inside the electric range, but who still values the flexibility of gasoline for longer journeys.

With more than 70 miles available before that engine is needed, Volvo is widening the number of households for which that description could apply.

Production and What Buyers Still Need to Know

Volvo says production of the new XC60 and XC90 T8 AWD Long Range plug-in hybrids will begin later this fall, with customer deliveries expected in early 2027.

Several important details have not yet been supplied in the press material.

Volvo has not announced U.S. pricing for the new long-range variants. Final EPA-certified range and complete efficiency figures will also matter, as will battery capacity, charging power and charging-time information for American customers.

Those numbers could significantly affect the vehicles’ value proposition.

A 78-mile electric range is compelling on paper, but the complete ownership calculation will depend on how rapidly the battery can be replenished, what the vehicles cost relative to conventional hybrids and full EVs, and whether the additional technology changes cargo capacity or curb weight in meaningful ways.

Volvo also says both the XC60 and XC90 will continue to be offered as mild hybrids, preserving a less electrified option for buyers who cannot or do not want to plug in.

The company plans regular over-the-air software updates for the two vehicles, another sign that software capability is becoming part of long-term vehicle ownership rather than something fixed at purchase.

For the broader market, however, the most important number remains the electric range.

A decade ago, a plug-in hybrid with enough battery capacity for more than 70 miles of electric driving would have occupied unusual territory. Today Volvo believes that formula may be one of the most practical ways to keep customers moving toward electrification.

The result is not quite an electric vehicle and not quite a traditional hybrid. For a significant group of American drivers, that may be precisely the point.

text:
FOR IMMEDIATE RELEASE September 22, 2026

PUBLIC HEALTH AND SAFETY EXPERTS URGE CONGRESS TO PASS BIPARTISAN ASBESTOS BAN AT 20TH CONGRESSIONAL BRIEFING

Speakers Connect Health, Legacy Exposure, Law, and First Responder Risk

WASHINGTON, DC — The Asbestos Disease Awareness Organization (ADAO), an independent nonprofit dedicated to preventing asbestos exposure through education, advocacy, and community initiatives, today held its 20th Congressional Staff Briefing, “Impact of Asbestos on Public Health, Environment, and Economy,” in the Capitol Visitor Center, sponsored by Senator Jeff Merkley (D-OR). A bipartisan group of congressional staffers attended the briefing, which took place during Mesothelioma Awareness Month.

Despite being a known carcinogen linked to more than 40,000 preventable deaths in the United States every year, asbestos remains legal and lethal in America. Speakers used the briefing to ask congressional offices to cosponsor the Alan Reinstein Ban Asbestos Now (ARBAN) Act, a comprehensive asbestos ban bill.

“Congress has a duty to protect the public health and safety of Americans and end the decades of unnecessary suffering and death caused by asbestos, a deadly carcinogen,” said Linda Reinstein, President and Cofounder of ADAO. “There is no safe or controlled use of this dangerous substance, and safer alternatives are readily available.”

Senators Merkley and John Curtis (R-UT) introduced the ARBAN Act of 2026 (S. 5235) on August 4, 2026, and the bill has since been referred to the Senate Committee on Environment and Public Works. Representatives Suzanne Bonamici (D-OR) and Don Bacon (R-NE) lead the House companion, H.R. 5373. The legislation would amend the Toxic Substances Control Act to ban all six asbestos fibers (chrysotile, crocidolite, amosite, anthophyllite, tremolite, and actinolite) along with Libby Amphibole asbestos. It would be a statutory ban that, unlike any regulatory rule, could not be reversed by a future administration.

The briefing featured the following experts:

Brent Kynoch, Managing Director, Environmental Information Association

Linda Reinstein, President and Cofounder, Asbestos Disease Awareness Organization

Greg Russell, Legislative Director, Federal Fire Fighters Joint Council, International Association of Fire Fighters

Bob Sussman, JD, Counsel for the Asbestos Disease Awareness Organization

The speakers discussed:

Health effects of asbestos exposure, including mesothelioma, lung, ovarian, and laryngeal cancers, and asbestosis, which can appear decades after exposure. All six fibers are carcinogenic.

Legacy asbestos in homes, schools, workplaces, and public buildings, and the exposure risk when renovation, demolition, fire, or disaster disturbs it

Regulatory updates, including the EPA Part 1 Chrysotile Asbestos Final Rule, the final Part 2 Legacy Asbestos Risk Evaluation, and the pending Part 2 risk management rule

Risks to firefighters and first responders, and the continuing health consequences 25 years after the September 11 attacks

The Alan Reinstein Ban Asbestos Now Act (S. 5235 and H.R. 5373), a comprehensive commercial asbestos ban

According to the U.S. Geological Survey’s 2026 Mineral Commodity Summaries, the United States imported no raw asbestos fiber from 2023 through 2025. The chlor-alkali industry, the only remaining domestic consumer, used an estimated 50 metric tons from stockpiles in 2025. EPA’s 2024 Part 1 chrysotile asbestos rule is under agency review while the agency has said its plans to propose its Part 2 risk management rule for legacy asbestos by June 3, 2027.

“ADAO supports completing strong EPA action on asbestos and enactment of the Alan Reinstein Ban Asbestos Now Act,” Reinstein said. “Nearly 70 countries have already banned asbestos. Prevention is the thread that connects every part of this problem and that is what we want every member of Congress and their staff to understand.”

Following the briefing, ADAO will host its 21st Annual Asbestos Awareness and Prevention Conference, “Asbestos: Awareness, Prevention, and the Law,” on September 25 and 26, 2026, at the AC Hotel Arlington National Landing in Arlington, Virginia. Staffers and lawmakers are invited.

Visit the 20th Staff Briefing page for more details on the briefing and speakers.

text:
49 global cities representing over 110 million people now back the Global Urban Data Centres Pact

C40 brings finance, city and community leaders together to cooperate on responsible AI and digital infrastructure

US mayors are leading the push for data centres that work for people and planet, with 22 US cities endorsing the Pact.

GRESB, Climate Bonds Initiative and NAACP Center for Environmental and Climate Justice are latest groups to support C40 mayors’ principles for what good data centres should look like

Phoenix Mayor Kate Gallego says that C40 Pact “creates greater certainty” for investors, developers and communities

New York, USA (22 September 2026) – Cities are spearheading a global push to ensure the next generation of data centres is cleaner, more efficient, and delivers benefits for the communities that host them.

As political leaders and policy makers, mayors are integral to data centre development. As New York Climate Week gets into full swing, C40 mayors are urging industry to support the Global Urban Data Centre Pact to ensure certainty, sustainability and local community benefits in AI and digital infrastructure investment and construction.

This New York Climate Week C40’s mayors are bringing together finance experts and business leaders to discuss the Pact’s call for sustainable AI and digital infrastructure development in cities. The dialogue comes as public concern over the rapid expansion of data centres and their impact on communities and natural resources grows across the world

US cities now make up nearly half the endorsers (22 out of 49 cities) of the Global Urban Data Centres Pact, a mayor-led initiative, co-founded by Mayor Kate Gallego of Phoenix and Melbourne’s Lord Mayor Nick Reece, that sets out clear expectations for responsible data centre development.

Whilst the US is experiencing a period of concentrated data centre growth, the Pact has been endorsed by cities on every continent, representing more than 110 million people. All signatories agree that it is time to move beyond data centres that threaten to spike energy costs, increase emissions and pollution, create health and safety risks for residents, and use critical water resources.

Climate Mayors and America Is All In support these efforts as organizational partners, and wider official support for the Pact has also come from GRESB, Climate Bonds Initiative and NAACP Center for Environmental and Climate Justice.

New developments must be designed around the needs of the communities that host them. This means protecting water supplies, avoiding unnecessary pressure on energy bills and power grids, using resources efficiently and delivering tangible local benefits.

The Pact, launched at London Climate Action Week in June, recognizes that mayors and city leaders, as those closest to residents’ concerns, must be empowered to act on a cleaner future for this essential infrastructure. The Pact brings together approaches already being pioneered by cities and sets four principles for future developments. These are that data centres should be:

strategically integrated into cities;

sustainable and resource efficient;

developed with and for local communities;

focused on driving down residents’ costs and delivering shared prosperity

That challenge is particularly urgent in the US, where opposition to new data centres is growing. Recent polling highlights that 79% of Americans are either skeptical or critical of data centres. Yet, if clean energy is integrated into data centres, net support increases from -33% to +16%. The rapid growth and low regulation of the industry has led some local governments to instigate temporary moratoriums while they decide how further development should proceed.

The principles of the Pact allow cities to agree with developers and investors on what a responsible and sustainable future looks like.

Clear standards can also provide greater certainty for investors. Setting expectations early can help capital flow towards sustainable projects that are more likely to get approved by cities, rather than dirty data centres that do not align with the Pact.

US mayors and city leaders met with investors, lenders and industry representatives in New York this week to discuss how the financial community can help deliver the next generation of digital infrastructure and leverage principles for long-term sustainability to build community trust and reduce exposure to material risks.

The meeting, co-hosted by C40 Cities and sustainable benchmarking organisation GRESB, brought together US cities, real asset investors, mission-driven investors, asset managers, commercial lenders and developers to discuss approaches to identify, mitigate, and finance solutions to the socio-environmental risks of data centre expansion, and make sure data centres generate shared value for both local communities and shareholders.

Kate Gallego, Mayor of Phoenix and C40 Cities Vice Chair, said: “US cities are at the forefront of defining the next era of digital growth and urban development. It’s essential that we work to ensure our cities, and our peers around the world, establish a standard for how our residents get the benefits of the AI and digital economy while protecting the communities that make that growth possible.

“Phoenix has seen first-hand the opportunities that come with investment in clean technology, advanced manufacturing, and 21st century infrastructure, but growth has to be managed responsibly. Our residents expect infrastructure to keep pace, health and safety to be prioritized, resources to be used wisely, and local communities to share in the benefits.

“The Pact offers a clear framework for collaboration among cities, investors and industry. By setting expectations now, we can create greater certainty for responsible investment and support innovation that strengthens our economies and improves quality of life.”

Brandon Johnson, Mayor of Chicago, said: “As data centers continue to expand across the country, mayors have both an opportunity and a responsibility to shape the growth of the industry and ensure new infrastructure is developed responsibly, transparently and safely.

“Establishing clear standards on critical issues, from air quality to energy use, will give industry the clarity it needs to plan and invest responsibly while giving communities confidence that new development will protect their well-being and deliver meaningful benefits.

“The Pact is a vital tool for cities, investors and industry to unite around a shared vision for responsible growth. The City of Chicago is proud to be part of the Pact and to put its principles into action by developing robust regulatory standards for data center development. Working with partners in industry, finance, academia and government, both locally and globally, we can build a future with clean energy, clean air and shared prosperity.”

Kate Johnson, C40 Cities Director for North America, said: “Mayors are showing global leadership on one of the defining infrastructure challenges of the AI age. They recognize the potential economic benefits of data centers, but they also know that dirty, inefficient developments which damage communities cannot be the future.

“But instead of closing the door on data centers, they’re raising the bar. Where cities have paused development, now is the moment for mayors, investors and industry to agree on the rules that allow the right projects to go ahead but only if they work for communities and the planet.

“When those pauses end, we want investment flowing into cleaner, more efficient data centers that communities can support. The Pact gives cities and investors a practical blueprint for making that happen.”

Chris Pyke, Ph.D., Director, Thought Leadership & Industry Engagement, Global Real Estate Sustainability Benchmark (GRESB), said: “GRESB recognizes the vital role cities play in setting a high bar for data center development. We share the goals of the C40 Global Data Center Pact, including sustainable and resource-efficient data centers that deliver tangible benefits for local communities.

“GRESB’s new Data Center Assessment supports these aspirations with a common language providing transparency and comparability, and, ultimately, building trust among financial stakeholders.”

Sean Kidney, CEO, Climate Bonds Initiative, said: “Cities are on the frontline of the data center boom, from hosting the infrastructure, managing the grid pressure, and bearing the community impacts.

“Climate Bonds Initiative supports the C40 Urban Data Centers Pact because sustainable data center development is not just an engineering challenge; it is a finance challenge.

“Getting the criteria right is how we ensure the capital flowing into this sector drives genuine climate action rather than greenwashing. We are proud to support this initiative and the ambition it represents”.

text:
Scientific evidence continues to make clear that the climate crisis is accelerating. The past few years have been the hottest on record, reaching surface temperatures of 1.44°C above the 1850 to 1900 average. Extreme weather events such as massive wildfires, drought, and flooding continue to upend lives as a result.

And yet 50 energy utilities in the United States are failing to transition off of fossil fuels—the primary driver of the climate crisis—toward clean energy sources, despite the clear evidence that change is needed, according to the Sierra Club's 2026 Dirty Truth report, released today.

The report gave the parent companies, which own 76 individual operations, an all-time-low score of seven out of 100 for their plans to transition from coal and gas to clean energy: wind, solar, and storage. This was the largest single-year drop since the Sierra Club started tracking. The score is eight points lower than last year's, and 11 points lower than that in the 2021 inaugural report.

“This year’s results were pretty alarming overall,” said Emma Pabst, a campaign manager for the Sierra Club’s Beyond Coal campaign and a study author.

Researchers graded companies based on their plans to retire coal by 2030 as of July 1. They also investigated their green energy strategy, including how they will build clean energy to replace fossil generation and meet energy demand without developing new gas plants throughout the next 10 years. The consensus was that companies are not moving toward green energy as quickly as they should.

“This is the science-aligned target,” said Noah Ver Beek, a senior energy campaigns analyst with the Beyond Coal campaign and one of the report’s authors. “It’s what basically every study and the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change says needs to happen in developed economies in order to stay on track with our climate targets.”

Hitting the snooze button on clean energy isn’t simply impacting our planet. It contributes to a slew of problems, including health and affordability issues. Households are having to pay higher rates for electricity. This trend, called energy burden, is affecting Americans disproportionately across the country, with people of color especially impacted. Even though clean energy is cheaper than what coal plants produce, utility companies refuse to fully unplug.

“Coal is the dirtiest and often the most expensive way to generate power, so we want utilities to be retiring those plants by 2030 at the latest,” Ver Beek said.

As of 2022, coal and gas were contributing between 45 and 53 percent of carbon emissions, according to the US Energy Information Administration. Fossil fuel emissions then drive rising temperatures and widespread global issues of extreme weather and marine heat waves, which are wreaking havoc on our ecosystems and populations.

The demand for energy

The energy appetite is largely connected to the hungry expansion of data centers and artificial intelligence, which is placing pressure on utility companies to meet energy demands, known as load growth. Rhodium Group, an independent think tank, estimates energy demand could push to 338 percent by 2030 because of data centers under a high-growth scenario. Some projections are even higher, according to the report.

But Pabst said that these companies could avoid relying on coal and gas for quick power generation if they took the time to look for greener sources like wind and solar. “Their failure to plan, combined with unprecedented load growth, is hitting us,” she said.

While nearly half of utilities have improved their clean energy scores, replacing 25 percent of fossil fuel production and leading to a reduction of costs in clean energy since the first report, many companies still stubbornly depend on coal and gas.

“This is also the consequence of an administration that is actively pushing for infrastructure that is harming people's wallets and health."

Effects of coal and gas

Gas is volatile and expensive. Eighty percent of companies continue to guzzle it for energy demand, according to the report. This year, utilities proposed 140 gigawatts of new gas capacity—more than in any previous report. The study found that 28 companies are pushing for more gas production than they need to meet demands through this decade. One company, Alabama Power, is planning to generate more than seven times what it needs through 2035. If these companies continue with that approach, it would increase current gas capacity by 25 percent nationwide, which is more than two and a half times the amount of gas utilities planned in the first report.

With coal, 60 percent of utilities made no improvement in their scores. While they plan to retire 25 percent of their generation by 2030, this falls short of what is needed economically. Pumping the brakes on coal would help reduce emissions and expenses—since 2015, companies could save $1 billion to $2 billion a year by avoiding coal—and devastating health impacts. One company’s coal-burning power plant, Ameren’s Labadie in Missouri, has been associated with the most premature deaths per year (315). Built in the 1970s, it lacks modern pollution controls. Coal-burning power plants are often correlated to increased mortality rates and significant health risks such as premature death, heart attacks, lung cancer, dementia, and Alzheimer's disease. Despite these facts, the report found that energy companies are planning for 75 percent of their remaining coal generation to be online beyond 2030, even as the costs climb and health implications mount.

“This is also the consequence of an administration that is actively pushing for infrastructure that is harming people's wallets and health,” Ver Beek said.

Under President Donald Trump, the One Big Beautiful Bill Act curtailed many of the clean energy incentives from the Biden-era 2022 Inflation Reduction Act. The Environmental Protection Agency also scrapped its emission regulations for power plants, and individual companies postponed closures. The report found that Georgia Power asked the Georgia Public Service Commission in 2022 to retire Plant Scherer’s Unit 3 and Plant Bowen’s Units 1 and 2 by 2028. But the utility is now extending the life of all three coal-burning units for the foreseeable future.

The Dirty Truth report finds that utilities can still meet load growth without new gas, but it will require planning and incentives, and public comment.

“Utilities listen to public pressure,” said Ver Beek. “People have the opportunity, and we have the technologies that we need to build that future, to achieve the goal of 100 percent clean energy by 2035.”

title: Google, Georgia Power Have Deal to Support Nuclear Power Plant Uprates
description:
Electric utility Georgia Power and tech giant Google said the companies have an agreement under which Google will support power uprates at two of the utility’s nuclear power plants.
The deal, which must be approved by the Georgia Public Service Commission (PSC), involves extended power uprates for units at Plant Vogtle and Plant Hatch that are owned by Georgia Power.
Georgia Power, which serves 2.8-million customers in Georgia, said that Hatch and Vogtle provide about a quarter of the electricity used in the state.
Google earlier in September signed its first international nuclear deal, a $15.1-billion agreement with Fortum, a Finland-based utility.
The company said it would buy up to 50% of the electricity from the Loviisa nuclear plant over a 22-year period to support at least three data centers in Finland.
text:
Electric utility Georgia Power and tech giant Google said the companies have an agreement under which Google will support power uprates at two of the utility’s nuclear power plants. The groups on September 21 said the moves would add some 96 MW of power generation capacity to Georgia’s power grid.

The deal, which must be approved by the Georgia Public Service Commission (PSC), involves extended power uprates for units at Plant Vogtle and Plant Hatch that are owned by Georgia Power. The utility filed documents Monday with the state PSC that include a new nuclear uprate tariff structure, along with a request to approve an extended power uprate (EPU) for Units 1 and 2 at Hatch, located in Baxley about 200 miles southeast of Atlanta. An EPU for Units 1 and 2 at Vogtle, located near Waynesboro, just more than 150 miles east of Atlanta, was approved by the PSC as part of Georgia Power’s 2025 Integrated Resource Plan. The utility on Monday said the deal could generate about $900 million in benefits for its customers over the life of the units.

Google, under a subscription-based program, will subscribe to the new NU-1 tariff and receive zero-emission credits, which represent the carbon-free attributes of nuclear energy associated with the power generated by the nuclear unit uprates.

“Many of our large customers have specific clean energy goals, and we continue to work with the Georgia PSC to create programs that not only help them meet their goals, but align with our Customer Protection Pledge, enhancing the reliability and resiliency of the power grid and creating savings for all customers,” said Aaron Mitchell, senior vice president of Strategic Growth for Georgia Power. “We appreciate Google’s continued leadership in this space and partnership in developing this program, which we see as the latest example of how large-load growth can benefit all electric customers.”

“Google data centers are long-term investments in the communities we call home, catalyzing local economic development and accelerating clean energy deployment. They also serve as a proof point for how we can unlock the significant opportunity to bring online new nuclear power through expanding the capacity of the existing nuclear fleet,” said Lucia Tian, director, Advanced Energy Technologies, at Google. “This collaboration with Georgia Power ensures that digital infrastructure growth goes hand-in-hand with positive local impact, helping to deliver hundreds of millions of dollars in direct customer benefits and supporting a more affordable, clean, and reliable energy system for all Georgia residents.”

The utility said that EPUs increase the electrical output of nuclear power generating units through modifications to equipment such as turbines, pumps, motors, and cooling systems. The work enables nuclear reactors to operate at higher licensed thermal power levels, producing additional heat that increases steam flow to the turbine generator. The unit then generates more electricity while continuing to utilize the existing reactor fuel design and plant infrastructure.

Georgia Power, which serves 2.8-million customers in Georgia, said that Hatch and Vogtle provide about a quarter of the electricity used in the state. The plants are managed by Southern Nuclear, a sister company owned by Southern Co. that specializes in nuclear operations.

Google earlier in September signed its first international nuclear deal, a $15.1-billion agreement with Fortum, a Finland-based utility. The company said it would buy up to 50% of the electricity from the Loviisa nuclear plant over a 22-year period to support at least three data centers in Finland.

title: Inequality and the (Climate) Preference–Behavior Gap | United Nations University
description:
The project investigates whether and through which mechanisms inequality shapes preferences for climate policies and climate behavior.
We show that the exposure to inequality increases support for green climate policies but decreases the willingness to take actions against climate change.
This puzzle seems to be explained by the fact that inequality shapes these outcomes through different trajectories.
For climate policy preferences, our findings show that participants exposed to inequality clearly identified the wealthy individuals and the government as responsible for environmental problems while also shows an increase in moral universalism.
In contrast, for climate-related behaviour, mediators play a limited role, while inequality has a direct effect on the willingness to take action against climate change.
text:
Funded by: ST4TE, a Horizon 2020 programme.

The project investigates whether and through which mechanisms inequality shapes preferences for climate policies and climate behavior. We address this question by designing and implementing a large-scale online experiment (nearly 5,000 participants) across five European countries (France, Germany, Italy, Spain, and the United Kingdom). We show that the exposure to inequality increases support for green climate policies but decreases the willingness to take actions against climate change. Specifically, participants exposed to inequality are more in favour of introducing a flying tax and a green climate fund to finance clean energy in low-income countries but they are less willing contribute time and effort toward the collective goal of environmental protection. This puzzle seems to be explained by the fact that inequality shapes these outcomes through different trajectories. For climate policy preferences, our findings show that participants exposed to inequality clearly identified the wealthy individuals and the government as responsible for environmental problems while also shows an increase in moral universalism. In contrast, for climate-related behaviour, mediators play a limited role, while inequality has a direct effect on the willingness to take action against climate change. Overall, these results have important policy implications, as rising disparities may influence the social foundations necessary for the design and implementation of effective climate action.

Key takeaways Small modular reactors, SMRs for short, could profitably integrate into the U.S. industrial sector, but they fail to compete with wholesale electricity prices in the power sector.

text:
Key takeaways

Small modular reactors, SMRs for short, could profitably integrate into the U.S. industrial sector, but they fail to compete with wholesale electricity prices in the power sector.

SMR success hinges on the Hydrogen Production Tax Credit. If used for heat processing and hydrogen production, SMRs could reduce U.S. industrial carbon emissions by 8% in the first wave of construction and 14% in the second wave.

The study is a collaboration between University of Michigan Engineering and the U-M School of Environment and Sustainability.

A technoeconomic assessment of small modular reactor development across the United States suggests stakeholders should shift focus from the power sector to industry, according to a University of Michigan Engineering and School of Environment and Sustainability study published in Nature Communications. The research was funded by Idaho National Laboratory.

Known as SMRs for short, the compact nuclear reactors are built off-site in factories and assembled on-site, providing flexible energy and hydrogen generation at a lower capital investment. Dozens of reactor designs are in progress, but none have been built for commercial use, and pathways for early scale-up remain uncertain.

The research team explored potential pathways and formulated a roadmap for commercially viable SMR deployment in the U.S. across electricity, industrial heat and hydrogen applications using site-specific needs. The roadmap evaluates economic performance, decarbonization potential and sensitivity to ballooning capital costs.

The Hydrogen Production Tax Credit, part of the Inflation Reduction Act of 2022, is crucial to SMR success. With the credit in place, producing hydrogen for use in ammonia, steel and refining is the most profitable path forward for SMRs. This would help the U.S. industrial sector gain independence from foreign oil and gas imports and build protection against fossil fuel price volatility—all while creating skilled jobs and reducing carbon emissions.

“This work can advise investors, companies and business leaders on where to deploy SMRs to maximize profits. It can also inform the federal government on effective policy tools for supporting increased deployment of nuclear energy,” said Brendan Kochunas, an associate professor of nuclear engineering and radiological sciences at U-M and co-author of the study.

The Hydrogen Production Tax Credit

The research team built an optimization model to find the number and type of SMRs needed to economically meet energy demands for 34 ammonia plants, 9 steel plants, 47 refineries and 955 industrial facilities that use process heat. A second model optimized cost-effective SMR dispatch in a wholesale electricity market.

“There’s a lot of momentum around increased deployment of nuclear energy and small modular reactors, but this study provides the first comprehensive analysis of where it actually makes business sense to build and operate them,” said Kochunas.

Running these models with and without the Hydrogen Production Tax Credit, which pays up to $3 per kilogram of clean hydrogen produced, revealed how this incentive could enable much broader deployment of SMRs, and sharper reductions in carbon emissions.

With the tax credit active, SMRs could produce 91 gigawatt-electric (GWe) during the first wave of construction while turning a profit, compared to just 4 GWe without it. In a second wave, when mass production could further reduce construction costs by about 20%, the tax credit would yield 171.9 GWe capacity, but deployment without the credit would only reach 7.8 GWe. For scale, 171.9 GWe is 1.8 times the current U.S. nuclear capacity.

“Our findings offer actionable insights for policy-makers to both restart nuclear infrastructure deployment in the U.S. and decarbonize one of the highest emitting industrial sectors,” said Marisol Garrouste, a doctoral graduate of nuclear engineering and radiological sciences at U-M, current Research Engineer at Électricité de France and lead author of the study.

High profit margins for ammonia and refining

Using SMRs to produce hydrogen—by supplying the high heat and electricity needed to split water molecules—proved the most lucrative. Process hydrogen for ammonia projected 300% profit margins while most refining sites had margins above 50% and steel around 20%.

Of the facilities that use process heat, only a handful had positive profit margins, and most were less than 10%. Ammonia and refining’s high margins make them the most resilient to cost increases that could run a project over budget.

SMRs do not seem able to outcompete renewables or large light water reactors, like the AP1000, when it comes to existing wholesale electricity market prices in the power sector. This limits the path forward for SMRs without subsidies or major construction cost reductions.

The U.S. industrial sector emitted 1,360 million metric tons of CO2 in 2020. If SMRs were incorporated into the sectors listed above, the researchers project they could reduce U.S. industrial carbon emissions by 8% in the first wave and 14% in the second wave of construction.

“It is common for new technologies to find early success in niche markets. By incentivizing SMR deployment for industrial applications, the tax credit would not only accelerate decarbonization in a hard-to-abate sector, but provide a proof of concept and ideally bring down the cost of SMRs such that they are more competitive in the power sector in the future,” said Jessica Lovering, a sponsored affiliate of nuclear engineering and radiological sciences at U-M and a postdoctoral researcher at Uppsala University in Sweden.

Michael Craig and Max Vanatta of the University of Michigan School of Environment and Sustainability also contributed to this study. This research was supported by the Idaho National Laboratory (contract no. F067620).

text:
US-based New Era Energy & Digital, through its subsidiary TCDC PowerCo, has entered into a 20-year power purchase agreement (PPA) with Luminant ET Services, an affiliate of Vistra.

The contract will see Luminant supply a minimum of 200MW and up to 207MW of electricity for phase one of New Era’s Texas Critical Data Center (TCDC) project near Odessa, Texas.

Under the agreement, Luminant will deliver power from Vistra’s 1.18GW natural gas-fired facility, which is adjacent to the planned data centre site.

The firm supply is scheduled to be available starting in the third quarter of 2027.

The contract contains automatic one-year renewal periods after the initial 20-year term, provided neither party opts out.

According to New Era, the agreement is intended to secure power for the first phase of its data centre project and support its long-term development plans.

New Era chairman and CEO Charlie Nelson said: “Having firm, contracted power for Phase 1 in New Era’s name is an incredible milestone, which we believe materially reduces Phase 1 development risk at TCDC.

“With the land secured, construction permits in hand, Phase 1 power contracted for 20 years and room to expand to multiple phases, we believe this is an attractive opportunity to any quality tenant currently in the market.”

Luminant’s obligations under the new PPA are contingent upon several conditions, including New Era’s provision of credit support.

This includes a letter of credit for $116m to be posted within 15 business days and additional security up to $82.8m before the delivery date.

The contract also contains standard terms including events of default, force majeure provisions, indemnification and insurance requirements.

In a concurrent move, New Era and Vistra signed a development framework agreement to explore future power development at the Odessa site and other locations.

The agreement gives Vistra a 5% non-voting equity interest in the project segment it supplies. It also grants Vistra a right of first refusal for future on-site power expansion and a right of first offer for certain future projects over the next five years.

Vistra corporate development and strategy senior vice-president Claudia Morrow said: “We are pleased to work with New Era on a long-term power arrangement for the TCDC project and to establish a framework that allows us to evaluate additional power opportunities together over time.”

New Era’s obligations also include reimbursing Vistra for certain construction costs related to substations and transmission lines, subject to further agreements.

text:
A series of investments, partnerships and projects have helped cut carbon emissions, increase recycling, create opportunities for future employment and protect the borough's natural environment.

One of the year's standout successes has been the launch of Renew North Tyneside, a new reuse shop created in partnership with SUEZ and North Tyneside Big Local. Since opening in March, the shop has sold more than 30,000 preloved household items, giving unwanted goods a second life, reducing waste and helping residents access affordable items for their homes.

Supporting the region's growing green economy has also been a key priority. We worked closely with Newcastle College and Shepherd Offshore to secure £8.9 million from the North East Innovation Zone to expand the Energy Academy in Wallsend and almost treble its capacity, taking it to over 1,000 learners in 5 years.

We also continued to make significant progress in reducing our carbon footprint. Our programme to convert all street lighting to LED technology is now in its final phase and, once complete, is expected to cut energy consumption by 74%, reducing both emissions and costs.

A range of heat decarbonisation projects across council buildings has further improved energy efficiency and supported progress towards net zero ambitions.

Residents have benefited from improved recycling services, with more materials now accepted for recycling and a programme of community recycling and waste events encouraging more people to reuse and recycle.

Investment in sustainable transport has also continued through the completion of the Sea Front Sustainable Route, linking Tynemouth and Whitley Bay. Delivered through external funding and partnerships with Active Travel England, Walk Wheel Cycle Trust and Capita, the route is encouraging more walking, wheeling and cycling along the coast.

We also strengthened our commitment to nature recovery and biodiversity. Through the North East Community Forest partnership, £73,000 was secured to plant 1,351 trees across the borough during 2025/26.

Further environmental improvements have been delivered through Section 106 funding, supporting projects including sand dune restoration in Tynemouth, woodland management at Rising Sun Country Park and habitat creation in Wallsend Dene.

Councillor Willie Samuel, Cabinet Member responsible for Environmental Sustainability, said:

"This has been a landmark year for environmental sustainability in North Tyneside, but also for the opportunities we're creating for local people.

"The success of Renew North Tyneside shows how small changes can make a big impact, preventing thousands of items from going to waste while helping residents access affordable goods.

"At the same time, our investment in the Energy Academy will help equip local people with the skills needed for the clean energy jobs of the future, ensuring North Tyneside is well placed to benefit from the growth of this sector.

"Alongside this, we've continued to reduce emissions, improve recycling services, invest in active travel and protect our natural environment. Together, these projects are helping us build a cleaner, greener and more sustainable borough for future generations.

“Contrary to what is often said, cutting our carbon footprint is also about cutting costs and by going green we are saving money in a number of ways.”

The achievements form part of our ongoing commitment to environmental sustainability and its ambition to create a cleaner, healthier and more resilient North Tyneside.

title: The Grassroots Revolt Against Pollution Is Growing | Opinion - Newsweek
description:
Holding polluters accountable is far more likely to mobilize people than tax credits for clean energy.
According to a recent analysis by BloombergNEF, proposed new data centers would increase pollution from electricity by 20 percent.
The fact that AI is driving a dirty gas boom is confusing, since market observers note that clean energy is cheaper than fossil-powered electricity.
Turns out, clean energy doesn’t have much of a cost advantage in a world without environmental regulations.
Though we sometimes struggle to build public goods like highways and affordable housing, we have no problem letting corporations build, build, build.
text:
We are in the midst of a widespread uprising of grassroots activism, from the data center rebellion sweeping the country, to Iowa where cancer is the number one issue this election cycle, to residents of Corpus Christi pushing back against industry’s rapacious use of water during a drought. The Trump administration is trying to squelch this activism, announcing recently that they are limiting public comment on new sources of pollution. But, thankfully, Americans across the political spectrum are saying yes—yes to clean air and water, safe food and local control—and an emphatic no to decisions that put their health, their neighborhoods and their livelihoods at risk.

Election day is coming quickly. If you’re a politician of either party, remember that voters and nonvoters alike value their health and safety. Environmental regulations are popular, corporations are not. If you’re a professional climate advocate, as I am, there’s an important lesson in what’s happening across the country—and in what didn’t happen to defend Biden’s signature climate achievement, the Inflation Reduction Act. Holding polluters accountable is far more likely to mobilize people than tax credits for clean energy.

Unfortunately, this cross-partisan revolt has not yet stopped what is happening in Washington. Under President Donald Trump, the Environmental Protection Agency's (EPA’s) agenda has shifted away from a mandate to protect the environment to now, “unleash energy dominance, bring back American auto jobs, pursue permitting reform and make America the AI capital of the world.” The White House has eviscerated protective regulations, abandoned enforcement of the regulations that remain and, under the guise of an "energy emergency," specifically accelerated the permitting of new infrastructure for data centers and the oil and gas industry—including the largest gas-fired power plant ever and a massive gas export terminal.

Read More on Opinion

The scale of what’s happening is too much to comprehend. Have you heard that the federal government recently approved testing mirrors in space that will direct more sunlight to specific locations to improve farm productivity and make it easier for construction workers to build at night time? No environmental review required. Too much to comprehend.

Back here on earth, EPA recently decided that massive private energy grids do not need to comply with a decades-long component of the Clean Air Act, unlike traditional power plants. According to a recent analysis by BloombergNEF, proposed new data centers would increase pollution from electricity by 20 percent. The fact that AI is driving a dirty gas boom is confusing, since market observers note that clean energy is cheaper than fossil-powered electricity. Turns out, clean energy doesn’t have much of a cost advantage in a world without environmental regulations.

Even after notching these victories, polluters are still asking for more. They are pushing Congress for what is euphemistically called "permitting reform" but is really a way to permanently weaken environmental laws and limit opportunities for people to push back on new sources of toxic emissions that contaminate our air and water.

This deregulatory agenda is unpopular, but also highly technical and confusing. Among Trump’s base, for example, two-thirds of conservatives believe EPA should prioritize protecting people’s health from toxic chemicals and pollution, even if it means higher costs. But most people aren’t even aware that Trump is weakening protective regulations. Since it’s hard to feel like you can influence the outcome in Washington, why bother?

Americans are paying close attention to what’s happening at home. They are investing their time and money to protect themselves. Political analysts have noted the Make America Healthy Again (MAHA) movement, motivated by concern about threats from pesticides like glyphosate and forever chemicals like PFAS, but that is just a small part of what’s happening.

People are showing up at public hearings across the country to say how important their environment is to them. And they are winning much of the time, through litigation, local zoning challenges and by passing moratoria against data centers in more than 500 communities. By stopping $130 billion of data center projects in the first quarter of 2026, local activists—from both parties—had almost as much success as they had in the previous year.

People are also punishing politicians. Given the breadth of public opposition, two remarkably different politicians—New York Governor Kathy Hochul and Texas Governor Greg Abbott—recently made a big show of hitting the pause button on new data centers. Both of these "moratoria" were likely crafted with significant behind-the-scenes input from industry and are deeply flawed: NY’s may eventually lead to a reduction in required environmental review, while Texas’ may drive data centers to weakly regulated private grids. But both governors felt the need to do something.

I am in awe of the power of "small d" democratic engagement by people throughout the country. If you are fighting a dirty data center, a toxic industrial farm, or any other polluting factory that is receiving special dispensation from the federal government right now—thank you.

As politicians keep telling us, America is a nation that builds. Though we sometimes struggle to build public goods like highways and affordable housing, we have no problem letting corporations build, build, build. Corporations have built massive new infrastructure to allow the United States to become the world’s largest exporter of gas and gasoline, as well as the largest producer of both oil and gas. Their appetite is insatiable: They want to keep building more, regardless of the harm they cause.

Instead, let’s tell our politicians that we want to rebuild our health, safety and environmental regulations. Those of us who work in politics every day should recognize the remarkable opportunity to rebuild the environmental movement around the pro-people activism emerging across the country. We can help politicians respond to what people care about: reducing pollution. We can draw connections between what happens at home, in our nation’s capital and what happens around the world. In partnership with grassroots activists, we can build a stronger foundation that gives the American people the freedom to build lives of health and prosperity.

title: Did the Sun Set Last Week on Suncor's Clean Air Act Preemption Theory?
description:
The oil companies, backed by the Department of Justice (DOJ) as amicus curiae, contend Boulder’s claims for compensation are preempted by, among other things, the Clean Air Act.
This post deals only with their Clean Air Act theory.
But the brief goes on to infer, wrongly, that EPA’s Clean Air Act authority to regulate those emissions preempts Boulder’s state-law claims for damages.
Monetary compensation is something the Clean Air Act simply does not address, let alone preclude.
The oil companies try to flip the script by claiming suits like Boulder’s are barred unless the Clean Air Act affirmatively authorizes them.
text:
When the Supreme Court hears arguments October 5th in Suncor Energy v. County Commissioners of Boulder, the oil companies will argue that municipalities cannot pursue state-law claims for damages caused by the marketing of fossil fuels. Boulder seeks to prove that it has suffered damages from the defendant companies’ contribution to extreme heat, storms, wildfires, and other harmful effects of climate change. The oil companies, backed by the Department of Justice (DOJ) as amicus curiae, contend Boulder’s claims for compensation are preempted by, among other things, the Clean Air Act.

Boulder has solid rebuttals to all of its opponents’ preemption arguments. This post deals only with their Clean Air Act theory. It shows how recent actions of the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) disclaiming any statutory authority to regulate climate-changing pollution have radically undermined that theory.

Relying on Supreme Court precedent in climate change cases, DOJ’s Suncor brief argues that the Clean Air Act gives EPA statutory authority to regulate greenhouse gas pollution at the federal level. Right so far. But the brief goes on to infer, wrongly, that EPA’s Clean Air Act authority to regulate those emissions preempts Boulder’s state-law claims for damages.

DOJ’s preemption theory is rickety enough on the correct understanding that EPA has statutory authority to regulate. But EPA has just thrown DOJ a big curve ball.

Last week EPA proposed to find that it has no authority under Section 111 of the Clean Air Act to regulate climate-changing emissions from power plants. That proposal comes atop a final EPA rule issued in February taking the same position under Section 202 of the Act regarding motor vehicles’ climate pollution. See 91 Fed. Reg. 59002 (Sept. 17, 2026); 91 Fed. Reg. 7686 (Feb. 18, 2026).

A broad coalition of states, public health and environmental groups, and industries is challenging EPA’s February action in the D.C. Circuit and will do the same in comments on last week’s proposal. But taking EPA’s current position at face value, if the Clean Air Act gives EPA no such regulatory authority, then DOJ’s already shaky statutory preemption theory in Suncor collapses entirely.

Let’s walk through the government’s statutory preemption theory first on DOJ’s premise that EPA does have Clean Air Act authority to regulate climate-changing emissions, and then consider the impact of EPA’s reversal of position.

DOJ’s brief in Suncor starts from the holding of American Electric Power v. Connecticut, 564 U.S. 410 (2011), that EPA does have authority to curb power plants’ climate pollutants, and this displaces federal common law claims for emissions abatement even if EPA has not exercised that authority. American Electric Power expressly declined to rule on whether that statutory authority preempts state-law claims. That is what the DOJ Suncor brief now argues for.

DOJ’s brief could not entirely avoid the inconvenient fact that EPA had already disclaimed its Clean Air Act authority to regulate climate pollutants from motor vehicles last February. The brief buried this point in a footnote on the last page. It asserts: “But that conclusion about Section [202] does not apply to EPA’s authority under Section [111] to regulate emissions from stationary sources.” Now EPA has knocked the legs out from that footnote, and DOJ’s straddle between vehicles and power plants has become impossible.

This is not the place to explain why the courts will likely reject both EPA actions; you can find good summaries here, here, and here, and in detailed submissions to EPA here and here.

But EPA’s comeuppance will not come before the Supreme Court considers the Suncor case next month. As in Puerto Rico Dept. of Consumer Affairs v. Isla Petroleum Corp., 485 U.S. 495, 504 (1988), EPA’s disclaimer of authority cannot “leave behind a pre-emptive grin without a statutory cat.”

To be clear, Boulder has strong arguments against preemption even if the Court ignores EPA’s disclaimer. Boulder emphasizes that it is seeking damages, not emissions abatement. Monetary compensation is something the Clean Air Act simply does not address, let alone preclude.

In very similar circumstances under the Clean Water Act, the Supreme Court held that “nothing in the Act bars aggrieved individuals from bringing a nuisance claim pursuant to the law of the source State.” International Paper Co. v. Ouellette, 479 U.S. 481, 497 (1987). Boulder argues that the source-state-law proviso should not apply to cases seeking monetary damages, as opposed to emissions reduction. But even if Ouellette’s source-state rule applies here, that case contradicts DOJ’s statutory argument for total preemption.

The oil companies try to flip the script by claiming suits like Boulder’s are barred unless the Clean Air Act affirmatively authorizes them. Neither Ouellette nor any other Supreme Court case supports that novel proposition.

text:
DHL is expanding its global battery logistics network to support the growing electrified value chain, including electric mobility, battery manufacturing, industrial equipment and energy storage systems.

The logistics company is bringing together the capabilities of DHL Supply Chain, DHL Global Forwarding and DHL Express through an integrated network of EV and Battery Centers of Excellence. The network links key stages of the battery and electric vehicle supply chain, covering manufacturing, transportation, warehousing, aftermarket services and battery lifecycle management.

The network currently connects more than 20 sites worldwide, with DHL planning further expansion across key markets to support the continued growth of the battery and electrified mobility sectors.

Growing demand for specialised battery logistics

Growing demand for electric vehicles, battery energy storage systems and renewable energy solutions is creating new supply chains that require specialised handling, regulatory expertise and global coordination. As electrification expands beyond passenger vehicles into industrial equipment, mining and energy infrastructure, logistics operations are becoming increasingly complex, with some battery systems weighing more than 50 tonnes.

These developments are driving demand for advanced battery logistics capabilities across major regions, including Europe, Asia-Pacific, the Americas, the Middle East and Africa.

Francisco Milián, Head of Inbound to Manufacturing, DHL Supply Chain EMEA and member of the DHL New Energy Board, said, "Customers need specialized capabilities throughout the entire battery lifecycle, from inbound logistics and manufacturing support to storage, distribution, refurbishment, returns and recycling. By building a connected global network that combines supply chain and transport expertise, we can bring these capabilities closer to production sites, energy projects and end markets while ensuring the safety, compliance and responsiveness that battery supply chains require."

Christopher Ong, Managing Director Singapore and New Energy Board Member for Express, said, “Through our Heavy Weight Express service and dangerous goods expertise across our global air and intra-European road networks, DHL Express is helping high-energy battery shippers move time-critical shipments reliably between production sites, customers, and end markets. We continue to invest in the network capacity, compliance expertise, and specialized equipment that this fast-growing segment demands across Europe and around the world."

New trade corridors emerge as electrification accelerates

The expansion comes amid significant structural shifts in global trade flows. While much of the world’s battery manufacturing capacity and new-energy production remains concentrated in Asia, demand is growing rapidly across Europe and other markets. The emergence of gigafactories worldwide is also creating demand for logistics services covering capital equipment, raw materials, battery chemicals and finished products.

At the same time, geopolitical uncertainty, energy security concerns and decarbonisation efforts are driving further investment in electrification and renewable energy infrastructure. DHL is supporting customers by developing resilient battery trade corridors linking established manufacturing hubs with emerging gigafactory clusters and energy infrastructure projects across global markets.

Hendrik Venter, Global CEO, DHL Supply Chain, said, “Customers are redesigning global supply chains to support electric mobility, energy storage and renewable energy deployment at scale. As manufacturing, consumption and infrastructure investments evolve across regions, companies need logistics partners capable of connecting markets seamlessly. DHL's global network and cross-divisional expertise enable us to support customers from component manufacturing, transportation, warehousing all the way to aftermarket and circularity solutions."

DHL’s dedicated battery logistics facilities combine specialised warehousing with technical services, including battery diagnostics, testing, charging, conditioning, repairs, reverse logistics and recycling preparation. In Halle, Germany, DHL has recently made 13,000 square metres of battery-ready warehouse capacity available to meet growing customer demand. In Hungary, the company is preparing an additional specialised battery logistics facility, which is expected to become operational in 2027.

Several locations also integrate transportation, customs and cross-border logistics services to provide end-to-end solutions for battery manufacturers, automotive companies and energy providers. Battery logistics is also playing an increasingly important role in mining electrification and critical mineral supply chains, supporting both resource extraction and decarbonisation efforts.

As battery and energy storage supply chains become more complex, customers are increasingly looking for logistics partners that can manage multiple stages of the value chain. Regulatory requirements are also becoming more detailed across national and local jurisdictions, increasing the importance of accurate documentation, dangerous goods handling, customs compliance and classification as key factors in supply-chain competitiveness.

Supporting large-scale energy storage and infrastructure projects

Beyond battery manufacturing and automotive applications, DHL is expanding its logistics support for utility-scale Battery Energy Storage Systems (BESS), grid infrastructure and renewable energy projects, where specialised project logistics and heavy-lift capabilities are increasingly required.

In the first half of 2026, DHL delivered more than 1,100 BESS units worldwide, highlighting the growing demand for specialised logistics solutions as energy storage and renewable energy infrastructure expands.

Martyn Lawns, CEO of DHL Industrial Projects and Senior Vice President of Growth for New Energy at DHL Group, said electrification is creating logistics requirements ranging from global battery supply chains to the deployment of grid-scale energy infrastructure.

He said DHL Global Forwarding and its DHL Industrial Projects unit combine international freight expertise, dangerous goods compliance, project logistics and heavy-lift capabilities to provide integrated solutions. These services cover the movement of battery materials across continents as well as the delivery of energy storage systems to remote project sites, supporting customers as they expand electrification and energy transition projects.

New Energy is one of DHL Group’s designated growth sectors under its Strategy 2030, with the company developing end-to-end logistics solutions through its DHL New Energy Logistics sector brand.

The business covers eight segments: wind, solar, electric vehicles and batteries, Battery Energy Storage Systems (BESS), EV charging, grid infrastructure, hydrogen and alternative fuels. DHL is investing in logistics capabilities across these areas globally to support the evolving energy supply chain.

The Group aims to grow its New Energy business to EUR 3 billion by 2030, driven by increasing investment in electrification, renewable energy, energy storage and resilient energy infrastructure.

Visitors are invited to meet the FSQuality Circuits team at Booth 730 to discuss advanced PCB solutions for electric vehicles, battery-management systems, energy storage, charging infrastructure, power conversion, and other demanding electronic applications.

The Battery Show brings together engineers, technology developers, battery manufacturers, automotive companies, suppliers, and business leaders working to advance battery and electric-vehicle innovation. FSQuality Circuits will use the event to demonstrate how its technical capabilities, expanding Thailand manufacturing operation, and customer-focused engineering support can help companies develop dependable electronics for the rapidly growing electrification market.

Today’s battery and electric-vehicle applications require printed circuit boards capable of operating reliably under demanding electrical, thermal, and environmental conditions. Battery-management systems must monitor voltage, current, temperature, state of charge, and overall battery health with exceptional accuracy. Power electronics, charging systems, converters, inverters, and vehicle-control systems also depend on PCBs that provide reliable signal integrity, thermal performance, current-carrying capacity, and long-term durability.

FSQuality Circuits offers a broad range of PCB technologies supporting these requirements, including multilayer PCBs, high-density interconnect technology, heavy-copper constructions, controlled-impedance boards, advanced thermal-management solutions, and complex high-layer-count products. The company also works closely with customers on stack-up development, material selection, design-for-manufacturability reviews, and production planning.

“The Battery Show is an important opportunity for FSQuality Circuits to meet the engineers and companies developing the next generation of electric vehicles, energy-storage systems, and battery technologies,” said Mr. Tianming Liu, founder of FS Quality Circuits. “These applications require much more than ordinary printed circuit boards. They require consistent quality, dependable thermal and electrical performance, strong engineering cooperation, and a manufacturing partner prepared to support long-term growth. Our expanding facility in Thailand allows us to provide advanced PCB technology while helping customers build a stronger and more flexible global supply chain.”

The FSQuality Circuits Thailand operation provides OEMs and electronics manufacturers with a valuable China-Plus-One PCB sourcing solution. This strategy enables customers to diversify their supply chains without sacrificing engineering expertise, manufacturing technology, responsiveness, or quality. The company’s continued investment in Thailand is designed to support customers seeking dependable Asian manufacturing capacity outside China while maintaining access to the knowledge and resources of an established global PCB organization.

FSQuality Circuits is also expanding its manufacturing capabilities through the development of its Phase II operation in Thailand. The expansion includes advanced equipment and processes intended to support increasingly sophisticated circuit-board requirements, including finer features, greater interconnection density, complex multilayer constructions, and future mSAP manufacturing capabilities.

The company’s technical roadmap includes advanced PCBs for artificial intelligence infrastructure, semiconductor test equipment, high-performance computing, automotive electronics, telecommunications, industrial controls, medical electronics, and other high-growth markets. Its experience includes the successful production of a recognized 42-layer automated-test-equipment board, while its continuing development program is targeting PCB constructions of up to 80 and 100 layers.
