title: Governor Abbott Directs TCEQ To Halt Data Center Permits
description:
Governor Greg Abbott today directed the Texas Commission on Environmental Quality (TCEQ) to halt all permits sought by data centers until the Electric Reliability Council of Texas (ERCOT) completes its audit.
“Simply put, Texans must come first,” said Governor Abbott.
“Data centers must pay their own way, protect our grid and water, and complete the ERCOT and TWDB audits.
Data center projects must cover all electrical infrastructure costs, result in lower residential electrical bills, and complete the ERCOT audit.
Next session, Governor Abbott will work with the Legislature to eliminate any financial incentives for data centers.
text:
Governor Greg Abbott today directed the Texas Commission on Environmental Quality (TCEQ) to halt all permits sought by data centers until the Electric Reliability Council of Texas (ERCOT) completes its audit. Because the Public Utility Commission of Texas (PUCT), ERCOT, and the Texas Water Development Board (TWDB) require that information to make informed decisions, no state agency shall move forward with regulatory approvals related to data center development until it is acquired.

“Simply put, Texans must come first,” said Governor Abbott. “Data centers must pay their own way, protect our grid and water, and complete the ERCOT and TWDB audits. Until they do, TCEQ will issue no permits sought by data center projects.”

Governor Abbott directed the PUCT and ERCOT to audit all data centers undergoing ERCOT’s interconnection process so their development does not compromise the reliability of the Texas electric grid and does not put Texans’ natural resources at risk. On September 14, he directed TWDB to compel data centers to comply with water-use reporting requirements, impose legal consequences for past and future failure to comply with state law, and partner with ERCOT on the audit to obtain additional water-use information. The PUCT, ERCOT, and TWDB will determine the impact of data centers on grid reliability and security and on the water resources needed by Texas communities.

Data center projects must cover all electrical infrastructure costs, result in lower residential electrical bills, and complete the ERCOT audit. Data centers must not use water needed by local communities, must report electricity and water usage, and must abide by setback requirements that will protect the communities in which they operate.

As ERCOT and TWDB conduct their audits, TCEQ must align its permitting decisions with the Governor’s directives and use the information from those audits. TCEQ shall provide an update to the Office of the Governor on its compliance with this directive by Monday, October 19, 2026.

Next session, Governor Abbott will work with the Legislature to eliminate any financial incentives for data centers.

title: LFP Cathode Materials to Surge to 5.24 Million Tons This Year, Commanding 77% of Total Market
description:
China Accelerates Transition to High-Density LFP Production expansion is even steeper in China, the world's largest LFP producer.
China's LFP production in the first half of this year reached approximately 2.7 million tons, up 73% year-over-year.
Prismatic Batteries Dominate the ESS Market The dominance of prismatic batteries in the ESS battery market is expected to strengthen further.
ESS Market to Enter the 1,000 GWh Era Next Year The growth trajectory of the ESS battery market is expected to continue for the foreseeable future.
With Chinese manufacturers dominating the market through LFP battery price competitiveness, South Korean companies are seeking business expansion opportunities in the U.S. market.
text:
Lithium iron phosphate (LFP) cathode materials have established themselves as the dominant force in the battery cathode materials market, riding surging demand from entry-level electric vehicles and energy storage systems (ESS). Global LFP cathode material shipments are projected to reach 5.24 million tons this year, up 51% from last year, with their share of the total lithium-ion battery cathode materials market expanding to 77%.

According to data released by market research firm SNE Research on the 21st, LFP's market dominance has risen sharply in recent years. In 2024, LFP accounted for 2.36 million tons, or 64%, of the 3.7 million tons of global cathode material shipments. Last year, that figure climbed to 3.47 million tons, pushing the share to 72%. In the first half of this year, LFP shipments grew 73% year-over-year, expanding the share to 76%.

Two factors are driving LFP growth. First is demand for entry-level EVs, which leverage LFP's price competitiveness, thermal safety, and long cycle life. While LFP has lower energy density than nickel-cobalt-based ternary cathode materials, its lower cost burden and reduced fire risk have accelerated adoption, particularly in entry-level EVs and commercial vehicles.

Second is the explosive growth of the ESS market. As AI data center power demand surges and renewable energy expansion increases the need for large-scale power storage, ESS has emerged as a new growth engine for LFP. Global ESS battery shipments reached 461.3 gigawatt-hours (GWh) in the first half of this year, up 71% year-over-year. The North American market grew 83% to 75.9 GWh, demonstrating that LFP demand is rapidly expanding beyond China.

China Accelerates Transition to High-Density LFP

Production expansion is even steeper in China, the world's largest LFP producer. China's LFP production in the first half of this year reached approximately 2.7 million tons, up 73% year-over-year. SNE Research estimates that average capacity utilization among Chinese LFP manufacturers has exceeded 80%, with some leading players approaching full-capacity operation.

However, with oversupply persisting in commodity-grade products, the competitive focus is shifting toward high-density, high-performance materials. Major Chinese manufacturers are moving their center of gravity from third-generation and earlier products to 3.5- to 4th-generation and above high-density LFP production. Recently, development of high-density LFP with compression density above 2.6 g/cc has emerged as a key direction, and competition in lithium manganese iron phosphate (LMFP), which has the potential to boost energy density by approximately 15-20% over LFP, is also intensifying.

Korean Battery Makers Accelerate North American ESS Market Push

South Korean battery makers are also moving quickly to build LFP production and supply chains targeting the rapidly growing North American ESS market.

South Korea's LG Energy Solution (373220.KS) began full operations at its Lansing, Michigan plant last month. The facility is a multi-purpose hub targeting annual production capacity of over 35 GWh, producing both LFP batteries for ESS and nickel-cobalt-manganese (NCM) batteries for EVs. The company has established five ESS production bases in North America, including the Lansing plant, to respond to growing local demand.

South Korea's Samsung SDI (006400.KS) plans to begin mass production of LFP batteries for ESS at its StarPlus Energy (SPE) plant in Indiana in the fourth quarter of this year. To secure its cathode material supply chain, the company signed a supply agreement with L&F worth approximately ₩1.6 trillion (approximately $1.2 billion) over three years starting next year. The strategy aims to connect North American production facilities with South Korean materials companies to secure a stable LFP supply chain for ESS.

South Korea's SK On also signed a supply agreement this month with L&F for high-density third-generation LFP cathode materials worth approximately ₩160 billion (approximately $116.0 million) through 2028. The company has been expanding its related business, having previously signed a 9 GWh ESS LFP battery supply agreement with U.S.-based Neovolta Power.

Prismatic Batteries Dominate the ESS Market

The dominance of prismatic batteries in the ESS battery market is expected to strengthen further. Prismatic batteries are estimated to account for 94% of the global ESS battery market this year. The share is expected to dip slightly to 92% next year before rising again from 2028, reaching 97% by 2035.

The temporary decline in prismatic share next year is attributed to increased pouch-type supply targeting the U.S. market. Industry sources explain that LG Energy Solution's production of pouch cells for the U.S. market will expand the pouch-type share next year compared to this year. However, the pouch cell share is expected to gradually decline thereafter.

Prismatic batteries' high market share aligns with the characteristics of ESS, which requires stable operation of large-capacity batteries. Prismatic cells are encased in rigid aluminum cans, providing structural rigidity, and it is relatively easier to scale cell sizes to meet required capacities. In contrast, pouch-type batteries offer advantages in energy density and space utilization but require structural reinforcement due to their thin film exterior, and safety design burdens increase as cells grow larger. Cylindrical batteries also face thermal management challenges during scaling, as larger diameters make it more difficult to dissipate internal heat.

South Korea's battery industry is also focusing on securing prismatic competitiveness. Samsung SDI has produced prismatic batteries as its mainstay since 2009. LG Energy Solution and SK On, which built their businesses primarily around pouch-type batteries, are also accelerating expansion into prismatic product lines.

ESS Market to Enter the 1,000 GWh Era Next Year

The growth trajectory of the ESS battery market is expected to continue for the foreseeable future. Annual ESS battery shipments are projected to rise from 984 GWh this year to 1,150 GWh next year, surpassing 1,000 GWh for the first time. Growth is expected to continue thereafter, reaching 1,870 GWh by 2035—approximately double this year's level.

The key challenge is converting ESS demand expansion into actual orders and market share gains. With Chinese manufacturers dominating the market through LFP battery price competitiveness, South Korean companies are seeking business expansion opportunities in the U.S. market. Industry assessments note that while Chinese battery makers have captured the market through low-price LFP strategies, South Korean battery makers are now pursuing a resurgence in the U.S. market based on prismatic technology.

The LFP market is expected to maintain its growth trajectory centered on entry-level EVs and ESS. However, large-scale capacity expansion by Chinese manufacturers is likely to intensify oversupply and price competition in commodity-grade products. South Korea's three major battery makers must differentiate beyond simply increasing LFP production volume, focusing on high density, fast charging, and low-temperature performance. Securing ESS demand for AI data centers and power grids, backed by North American local production and supply chains, will determine the success or failure of their LFP businesses going forward.

text:
Client Alert

On September 14, 2026, the Environmental Protection Agency (“EPA”) issued a final rule that repealed substantially all of the carbon pollution standards set in 2024 with respect to fossil fuel-fired power plants. The EPA supplemented its repeal with a proposal to rescind the remaining standards by repealing its Greenhouse Gas Standards for Fossil Fuel-Fired Power Plants and Regulations for Power Plant Greenhouse Gas Emissions under Clean Air Act Section 111.

Background and Rescission

The EPA forecasted this move when, in February 2026, it rescinded its Greenhouse Gas Endangerment Finding and subsequent federal greenhouse gas emission standards for cars and trucks. The EPA asserts that its actions will ensure “affordable and reliable energy supplies and drive down costs of transportation, heating, utilities, farming, and manufacturing while boosting our national security.” The EPA estimates that the final rule will save the power sector up to $310 billion in compliance costs.

In 2024, the Biden Administration finalized a rule that set standards under the Clean Air Act to reduce greenhouse gas emissions from new gas plants and existing coal-fired power plants. Among other things, the standards required the use of carbon capture and sequestration technology on coal-fired power plants operating past 2039 and on modified or reconstructed units. The 2024 carbon pollution standards represented a second attempt to regulate greenhouse gas emissions from fossil fuel-fired power plants. The Obama Administration issued the Clean Power Plan in 2015, which aimed to cut greenhouse gas emissions by 870 million tons by 2030. The Clean Power Plan was subsequently struck down by the Supreme Court.

Environmental and public health groups have already filed lawsuits against the EPA challenging its repeal of the 2024 carbon pollution standards. Additional lawsuits are expected to follow.

Providence, RI - A Trump-appointed judge on the U.S. District Court for the District of Rhode Island ruled against the Trump administration’s attempt to slash $7 billion of funding for solar energy projects.

The Solar For All program provides grant funding to regions across the country in order to expand affordable solar energy to over 900,000 households. Last summer, Donald Trump’s Environmental Protection Agency announced it would rescind the funds and ended the program.

Solar energy is one of the cheapest forms of energy, and in June 2026, solar production in the U.S. overtook coal production for the first month on record. Despite the administration’s attempts to cut funding and end projects, renewable energy has continued to grow in popularity and production in the country.

In response, Sierra Club Climate Policy Director Patrick Drupp issued the following statement:

“Solar energy is cheap, reliable, and quick to get online. It is a common sense solution to address the record-high electricity bills that families are seeing, while improving public health and cleaning up our air and water. We are glad to see the courts agree with Sierra Club that the administration’s attempt to end the Solar For All program is unlawful, and we will continue to defend this program to ensure families everywhere can reap the benefits of solar energy.”

text:
Matthew Chen, External Affairs Manager, North America, ABB E-mobility Inc. and Electric Vehicle Charging Association Chair:“ Meeting California’s clean transportation goals means building more than 400 new chargers a day, every day, through 2030. In a difficult budget year, as federal support retreats, the Governor and the Legislature delivered a package of bills that address permitting delays and cut unnecessary costs to accelerate EV charger build-out. The Electric Vehicle Charging Association (EVCA) appreciates this leadership and the willingness to advance practical solutions that do not depend on new spending. From charging infrastructure to the vehicles themselves, California is backing every part of the clean transportation transition, and industry is ready to deliver the affordable, reliable charging Californians expect.”

Laura Renger, Executive Director, California Electric Transportation Coalition: “Thank you, Governor Newsom, for signing SB 1213 and SB 1283 today. These bills are good news for California’s electric-transportation future, bringing greater transparency to zero-emission incentives for medium- and heavy-duty vehicles while making it easier to build the charging infrastructure Californians need. CalETC applauds the Governor and bill authors for clearing unnecessary barriers and keeping California moving forward.”

Bill Mcgavern, Policy Director, Coalition for Clean Air: “Electrifying transportation is an essential tool for cleaning up California’s air, fighting catastrophic climate change, and creating quality jobs. These new laws will help build the infrastructure to enable all Californians — including residents of multi-family housing — to benefit from clean electric mobility. In addition, price transparency requirements will help build a more affordable market for the zero-emission trucks we need to reduce the toxic diesel exhaust poisoning our communities.”

Guillermo Ortiz, Senior Clean Vehicle Advocate, Natural Resources Defense Council: “The transition to clean vehicles is a smart business move, not a financial burden. By bringing transparency to the marketplace and enhancing our voucher programs, this bipartisan legislation will drive down costs, protect our small businesses from fuel price volatility, expedite EV charging and ensure California remains a leader in both environmental and economic innovation.”

Daniel Barrad, Western States Associate Director, Union of Concerned Scientists: “As the Trump administration rolls back life-saving policies and raises costs, California’s progress on zero emission transportation is more important than ever. We applaud the legislature and governor for enacting laws that will advance clean, affordable and sustainable transportation. From increasing charging access to laying the groundwork for battery recycling, these laws show the world that a safe, clean and reliable transportation future is possible.”

Gracyna Mohabir, Sr. Regulatory Advocate, California Environmental Voters: “Transportation is California’s largest source of pollution and a major contributor to the state’s poor air quality. At a time when the federal government is systematically dismantling our clean air and health protections, this is an important step toward building a cleaner freight future. “We need practical solutions that make it easier to choose zero-emissions vehicles and create a freight system that doesn’t come at the expense of Californians’ health and clean air, and SB 1213 is exactly that.”

Jakob Evans, Senior Policy Strategist, Sierra Club California: “Signing this package of bills shows that California is stepping up to lead on clean air at a time when the federal government has undermined the electric vehicle market and attacked our state’s regulatory autonomy. Bills like SB 1213 will ensure that California is able to take more effective action to accelerate deployment of zero-emission trucks and address our largest sector of pollution. Sierra Club California will continue to work closely with state leaders to fight for California’s air quality and public health.”

California’s clean transportation leadership

The Golden State has more than 216,445 public and shared charging plugs statewide, including more than 20,000 DC fast-charging ports. Chargers are being installed at places Californians already go, including workplaces, multifamily housing, retail centers, park-and-ride lots, medical offices, and travel corridors.

The California Energy Commission allocated $98.5 million in light-duty ZEV infrastructure funding for fiscal year 2025-26, emphasizing Level 1 and Level 2 chargers in locations where cars are parked for longer periods, including homes and multifamily residences.

California is one of the top states for EV buyers and drivers. California has surpassed its original goal of 1.5 million zero-emission vehicle sales by 2025, reaching more than 2.7 million cumulative ZEV sales. In the second quarter of 2026, Californians purchased 86,857 new ZEVs, representing 19.1% of all new vehicle sales in the state.

Key takeaways Amazon’s carbon-free energy projects contributed nearly $11 billion to U.S. GDP from 2023 through 2025.
Amazon's carbon-free energy projects don't just keep the lights on for our operations—they put people to work, support tax revenue generation into local communities, and drive economic growth.
That’s across our full portfolio of carbon-free energy projects—including solar farms, wind farms, nuclear energy, and battery storage systems.

text:
Key takeaways

Amazon’s carbon-free energy projects contributed nearly $11 billion to U.S. GDP from 2023 through 2025.

These investments supported nearly 22,000 jobs annually across the country.

Amazon covers all costs associated with powering its data centers, so communities benefit from these investments without bearing expenses.

Amazon's carbon-free energy projects don't just keep the lights on for our operations—they put people to work, support tax revenue generation into local communities, and drive economic growth.

A new independent study by Oxford Economics puts a number on it: Amazon's carbon-free energy investments contributed nearly $11 billion to United States gross domestic product (GDP) and supported nearly 22,000 jobs annually from 2023 through 2025. That’s across our full portfolio of carbon-free energy projects—including solar farms, wind farms, nuclear energy, and battery storage systems.

What happens when Amazon invests in carbon-free energy?

Amazon's carbon-free energy portfolio spans more than 700 projects across 28 countries, totaling more than 40 gigawatts (GW) of capacity—enough to power more than 12.1 million U.S. homes.

Every project creates jobs in layers. Construction crews, welders, and electricians build the project, while local vendors, suppliers, and logistics companies support the building. Those paychecks get spent at nearby restaurants, shops, and service businesses. After construction wraps, plant managers, maintenance teams, and technical specialists keep things running for decades. Oxford Economics found these projects enabled billions in estimated tax revenue from 2023 through 2025—money that increases public funds to support schools, roads, first responders, and public services in the communities where they operate.

“Investment in America’s energy infrastructure has benefits that extend well beyond the electricity it generates,” said Pete Collings, managing director of economic footprint and sustainability at Oxford Economics. “Amazon's purchases of carbon-free power support jobs and economic activity across the country, stimulate tax revenues that can pay for public services, and contribute to a more secure and resilient energy system.”

These projects last anywhere from 25 to 60 years depending on the technology. Oxford Economics estimates that through 2034 alone, the total contribution will top $61 billion in GDP while supporting roughly 23,500 jobs annually.

How do these projects benefit local communities?

Mississippi

In Tunica County, Mississippi, Amazon's Delta Wind project is the first utility-scale wind farm in the state. Developed by AES and operational since April 2024, the 184.5-megawatt project generates enough carbon-free energy to power the equivalent of nearly 80,000 Mississippi homes a year. Landowners continue to farm the acreage around the turbines, preserving the county's agricultural heritage alongside its new energy infrastructure.

“These are powerful examples of how we're not only providing the carbon-free energy that companies like Amazon need to grow, but helping states like Mississippi attract critical investment, create new sources of revenue for landowners and local communities, and support sustainable economic growth for decades to come,” said Amanda Smith, vice president of external affairs, U.S. renewables and power, at AES.

Statewide, Amazon's carbon-free energy projects contributed $212 million to Mississippi's GDP from 2023 through 2025, supporting approximately 280 jobs annually and enabling more than $22 million in tax revenue.

The benefits extend to everyday ratepayers as well. Entergy Mississippi reports that revenue from large customers like data centers is beginning to deliver direct benefits, helping keep electricity rates flat through the peak summer months. Through its Fair Share Plus Pledge, the utility projects more than $2 billion in savings for Mississippi customers over the next two decades and has credited large-customer revenue with supporting reliability improvements across its system.

Virginia

Amazon's carbon-free energy projects in Virginia contributed more than $331 million to the state's GDP from 2023 through 2025, supporting more than 150 jobs annually and enabling over $15 million in tax revenue.

The benefits also reach communities in more direct ways. In Louisa County, Amazon awarded a $135,000 grant to fully fund a solar project for the Louisa County Resource Council (LCRC), the county's primary source of free food for nearly 4,000 residents each month. The new solar system is expected to cut roughly $1,000 from LCRC's monthly utility bill, savings it estimates could put nearly 48,000 meals on its clients' tables each year.

Indiana

In Indiana, Amazon has worked alongside local leaders who see firsthand how our carbon-free energy projects translate into jobs, new sources of tax revenue, and long-term economic development for their communities.

“What's exciting for our region is the ripple effect. While we see Amazon’s investment in data centers, we also understand what their investment across the state has enabled in carbon-free energy (CFE),” said Jeff Rea, president and CEO of South Bend Regional Chamber. “We're proud to have a company investing in the South Bend Region which pushes beyond its project boundaries to support Hoosiers across the state.”

Statewide, investments made by developers for Amazon's carbon-free energy projects contributed $160 million to Indiana's GDP from 2023 through 2025, supporting approximately 116 jobs annually and enabling more than $11 million in tax revenue.

Texas

Amazon's carbon-free energy portfolio in Texas is the largest of any state, with more than 10 gigawatts of capacity across solar, wind, and nuclear projects—enough to power approximately 8 million U.S. homes. From 2023 through 2025, Amazon’s carbon-free energy projects contributed over $1 billion to the state's GDP, supported over 1,300 jobs annually, and enabled over $143 million in tax revenue across the state.

“Corporate commitments to carbon-free energy are strengthening Texas's reputation as a great place to do business,” said Bryn Baker of the Texas Energy Buyers Alliance. “Amazon alone has 10 gigawatts of carbon emissions-free energy capacity in the state, spanning solar, wind, and nuclear. Large energy customers want to grow their operations in the Lone Star State, and they are ready and willing to invest in the low-cost, reliable, carbon-free energy resources that can support that growth.”

What's the future for Amazon's carbon-free energy portfolio?

Amazon builds the energy it needs in ways that also benefit surrounding communities—with sources that will last for decades. As we work toward our Climate Pledge goal of net-zero carbon by 2040, every carbon-free energy project we bring online gets us closer and leaves the local economy stronger in the process.

Learn more about all of Amazon's sustainability initiatives.

Learn more about our model methodology.

*Tax revenue is enabled through the economic activity of the energy developers building these projects.

title: LSU Sensors Pinpoint Escaping Gases, Prevent Catastrophic Pipeline Failure
description:

Add moisture, and CO₂ can form carbonic acid, accelerating corrosion that could lead to catastrophic pipeline failure.
The research team lab-tested its system but mixed in humidity to simulate field conditions.
The research team tailored MOF coatings to detect individual gases.

text:
Current pipeline monitors detect leaks without identifying the escaping gas, creating a blind spot that can delay emergency responses and endanger communities.

A new LSU system uses unique fiber-optic sensor coatings to tell the difference between carbon dioxide, nitrogen, methane and ordinary air flow, as well as humidity. The sensors could slash millions from monitoring, repairs and leak prevention costs.

“The gas identity tells you what danger you face. Humidity tells you how the danger will behave and how fast the pipeline may deteriorate,” said FNU Jyoti, a postdoctoral research associate in the Department of Petroleum Engineering.

CO₂ displaces oxygen, can pool in low-lying areas, suffocate people and animals and make metal pipes brittle. Add moisture, and CO₂ can form carbonic acid, accelerating corrosion that could lead to catastrophic pipeline failure.

The research team lab-tested its system but mixed in humidity to simulate field conditions.

“Moisture can influence sensor performance. We wanted to analyze how humidity affects our CO₂ sensing response to reduce the threat of carbonic acid formation,” Jyoti said.

The research team includes LSU Petroleum Engineering Associate Professor Jyotsna Sharma, LSU Mechanical and Industrial Engineering Associate Professor Manas Ranjan Gartia, Jyoti and Satyendra Kumar Mishra, a senior researcher at the Centre Tecnològic de Telecomunicacions de Catalunya in Spain.

The new monitoring system builds on Sharma’s earlier work using fiber-optic sensors to track leaks by measuring physical changes inside a pipeline, such as temperature, pressure and stress. However, external or environmental conditions, like temperature or traffic vibration, can compromise those measurements.

The researchers coated the fiber with metal-organic frameworks (MOFs), porous hybrid materials whose development was recognized with the 2025 Nobel Prize in Chemistry.

MOFs’ crystalline structures form precisely sized pores just nanometers wide. The pores can grab and hold specific molecules. The research team tailored MOF coatings to detect individual gases.

The team also built a numerical model that predicts MOF performance with more than 95% accuracy. Researchers can digitally screen dozens of potential materials before moving to lab testing, saving months of work.

After lab testing, the researchers’ next step will be large-scale experiments in a 5,000-foot wellbore.

“Our goal is to show there is a clear path from our research prototype to a real-world solution,” Jyoti said.

The research team is working with the LSU Office of Innovation & Technology Commercialization to find partners or funding to advance the leak detection system.

“This pipeline safety breakthrough illustrates how LSU is advancing toward our goal of becoming a Top 50 research institution,” said Robert Twilley, vice chancellor of research and economic development. “By turning research into practical solutions, our scientists are tackling global energy challenges head-on, protecting communities and saving industry millions of dollars.”

text:
Two months after Louisiana became a finalist for a national initiative to modernize nuclear power, state officials have begun meeting with local officials — most recently in East and West Feliciana parishes — about interest in new nuclear development.

Such companies could include those engaged in recycling spent radioactive fuel rods, nuclear fuel enrichment and permanently storing nuclear waste.

The state Department of Conservation and Energy, which is leading Louisiana’s effort to win the federal competition, met with local officials last week in south Louisiana and will hit the northern part of the state soon.

“We’re visiting different areas saying, ‘Hey, here’s the kind of things that are out there that might be part of it. Is there anything you’ve got an interest in?’” said Patrick Courreges, a state energy department spokesman.

One such meeting took place with East Feliciana officials late last week, said Police Juror Richard Oliveaux. The police jury is considering whether to support the state’s effort to land a “Nuclear Lifecycle Innovation Campus,” a designation that federal officials say could attract up to $50 billion in private-sector investment.

Neighboring West Feliciana is home to one of the state’s two nuclear power plants, River Bend near St. Francisville.

West Feliciana Parish President Kenny Havard said he has taken part in the talks and has also spoken to officials at Curio Energy, a startup company pitching a fuel-rod recycling plant. Courreges said officials with Curio have participated in some of the state meetings with local officials.

Curio wants to build a plant to recycle spent rods now being stored at nuclear plants across the nation into reusable nuclear fuel or into other material for commercial and medical purposes, according to the company.

In addition to River Bend, West and East Feliciana have ample land and Mississippi River and railroad access to attract nuclear industry companies, officials have pointed out.

Havard said he believes Louisiana may have three or four potential areas for one of the campuses. He stressed the preliminary nature of the discussions in the Felicianas.

"There's been nothing set in stone, no property purchased or bought, you know, any of that stuff, but we are having conversations," he said.

Oliveaux cautioned that he didn't know what talks other East Feliciana officials may have had, noting the concept is still in the early stages and would not move forward without public input first.

Courreges said the state isn’t ruling out locating different nuclear industries in different parts of the state.

Officials with Curio — based in Washington, D.C. — couldn’t be reached for comment.

Company CEO Ed McGinnis spoke to Louisiana lawmakers in a committee hearing last year. McGinnis, a Jefferson Parish native, said material from the recycled rods is an untapped energy source.

McGinnis said the spent rods, which would be held in specialized containment, could be moved to the recycling site by road, rail or water. He pointed out that the federal government's site for permanent storage for nuclear waste, Yucca Mountain in Nevada, hasn't opened nearly three decades after its planned start date.

title: Methane reductions are critical to ensuring Canada's oil and gas is ready to ... - News and stories
description:
Many of the Major Project Office’s priority projects are aimed at growing Canada’s energy and resources sectors, including a plan to export more oil and gas by way of British Columbia.
While BC is a leader in low-emission production, oil and gas from Alberta, Canada’s largest producing province, emits too much methane to meet the most common international methane standards.
The European Union has already announced its methane regulation that imposes methane emission limits on imported oil and gas starting in 2030.
The most commonly used intensity standard for natural gas production is to have methane emissions less than 0.2% of the volume of the sold gas.
Building on momentum to get across the finish line Canada has announced new regulations to reduce oil and gas methane by 72% below 2012 levels by 2030.
text:
By Ari Pottens and Scott Seymour

Canada’s trade priorities are shifting quickly as its largest trading partner, the United States, proves less reliable with every passing month. Prime Minister Carney is travelling the world seeking new markets to diversify our customer base.

He asserts that “Canada has what the world wants” and touts our status as a clean energy superpower. Many of the Major Project Office’s priority projects are aimed at growing Canada’s energy and resources sectors, including a plan to export more oil and gas by way of British Columbia.

However, with global markets increasingly calling for lower emissions of methane from oil and gas supplies and the growing urgency of energy security, does Canada truly have what the world wants?

The short answer is not yet, and not in all major producing provinces. While BC is a leader in low-emission production, oil and gas from Alberta, Canada’s largest producing province, emits too much methane to meet the most common international methane standards. Luckily, Alberta can implement policies to help get there.

Importer standards equal external pressures

Some of Canada’s new trade partners are countries that are leading the way on methane standards, which means Canada must align with them to unlock new export opportunities. The European Union has already announced its methane regulation that imposes methane emission limits on imported oil and gas starting in 2030. Buyers in Asia are also expressing a preference for low-emission energy: Japan, the world’s second-largest importer of liquefied natural gas, has joined together with South Korea to launch the CLEAN initiative to improve LNG supply chain transparency and drive down methane emissions. Just two weeks ago Japanese and Canadian officials gathered at the Canadian Embassy in Tokyo for a productive discussion on the interconnection between methane mitigation and energy security.

The best way for major buyers to decide which fossil fuels are cleanest is to compare each production region’s methane emission “intensity”—the amount of methane emissions per unit of oil and gas. The most commonly used intensity standard for natural gas production is to have methane emissions less than 0.2% of the volume of the sold gas.

How close to ready are we?

Many leaders in Government describe Canada as having some of the lowest-emission gas on Earth, but aerial measurements have shown that not all oil and gas is produced equally across western Canada:

British Columbia: Based on recent analysis, BC’s oil and gas is calculated to carry less than 0.2% methane emissions intensity, meeting the most common international intensity standard.

Alberta: The oil and gas produced in Alberta carries a much higher emissions intensity at 1.3%, about 7x higher than that 0.2% target and leaving plenty of room for improvement.

The reality is that if Canada wants to export truly low-emission energy at scale to new customers overseas, Alberta—which accounts for 84% of Canada’s oil production and 61% of Canada’s gas production—will have to reduce its methane emissions substantially.

The best way for Alberta to bring down its emissions is by bolstering its provincial regulations to a level equivalent to or stronger than the recently finalized federal standard. Any finalized equivalency agreement should be based on an assessment made by a truly independent third-party and based on credible federal emissions data.

Building on momentum to get across the finish line

Canada has announced new regulations to reduce oil and gas methane by 72% below 2012 levels by 2030. Provinces can adopt the federal regulations, or, under an “equivalency agreement,” develop their own regulations provided they meet or exceed the federal standard. The federal government has the power to approve these agreements and with that power, ensure Alberta’s new regulations result in meaningful reductions that can help enable the transpacific energy trade that the Carney government has sought.

There are clear market signals coming from overseas energy customers, and Alberta cannot afford to mute or ignore these signals as our nation pursues new trading partners. As Ottawa fast-tracks massive infrastructure investments to build complex, expensive pipelines to serve new customers, this is no time to skimp on regulatory strength to ensure we deliver truly low-emission oil and gas. If Canada wants to build stronger, stabler, trade relationships, then we need stronger regulations and more transparency when it comes to one of our marquee products.

text:
The 1990s produced a lot of bad ideas, from grunge fashion to New Coke. But there’s one Leah Stokes particularly dislikes: the notion of a “carbon footprint.”

You remember that one. To protect the planet from the ravages of climate change, we were told that each of us needed to alter our lifestyles. Carpool to work. Limit your use of heating and air conditioning. Don’t even think about flying.

In retrospect, all of those recommendations have one thing in common, noted Stokes, the Anton Vonk Associate Professor of Environmental Politics at UC Santa Barbara. Each of them is about “making a behavioral change within a fossil-fuel energy structure.” The energy companies aren’t asked to compromise: We are, because we, apparently, are the problem.

Stokes understands the threat of rising global temperatures better than most, but she approaches the issue from an entirely different perspective. We can still use as much energy as we need; we just need to upgrade the machines that provide it.

“I am talking about swapping out the hardware,” she said. “Replacing a gasoline-powered car with an electric vehicle isn’t behavioral change — it’s infrastructure change.”

Today, electricity can be, and increasingly is, generated in ways that don’t involve burning fossil fuels. So, electrifying your household — swapping out your gas stove for an electric one, or replacing your gas heating system with a heat pump — is a way to lessen your environmental impact that does not require sweating through the summer or wearing wool sweaters all winter.

“Now, you don’t have to stop at your own home,” Stokes added. “You can work with others in your community to electrify your local school or church, or lobby for your city’s car fleet to be EVs. Change happens one person at a time, joining with others to shift the system.”

Furthermore, at a critical point during the project, Stokes gave birth to premature twins. That story provides some harrowing moments, and emphasizes the stakes of what she and her colleagues were trying to accomplish.

It’s worth asking why it is worth chronicling this period, given that since he returned to office, Donald Trump has managed to gut many of the law’s key provisions. Stokes has two answers.

First, she wanted to provide a vivid example of how people working together on a difficult problem can make real progress. Second, the cliché that the current administration has effectively killed the bill is, in fact, vastly oversimplified.

“The law has proven more resilient than a lot of people predicted or understand,” she said. “Some of its most important provisions were the tax credits to build clean-energy manufacturing plants around the country. There were more than 500 of these, and nine out of 10 are still moving forward.”

On the other hand, “the tax credits for everyday people, the grants for disadvantaged communities — those got gutted,” she said. “That was a heartbreaker. Corporations are still going to manufacture clean energy, which is good. But individuals should also be able to get heat pumps and solar panels.”

In retrospect, Stokes concedes that the process was hindered by the Democratic Party’s “too lawyerly approach” to awarding grants. Echoing the argument of journalists like Ezra Klein, she now emphasizes the importance of getting projects underway quickly, so that voters see tangible results before the next election.

“I wish we had gotten money out the door faster,” she said. “I see no inherent tension between supporting equity, justice and labor rights and moving fast. As Klein told me a few months ago when he was in town, ‘Speed should be a progressive value.’”

Stokes brings a glass-half-full perspective on the climate crisis to her work. In spite of polls showing environmental protection is less and less salient to Americans as an issue that influences how they vote, she insists that “more and more people want to do the right thing.”

While that is debatable, everyone wants to save money, and Stokes argues the technological revolution is rapidly making green energy more affordable than traditional power sources. “EVs are cheaper than gas vehicles, in terms of total cost of ownership,” she said. “With the wars in Ukraine and Iran pushing fossil-fuel prices through the roof, the whole world is waking up.”

The political clout of the fossil-fuel industry, particularly in America, remains a problem, she said. “But the clean-energy industry is starting to get politically savvy as well,” she added. “We’re at an inflection point politically as well as economically.”

An American citizen who was born and raised in Canada — “I’m proud to be Canadian at this moment,” she declared in reference to the current trade war — Stokes insists her approach is pragmatic rather than pollyannaish or utopian.

“It’s heartbreaking to me to watch Canadian forests burn,” she said. “But the best way to channel those negative emotions is to take action. Sitting around and feeling sad isn’t going to help anything.”

Yes, humanity seems poised to blow past the 2.5-degree Celsius rise in average global temperature that scientists have long argued is crucial if we are to avoid major climate disruptions. “But there are degrees of bad,” she said. “Things will get a lot worse if we get to three degrees. Everything we do matters, and I think we should do everything we can.

text:
Zionsville doesn't want the LEAP district's wastewater, town councilors unanimously agreed in a resolution passed Monday, Sept. 21. But if the LEAP water supply program does decide to discharge treated wastewater into town's waterways, there may not be much Zionsville officials can do to stop it.

Boone County's up and coming tech park, the LEAP Innovation District in Lebanon, has long been embroiled in a contentious water saga. Lebanon and, by extension, LEAP need more water to support development – which includes an Eli Lilly manufacturing plant and an upcoming Meta data center. Citizens Energy, a utility local to Indianapolis, will provide Lebanon with upwards of 25 million gallons of water a day. After the resource is used by the likes of residents, manufacturers, data centers and future tech park residents, Lebanon Utilities will treat it.

Central Indiana residents want to know where that wastewater will go.

Controversial plans to discharge it into Eagle Creek Reservoir have been scrapped, according to Lebanon Utilities, and the utility has been considering several other options. As of June, some of the options were in Zionsville.

Lebanon Utilities did not immediately respond to IndyStar's inquiry about which locations are still under consideration. Jason Plunkett, Zionsville town council president, confirmed at the Monday meeting that the town has not entered into any agreements pertaining to the LEAP wastewater discharge.

A new discharge site would need to adhere to strict pollution standards, but Zionsville officials have still been fielding concerns from residents. Scientists, including a retired hydrologist from the Indiana Department of Environmental Management told IndyStar earlier this year that wastewater – even when properly treated and permitted – can still alter ecosystems.

Zionsville councilors voted 7-0 to formalize their stance on LEAP discharge coming to town.

"I think this is an effort to clear the air a little bit. There's been a lot of confusion and misinformation with the public about what Zionsville can and cannot do, what we have and have not done," Plunkett said.

The resolution asked Lebanon officials to eliminate any plans or permits that involve the discharge of treated wastewater into Zionsville's waterways, and it asked IDEM to avoid approving any such plans or permits.

Voting for the resolution was a "no-brainer," said Councilor Evan Norris. But for at least one resident, the resolution wasn't enough.

"I support the town speaking up, so thank you for that. But I am asking the council to make the resolution stronger, said Jeni Jenkins, a Zionsville resident who works for the Hoosier Environmental Council.

She asked the council to assign someone from the city to follow the issue closely and keep residents informed.

Beyond that, Zionsville's legal authority is limited.

The town isn't in charge of Lebanon Utilities' discharge plans or the associated permits, said Heather Harris, an attorney who prepared the resolution. She said Zionsville Mayor John Stehr is in talks with the city of Lebanon about the issue and plans to engage in the public comment process if plans for discharging in Zionsville develop. But the final authority rests with IDEM.

text:
The proposed BESS mandate comes as battery makers look beyond electric mobility towards stationary energy storage.

The Central Electricity Authority (CEA) has proposed making battery energy storage systems (BESS) mandatory for all new ground-mounted solar and onshore wind projects commissioned from 1 July 2027, a move that could accelerate the battery industry's shift beyond electric mobility into stationary storage.

Under the draft rules, a 100 MW solar or wind project would need at least 10 MW of storage capacity with a minimum two-hour duration. The requirement would rise to four hours for projects commissioned from July 2029.

The proposal comes as India's need for grid-scale storage is expected to expand sharply. The country added 2,668.54 MW of BESS power capacity, equivalent to 7,785.6 MWh of storage in 2026. Solar capacity stood at 164.59 GW and wind at 58.14 GW as of 31 July.

For battery manufacturers that built their businesses largely around electric two-wheelers, three-wheelers, four-wheelers and light commercial vehicles, the emerging stationary-storage market offers another major source of demand.

A Formalisation, Not A Surprise

The proposed mandate largely formalises a transition that is already visible in procurement. “Buyers have stopped asking for vanilla solar in the last few months — every serious conversation in the last months has been peak-power or solar-plus-storage,” said Sudharman Ezhil, Director & CEO, Natrinai Ventures (NGE Green Energy).

Ezhil said storage makes renewable assets more useful to lenders and offtakers by allowing projects to schedule power, manage deviation settlement and participate in evening demand periods, when time-of-day tariffs and exchange prices can be significantly higher than daytime solar rates. it's a welcome move,” he said.

Ezhil expects storage to become standard within two to three years, irrespective of the mandate, as buyers look for projects that can provide power beyond solar generation hours. NGE Green, for instance, already treats BESS as a default line item. The system is sized according to the offtaker's load rather than the regulatory minimum.

Beyond Electric Mobility

The emerging BESS market is also allowing lithium-ion battery manufacturers to diversify beyond electric mobility. Pratik Kamdar, Co-founder & CEO, Neuron Energy, said BESS “has the potential to become a significant new market for Indian lithium-ion battery manufacturers”, pointing to India's projected requirement of more than 236 GWh of BESS by 2031-32.

“This creates an opportunity to diversify beyond electric mobility and participate in utility-scale as well as commercial and industrial storage applications,” Kamdar said.

The shift is also beginning to appear in manufacturers' strategies. Amara Raja Energy & Mobility told investors after its FY26 results that it was giving BESS a larger role in its mix. “A major change in our strategy is the introduction of BESS as a larger part of our mix. Earlier, we had largely focused on EVs,” the company's management said.

For manufacturers, the opportunity extends beyond cells and battery packs to areas such as battery management systems, thermal management and monitoring technologies.

Same Cells, Different Engineering

The move into stationary storage, however, is not a straightforward extension of EV battery manufacturing. “BESS cannot be treated as a simple extension of an EV battery platform,” Kamdar said, pointing to differences in operating requirements, including long-duration operation and frequent charge-discharge cycles.

“Battery pack architecture, BMS software, monitoring and thermal-management systems need to be designed around the specific operating profile of stationary storage,” Kamdar added.

At the same time, the underlying expertise developed through EV battery manufacturing remains transferable, giving existing lithium-ion manufacturers a starting point as they move into grid-scale and commercial storage.

Regulatory Gaps Persist

While the market opportunity is expanding, developers point to commercial and regulatory issues that could affect the pace of deployment.

Ezhil said one challenge is the way solar-plus-storage projects are priced. “The industry keeps trying to sell a blended Rs /kWh tariff that folds battery costs into solar energy. That structure fails bankability,” he said.

Ezhil argued that solar and storage need separate capacity and energy charges, or that batteries should be deployed behind the meter, to better reflect the different functions and costs of the two assets.

State-level rules also remain inconsistent, particularly around banking and surcharge provisions for commercial and industrial storage projects, Ezhil said.

Tamil Nadu's resource adequacy plan, for instance, projects a need for more than 11 GW of additional storage by 2035 and flags evening-hour power shortages between October and April. “The regulatory framework should be pulling private storage into that gap, and we are waiting eagerly for the new policy to get going,” Ezhil said.

The CEA has invited comments on its draft proposal until 4 October 2026, before the regulations are finalised.

For India's battery manufacturers, the proposed mandate could provide further impetus for stationary storage to develop from a supplementary market into a significant part of the country's power infrastructure.

text:
New Jersey environmental advocates are disappointed by today’s rollback of Resilient Environment and Landscapes (REAL) flood rules designed to lower costs and protect public safety in the face of increasingly severe weather.

Coming off a summer of serious flooding that caused millions of dollars of property damage for families and local businesses, advocates are calling on the Sherrill administration work quickly to implement updated rules that set a new national standard for storm protection, saving working families, local businesses and state and local governments countless millions in rebuilding costs, lowering flood insurance premiums and saving lives.

“Rolling back flood protection regulations puts the people of New Jersey directly in harm's way. Today, the Sherrill administration reinstated old flood regulations that use maps and standards that we know are wrong. This regulatory backsliding is at the request of big developers who have sowed disinformation about the REAL rules to the benefit of their own profit margins,” said Jennifer M. Coffey, Executive Director of the Association of New Jersey Environmental Commissions (ANJEC). “We urge Governor Sherrill to re-adopt strong flood protection regulations immediately to protect the lives and homes of New Jersey residents.”

The New Jersey Department of Environmental Protection’s own website explains that the REAL land resource protection rules “better support New Jersey communities, residents, and businesses in building their resilience to sea-level rise, extreme weather, chronic flooding, and other impacts of our changing climate. Almost two-thirds of New Jersey’s coastline is already at high or very high risk to coastal erosion and 98% of the coastline is projected at medium or very high risk to sea level rise. Over half a million acres of New Jersey land are highly vulnerable to coastal hazards.”

“Any delay in implementing the REAL rules endangers our preserved lands, including the delicate ecosystem within the one million acres of the Pinelands, particularly the 17-trillion-gallon Kirkwood-Cohansey aquifer that provides drinking water for about one million people, irrigation for 200,000 acres of farmland, and habitat to dozens of endangered species. Flooding threatens the quality of this vital water supply,” said Michael Klein, director of government relations for the Pinelands Alliance.

“In a densely developed state surrounded by water, the REAL rules address two of our biggest issues: flood safety and affordability,” said Danielle McCulloch, Executive Director of the American Littoral Society. “Strong, evidence-based construction standards will help New Jerseyans build safer homes and communities today, rather than leaving families and taxpayers to pay for preventable flood damage tomorrow.”

Many of the roads and buildings in service today on New Jersey’s coast will likely be unusable by the year 2100 given the increasing flooding impacts of sea level rise. New Jersey is one of the states most impacted by climate change — with the fastest increase in warming temperatures and the third-highest number of flood insurance claims in the nation. From 1980 through 2024, there were 72 confirmed weather disaster events with losses exceeding $1 billion each that affected New Jersey, according to the National Center for Environmental Information. On average, New Jersey experiences a $1 billion weather event every 32 weeks — an astounding figure that serves as a clarion call for adopting science-based rules designed to lower recovery costs.

“Delaying the NJPACT REAL rule delays the protections New Jersey families, businesses, and communities need from worsening floods,” said Jim Waltman, Executive Director of The Watershed Institute. “These commonsense, science-based standards would ensure that new homes and critical facilities are built above current and projected flood levels, while stronger stormwater requirements help reduce the runoff that overwhelms neighborhoods and infrastructure. At a time when extreme storms and chronic flooding are becoming more frequent, New Jersey must move forward with rules that protect people, property, and the natural systems that make our communities more resilient.”

In addition to adopting building elevation requirements for new residential development, the REAL rules include new stormwater management requirements for redevelopment projects previously exempt, new nature-based solutions permitting designed to accelerate restoration projects and additional protections for wetlands.

title: EPA and Army Corps Issue Supplemental WOTUS Proposal: How It Could Affect Your Projects

text:
On September 9, 2026, the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) and the U.S. Department of the Army, including the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers (the "Corps," collectively with EPA, the "Agencies") published a Supplemental Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (Supplemental Proposed Rule) addressing the definition of "waters of the United States" (WOTUS) as used under the Clean Water Act (CWA). The Supplemental Proposed Rule augments targeted portions of the Agencies' November 20, 2025 Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (NPRM), effectively and further narrowing jurisdictional WOTUS following the Supreme Court's decision in Sackett v. Environmental Protection Agency, 598 U.S. 651 (2023) (Sackett), after receiving and reviewing approximately 220,000 comments.

The most immediate practical takeaway is that the Supplemental Proposed Rule would not change current law or permitting obligations; rather, it seeks additional public comment before final action. Stakeholders should evaluate potential effects of the Supplemental Proposed Rule on Section 404 permitting and mitigation, Section 402 NPDES permitting, Section 401 certification, and potential downstream impacts on state and Tribal programs.

Any comments on the Supplemental Proposed Rule must be received by October 9, 2026. The deadline creates an urgent opportunity to address the proposed perennial-only standard, the 30-day interruption rule, the five-year drought concept, and potential effects on projects and state or Tribal programs.

Overview of the Supplemental Proposed Rule

The Agencies say the Supplemental Proposed Rule is intended to provide greater certainty in implementing the post-Sackett WOTUS framework.

What the Supplemental Proposed Rule Would Add

The Supplemental Proposed Rule would add several new definitions.

First, the Agencies propose defining "relatively permanent" as "perennial bodies of water," with standing or continuously flowing water every day of the year during ordinary conditions. Moreover, a perennial water body would retain that jurisdictional status under two scenarios. Under the first scenario, a perennial water would remain a jurisdictional WOTUS if flow is interrupted by an anomalous event, such as drought or an unusual dry spell (the Agencies are considering whether only extreme (D3) and exceptional (D4) droughts should qualify as anomalous events), so long as the interruption lasts no more than five years. After five years of a continuous anomalous event, a perennial water body would no longer be considered jurisdictional because the interruption will no longer be deemed anomalous. Under a second scenario, an otherwise perennial water body would retain its jurisdictional status where non-anomalous events occur, such as low tide or a regularly occurring dry spell, so long as the event only lasts for a single period of up to 30 consecutive days in any given year.

Second, the Agencies propose defining "continuous surface connection" to require perennial surface water in a wetland that is continuously connected to the surface water of a jurisdictional water, making it difficult to determine where the jurisdictional water ends and the wetland begins. The same anomalous and non-anomalous interruption concepts included in the "relatively permanent" definition would apply to "continuous surface connection." Only that portion of the wetland that is indistinguishably part of the jurisdictional water would be jurisdictional. The Agencies anticipate that the majority of wetlands currently treated as jurisdictional under the adjacent wetlands regimes would no longer satisfy this proposed supplemental definition.

Third, the Agencies propose defining "perennial" as "having standing or continuously flowing water every day of the year during ordinary conditions."

Departure from Sackett's Formulation

Although the Supplemental Proposed Rule invokes the Sackett majority's "relatively permanent" language, the proposed "perennial" standard arguably narrows that concept more than Sackett facially required. Sackett borrowed the phrase "relatively permanent" from Justice Scalia's plurality opinion in Rapanos v. United States, 547 U.S. 715 (2006) (Rapanos), which stated that WOTUS encompasses "only those relatively permanent, standing or continuously flowing bodies of water 'forming geographic[al] features' that are described in ordinary parlance as 'streams, oceans, rivers, and lakes.'" The qualifier "relatively" indicates something less than absolute permanence, and the Rapanos plurality expressly noted that its test did not "necessarily exclude streams, rivers, or lakes that might dry up in extraordinary circumstances, such as drought." Justice Scalia's Rapanos plurality also acknowledged that "seasonal rivers" could qualify as relatively permanent where they "chann[el] water in a permanent channel"—a concession that leaves room for waters flowing continuously for extended periods but not every day of the year, a key factor in many arid western jurisdictional waters.

The above statements leave room for argument that "relatively permanent" was intended only to exclude ephemeral or ordinarily dry channels, but not necessarily every waterbody lacking uninterrupted year-round flow. Sackett adopted the Rapanos plurality's formulation, but it did not go so far as to independently define "relatively permanent" to require standing or continuously flowing water every day of the year. The Supplemental Proposed Rule acknowledges that ambiguity but would resolve it in favor of a perennial-flow standard, reasoning that "'relatively' cannot stretch the meaning of 'permanent' to the point that 'permanent' would encompass flow for significantly less than the majority of the time."

In doing so, the Supplemental Proposed Rule potentially goes beyond what Sackett expressly required in a few ways. First, it would equate "relatively permanent" with "perennial," effectively categorically excluding intermittent streams. Second, it would introduce a 30-day bright-line threshold for non-anomalous interruptions—a numeric limit found nowhere in Sackett, Rapanos, or elsewhere in the extended WOTUS judicial history. Third, it would limit "anomalous" drought to extreme (D3) and exceptional (D4) drought classifications under the U.S. Drought Monitor. Fourth, it would treat drought lasting more than five years as the "new normal," potentially eliminating future jurisdiction over currently perennial waters. These features reflect the Agencies' policy interpretation of Sackett rather than direct codifications of the Court's holding.

The Agencies' policy interpretations are particularly relevant under the Administrative Procedure Act (APA). Neither Sackett nor Rapanos supplies a 30-day limit for ordinary interruptions. The Supplemental Proposed Rule concedes that there are "no precise, scientifically-grounded, nationally consistent time limits" for such interruptions and explains that it selected 30 days because the period "roughly" corresponds to a month and is "predictable, transparent, and easy to administer." The Supplemental Proposed Rule also acknowledges that the proposed five-year drought limit tracks the five-year expiration period for approved jurisdictional determinations outlined in the Corps' Regulatory Guidance Letter 05-02. The Agencies reason, though, that the 30-day and five-year timeframes are being proposed because they are easily administrable. However, the Agencies also acknowledge that commenters have objected to time-based thresholds as being artificial and not accounting for regional variability. There remains a significant risk that the Agencies' use of such bright-line time-based rules could be challenged in court as arbitrary and capricious under the APA without an adequate basis in the CWA or Supreme Court interpretations. Given these known objections, if adopted, the Supplemental Proposed Rule would almost certainly be subject to continuing litigation.

The Agencies' policy choices likely create vulnerabilities: the perennial-only standard may narrow what Sackett requires, while the 30-day and five-year thresholds may be arbitrary numerical limits lacking scientific foundation or adequate reasoned explanation.

What the Supplemental Proposed Rule Would Not Change

The Supplemental Proposed Rule would be limited in scope. It would not modify the proposed changes to the "interstate waters" and "lakes-and-ponds" categories. It also would leave unchanged proposed exclusions for waste treatment systems, prior converted cropland, certain ditches, and groundwater, and the definitions of "ditch," "prior converted cropland," "tributary," or "waste treatment system." The Agencies will continue to consider each of those proposals through the original NPRM.

Practical Implications

The Agencies characterize the Supplemental Proposed Rule as an Executive Order 14192 deregulatory action and state that they anticipate that the supplemental definitions will significantly reduce federal jurisdiction over streams and wetlands relative to the 2023 WOTUS rule, with the greatest effects in the arid West. The practical effect of the Supplemental Proposed Rule, if it becomes final, is that the Section 404 program is likely to see fewer permits and less required mitigation.

In practice, the proposed perennial-only standard would make the flow history of nearby waters central to any Section 404 analysis. For example, a waterbody that ordinarily lacks standing or continuously flowing water every day of the year would generally not qualify as "relatively permanent," subject to the proposed exceptions for anomalous events and a single non-anomalous interruption of up to 30 consecutive days. This would include most intermittent streams. Additionally, only the portion of wetlands with perennial surface water continuously connected to, and indistinguishably part of, a jurisdictional water would qualify as jurisdictional. If adopted, these changes could reduce federal permitting costs and timelines. However, state and local requirements could still apply.

State Regulatory Responses

The Supplemental Proposed Rule expressly recognizes that states and Tribes may regulate waters that fall outside federal CWA jurisdiction. The proposed federal narrowing may ultimately shift compliance work rather than eliminate it: state or Tribal permits, mitigation, and water-quality requirements would still apply and could, in fact, become more onerous to fill the gap left by the federal retrenchment.

For example, in California, the State Water Resources Control Board adopted its own definition of "waters of the state" that is not limited to perennial surface waters, does not require wetlands to have a continuous surface-water connection to another jurisdictional water, includes groundwater, and may encompass certain artificial wetlands.[1] Additionally, the Washington Department of Ecology is currently conducting rulemaking (under WAC 173-217 et seq.) to establish a formal State Waters Alteration Permit program to regulate dredge-and-fill and other impacts to waters of the state that are no longer covered by the federal CWA jurisdiction post-Sackett.

Due Diligence Considerations for Transactions

For now, buyers', lenders', and investors' due diligence should distinguish existing law from the NPRM and Supplemental Proposed Rule. Environmental review should identify intermittent streams, perennial waters, wetlands, and potential surface connections; evaluate current federal, state, and Tribal requirements; and assess whether the Supplemental Proposed Rule could affect development potential, mitigation exposure, or environmental liability if adopted.

The Supplemental Proposed Rule is silent on the transitional treatment of existing approved jurisdictional determinations (AJDs), preliminary jurisdictional determinations (PJDs), pending permit applications, or existing mitigation commitments. In other words, the Supplemental Proposed Rule does not state whether, if it becomes final, pending applications would be processed under the new framework, whether prior jurisdictional determinations would retain effect, and how existing mitigation obligations would be treated. Stakeholders with pending applications or existing AJDs should evaluate whether—if the NPRM and Supplemental Proposed Rule become final—withdrawal and resubmission could be beneficial, while recognizing the associated timing, cost, and permit-risk implications. Any such strategy should be considered while monitoring the Agencies' responses to comments and any transition guidance included in the final rule.

title: RFA Challenges EPA's Latest Round of Small-Refinery Exemptions in Appeals Court
description:
Circuit on the EPA's handling of the exemption petitions, focused primarily on the same legal arguments against the actions.
RFA President and CEO Geoff Cooper said in a statement to DTN his group will press EPA on its decisions.
EPA's own analyses show that RIN compliance costs are passed through to wholesale fuel buyers, meaning small refineries are not bearing a disproportionate burden.
The Renewable Fuels Association filed two previous rounds of SRE challenges after the EPA granted petitions in 2025.
"Our new filing ensures the August 2026 exemptions are properly preserved for judicial review while allowing the court to resolve the fundamental legal issues first."
text:
LINCOLN, Neb. (DTN) -- The Renewable Fuels Association filed two legal challenges to the Trump administration's granting of small-refinery exemptions to the Renewable Fuel Standard, three weeks after the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency granted exemptions on Aug. 31, 2026, totaling 1.76 billion gallons.

The RFA petitioned the U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit asking for review of that decision, as well as another decision on six other SRE petitions announced on Aug. 3, 2026.

In all, more than 30 petitions for review have been filed by a variety of interests with the D.C. Circuit on the EPA's handling of the exemption petitions, focused primarily on the same legal arguments against the actions.

The EPA announced at the end of August plans to issue a rulemaking to reallocate all gallons waived as part of the Aug. 31, 2026, announcement.

Such a proposal has yet to be put forward by the EPA.

RFA President and CEO Geoff Cooper said in a statement to DTN his group will press EPA on its decisions.

"These exemptions are unjustified and based on flawed analysis by the Department of Energy," Cooper said.

"We intend to challenge these decisions vigorously. EPA's own analyses show that RIN compliance costs are passed through to wholesale fuel buyers, meaning small refineries are not bearing a disproportionate burden. Congress never intended the SRE program to be a permanent entitlement for highly profitable oil refining companies."

The EPA, however, made a change in policy when it comes to cost passthrough.

The agency spent years arguing that refiners generally recover the cost of buying renewable identification numbers, or RINs, through fuel prices. The EPA still maintains that its analysis of the markets supports that passthrough nationally.

After a key 2024 decision in the DC Circuit on Sinclair IV v. EPA, the agency says it was no longer assuming every refinery fully passes through RIN costs, when evaluating hardship petitions.

EPA now says a refinery can experience "partial" disproportionate economic hardship, meaning refineries can receive full or partial exemptions, or denials on their SRE petitions. The EPA also uses a Department of Energy matrix that includes several different factors including refiner access to capital and credit, refining margins compared to industry averages, renewable fuel blending capacity, and other factors.

Essentially, the EPA has moved away from blanket denials of petitions and toward a case-by-case system to make that decision.

EPA granted exemptions for 2023 and 2024 totaling 160 million RINs, and then 29 more SREs totaling 1.76 billion gallons at the end of August -- the second-highest exempted volume in the history of the RFS.

The Renewable Fuels Association filed two previous rounds of SRE challenges after the EPA granted petitions in 2025.

Briefing in those consolidated cases is underway and involves the same core legal issues, including EPA's methodology for evaluating disproportionate economic hardship under the Clean Air Act.

"The D.C. Circuit is already considering these same legal questions in the case regarding SREs granted in late 2025," Cooper said. "Our new filing ensures the August 2026 exemptions are properly preserved for judicial review while allowing the court to resolve the fundamental legal issues first."
