text:
WASHINGTON, D.C. — The Texas Energy Buyers Alliance (TEBA) is pleased to announce Dawn James as its inaugural executive director, bringing an experienced Texas energy and business leader to the helm as the alliance expands its work on behalf of large energy customers across the state.

“This is a critical moment for Texas. We face unprecedented electricity demand growth, but the opportunities that come with that growth are even greater,” James said. “By advancing smart, durable energy policies, we can meet these challenges and cement the state’s economic and energy leadership for another century.”

James brings more than 25 years of experience spanning energy, technology, business strategy, and infrastructure to TEBA, the Texas chapter of the Corporate Energy Buyers Association (CEBA). Most recently, she led the executive consulting firm Sustainability Leadership & Training LLC, advising energy organizations on growth strategy, market development, and business transformation. She previously held executive roles at Microsoft and Deloitte, where she worked with Fortune 100 companies, utilities, and major corporate energy users on complex energy and technology challenges. Her career also includes energy industry experience, grounded in an early technical foundation in geoscience and engineering, with Halliburton and Schlumberger in Houston.

“Texas’ economy is booming, and it’s imperative that the power grid keeps up,” CEBA Senior Vice President for Policy Nidhi Thakar said. “Dawn will be a vital leader for TEBA — and a tremendous asset for Texas energy consumers — as she helps shape the issues that will dramatically influence the state’s economic future.”

As executive director, James will lead TEBA’s strategy, policy engagement, and growth in Texas, representing major energy customers before the Texas Legislature, Public Utility Commission of Texas, and the Electric Reliability Council of Texas.

Over the past five years, TEBA has become an active voice on a wide range of legislative and regulatory issues driving energy development in Texas. TEBA advocates for competitive energy policies that strengthen grid reliability and affordability, expand critical infrastructure, support innovation, and enable continued economic growth across Texas.

name: Louisiana Environment
title: Liberty vs. the Leviathan: Banning Diesel Exports Won't Lower Your Fuel Bill — It'll Raise It
description:
Diesel prices have gotten out of hand.
You read that right: a policy sold as lowering diesel prices would tighten the gasoline market too, hitting every driver in the state, not just truckers.
Once government gets a taste of picking winners and losers in energy markets, it rarely gives that power back.
Finalizing that rule with the current small refinery exemptions preserved or, better yet, repealing it altogether, would do more to ease prices than a new export ban ever could.
The honest fix for high diesel prices isn’t a ban, it’s more supply.
text:
Diesel prices have gotten out of hand. Every trucker, farmer, and small business owner in Louisiana feels it every time they fill up. So when Washington starts talking about “fixing” it, it’s worth paying close attention. Unfortunately, the fix on the table right now would make things worse, not better.

Here’s the idea making the rounds in the Capitol: ban U.S. companies from exporting diesel. Senate Majority Leader John Thune said this week he’s willing to consider the idea, reasoning that if we’re producing diesel and shipping it overseas while Americans pay record prices at home, keeping that fuel here should bring prices down. It sounds simple. It sounds like common sense. It is neither.

It’s important to note that refiners don’t make diesel in isolation. Rather, they make it alongside gasoline.Every barrel of crude that goes into a refinery comes out as a mix of fuels, diesel included. Take away the export market and refiners can’t just keep making the same amount of diesel and stockpile the rest. They have to cut how much crude they run, period. The American Fuel & Petrochemical Manufacturers (AFPM) trade association estimates that could mean up to 4 million fewer barrels of crude processed per day, which would drag gasoline output down with it by something like 2 million barrels a day. You read that right: a policy sold as lowering diesel prices would tighten the gasoline market too, hitting every driver in the state, not just truckers.

This is price-control logic wearing an “energy security” costume, and we’ve seen this movie before.Whether it’s rent control, wage caps, or the credit card interest rate cap Washington flirted with earlier this year, government intervention in prices always produces the same result: less supply, not more, because you can’t repeal the law of supply and demand by executive order. Diesel would be no exception.

Louisiana would take a direct hit.As AFPM’s refiners have laid out, most U.S. refining capacity, and most of the diesel we export, sits right here on the Gulf Coast. The East Coast and West Coast rely on imports because there isn’t enough pipeline or shipping capacity to move fuel from us to them cheaply, so a ban wouldn’t even reroute much Gulf Coast diesel to those markets. What it would do is shrink the market for the fuel Louisiana refiners make, threaten Louisiana refining jobs, and leave import-dependent regions of the country more exposed to a shaky global diesel market, not less.

There’s also a bureaucratic problem lurking underneath all of this. An export ban would hand Washington the power to decide, barrel by barrel, who gets to sell fuel and to whom — a licensing regime run by unelected officials deciding which companies win and which lose, dressed up as a consumer protection. That’s not how free markets work, and it’s exactly the kind of quiet expansion of federal control that starts as an “emergency measure” and never quite goes away. Once government gets a taste of picking winners and losers in energy markets, it rarely gives that power back.

Foreign refiners, meanwhile, would be thrilled.They’d keep buying cheap American crude and exporting the diesel it makes into markets we walked away from — Mexico, Latin America, Europe — while hostile competitors like Russia expand their footprint in those same markets. We’d be handing away energy influence we spent decades building, all while doing nothing to fix the actual cause of high prices: a global supply crunch tied to the wars in Ukraine and the Middle East.

Washington could also help without banning anything at all. EPA is sitting on an overdue Renewable Fuel Standard rule for 2026 and 2027, and the uncertainty around it, including whether small refinery exemptions will be granted or clawed back, is adding its own cost and volatility to diesel markets. Finalizing that rule with the current small refinery exemptions preserved or, better yet, repealing it altogether, would do more to ease prices than a new export ban ever could.

The honest fix for high diesel prices isn’t a ban, it’s more supply. That means permitting reform, pipeline capacity, and policies that let American refiners run flat-out instead of policies that force them to throttle back. At the Pelican Institute, we’ve made that case again and again on energy: Louisiana’s road to lower costs and real energy dominance runs through unleashing production, not restricting it.

text:
Democratic nominee Cait Conley will face incumbent Republican Mike Lawler in NY-17, one of the nation’s most closely watched House races. Here’s where the candidates stand on the environmental issues defining the district.

By Leana Carbonez for Inside Climate News

The Hudson River bisects New York’s 17th Congressional District, with basalt bluffs lining its western bank 40 miles north of New York City.

The district, which includes Putnam and Rockland counties, as well as parts of Dutchess and Westchester, boasts acres of protected parkland. Its lakes and reservoirs feed the Croton Watershed, a significant source of New York City’s drinking water.

This fall, the 17th district is among the most closely watched House races in what many consider the most consequential midterm elections in American history. The Cook Political Report has the district as one of 18 House “Toss-Up” races, and rates it as one of only two with a Democratic lean. This makes it one of the Democrats’ best pickup opportunities, with Republicans holding a slim 218–213 majority in the House.

The race pits Republican incumbent Mike Lawler against Democrat Cait Conley, a veteran and national security expert. She won 49.5 percent of the vote in the June 23 primary, beating Rockland state legislator Beth Davidson, who took 31.8 percent.

With President Donald Trump’s net approval rating at minus-30 among New York voters, according to polling by The Economist, Democrats hope to win over moderate Republicans.

“I am willing to cross party lines and vote for Cait Conley,” said William Knox, a resident of Dutchess County who supported Lawler in both 2022 and 2024. “He has consistently voted along lines that support the president’s agenda, rather than voting in ways that would support us, his constituents.”

Should Democrats win both the House and Senate, the midterms could put Trump’s political future in jeopardy and determine whether the United States returns to the emissions-reduction path set by the Biden administration. As it stands, Climate Action Tracker rates U.S. climate action as “Critically Insufficient.”

As the campaign has worn on, both candidates have sought to cast the other in a partisan light: Conley has painted Lawler as a lapdog of Trump’s “Make America Great Again” agenda, while Lawler has labeled Conley a Democrat allied with New York’s “radical, far-left socialists.” The race has become a mudslinging contest, rife with half-truths, over the Hudson Valley’s pocketbook issues.

Conley has focused her campaign on affordability issues, tying higher gasoline and grocery prices to Lawler’s support for Trump’s war with Iran. Lawler, meanwhile, has blamed Albany Democrats and Gov. Kathy Hochul for soaring utility costs driven by the closure of Indian Point Energy Center, the district’s retired nuclear power plant, and New York’s climate law.

Related | Is this vulnerable New York Republican trying to lose his House seat?

Data centers are another flashpoint. Rockland, where Lawler lives, has five. Lawler has seized on growing public unease over AI, spotlighting more than $328,000 in payments from two AI surveillance companies disclosed in Conley’s financial filings. He has turned a remark made in April, isolated from its context and since clarified by Conley, into a campaign cudgel; her comment, “we need data centers,” anchors a new campaign ad. Conley, in turn, has pointed to Lawler’s record, accusing him of helping turn Rockland into a data-center hub, highlighting campaign donations from Big Tech.

The campaigns have devoted considerable energy to undercutting each other’s claims, while poring over one another’s records.

Lawler won his second term in 2024, picking up 52.1 percent of the vote. He was one of only three Republicans to win a congressional district that Democrat Kamala Harris won in her unsuccessful run for the presidency.

Democrats will be buoyed in the tight race by a sizable voter registration advantage in the district. As of February 2026, there were 194,295 registered Democrats and 138,421 Republicans, widening the gap since the 2024 election.

Many environmentalists across the district are looking for change.

“I’m concerned with the direction in which things are going. And I’m not looking for perfection,” said Kate Schlott, who serves on the Ossining Environmental Advisory Council.

Many of NY-17’s environmental assets are already blighted or under threat:

In the village of Buchanan, in Westchester County, Indian Point is undergoing a $2.3 billion decommissioning project. During its more than 50 years of operation, the plant routinely discharged low levels of treated radioactive wastewater into the Hudson River. But plans to release roughly 45,000 gallons of radioactive wastewater during decommissioning, approved by a court but now under appeal, along with calls to reopen the plant, have made Indian Point a hot political issue ahead of the November elections.

PFAS, man-made “forever chemicals,” contaminate Rockland County’s drinking water, with the Trump administration moving to roll back limits on some PFAS.

A data center in Orangetown, in Rockland County, has plans for a tax-subsidised expansion. The town has passed its own data center moratorium, but it does not apply to the project, and concerns surrounding noise pollution, diesel backup generators and the potential for contaminating the adjacent Lake Tappan Reservoir have mobilized local residents.

In early 2025, Politico reported that $26 million in Biden-era clean energy and climate funding was cut from the district by the Trump administration, including a $19.7 million IBM project set to characterize, track and mitigate methane emissions.

Throughout Conley’s campaign, she has argued that the climate crisis is a national security threat, not simply an environmental issue, a position couched in her experience as director for counterterrorism on the National Security Council during the Biden administration.

Conley opposes cuts to federal residential solar tax credits, supports reinstating clean energy grant programs and has called for modernizing the electric grid. She has also advocated moving away from fossil fuels in favor of solar, geothermal and wind power, while calling for greater accountability from utility companies, promising to haul them into public hearings and subpoena their records.

Conley does not oppose data centers outright.

“My policy on data centers has been very clear. If they’re going to be built, they need to be a net positive for the communities, not extorting the communities that they’re being built in,” she said in an early September interview on CNN’s “State of the Union.”

Lawler, who appeared on the same CNN program, emphasized the importance of preserving local authority over data-center development. Asked about his vote for the House version of the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, which would have barred state and local governments from regulating AI systems, he pointed to the provision’s removal from the final bill and his record of preserving local zoning authority.

He argued that New York’s decision to shut down nuclear plants, ban natural-gas extraction and block pipeline construction is part of the reason New York is struggling to deal with the issue of data centers.

“It’s my opponent, Cait Conley, who is bought and paid for by AI and Big Tech,” he said.

Conley opposes reopening Indian Point, unlike Lawler, who recently brought Energy Secretary Chris Wright to the site. She argues that the plant’s closure reflected the safety standards and technological limitations of its era.

She has not taken a broadly anti-nuclear position. Her stance may reflect a shift in public opinion: about 60 percent of Americans now favor building nuclear power plants, up from 43 percent in 2020, according to a 2025 Pew Research Center survey. And companies like Meta, Microsoft and Amazon are turning to nuclear energy to power their data centers.

After two terms in Congress, Lawler has a more concrete environmental record for voters to consider.

The League of Conservation Voters, which tracks members of Congress’ voting records on environmental legislation, gave Lawler a 12 percent score for 2025. He voted in favor of the environment just four of 33 times, the group found. This marks a decline from his score of 18 percent in 2024 and 19 percent in 2023.

Still, among New York’s seven House Republicans, Lawler, former executive director of the New York State Republican Party, was tied with U.S. Rep. Nick LaLota for the highest 2025 score. He also ranked among the highest-scoring House Republicans nationally. He has supported clean air and water legislation, co-sponsoring the NJ-NY Watershed Protection Act in 2023, which would have established an annual $20 million fund to keep the Hudson River clean, and supporting New York’s Environmental Bond Act, which makes $4.2 billion available for environmental and community projects.

He has also secured $35.9 million in funding for 17 projects across the district, the majority supporting environmental infrastructure, including clean-water and wastewater projects, PFAS treatment, stormwater management and dam rehabilitation aimed at reducing the risk of pollution and flooding.

Lawler has been less supportive of green energy investments, arguing that New York’s climate policies place an undue burden on taxpayers. He was among a group of House Republicans who urged leaders to preserve clean-energy tax credits, warning that eliminating them could jeopardize investments and projects in their districts, but ultimately voted for the One Big Beautiful Bill Act that rolled back many of those subsidies. He has called for the repeal of the state’s landmark Climate Leadership and Community Protection Act.

In op-eds, he pits “basic economics and science” or “commonsense” against “fad green energy policies” advanced by what he calls “far-left” ideologues.

“I am somehow anti-environment for wanting to expand natural gas and nuclear—nonsense,” Lawler wrote.

Lawler co-chairs the House’s Extreme Heat Caucus and the Appalachian National Scenic Trail Caucus, and belongs to the Climate Solutions Caucus, PFAS Task Force and Conservative Climate Caucus. The latter advocates for an energy strategy that emphasises the continued use of fossil fuels—which are damaging the climate, with disastrous effects for New York and the rest of the world—alongside emerging technologies.

Related | Climate ‘overshoot’ is coming—are we ready?

Before entering Congress, Lawler was a registered lobbyist and executive director of New Yorkers for Affordable Energy, a natural-gas advocacy group whose backers included utilities and fossil-fuel interests. And, in this election cycle, Lawler has received campaign donations from a range of oil and gas interests, including $10,000 from Koch Inc.; $5,000 from California-based utility company Edison International; $4,500 from Williams Cos.; and $1,000 from Entergy, the former owner of Indian Point. He has also received personal contributions from industry executives and owners, including $8,300 from the owner of Sunshine Gasoline, a Florida-based oil retailer; $7,000 from the chairman of United Refining Co., based in Warren, Pennsylvania; and $9,500 from the president of Texas Crude Energy.

Conley is part of Unrig Washington, a program in which candidates reject corporate PAC money. While Conley’s campaign website lays out her approach to “Fighting Climate Change as a National Security Priority,” she has not made the issue a major focus of her campaign.

Neither the Conley nor Lawler campaign responded to requests for comment.

Conley and Lawler will face off in a televised debate on Sept. 28 at 8 p.m. Eastern on News 12, followed by another on Oct. 14 at 7 p.m. on PIX11. As the general election draws closer, many are hoping the debates will force the candidates to take clearer, more specific positions on the environmental issues facing the district.

text:
The following is a transcript of a speech delivered by UN Climate Change Executive Secretary Simon Stiell at the Build Clean Now Industry Acceleration Summit on Monday 21 September 2026 in New York City.

Good morning.

It’s a pleasure to join you today.

And I thank the ITA for hosting us.

The new King of New York – Knicks basketball star, Jalen Brunson said: "You’re allowed to think about the worst possible scenario. But you’ve got to go out there and do something about it."

He’s right.

Holding the rise in global temperature to 1.5 degrees Celsius this century is demanded by science, agreed by nations, and essential to protect every person and economy.

Yet exceeding that limit is now guaranteed, at least temporarily. A recent report by the UN Environment Programme reaffirms it.

How to respond?

By doing something about it: Building resilience. And cutting greenhouse gas pollution faster – to bring the temperature rise back below 1.5 degrees as quickly as possible.

That demands international cooperation, laser-focussed on implementation, supporting delivery of the targets, plans and commitments countries have agreed.

Our systems have proven they can drive real change.

UN-convened cooperation – and national efforts – have reduced the projected global temperature rise – from well over 4 degrees Celsius, to 2.6 degrees Celsius – undeniable progress but not enough to avoid catastrophe.

And the Paris Agreement – and other COPs – have helped unleash an energy revolution – even if it’s still globally uneven, and vulnerable countries need support to get fully on board.

Take new data released today by the International Renewable Energy Agency: last year, renewable capacity additions reached a record high: 693GW. That’s over half the installed power capacity of the entire United States.

And thanks to global renewables, humanity avoided almost half a trillion US dollars in fossil fuel costs. Almost half a trillion – that’s a mammoth decarbonisation dividend – that’s more than the national GDP of over three quarters of countries on Earth.

And clean energy’s attracting extraordinary investment: over USD 2 trillion last year alone. While driving jobs and growth the world over.

Friends,

Pointing to progress is not about complacency. It is essential. To combat disinformation and show that this is a fight we can win.

This is the moment to mobilise more. To narrow the gap between pledges and action on the ground.

That will be a central focus of COP31 in Türkiye, and COP32, in Ethiopia next year.

By the second global stocktake in 2028, we must show substantial progress against commitments made in the first. And, from there, identify what’s needed to close the gaps – on both implementation and ambition.

At UN Climate Change, we’re committed to finding ways to help the international process to deliver more. For example, we’re looking at whether countries could designate a representative to coordinate across governments and the private sector – to drive the transition in every industry.

And we are exploring operational opportunities to provide spaces to enhance action. For example, an Action Agenda closing plenary at COPs, alongside the negotiation closing plenaries.

The Action Agenda is a vital part of the work ahead. It's where business, investors, governments, cities and regions, and many more, come together to deliver real economy actions.

In other words, it’s the fast lane to more implementation. Key to helping countries to put their national climate plans into practice.

And there is value in strengthening it within the international process, to complement negotiations, which will remain front and centre.

Getting almost 200 countries to agree on every word is incredibly hard but incredibly important.

No single COP can fix this global crisis, but each takes meaningful steps forward.

COP31 negotiations can support accelerated implementation: enabling stronger institutions and faster technology transfer, improving flow and access to higher-quality finance, and helping countries with their own just transitions.

The Action Agenda can also drive much needed real-world progress.

The Turkish COP31 Presidency – working closely with Australia – has set clear Action Agenda targets, including for electricity to reach 35% of global energy use by 2035.

I urge countries, business leaders, investors and more to respond to the Presidency’s call. And to come to Antalya with solutions that help drive implementation at greater speed and greater scale.

That includes delivering real results to get projects off the ground in developing countries. The UN carbon market is up and running, providing potential new channels for investment.

And our focus this year is meeting existing finance commitments, boosting quality and access. Mobilising every part of the system: from public and private finance, to climate funds, Multilateral Development Banks, and more.

Together, they can get capital flowing, and move the Baku to Belém Roadmap to USD 1.3 trillion closer to reality.

This is no time to backtrack.

This is the time for all shareholders who believe in science, facts, and saving millions of lives to stand firm and step-up on climate.

Friends,

COP31 will be a big tent. Anyone with real solutions is welcome.

The ITA shows that this is what it takes to drive progress.

And your efforts are moving clean industry closer to reality, at scale.

19 commercial-scale projects reached final investment decisions in the first half of this year alone. Together, worth an estimated USD 43 billion.

You are tackling hard problems head on. Which is what this moment demands.

The UNEP Overshoot report is clear.

Bringing global temperature rise back down to 1.5 Celsius will require much greater cuts to planet-heating fossil fuel pollution.

We’ll also need carbon dioxide removals, or CDR – as the IPCC has long assumed – absolutely not as a replacement for transitioning away from all fossil fuels. But in addition to it.

Protecting and enhancing natural carbon sinks will be vital.

Despite some isolated initial efforts, the world is nowhere near ready to deliver, partly due to fears that talk of CDR hands polluters a free pass to continue business as usual.

Many of those fears may well be valid. But simply ignoring CDR is no longer viable.

More policy leaders, investors and innovators need to start tackling this issue – while recognising that transitioning away from fossil fuels can never be circumvented.

Cutting emissions – like building resilience – will always be essential.

Tech titans are increasingly central to that fight.

If AI can solve a 90-year-old math problem in days, it can do more on key climate challenges: building on existing efforts, in areas such as improving early warning systems for climate disasters. And accelerating grid efficiency.

We need every country to benefit from AI today – not vague promises of future solutions.

That means addressing the barriers faced by developing countries. And creating accessible, efficient solutions.

In the world's climate fight, there’s already a worrying two-speed global transition. AI must help bridge, not inflame, this divide.

We also need the industry to respect science and start aligning with global climate efforts – urgently.

Energy guzzling Artificial Intelligence is driving up planet-heating pollution from coal, oil and gas, while ratcheting up energy costs for households and businesses. All while fuelling disinformation, social division, and even larger inequalities of wealth.

AI leaders are now on thin ice when it comes to license to operate, and sinking deep underwater when it comes to public support.

In this country, from the Empire State, to the Lone Star State, datacentres are being put on hold. It’s a similar story in many other parts of the world.

Industry leaders need to step up, including CEOs and boards.

Tech titans need to start showing why the benefits of AI outweigh its skyrocketing costs – for the many, not just the tiny few.

By setting and delivering credible climate targets if they haven’t already.

Investing in efficiency, building on existing gains.

Coming clean about their energy and water use, and powering data-centres with renewable energy – as the UN Secretary-General has said.

Friends,

In almost all places, we're seeing an historic disconnect: between the spiralling scale of the climate crisis impacting billions of daily lives, and the calibre of the response.

This makes no sense, morally, economically or politically.

From the tragedy of the Himalayas. To brutal, economy-slowing heatwaves. And the supercharged impacts of El Niño, set to get worse. The climate crisis is now a national economic and security emergency for all nations.

It should be top of every government's agenda.

Lives and livelihoods are being wrecked. Health impacts and costs are soaring, and health systems are coming under huge strain.

Climate-disasters are hitting crop yields, driving up food prices and wider inflation.

Billions of people around the world are realising that fossil fuel dependence is hitting them hard at the fuel pump each week.

It’s been estimated that since this Middle East conflict began, fossil fuel dependence has heaped over USD 100 billion in extra costs on US consumers alone, just in higher gas and diesel prices.

Any leader serious about combatting inflation, building strong economies, and protecting their citizens, must be serious about cutting the planet-baking fossil fuels driving this climate crisis, and about building resilience.

It's clear now that countries that choose to resist the clean transition aren't protecting old industries – they're sending new innovations, sectors, jobs and pay checks to competitor economies.

Renewables are now cheaper in almost all places. The brute power of market forces is taking hold.

Last year renewables overtook coal as the world's top electricity source.

The shift to clean energy is now irreversible – as all countries at COP30 said in unison.

So friends,

For these reasons and more, we are still absolutely in this fight.

But to win will take far more.

Now's the time to double down on climate multilateralism – the bedrock of the world's progress so far.

At COP30 every nation agreed – the Paris Agreement is working, and we will make it go further and faster.

Let's get to work.

Thank you.

text:
Bipartisan lawmakers, two governors, and senior administration officials spent two days in Washington focusing on permitting, geothermal energy, nuclear power, and household energy bills during the tenth annual National Clean Energy Week, hosted by the Citizens for Responsible Energy Solutions (CRES) Forum.

The Legislative Effort

Sen. Sheldon Whitehouse (D-RI), one of four senators negotiating a permitting package, said that the group recently held a productive meeting. While declining to detail specifics, he highlighted two key provisions. The first would require developers to document prior stakeholder engagement, arguing that early engagement separates the projects that get built from those that do not. The second would establish “waypoints with spotlights” throughout the interagency review process to make clear which agency is causing a delay. Emphasizing the urgency of the work, Whitehouse described climate risk as “systemic” and compared it to economic threats such as uninsurability.

Sen. John Curtis (R-UT), who founded the Conservative Climate Caucus, cautioned about the potential consequences of permitting reform. It will not matter, he said, if a project can be canceled after it is permitted and billions spent. The market needs “predictability, consistency, and reliability,” and a tariff or reversal imposed after the money is committed is among the worst things Washington can do.

Conservative Climate Caucus Chair Rep. Mariannette Miller-Meeks (R-IA-01) noted that the House has already passed its package, warning that serial litigation against fully permitted projects creates unnecessary costs. Rep. Marc Veasey (D-TX-33), who is retiring after seven terms, urged lawmakers to act now rather than wait for the next Congress. Meanwhile, Rep. Nikki Budzinski of Illinois (D-IL-13) pointed out that permitting a single transmission line takes about seven years, framing American energy infrastructure as being at an “inflection point.”

The Agencies

Sworn in May as the 20th director of the Bureau of Land Management, which oversees roughly 245 million acres of public land, Steve Pearce grew up in an oilfield family in rural New Mexico. Raised as one of eight children on roughly $90 a paycheck, Pearce emphasized that he views affordability as a household question rather than a policy abstraction. Under his leadership, environmental assessments that took a year now take fourteen days, he said, and impact statements that took two years now take twenty-eight. He also committed the bureau to plugging every orphaned well on its land by the end of next year, and put its roughly 58,000 abandoned mines on a ten-year schedule.

Alex Fitzsimmons, an associate deputy secretary at the Energy Department, described the same push from his side. The agency has approved more than 18 billion cubic feet per day of new liquefied natural gas export capacity and prevented the early retirement of more than 20 gigawatts of dispatchable generation, which helped during Winter Storm Fern. He also pointed to a $26.5 billion loan package to Georgia Power and Alabama Power projected to save ratepayers $7 billion through lower borrowing costs.

Lastly, Jeffrey McClure, a senior advisor in the department’s Office of Energy Dominance Financing, said his office holds roughly $350 billion in lending authority, and has committed about $100 billion in the past year and intends to deploy the rest during this administration.

Photo Courtesy National Clean Energy Week

Where The Parties Agree

Geothermal drew more bipartisan enthusiasm than anything else on the agenda. Rep. Jake Auchincloss (D-MA-04), who wrote the Hot Rock Act, explained the politics plainly: Democrats like it because it is clean, and Republicans like it because it involves drilling and the techniques that make it viable came out of the American oil and gas industry. He lives in a state that pays roughly twice the national average for power, and said that abundant, affordable power is the input everything else runs on. He is betting on a microwave drilling method out of MIT’s plasma fusion lab and says it is now a question of whether it can be industrialized into the next great American industry.

Rep. Susie Lee (D-NV-03) highlighted Nevada’s role in clean energy as host to Fervo’s Project Red, the country’s first advanced geothermal plant. Geothermal runs around the clock, she noted, and the U.S. holds more than five terawatts of the resource, enough to meet the electricity needs of the entire world; the Energy Department estimates it could affordably power more than 65 million homes within 25 years. She co-led a six-bill package with a Republican colleague from Colorado that she called the most significant geothermal legislation since 1970, including a measure requiring permits under an existing lease to be processed within sixty days. All six passed the House unanimously. Any permitting deal, she added, should treat solar and wind on the same terms.

Photo Courtesy National Clean Energy Week

Pearce reported the same momentum on federal land. Fifty-one geothermal plants now operate on BLM acreage producing 2.6 gigawatts, and a recent lease auction drew 200 bidders and a record tract price. Fitzsimmons said the department has opened its largest competitive geothermal funding opportunity, at $174 million.

Nuclear ran a close second. Fitzsimmons said four executive orders aim to quadruple American nuclear capacity from roughly 100 gigawatts to 400 by 2050, backed by a $17 billion loan package. The golden age of nuclear power, he said, is here. He made a similar case for hydropower, the first renewable resource America used, noting that only about 3% of the country’s dams generate electricity and that powering a fraction of the rest could add tens of gigawatts without building anything new. The department is also funding reconductoring, which he said can double or triple the capacity of an existing line at roughly half the cost and half the time, using rights of way the country already holds.

Veasey, first elected in 2012, said that when he arrived in Congress only a handful of Democrats were bullish on nuclear, and that has changed. New Hampshire Governor Kelly Ayotte, in a recorded conversation marking the week’s tenth anniversary, said the state’s legislature has moved on a bipartisan basis to put the state at the front of small modular reactor deployment.

The Bills At Home

Sen. Curtis argued that three things now decide which energy sources win: affordability, reliability, and cleanliness, and that ignoring any one is how policy goes wrong. Government efforts to regulate toward cleaner power have mostly underperformed, he noted. The marketplace moves faster.

Rep. Miller-Meeks made the case for a technology-neutral federal framework and for biofuels, which she said are not an emerging technology awaiting a breakthrough, but something American farmers produce today. Every gallon of ethanol grown here, she added, is a gallon not bought from a foreign supplier. Citing the Energy Department, she put employment across energy and efficiency at 8.5 million Americans. When more American workers and communities hold a direct stake in what gets built, she said, the policy supporting it becomes much harder to dismantle. Iowa leads every state in wind share, generating 63% of its electricity that way in 2024 while keeping among the lowest rates in the country.

Rep. Budzinski co-convened a House working group on gas and utility affordability that heard from more than 100 stakeholders. Regular unleaded gas runs more than $4.50 a gallon in Illinois, and diesel has passed $6 for the first time, she said, arriving as harvest begins. She has pushed a bipartisan bill, already through the House, for year-round E15, a homegrown fuel she said lowers pump prices, reduces emissions, and supports American producers.

Rep. Auchincloss pointed to a lever states can pull without waiting on Washington. There are gigawatts of hidden supply already sitting on the grid, he said, and tapping it through virtual power plants and strategic battery deployment to shave peak demand could bring rates down significantly.

Rep. Juan Ciscomani (R-AZ-06) looked to copper, which supports roughly 50,000 jobs in the southwestern part of his state. He framed domestic extraction and processing as both an economic and an energy security priority, and he has moved a bill aligning the federal government’s competing critical mineral lists so that copper qualifies for expedited permitting. He also pointed to $180 million going into mining education at a time when few American universities still run a mining school, and described the work as the kind of career that keeps people outdoors and employed. He argued that Arizona can be both the “Grand Canyon State” and a copper-producing state; environmental protection and economic development are not mutually exclusive.

American Leadership

Alaska Governor Mike Dunleavy highlighted how the state tests every form of clean energy. Alaska is two and a half times the size of Texas with about 740,000 residents, and more than 220 communities sit off the grid, leading him to call it the microgrid capital of the world. Cook Inlet holds one of the world’s largest tidal resources, Southeast Alaska runs almost entirely on hydropower, and villages along the rivers are installing in-river turbines to let the salmon pass. Wind turbines run above the Arctic Circle at forty below, and solar panels work north of the Arctic Circle, and better in the cold than most assume, with clear skies and snow reflecting light back onto the array. Dunleavy noted that his personal solar setup generates a net credit on his monthly power bill.

Sen. Curtis, reflecting on a decade of National Clean Energy Week, said the movement undervalues small wins. He changed his light bulbs, rode his bicycle to work, and, as a mayor, asked residents to take one fewer car trip a week in a state with half a million vehicles. He also thinks the country can sell the combination abroad, delivering affordable, reliable, clean energy to the world and teaching others how to follow suit.

title: Climate Week Keynote Address | Prime Minister of Australia
description:
Thank you for the invitation to officially open Climate Group’s Climate Week NYC 2026.
It’s great to be here with so many champions of climate action.
Climate Group and Climate Week NYC are needed now more than ever.
And for that we have Climate Group and Climate Week NYC and so many great worldwide organisations to thank.
This is why we continue to back Pacific-led climate action and innovation to protect livelihoods, security and cultures.
text:
Thank you for the invitation to officially open Climate Group’s Climate Week NYC 2026.

It’s great to be here with so many champions of climate action.

Your CEO – Helen Clarkson.

Your Chair – my friend Mike Rann.

And of course, Ed Milliband.

Last year my Minister for Climate Change and Energy, Chris Bowen, addressed this gathering with a message of hope about the vast global move towards renewables now underway.

Climate Group and Australia have a long and strong relationship, going back to the organisation’s early days.

Climate Group and Climate Week NYC are needed now more than ever.

We understand the scale of the problem better and the need to tackle it on a far broader front.

And for that we have Climate Group and Climate Week NYC and so many great worldwide organisations to thank.

The reality of our changing climate is becoming more obvious with every season.

In the northern summer just past, there have been record-breaking temperatures and unprecedented wildfires in Europe.

Not every extreme weather event can be directly attributed to climate change. Global weather has always been treacherous.

But the science told us unmistakably that as the world warms these events will become more frequent and intense.

And those scientific forecasts have come to be.

This means the global community cannot afford to be frozen in time as the world warms around us.

Australia understands the dangers of global warming and the urgency of climate action as well as any nation.

We have seen it up close – from increasingly intense bushfires and floods, to the damage warming oceans are wreaking on our vulnerable coastlines.

In Australia, spring has arrived. With a record-breaking El Nino forecast, Australia and the Pacific nations are preparing for a potential summer of extreme heat, bushfires and floods.

As we know, in the worst of times, we often see the best of humanity.

Selflessness.

Bravery.

Compassion.

We see it in our professional and volunteer firefighters and special emergency service workers, battling for their communities.

Stepping up, volunteering to fight fires and respond to floods in countries far away – in places like Canada, the United States and or France. Part of an international fraternity of bravery.

In times of crisis, community comes to the fore.

From people who take in evacuated neighbours and give them shelter while their own homes are under threat.

To those who rescue and care for our wildlife.

Their kindness and generosity bring light in the darkest times.

As leaders, we must match their bravery.

Unfortunately, without strong action the science tells us these events will get worse and more intense.

That’s more communities facing repeated trauma.

Knowing the next flood or fire isn’t a matter of if, but when.

That’s not just true for Australia, but for every nation represented here today.

We can’t rely on the fortitude of our people alone, as tough as they are.

We need to come together, to meet the problem head on.

There’s no avoiding the scale of our responsibility – or the cost of inaction.

But there’s no denying what it also represents – another clear and urgent reason to advance the clean energy transition.

Australia understands the important role we must play.

To get behind something positive.

To move forward with a common purpose.

And to build a better future for the next generation.

Last year, I stood in the UN headquarters and announced Australia’s Nationally Determined Contribution.

Our 2035 target is to reduce emissions by 62 to 70 per cent on 2005 levels.

It is ambitious. But achievable.

Australia’s abundant renewable potential firmed by gas will get us there.

Before my government came to office just four years ago, renewables accounted for around a third of Australia’s energy grid.

At the peak of the last Australian summer, they made up half.

And we’ve since broken records in each quarter of this year.

We are now a leader in home battery installation, with Australians installing ten thousand batteries each week – more than half a million in the past year.

And we’ve now added enough wind and solar capacity to power six million households.

This in a nation of 28 million people.

Across homes and businesses, Australians are choosing to electrify.

Seeing the obvious benefits of clean, reliable, more affordable energy.

Electrification is the way to reduce emissions while maintaining economic growth.

This is why Australia is backing global efforts for electrification.

Australia is working with our partners to build new renewable energy markets and enable our region to electrify.

More solar and wind power, more batteries and storage.

And, of course, more of the critical minerals and rare earths this technology depends on.

So, we are backing our sovereign capability and renewable energy value chains.

Across everything from critical minerals processing to green metals and clean energy manufacturing.

Helping economies in our region grow – and helping the world meet its net zero goals.

Nowhere does this matter more than in the region that is our home – the Pacific.

A region where those who have contributed the least to the climate crisis are among the most vulnerable to its consequences.

This is why we continue to back Pacific-led climate action and innovation to protect livelihoods, security and cultures.

Last year, with other Pacific nations, we established the Pacific Resilience Facility.

It is the first Pacific-led regional climate financing mechanism.

It is also a promise to our Pacific family that they will not face the climate crisis alone.

We’ve backed that promise with a contribution of $100 million towards the Fund’s goal of reaching $1.5 billion capitalisation.

And we’re contributing $350 million to support climate resilient infrastructure in the Pacific as well.

This week we focus on ‘Impact’ – something I saw firsthand when I visited Palau earlier this month.

With Australia’s backing, Palau’s first large scale solar and battery project is on track to supply more than 20 per cent of its energy needs.

And displace more than a million litres of diesel consumption each year.

Elsewhere, our REnew Pacific Program is delivering everything from climate resilient classrooms in Vanuatu and Fiji to clean energy and water on one of Kiribati’s most remote islands.

The program has directly improved 300,000 lives.

Australia’s pledge to our Pacific family goes deeper than investment.

In 2023, we signed a world first agreement with Tuvalu.

The agreement not only helps Tuvaluans live and thrive in their island home, it gives them the chance to live, study and work in Australia, too.

This agreement is known the Falepili Union Treaty – after the Tuvaluan word, meaning good neighbourliness, care and mutual respect.

Australia is engaging with our entire region in this spirit.

We are backing Pacific action and innovation – turning up, following through, and creating a more connected and unified region.

Pacific nations have long been the strongest advocates for climate action.

And the value of listening to their perspectives has never been clearer.

Which is why we are working with Türkiye – and with the Pacific – through our innovative COP31 partnership this year.

And why we are working with the governments of Tuvalu and Fiji to deliver the Pre-COP Leaders’ event next month.

We will bring the eyes of the world to our region, highlight the threat climate change poses to it, and show how Pacific voices are shaping global action to counter it.

Deepening ties with our closest neighbours as we accelerate the global transition to net zero.

Australia will always advocate for stronger climate action.

Through cooperation, collaboration, investment, partnership and implementation.

We all have a role to play – with ideas, financing and energy.

Leaving no region of the world out of the solution.

And build a fairer, safer and prosperous future for all.

Thank you.

About RWE Americas RWE Americas, a subsidiary of RWE, is a US-based energy company that is helping to meet the growing demand for energy across the United States.
Backed by RWE's 125-year global legacy of managing diverse power assets, RWE Americas operates over 13 GW of power projects across 27 states.
Committed to responsible development, RWE Americas invests in local and rural communities, creating jobs and partnering with stakeholders to support and strengthen the places where we live and work.
Learn more about how RWE Americas is generating impact at americas.rwe.com.
text:
Heron is headquartered in California and plans to manufacture in the state as well. In August 2026, the company announced Heron Factory One, a 286,000 square foot facility in Morgan Hill designed to produce up to 10,000 Heron Links a year, or over 40 gigawatts (GW) of annual capacity. The plant requires more than $100 million in investment and will add over 600 jobs, with mass production beginning in late 2027. Domestic manufacturers supply less than 10 percent of the utility-scale US solar inverter market today, and few of them can meet the demand of a large renewable energy portfolio.

With more than 13 GW of operating capacity in 27 states, RWE operates one of the nation's largest renewable energy portfolios, including approximately 6 GW of solar PV and 1.2 GW of battery energy storage assets. As the company continues to expand its generation and storage footprint, RWE is evaluating technologies that can improve system performance, simplify project architectures and enhance lifecycle economics. The Heron Link pilot represents an important opportunity to assess an innovative U.S.-manufactured solution within a utility-scale operating environment and support the advancement of next-generation grid infrastructure.

About Heron Power

Heron Power Electronics Company builds hardware for a better grid, helping the electricity sector grow faster with scalable, reliable and software-controlled infrastructure. Heron's first product, the Heron Link, enables renewable energy, battery storage, and data center developers to connect directly to medium voltage transmission without a transformer. title: Mexico's Executive Branch Publishes Proposed Comprehensive Overhaul of LGEEPA
description:
Highlights Mexico's Executive Branch has proposed a comprehensive rewrite of the General Law of Ecological Balance and Environmental Protection, introducing new environmental principles, regulatory instruments and institutional arrangements.
The proposed reform is a full rewrite – not a simple amendment – replacing the current law's structure with new instruments, enforcement mechanisms and institutional arrangements.
Penalties: A Dramatic Increase The proposed reform would multiply maximum fines by up to 40 times compared to current levels.
Mexico's Federal Attorney for Environmental Protection (Procuraduría Federal de Protección al Ambiente or PROFEPA) would be renamed the "Federal Environmental Justice Agency" (Procuraduría Federal de Justicia Ambiental).
Holland & Knight's Environmental Team will continue monitoring developments related to this proposed reform and update clients accordingly.
text:
Highlights

Mexico's Executive Branch has proposed a comprehensive rewrite of the General Law of Ecological Balance and Environmental Protection, introducing new environmental principles, regulatory instruments and institutional arrangements.

The proposed reform would significantly expand environmental enforcement, including maximum fines up to 40 times higher than current levels, a new Environmental Offenders Registry and broader inspection and enforcement authority.

Companies with operations or investments in Mexico could face new environmental impact assessment requirements, longer permitting timelines, expanded environmental insurance obligations and changes to the authorities responsible for environmental permitting and compliance.

Mexico's executive branch published a draft of a bill on August 18, 2026, proposing a comprehensive renovation of the General Law of Ecological Balance and Environmental Protection (Ley General del Equilibrio Ecológico y la Protección al Ambiente or LGEEPA). LGEEPA is Mexico's primary environmental framework law and has been in effect since 1988. It is comparable to a combination of the National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA), Clean Air Act and Clean Water Act in the United States. The proposed reform is a full rewrite – not a simple amendment – replacing the current law's structure with new instruments, enforcement mechanisms and institutional arrangements. The bill is expected to enter Mexico's Congress in September 2026, with the legislative session already underway.

This Holland & Knight alert summarizes the most significant proposed changes and potential implications for companies with operations or investments in Mexico.

Background and Legislative Context

LGEEPA has been in force since 1988 and has undergone multiple amendments, but the current initiative represents the first attempt at a complete structural renovation of the statute.

The current initiative was first published on June 20, 2026, with a revised second version released on August 18, 2026.

The bill was prepared by the executive branch and is expected to be submitted to Congress during the September 2026 ordinary legislative session (periodo ordinario).

The final text is subject to modification during congressional debate.

Key Policy Principles and Guiding Framework

The bill introduces or reinforces several guiding principles, including in dubio pro natura (in case of doubt, decisions must favor environmental protection), the precautionary principle, intergenerational solidarity and environmental justice.

A new "right to a healthy environment" is explicitly codified, along with a prohibition on "environmental regression" (retroactividad ambiental), meaning that future regulations may not weaken existing environmental standards.

These principles could significantly expand the legal basis for regulatory challenges, citizen enforcement actions and judicial interpretation of environmental obligations.

Penalties: A Dramatic Increase

The proposed reform would multiply maximum fines by up to 40 times compared to current levels. The following summarizes the key changes:

The current maximum fine for general violations is 50,000 Unidad de Medida y Actualización (UMA) days (MX$5.43 million / US$271,500).

The proposal increases fines to 2 million UMA days (MX$217.26 million / US$10.86 million).

For violations involving natural protected areas or threats to human health, the proposed maximum doubles to 4 million UMA days (MX$434.52 million/US$21.73 million).

Minimum fines would also increase substantially, from 30 UMA days (MX$3,258 / US$163) to 200 UMA days (MX$21,726/US$1,086).

Fines may be doubled on a second offense, effectively quadrupling the maximum exposure for repeat violators.

These increases represent a transformative shift in enforcement economics and could materially affect compliance cost-benefit analyses for companies operating in Mexico.

Environmental Offenders Registry

The bill creates a new Environmental Offenders Registry (Registro de Infractores Ambientales), a database of individuals and entities that have been sanctioned for environmental violations.

Inclusion in the registry could result in reputational harm, restrictions on government contracting and potential impacts on financing and insurance, including posting of financial guarantees before obtaining new environmental permits or delays in securing additional environmental permits.

Registered entities are barred from federal government support programs, and restriction could last for seven to 10 years.

The registry introduces an environmental, social and governance (ESG)-relevant risk factor for companies, as listed entities may face scrutiny from investors, lenders and business partners.

Strategic Environmental Assessment (EAE)

The reform introduces the Strategic Environmental Assessment (Evaluación Ambiental Estratégica or EAE), a new instrument requiring environmental review of public policies, government programs and development plans – not just individual projects.

Institutional and Structural Changes

The bill proposes the creation of new institutional bodies, including a National Environmental Planning Council and strengthened technical advisory committees.

The internal structure of Mexico's Ministry of Environment and Natural Resources (Secretaría de Medio Ambiente y Recursos Naturales or SEMARNAT) would be reorganized to align with the new law's expanded scope, with dedicated units for climate change, biodiversity and circular economy.

The reform envisions greater coordination between environmental authorities and other government agencies (e.g., energy, mining, agriculture) through mandatory inter-institutional consultation mechanisms.

Mexico's Federal Attorney for Environmental Protection (Procuraduría Federal de Protección al Ambiente or PROFEPA) would be renamed the "Federal Environmental Justice Agency" (Procuraduría Federal de Justicia Ambiental).

Expansion of Enforcement and Inspection Powers

The Federal Environmental Justice Agency would receive expanded authority, including the issuance of precautionary measures (medidas cautelares) to prevent imminent environmental harm or act as the "offended party" in criminal proceedings.

The bill introduces new enforcement tools, including environmental audits with binding corrective action plans, enhanced whistleblower protections and broader standing for citizen complaints (denuncia popular).

Companies should expect a more aggressive enforcement posture, with greater emphasis on deterrence and compliance monitoring.

Centralization of Environmental Authority

The reform would recentralize several environmental competencies currently delegated to state and municipal governments, consolidating authority at the federal level under SEMARNAT and the Federal Environmental Justice Agency.

This could reduce regulatory fragmentation but may also create bottlenecks in permitting, particularly for projects that currently benefit from streamlined state-level procedures.

Companies with multijurisdictional operations should assess how the shift in regulatory authority could affect their permitting timelines and compliance obligations.

Environmental Impact Assessment (EIA): Revised Timelines and Procedures

The bill proposes significant changes to the Environmental Impact Assessment (Evaluación de Impacto Ambiental) process, including revised timelines for review and resolution.

Proposed timelines include 60 business days for standard EIA resolution, 90 business days for regional modality and 120 business days for projects requiring public consultation.

New requirements include mandatory climate change impact analysis, biodiversity impact assessment and a social impact component for projects affecting indigenous or local communities.

The shift from calendar days to business days effectively extends review periods by approximately 40 percent, potentially adding weeks or months to project development timelines.

Environmental Insurance

The reform would expand mandatory environmental insurance (seguro ambiental) requirements, potentially extending coverage obligations to a broader range of activities and increasing minimum coverage amounts.

Companies currently operating under existing environmental insurance policies should evaluate whether expanded requirements would require additional coverage or policy modifications.

The insurance provisions are designed to ensure financial capacity for environmental remediation, consistent with the "polluter pays" principle.

Transitional Regime and Implementation Timeline

The bill includes a transitional regime providing for a phased implementation period.

Existing environmental authorizations, permits and licenses would remain valid through their original terms, but renewal processes would be subject to the new law's requirements.

Secondary regulations (reglamentos) and official Mexican standards (Normas Oficiales Mexicanas or NOMs) would need to be updated within specified deadlines following the law's enactment.

Companies should monitor the transitional provisions closely, as the timeline for regulatory adaptation will directly affect compliance planning and operational continuity.

What Should Companies Do Now?

Conduct a gap analysis comparing current environmental compliance programs against the proposed new requirements, with particular attention to penalty exposure, insurance obligations, and permitting timelines.

Review existing environmental authorizations and assess potential impacts of the transitional regime on updates or renewal processes and ongoing operations.

Evaluate ESG disclosure and reporting implications, including potential listing on the Registry of Environmental Offenders.

Engage with industry associations to participate in the legislative process during the congressional debate period to advocate for workable implementation frameworks.

Develop a compliance roadmap and risk mitigation strategy tailored to your company's specific operations and risk profile in Mexico.

Holland & Knight's Environmental Team will continue monitoring developments related to this proposed reform and update clients accordingly. If you have any questions about the bill's potential impact on your operations or other environmental matters in Mexico, please contact our Environment Team.

description:

text:
In the heart of the lower Mississippi Alluvial Valley, some of the nation’s most productive farmland overlaps with one of its most important ecological corridors. Bottomland hardwood forests, wetland habitat and working fields all intersect the floodplain of the nation’s largest river basin.

But over the course of a century, the delicate balance of this landscape has shifted. More than 20 million acres were drained and cleared for cropland – and not always successfully. For as innovative as modern agriculture has been at transforming land, in the valley, the power of the river has proven even more powerful.

“It’s an excessive wetness problem,” says Ron Seiss, Lower Mississippi River program director and coordinator of the Tri-State Conservation Partnership, which encompasses Mississippi, Arkansas and Louisiana. “If your land frequently floods, farmers are going to struggle to make a profit on that land.”

For Ron and the partnership, restoring balance to the valley has required significant buy-in from the valley’s landowners, where between 90–95% of the land is privately owned.

To return as many acres of land back to nature as possible, Ron and the Tri-State partners connect farmers and landowners with the Wetland Reserve Easement Program, administered by the Natural Resources Conservation Service. The federal program pays landowners to take frequently flooded lands out of agricultural production, allowing restoration teams to replant native trees and reestablish wetlands.

Easements compensate landowners for the public benefits their land provides. As marginally productive farmland returns to nature, wildlife habitat is restored. The soil also holds more floodwater, preventing soil erosion and cleaning up water bound for the Gulf. For farmers, they can keep their land as an asset while continuing to farm their best acreage. For taxpayers, easements retire cropland and avoid federal payments for commodity programs, crop insurance and disaster assistance.

At the Walton Family Foundation, we believe that the most viable and lasting solutions work with the power of nature to improve water outcomes while also strengthening surrounding communities and ecosystems.

To get there, the foundation works to connect landowners to local, on-the-ground partners like the Tri-State Conservation Partnership to ensure that federal programs like the Wetland Reserve Easement Program deliver the greatest possible benefit to people and nature.

To date, more than one million acres have been placed into easements in the Mississippi Alluvial Valley.

To reach this impressive milestone, Seiss and his team have built a deep bench of local support, like The KKAC Organization, a land retention and agricultural organization serving farmers and landowners with limited resources based in the Arkansas Delta.

Across the rural South, Black farmers and landowners once owned nearly 20 million acres. A combination of discriminatory practices and a lack of proper estate planning caused this number to crater, and by 1997 around 90% of this land was lost. Currently, Black landowners own between 7–10% of the land in the valley.

The KKAC Organization provides education and technical assistance on estate planning and heirs’ property issues, and helps connect landowners to federal and state conservation programs, such as the Wetland Reserve Easement program.

Wilbur Peer is the founder of The KKAC Organization. Growing up on 40 acres of farmland, Peer says his large family had a strong work ethic and “grew everything that we ate. We had cows. We had chickens, guineas and ducks. The garden was not far from the house, and we grew tomatoes, cucumbers, cabbages and greens. We milked the cow. My daddy did what he had to do to feed all of us. He sold moonshine and barbecue on the weekends. We didn't focus a lot on natural resources. It was just survival.”

When Peer was 12 years old, he asked his father why he wouldn’t just sell his land and move the family to Chicago.

“He was a lot smarter than me, because I didn't realize how valuable land was at the time. That’s part of why we are doing this with the people here today.”

Rather than selling their land, Peer and the team at KKAC help landowners find other ways to keep it in the family through conservation, creating generational wealth and connecting younger people to their roots in the Delta.

“Farming is a good life,” says Peer. “Owning land, walking outside into a forest that you own and just listening to nature, fishing or hunting makes you feel a sense of self-worth.”

Working with organizations like KKAC, the Tri-State Conservation Partnership has become a nationwide model of how communities can work with nature to become more climate resilient.

text:
Keeping Up with Data Centers

From the Western Ag Network, I’m Bob Larson. More data centers are bringing new challenges for utilities across rural America.

Jim Matheson, CEO of the National Rural Electric Cooperative Association, says as electricity demand continues to rise, utilities will need both new and existing resources to maintain reliability …

MATHESON … “It’s going up, and it's going up a lot, and it requires a significant amount of new generating capacity to meet that need. It also requires us to stop shutting down power plants that still have useful life, which public policy has been encouraging over the last few years in this country, and we've got to stop doing that because we need to make sure we can keep the lights on at an affordable price."

Despite the growing debate around data centers, Matheson says the issue is not whether or not communities should support data centers, because that’s not the right question …

MATHESON … “But what we are for is making sure that our utilities have the ability to make the decision that's right for them in their local community. We don't like one-size-fits-all mandates on data centers or any other policy, quite frankly, that's out there. Because different geographic locations have different characteristics, different capacities, different needs, and different challenges. And the extent that you can maintain that autonomy and local control in making decisions from an electric cooperative standpoint, that drives through all of our policy advocacy that we do.”

Jim Matheson, CEO of the National Rural Electric Cooperative Association.

name: North Carolina Clean Energy
title: The Trump Administration's Actions Are Increasing Utility Bills in Arizona
description:
Working-class Americans are concerned about being able to afford their utility bills, and the Trump administration is not helping them; in fact, in states such as Arizona, the administration’s actions are resulting in increased costs for Americans.
Arizona households are projected to pay an additional $140 per year on their energy bills by 2030 due to the One Big Beautiful Bill Act (OBBBA) that congressional Republicans passed and President Trump signed into law last summer.
The administration’s actions will ensure that electricity prices continue to rise in Arizona and beyond.
Despite President Trump’s promises on the campaign trail to lower costs, the administration’s actions will ensure that electricity prices continue to rise in Arizona and beyond.
The tracker is not comprehensive and does not include every utility that is currently seeking an increase in utility rates.
text:
Despite President Donald Trump’s campaign promise to lower electricity prices, they have continued to rise since he took office and have even outpaced wage growth, meaning household electric bills are rising faster than paychecks. With rising energy demand, an aging grid in need of modernization, and increasingly severe weather threats, millions of customers across the country are either already paying more for their electricity or will see higher prices in 2026 and beyond. Working-class Americans are concerned about being able to afford their utility bills, and the Trump administration is not helping them; in fact, in states such as Arizona, the administration’s actions are resulting in increased costs for Americans.

Arizona households are projected to pay an additional $140 per year on their energy bills by 2030 due to the One Big Beautiful Bill Act (OBBBA) that congressional Republicans passed and President Trump signed into law last summer. The OBBBA reduces new energy capacity additions at a time of rising energy demand compared with the trajectory before the law was enacted. In addition, Arizona Public Service (APS) and Tucson Electric Power (TEP)—which together serve about 1.85 million people, or 52 percent of the state’s electric utility customers—are seeking approval for annual rate increases that would further increase electric bills in the coming year. APS’ request would yield $608.7 million in additional revenue and, if approved, is likely to go into effect in early 2027, while TEP’s request would yield $135 million in additional revenue and would likely go into effect by December 1, 2026.

According to Center for American Progress research and calculations, if the requests are approved, APS and TEP customers would together pay an additional $1.50 billion across all sectors through 2028 and an additional $240 and $186 per year, respectively, on average residential electricity bills.*

In general, more investment in the power system is a good thing. The country needs to replace aging grid infrastructure, increase generating capacity to meet growing demands for electricity, and prepare for climate change. However, those needed investments are now coming at a higher cost as both companies request rate increases. In their applications, APS and TEP cited current federal policies and administrative actions that contribute to higher costs for both the companies and their customers.

$1.50B

Total increase in APS and TEP customers’ payments across all sectors

$240

Average annual increase in each APS customer’s residential electricity bills

$186

Average annual increase in each TEP customer’s residential electricity bills

Uncertain economic conditions increase costs for utilities

Utilities are a capital-intensive industry sensitive to changing market conditions, including high inflation and interest rates. In testimonies before the Arizona Corporation Commission, representatives for both APS and TEP warned that Trump administration policies could potentially lead to higher inflation and interest rates.

APS witness testimony cited changes in U.S. trade policy, such as the implementation of the current administration’s tariffs, as likely to drive up inflation and interest rates, consequently concluding that these policies would increase the cost of debt and equity for APS. Despite the U.S. Supreme Court’s reversal of some of the tariffs in February 2026, APS’ witness testified during an April hearing that the ruling itself was a new source of economic uncertainty. Similarly, a TEP witness testified that significant policy changes—particularly the tariffs—would lead to higher inflation and unemployment rates, resulting in higher cost of debt and equity.

Now, both the utilities have requested higher returns on equity, which is the rate of shareholder profit that investor-owned utilities are allowed to collect from customer bills—meant to reflect the cost of capital. APS requested a return on equity of 10.7 percent, up 0.45 percentage points from its prior rate case request, while TEP requested a return on equity of 9.75 percent, the same return on equity TEP requested in its prior rate case but up 0.20 percentage points from what was ultimately adopted.

Energy generation and grid investments are being restricted or lost

Cuts to federal funding are also taking a toll. On January 7, 2025, APS also received a conditional commitment for a loan guarantee of up to $1.81 billion through the Inflation Reduction Act’s Energy Infrastructure Reinvestment program to help finance the utility’s investments in transmission projects, renewable generation, and energy storage systems. APS’ first investment supported by the loan was the construction of a four-hour 150-megawatt battery storage facility sited next to an existing solar facility. However, in January 2026, the U.S. Department of Energy confirmed that the loan commitment for APS was canceled. While it has not been confirmed who initiated the cancellation of the loan, Arizonans will lose out on approximately $250 million in total savings for customers over the life of the loan guarantee.

The administration’s actions will ensure that electricity prices continue to rise in Arizona and beyond.

APS also confirmed that potential changes to the tax benefits received through the Inflation Reduction Act tax credits could directly affect customer rates. APS witness testimony revealed that the IRS notified the company of the intent to examine its federal tax returns. The witness mentioned that the examination would likely be on the company’s 2023 and 2024 general business tax credits—including investment tax credits for a battery storage facility and nuclear production tax credits—and could potentially result in adjusted tax benefits. Further APS testimony also stated that the company is awaiting federal guidance on eligibility and phase-out requirements before passing on benefits from nuclear production tax credits.

A Plan for American Electricity Affordability

A Plan for American Electricity Affordability

Trevor Higgins, Shannon Baker-Branstetter, Michael Negron, 2 More Lucero Marquez, Kendra Hughes

Conclusion

Arizonans, particularly those who are customers of APS and TEP, will likely pay more on their electricity bills in the coming years. Despite President Trump’s promises on the campaign trail to lower costs, the administration’s actions will ensure that electricity prices continue to rise in Arizona and beyond.

* Authors’ note: These estimates are based on the methodology used for CAP’s “Electric and Natural Gas Utility Rate Hikes Tracker,” last updated on August 5, 2026. The tracker is not comprehensive and does not include every utility that is currently seeking an increase in utility rates. Please also note that both APS and TEP have revised their requests since the last “Electric and Natural Gas Utility Rate Hikes Tracker,” which this column has accounted for in its calculations as of September 17, 2026.
