text:
JUST weeks after the United Nations Environment Programme released its grim report concerning climate change and the future of humanity, the Trump administration has repealed pollution limits on fossil-fuel power plants. This rule change is happening despite the fact that power plants are the second-largest source of greenhouse gas emissions – the very same emissions scientists and climate activists say are the cause of global warming.

The reversal was announced by Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) administrator Lee Zeldin at the G20 Energy Abundance Ministerial Meeting on September 14 in Houston. He claimed the move “delivers reliable and affordable energy in the largest power sector deregulatory action in US history,” and that it is “expected to unleash the full potential of America’s vast energy resources, including coal and natural gas.”

Zeldin alleged that former presidents Joe Biden and Barack Obama implemented “a war on coal to destroy reliable and affordable energy” and boasted that the Trump administration “has come to protect American energy.”

The administrator’s comments continue a pattern where the EPA, under a president who said climate change is the “greatest con job ever perpetrated on the world,” has prioritised exalting the fossil fuel industry and thwarting the growth of clean energy initiatives such as solar, wind, and hydropower.

In February, Trump announced the official termination of the EPA’s 2009 landmark determination that greenhouse gases warm the planet and threaten the health and welfare of those who inhabit it. In 2025, the president referred to oil as “liquid gold” and created the National Energy Dominance Council as a means to expand US fossil fuel and energy production.

Doug Burgum, who serves as secretary of the Department of the Interior (DOI) and chairs Trump’s National Energy Dominance Council, stood alongside Zeldin during the announcement on power plants. He claimed that the EPA’s repeal of pollution rules would save Americans “hundreds of millions of dollars” and put an end to “the Biden administration’s disastrous Green New Scam policies.”

The EPA’s lofty claim of delivering $300+ billion (£224 billion) in savings to Americans might sound appealing in the middle of an affordability crisis, but independent researchers and advocates question whether Trump’s EPA is making false promises and ignoring the science.

While Zeldin and his colleagues claim that during periods of peak electricity demand coal and natural gas continue to “keep the lights on,” recent reports show that coal is actually driving higher utility costs for consumers. The non-partisan think tank Energy Innovation noted that coal power was 28 per cent more expensive in 2024 than in 2021 and that “coal’s already poor economics are getting worse as aging plants make coal power more expensive.” The organisation also referred to another study that showed “coal plants were more expensive to continue operating compared to replacement with local wind or solar.”

In nearly every part of the United States, people are seeing a rapid rise in their energy costs lately. Electricity and home energy bills have risen faster than inflation—climbing an estimated 21 per cent to 30 per cent over a three- to four-year period.

The quick jump for power bills has been attributed to a number of influences.

The top two reasons experts point to are, first, the high energy demand of AI data centres straining existing energy capacity (data centres which Trump champions) and, second, the extreme weather of hotter summers and freezing winters resulting from the climate change that the president doesn’t believe in.

In a press release announcing the power plant pollution rule elimination, the EPA maintained that “models” show greenhouse gas emissions from power plants have no “material impact on global climate change.” The claim provided no details on what models the agency was referring to or what science it relied on to make such an assessment.

Environmental advocates and scientists paint a different picture, one where continued pollution will impose detrimental costs for millions, both medically and financially.

Resources for the Future, an independent nonprofit research institution based in Washington, asserts that any savings made from the EPA’s continued deregulation of fossil fuels will be surpassed by the health damages many people will face as a result of increased emissions. The organisation estimates that the free flow of power plant air pollution will increase health issues among the public, bringing additional health costs of up to $476 billion (£355bn).

Advocates, political leaders, and medical professionals are also sounding the alarm on what they see as the immense danger the latest EPA move poses to working people.

“The administration is once again green-lighting massive corporate pollution with no regard to how it will harm our environment, climate, or Hoosiers struggling to afford their daily lives,” said Robyn Skuya-Boss, director of the Sierra Club Hoosier Chapter in Indiana. Hoosiers is a nickname give to residents of Indiana. Last year, that state’s coal plants released more than 5.2 million metric tons of carbon dioxide.

“These protections have been essential guardrails to improving the health and safety of our communities from soot, smog, and toxic air pollutants. This dirty and dangerous rollback comes at the same time the administration is using illegal bailout orders to keep two of Indiana’s coal plants online at Hoosiers’ expense rather than close as planned in December 2025.

“Over and over again, the Trump administration demonstrates it cares more about forcing Indiana to burn coal than it does the health and welfare of Hoosiers,” Skuya-Boss asserted.

American Lung Association President and CEO Harold Wimmer noted in a statement that leaving the rules in place would have “resulted in other immediate health benefits,” such as reducing emissions of harmful oxides of nitrogen, sulphur dioxide, and particulate matter from coal-fired power plants, preventing “1,200 premature deaths in 2035.”

Though the Trump administration is wasting no time in moving forward with its fossil fuel initiatives, the fight for clean air may not be over just yet. Just days after Zeldin’s announcement, a number of organisations have come forward to sue the administration to stop the rule elimination.

The Natural Resources Defense Council (NRDC), American Lung Association, American Public Health Association, Clean Air Council, Clean Wisconsin, and the Environmental Defense Fund filed suit, alleging that the EPA was failing in its “legal responsibility to protect health and the environment.”

The federal climate legal director at NRDC, Meredith Hankins, wrote in a statement: “The Clean Air Act and Supreme Court precedent demand that the EPA address climate pollution from the largest industrial source in the nation. The EPA’s legal reasoning is fatally flawed, so we are going to court.”

authors: Kelly Hinchcliffe, NC Local, Engin Akyurt

text: North Carolina leaders announced a $590 million deal last week with DuPont and Chemours for damages related to contamination by "forever chemicals" in the state. The settlement, which includes money to protect future drinking water and clean up pollution, is the largest total environmental damages recovery in North Carolina's history, according to N.C. Attorney General Jeff Jackson. This week, NC Local answers questions about the settlement and explains what PFAS are, why it's so dangerous and who is most affected in North Carolina. What are PFAS? PFAS, short for per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances, are a group of man-made chemicals that can be found in everything from drinking water to food packaging and shampoo. Known as "forever chemicals," they don't fully break down in the environment and can build up in humans' and animals' blood, causing health issues. Where are PFAS found? PFAS can be found in people, animals and the environment around the U.S. and the world. The most common way people are exposed is through drinking water, because most towns' and cities' drinking water treatment systems are not built to filter out PFAS. Until recently, testing labs were not able to detect them at lower levels, according to the North Carolina Department of Environmental Quality. Showering and bathing in water containing PFAS should not significantly increase exposure, according to the federal Agency for Toxic Substances and Disease Registry. Some common places you might find PFAS include: Drinking water Firefighting foams Water-repellent clothing Stain-resistant fabrics and carpets Fish from contaminated bodies of water Grease-, water- and oil-resistant products Crops and livestock raised in polluted soil or water Cleaning products and paints, such as polishes, waxes, varnishes and sealants Personal care products, such as cosmetics, dental floss, shampoo, nail polish, etc. Who is most affected by PFAS? Most Americans have been exposed to PFAS, according to the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency. Most people have relatively low levels in their body, but some can be high, especially if they are exposed to a concentrated source over long periods of time, especially through drinking water. In 2016, North Carolina officials found that Chemours had been releasing PFAS from its Fayetteville Works industrial plant into the Cape Fear River and surrounding groundwater, soil and air. The river provides drinking water to more than 500,000 people. The 11 areas most affected by the pollution include: Bladen County Brunswick County Columbus County Cumberland County New Hanover County Robeson County Sampson County Town of Wrightsville Beach City of Lumberton Village of Bald Head Island Lower Cape Fear Water and Sewer Authority How will the settlement money be used? Last week's settlement gives $455 million to the state and 11 local governments, paid over the next 10 to 15 years. Of that amount, $75 million will be given to the state with about $55 million going to an Emerging Contaminant Mitigation Fund recently created by the North Carolina General Assembly. The fund supports efforts by local governments to detect and reduce contaminants in drinking water. The remaining $380 million will be divided among the 11 local governments that were affected by Fayetteville Works' pollution and previously sued Chemours and DuPont. The deal also establishes a $135 million reserve fund from DuPont and sister company Corteva to guarantee the work that Chemours must continue to complete for decades under the NC Department of Environmental Quality's 2019 consent order. The consent order requires Chemours to provide clean drinking water to families whose well water is polluted with PFAS from Fayetteville Works. If Chemours can't pay due to financial problems, the state can tap into a reserve fund of $135 million to make sure families continue receiving clean drinking water. Cumberland County leaders say efforts to give residents safe, clean drinking water were already underway before the settlement, thanks to $50 million in federal and state funding. But, the new money will help continue that work. Phase 1 of the county's Gray's Creek Water System includes more than 5 miles of water main and is planned to provide public water service to 218 existing homes, including 184 properties impacted by PFAS contamination, according to the county. "The board has not yet made specific decisions about how the settlement funds will be allocated," Cumberland County Commissioners Chairman Kirk deViere told NC Local. "Those decisions will be made as the county continues developing permanent infrastructure and other long-term water solutions." "The lawsuit was about accountability," deViere added. "The settlement provides resources. The work ahead is about solutions. The settlement is not the finish line. We will continue pursuing state, federal and other available resources as we expand access to clean, safe, regulated drinking water." In Bladen County, commissioners have not formally voted on how to use the settlement money, but their "unanimous desire" is to make significant repairs to the existing water systems, Chairman Cameron McGill told NC Local. "Because of the age of the infrastructure, there are many areas in our county that are either underserved, poorly served, or not served at all by county water," he said. "We are currently going through a very extensive and exhaustive study and have been getting reports at each of our commissioner meetings regarding water issues that our citizens are experiencing. We will do everything in our power to stretch these funds as far and that wide across our county as possible." Sampson County commissioners also have not voted on how to use the money but have entertained some ideas, Chairman Allen McLamb told NC Local. They hope to get the first settlement check in October or November, but the exact amount is unclear at this time. "We want to definitely use it in the direction of our enterprise water system to assist some people who are not able to get water. I think that would be a big push of what we're looking at," McLamb said. "When the money starts coming, I can promise you it won't just be put in the general fund and wasted. It's going to be used in a way that will benefit the county and the citizens that have been affected by PFAS." Why are PFAS so dangerous? Studies have shown that exposure to higher levels of PFAS have been linked to a number of health problems, including increased risk of cancers, such as kidney and testicular cancers, fertility issues, developmental delays in children and other ailments, according to the EPA. The highest-risk populations include children, pregnant women, industry workers and people who live or work near high-risk facilities, such as military bases, shipyards, chemical plants, refineries, or airports, according to the Massachusetts Medical Society. Other issues associated with PFAS exposure include: Bone variations Low birth weight Behavioral changes Accelerated puberty Reduced vaccine response Interference with the body's natural hormones Increased cholesterol levels and/or risk of obesity Increased high blood pressure in pregnant women Reduced ability of the body's immune system to fight infections Babies born to mothers who were exposed to PFAS can also be exposed: Before they are born While breastfeeding Drinking formula mixed with PFAS-contaminated water. What should I do if I'm worried about PFAS in my water? If you are a customer of a public water system, contact your water provider to find out whether they have sampled for PFAS and what steps they are taking to address any issues. Find your county contact here. Some systems are voluntarily monitoring for PFAS. North Carolina DEQ officials say they have also sampled 580 water systems and will continue to test systems to assess the impacts of PFAS across the state. If you have a private well, consider having your water sampled by a certified lab. In most cases, private well owners are responsible for well sampling. The NC DHHS Filtration Options and Sampling Factsheet includes information on how to have your well sampled. DEQ has launched a pilot program under the Bernard Allen Emergency Drinking Water Fund to support North Carolina residents with PFAS contamination in their private water wells. Funding for treatment systems will be provided to eligible residents with PFAS contamination that equals or exceeds health advisory levels, on a scale based on household income. The program is meant to help when there is no designated responsible party that provides alternate drinking water. If you are a resident of the Cape Fear River Basin, you may already be eligible for well testing related to GenX contamination and other PFAS chemicals attributed to the Chemours facility: Bladen, Cumberland, Robeson, or Sampson counties Brunswick, Columbus, New Hanover, or Pender counties Potentially affected residents can call (910) 678-1101 or register online to request testing. If your water is found to be contaminated, you may be entitled to alternative water options, including bottled water service or filtration systems. Can I get tested for PFAS exposure? PFAS can be measured in the blood, but that type of blood test is not widely available. The CDC and Agency for Toxic Substances and Disease Registry developed a PFAS Blood Estimation Tool to help people understand how they might be exposed to PFAS and offer options for reducing exposure. PFAS leaves the body through excretion, mostly through urine, menstruation and breastmilk. People who have kidney disease may not excrete as much from their body as healthy individuals. Some PFAS leave the body slowly over time. Exposure and excretion are different for each person and two members of the same household may have very different PFAS levels in their bodies, according to the Agency for Toxic Substances and Disease Registry. Why were PFAS created? PFAS have been used since the 1940s for practical reasons, such as keeping food from sticking to packaging or cookware and making clothing and carpets water and stain resistant. Thousands of different PFAS exist, but some have been more widely used and studied than others, including Perfluorooctanoic Acid (PFOA) and Perfluorooctane Sulfonate (PFOS). They have been replaced in the U.S. with other PFAS in recent years. Some may have properties similar to the existing PFAS, while others may be less persistent in the environment. There are very few scientific studies on new PFAS, so more research is necessary to discover whether they may be a health concern, according to the federal Agency for Toxic Substances and Disease Registry. text:
The U.S. EPA is continuing its effort to repeal air quality regulations with proposals to rescind rules for power plant emissions, a move Indiana environmental advocates say strips the agency of its tools to combat climate change.

The repeal, which EPA Administrator Lee Zeldin called the "largest power sector deregulatory action in U.S. history," undoes most Biden-era greenhouse gas requirements for fossil-fuel-burning power plants. The agency estimates the rollbacks will save Americans $300 billion.

The rollbacks target two regulations – carbon pollution standards and greenhouse gas emission standards for power plants burning fossil fuels. Greenhouse gases, such as carbon, trap heat in the atmosphere when emitted.

The agency's actions remove "burdensome regulations that threaten America's power supply," Gov. Mike Braun said in a Sept. 17 written statement praising the move. "This commonsense approach will support American workers, strengthen energy security and help lower costs for families and businesses."

President Donald Trump's EPA rolled back the rules in response to what Zeldin called former Presidents Barack Obama and Joe Biden's "war on coal."

"The Trump administration has come in to protect American energy and to make sure you can afford to keep the lights on," Zeldin said in a Sept. 17 news release. "Americans will see a decrease in electricity prices, but this is just the beginning."

Public health and environmental groups disagree with the premise the rollbacks will save Americans money and expressed concern that the change in policy might endanger people's health.

"The Administration is once again green-lighting massive corporate pollution with no regard to how it will harm our environment, climate, or Hoosiers struggling to afford their daily lives," Robyn Skuya-Boss, Sierra Club Hoosier Chapter director said in a release. "Over and over again, the Trump administration demonstrates it cares more about forcing Indiana to burn coal than it does the health and welfare of Hoosiers."

National health and environmental groups have already filed a lawsuit against the rollbacks.

Indiana group says rollbacks target 'essential guardrails'

September's rollbacks follow EPA's recent repeal of the Endangerment Finding for motor vehicles. The back-to-back actions led the Sierra Club Hoosier Chapter to charge in a Sept. 16 news release that the EPA is engaged in a "sweeping effort to dismantle the legal foundation for federal climate regulation."

"These protections [the ones that EPA proposes rolling back] have been essential guardrails to improving the health and safety of our communities from soot, smog, and toxic air pollutants," Skuya-Boss said.

The recent proposed rollbacks are taking place when renewable energy sources, such as solar and wind, outperform coal in the energy marketplace, according to the release. This May, the U.S. reached a new milestone when solar supplied more energy than coal in the U.S.

Renewable energy sources do not emit harmful pollutants or compounds that trap heat in the atmosphere and warm the Earth. Burning coal and other fossil fuels releases toxins such as carbon monoxide, sulfur dioxides and nitrogen oxides.

Indiana calls repeal 'overwhelmingly positive'

But state officials say there's no reason for concern.

EPA's proposed rollbacks don't weaken or remove rules or standards that protect public health, Indiana Department of Environmental Management Commissioner Clint Woods wrote in an email to IndyStar.

"U.S. EPA's proposed repeal of burdensome greenhouse gas regulations for power plants represents an overwhelmingly positive development for Hoosiers across the state," Woods wrote.

Nearly all of Indiana's counties meet federal air quality standards, Woods wrote, and repealing the greenhouse gas rule would not change current protections or negatively impact local air quality.

IDEM last year submitted comments saying the Biden-era standards would have forced economic and environmental trade-offs.

"Instead of improving air quality, these unscientific regulations would have passed enormous costs on to American utilities, ratepayers and state agencies to the tune of $300 billion nationwide while producing minimal greenhouse gas reductions and with no measurable impact on global temperatures or climate-associated events," Woods wrote.

The Indiana Energy Association, a trade group representing the energy sector in the state, is still evaluating the overall impact of the repeal, Danielle McGrath, president of the group, wrote in an email to IndyStar.

"We are supportive of efforts by the administration that prioritize electric reliability and help drive down costs for customers," McGrath wrote. "A reliable and affordable electric system requires a balanced approach to environmental policy, resource planning, and the investments needed to meet Indiana's growing energy needs."

Rollbacks benefits may not trickle down

Some experts, however, question the claim that the measures would save Americans $300 billion.

"Yeah, that number is completely bogus," said Gabe Filippelli, executive director of Indiana University's Environmental Resilience Institute. "It's not analogous to any kind of real savings."

The EPA figures likely represent savings for the energy industries, but do not take into account the global health impacts and costs of continued reliance on fossil fuels, Filippelli said.

Regulations, Filippelli said, come from understanding the negative impacts certain operations have on human health and how to reasonably lessen those impacts. Because capitalism does not strive to make communities safer or healthier, regulations make sure things are done right and cleanly, he said.

"The fact we have such a strong body of knowledge to reinforce why the regulations are necessary to protect people, it's really disheartening to see them simply disregarded for the benefit of fossil fuel corporations," Filippelli said.

A history of greenhouse gas regulations

The regulations these rollbacks target date back to the robust 1970 Clean Air Act, which grants federal administrative agencies the authority to set rules around air pollution.

In the 1990s, a group of non-governmental organizations asked the EPA to regulate motor vehicle emissions, which can harm public health and the environment.

In 2003, the George W. Bush administration decided not to act for reasons that remain vague, said Janet McCabe, visiting professor at Indiana University and former deputy administrator for the EPA under Biden.

Then, in 2009, the EPA agreed to move forward with regulating mobile greenhouse gas emissions. This idea expanded to stationary emissions in 2015 when regulations were designed for coal- and gas-fired power plants.

During Trump's first term, the administration had a very different view of climate change and regulations, McCabe said. The battle of regulations moved from executive decisions into the court system where a series of cases dictated EPA's authority regarding the regulations.

When Biden took office, the EPA started working on new power plant rules consistent with previous court rulings that were more proactive than what Trump's first administration put forward.

The most recent moves represent a 180-degree turn on climate change regulations.

"This time, they are making an effort to legally undermine EPA's ability to ever use the Clean Air Act to regulate greenhouse gas pollution," McCabe said.

Current rollbacks open for public comment

The EPA has a comprehensive webpage for these rollbacks, complete with the prior rules, additional resources and information on how to make public comments.

The agency is holding a public hearing Oct. 1 online.

text:
WASHINGTON — Dozens of U.S. Army Corps projects in New Jersey, drawn up with meticulous paperwork, congressional legwork and painstaking engineering, are about to get approval from Congress.

Meanwhile, the Army Corps, the nation’s public-works agency known for dredging, dams and flood studies, has moved to revoke the approval of eight projects in New Jersey because they have received limited or no funding. The potential cancellation of those projects is part of a nationwide decision the Corps completed Aug. 20 to “deauthorize” hundreds of its projects nationwide.

The Army Corps said in May it was reviewing projects Congress authorized but had yet to fund. “This process is intended to identify projects for Congress to deauthorize and allow the continued authorization of projects that remain viable for construction,” Adam Telle, assistant secretary for the Army’s civil works division, said in a public notice.

The eight in New Jersey have been on the books for decades, and while they each had congressional approval, they lacked the other essential ingredient: money.

Before the House left town Wednesday night, members overwhelmingly passed a bipartisan bill — the vote was 415 to 9, with every New Jersey member in favor — to approve thousands of Army Corps projects across the country. The bill, known as the Water Resources Development Act, is widely popular and a clear way for members to draw attention to specific projects they helped pass. Once the Senate finishes its draft of the bill, the chambers will negotiate one final version that can become law.

A significant element contained in the House bill for New Jersey is construction approval for a flood-mitigation Corps project in the Meadowlands expected to cost more than $278 million, about $181 million of which would come from the U.S. government. That project, known as the “East Riser,” is one piece of a multi-step program across New Jersey and New York that has been underway for years.

Construction for some of the East Riser would take place just south of Teterboro Airport. The project “will allow for construction of these drainage improvements to maintain continuity of operations at Teterboro Airport during heavy local rainfall without inducing flooding downstream,” Lt. Gen. William Graham Jr. of the Corps said in a report, dated July 6, which recommended the project to the Pentagon.

The plan calls for removing and replacing two culverts under bridges, upgrading a different railroad bridge and replanting vegetation, among other steps — all moves the Corps says could cut flood risk by 26% to 29%.

“In our North Jersey communities, flooding is not some distant threat. In just the last few weeks, our communities have seen terrible flash floods turn streets into rivers, destroying homes, cars, and small businesses and upending lives,” Rep. Nellie Pou (D-9th), a member of the House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee, which wrote the bill, said in statement Thursday.

Pou folded 10 projects and studies into the House bill, including one to expedite a project in Clifton and another in the Meadowlands about potential reuse of dredged materials.

Once a federal project gets congressional approval, it still needs funding. That money almost always comes through the yearly appropriations process.

“When mom and dad say that you get an allowance, they don’t say, ‘Go to the bank and pick it up,’” Donald Norcross said in an interview with NJ Spotlight News.

Norcross, a Democrat who represents a South Jersey seat, said it can take decades for Army Corps projects to be completed. Sometimes, he said, the money comes in multiple batches.

“Many of them hit a limit each year. So you go up the authorized amount,” Norcross said. Often a Corps project begins with a congressional study. For example: a study Norcross attached to the bill to examine flooding from Little Tiber Creek, a tributary of the Delaware River, and across Gloucester and Camden counties.

“If the study comes back showing that we need work, then there’s the appropriations for the actual design of the project and then we get into the point of money,” Norcross said.

“Anywhere on the Delaware and the tributaries feeding into it, we have general problems,” Norcross said of the Delaware River, noting that many towns he represents were built long before modern flood mapping and engineering.

“It is not going to be a cheap fix because it encompasses such a large area,” he said of the Little Timber project.

Rep. Jeff Van Drew (R-2nd), whose coastal district is acutely vulnerable to flooding, said his fingerprints are on 11 elements of the bill, including a study on “hot spot” erosion affecting Atlantic City.

“South Jersey is surrounded by water, and our towns deal with flooding, erosion, aging dams, and waterways that need our full attention,” Van Drew said in a statement. “I fought to get these priorities into the bill because they will directly address these concerns and make a real difference in the safety of the residents of South Jersey.”

Democrat Rob Menendez (D-8th) secured approval for a study to “improve navigation south” of the Elizabeth Port Authority Marine Terminal, a significant port for large vessels like container ships.

“Among the priorities I fought for, I am especially proud to have secured the first step toward improving the waterways serving the Elizabeth Marine Terminal,” Menendez said in a statement to NJ Spotlight News. “We’re going to keep fighting to get this project to the finish line because it means better infrastructure, cleaner air, and a stronger economy for our state.”

The Corps’ proposal to cancel hundreds of projects, including the eight in New Jersey, is not final, according to a Menendez staffer.

The Corps did not reply to questions from NJ Spotlight News about the status of its proposed cancellations.

The previously-authorized New Jersey projects received approvals from Congress decades ago, including two, one for Rogers Pond in Franklin Township and another for McCarter Pond in Fairhaven, in the mid-1980s. Others received approval in the 1990s. Only one, a beach-nourishment project for Raritan Bay and Sandy Hook Bay, was funded. That money was approved more than 15 years ago.

Rep. Analilia Mejia (D-11th) was pleased six projects she wanted are in the bill. One addresses algal blooms, which grow worse due to chemical runoff, in Lake Hopatcong, which straddles Sussex and Morris counties.

“The heat creates additional algae bloom, which then chokes out the fish and wildlife in the lake,” Mejia said in an interview with NJ Spotlight News. “It’s the double whammy of ignoring climate change and not updating our infrastructure to the point that actually meets the needs of New Jersey.”

Overall, flooding is a big deal in her district, driven in part by the regional geology, Mejia said. “It’s a basin.”

“From Day 1,” she said, “[I’ve been working with] mayors in Glen Ridge, Bloomfield and Montclair, trying to tackle the fact that every time there’s a rainstorm peoples’ houses are flooding.”

“Same thing in Morris County, same thing in Passaic,” Mejia added.

Lee Zeldin, 17th Administrator of the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA), said “Americans will see a decrease in electricity prices, but this is just the beginning”. He unveiled the reversal of the 2024 carbon pollution standards on Monday.

name: Detroit and Evs
title: Detroit's Worst Nightmare Is Already Happening In Australia - Yahoo Finance
description:
The land of Crocodile Dundee imposes no punitive tariff wall against Chinese vehicles.
The result is one of the world's most competitive automotive markets, with more than 20 Chinese brands—including BYD, MG, GWM, Chery, Geely, Zeekr, Xpeng, Leapmotor and Deepal—fighting for buyers.
GWM and BYD had each delivered roughly 33,000 to 34,000 vehicles during the first eight months of the year.
Kia sold more than 80,000 vehicles in Australia in 2024, achieving a record year and finishing fourth overall.
The Sealion 7 electric SUV alone recorded more than 15,000 sales.
text:
America does not have to imagine what might happen if Chinese automakers were allowed through the front door. It just needs to look at Australia.

The land of Crocodile Dundee imposes no punitive tariff wall against Chinese vehicles. The result is one of the world's most competitive automotive markets, with more than 20 Chinese brands—including BYD, MG, GWM, Chery, Geely, Zeekr, Xpeng, Leapmotor and Deepal—fighting for buyers.

Their rapid advance has already pressured Japanese manufacturers such as Toyota, Mazda, Nissan, Honda and Subaru. But Japan is no longer the whole story. South Korea's Hyundai and Kia, two brands that built their Australian success on value, equipment and long warranties, are now being challenged by Chinese manufacturers using essentially the same playbook—only with lower costs, faster development cycles and formidable electric-vehicle technology.

BYD's monthly sales in Australia almost quadrupled

In August 2025, the Guardian reported that BYD, GWM, MG and Chery all appeared in Australia's top 10 brands for the first time. Chinese-made vehicle sales increased by approximately 8,000 units from a year earlier, while BYD's monthly sales almost quadrupled. GWM and BYD had each delivered roughly 33,000 to 34,000 vehicles during the first eight months of the year.

The effect on Hyundai and Kia requires some nuance. Chinese competition has not simply destroyed Korean sales. Kia sold more than 80,000 vehicles in Australia in 2024, achieving a record year and finishing fourth overall. Its Sportage SUV, Carnival people mover and expanding electric range have helped create a mature brand capable of competing on more than price.

But market disruption is often visible first in rankings and pricing power—not outright sales collapses.

By mid-2026, BYD had reportedly sold more than 60,000 vehicles in Australia, capturing an 8.5% share and overtaking Ford, Mazda and Hyundai to become the country's second-largest automotive brand. Its share had more than doubled from 3.9% during the comparable period a year earlier. The Sealion 7 electric SUV alone recorded more than 15,000 sales.

That is an extraordinary reversal. Hyundai and Kia once played the role now occupied by BYD and Chery: ambitious Asian outsiders offering generous equipment at prices established manufacturers struggled to match. Over several decades, the Korean companies transformed themselves into respected global competitors with attractive designs, strong quality and sophisticated EVs.

Now China is compressing that decades-long development story into a few years.

name: EPA
title: This farm raised thousands of pigs for slaughter. Now it's growing mushrooms instead - NPR
description:
The Faaborg family recently transitioned from pigs to mushrooms with technical and financial support from The Transfarmation Project, an initiative of the charitable organization, Mercy for Animals.
They retrofitted existing buildings on the farm to raise 2,000 hogs at a time.
Tanner Faaborg said he was also bothered by the reshaping of rural Iowa by industrial animal agriculture.
Where Tanner Faaborg saw an opportunity for change, his brother Tyler said he needed more convincing.
A Natural Resources Conservation Service grant program, part of the U.S. Department of Agriculture, partially funded the remediation, Tanner Faaborg said.
text:
Inside a long, dimly lit building, Tyler Faaborg slipped into a "fruiting room" cordoned off by what looked like plastic curtains.

Fog rolled over shelves of sprouting mushrooms. A bulbous fungi called lion's mane still had another week before harvest, he explained.

"You can see they're sort of, a little bit pinkish," Faaborg said. "When they get mature, they're going to be almost all the way white."

Faaborg, along with his parents and brother, grows specialty mushrooms on their family farm in central Iowa and sells them as tinctures, coffee blends and flavored salt.

They call their operation 1100 Farm, which is a nod to the number of hogs this building and the one beside it each held for decades. The Faaborg family recently transitioned from pigs to mushrooms with technical and financial support from The Transfarmation Project, an initiative of the charitable organization, Mercy for Animals.

"We primarily work with industrial animal farmers to help them transition out of that way of farming and into sustainable practices, and that can be growing mushrooms, growing diversified vegetables, incorporating trees and agroecology," said Katherine Jernigan, who directs the project.

In addition to resources online and a network of experts to help farmers grow new crops and start small businesses, Transfarmation provides open-source blueprints for converting industrial pig, poultry and dairy barns.

"That's really what makes Transfarmation unique," Jernigan said. "We're finding ways to repurpose the infrastructure that the farmers already have."

The Faaborgs just finished converting half of one 200-foot-long hog barn this summer. They say the retrofitted space will allow them to scale up their mushroom production after a successful pilot project.

The new mushroom operation is also designed to be a resource for other farmers as Transfarmation's second demonstration hub in the U.S. The first is a former chicken farm in North Carolina.

"The reason we established this as a demonstration hub is very much so the doors can be opened, so people can come and see firsthand," Jernigan said. "They can ask questions, and also, importantly, we're collecting data from this hub with the whole transition, as well as their production."

That data includes the Faaborgs' costs, hours of labor and product margins, along with lessons learned along the way. A Transfarmation spokesperson said the Faaborgs are being compensated $216,000 through a four-year contract for tracking and sharing their information with other farmers in the Transfarmation program.

Jernigan said other farms enrolled in the program have shown it's possible to be profitable switching from industrial-scale farms — known as concentrated animal feeding operations, or CAFOs — to specialty crops. Transfarmation's website includes estimated budgets for farms that grow strawberries, tomatoes and microgreens.

Having more test cases and being transparent about both the challenges and opportunities could help other farmers make the leap, she said.

Tanner Faaborg, who brought the vision of 1100 Farm to the family several years ago, wants their mushroom operation to be another "proof of concept."

"It just takes someone doing something a little different to help folks realize that it is possible," he said.

His parents, Rand and Tammy, bought their 25-acre farm in the 1980s with the dream of a homesteading lifestyle, he said. The family of seven harvested and preserved produce from their garden and fruit trees. They had a wood-burning stove and raised chickens for eggs.

Rand Faaborg said they started out by raising a few market hogs for "pocket money" to supplement his income as a welder. But it didn't work out.

"I lost money," Faaborg said. "And then I saw in the paper this advertisement of contract feeding."

Becoming a CAFO

Under contract feeding, a company provides the animals and pays for the feed while the farmer contributes the labor and covers the costs of the infrastructure.

This legal arrangement is a key component of CAFOs, which the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency defines as operations that meet certain animal number thresholds and confine them in an area without vegetation for at least 45 days out of the year.

Large CAFOs in Iowa increased from 789 in 1990 to 4,444 in 2025, according to an analysis by the Environmental Working Group, an organization that advocates for greater regulation of CAFOs. Together with small- and medium-sized operations, EWG estimates 66% of all the CAFOs in the state housed a total of 33.4 million hogs.

Rand Faaborg said contract feeding seemed like a good opportunity at the time.

The family did not put up new buildings for the enterprise at first. They retrofitted existing buildings on the farm to raise 2,000 hogs at a time.

Faaborg said once the farm scaled up and became a CAFO, it was "very profitable" but required more work than he expected on top of his day job.

"I was working 16-hour days, sometimes 24-hour days, going to work without even sleeping," he said.

After a few years, Faaborg said they borrowed $400,000 to build two new hog barns designed to improve efficiency. They had automatic feeder lines and systems to move the manure out to an open-air holding pit.

"Fortunately, we could make cash flow until we got the buildings paid off," Faaborg said, explaining it took 12 years to get out of debt.

But raising hogs was physically demanding work and became less profitable for the family over time, Faaborg said.

"In my day job, my pay over 35 years increased tenfold, and my pay raising hogs dropped by two-thirds," he said. He believes the decrease in profits was due to the proliferation of CAFOs across the state.

A new chapter for the Faaborgs

Rand and Tammy Faaborg decided several years ago they were ready to exit the hog business. Rand said they didn't have a deep love for raising pigs, but they'd poured so much money and time into the buildings that he didn't want to see them fall into disrepair or be bulldozed.

They asked their family if they had ideas to use the buildings for something else. That's when their son Tanner Faaborg began to lay out his vision.

"We have this infrastructure," he said. "We could retrofit it, change it, and do something that is a lot healthier on us, healthier for the planet, and actually is profitable, that'll be a job creator for the family, but for the community, as well."

Tanner Faaborg said he developed a passion for sustainability and climate change mitigation in college. He joined Urban Ambassadors, a volunteer-driven nonprofit that promotes sustainability in the Des Moines area, and was part of the steering committee for the city's climate action and adaptation plan.

But his work in Iowa's capital felt out of line with other parts of his life.

"I would come back [to the farm] and help out with pig chores and kind of living a double life that I felt terrible about," Tanner Faaborg said.

The Faaborgs raised around 8,000 hogs each year, producing roughly a million gallons of liquid manure. They stored it in an open pit until Rand Faaborg could find row-crop farmers to haul it off to spread on their fields during tight windows in the spring and fall.

While manure can provide essential crop nutrients, it's a major contributor to climate change. Manure pits and lagoons release methane, which is "28 times as potent as carbon dioxide at trapping heat in the atmosphere," according to the EPA. Excess manure in fields can also increase nitrous oxide emissions and pollute nearby bodies of water when it rains.

Tanner Faaborg said he was also bothered by the reshaping of rural Iowa by industrial animal agriculture. Near his childhood home, he pointed to long buildings surrounded by cornfields down the road.

"There used to be a house over there. Now, instead, there's turkey barns," he said. "There used to be a house over there, and now it's hog barns."

These local changes have a ripple effect, he said. The small school he attended no longer exists.

"There's just not enough people," Faaborg said. "There are small towns and rural communities that are losing population every single year, and it's really devastating."

Where Tanner Faaborg saw an opportunity for change, his brother Tyler said he needed more convincing.

Tyler Faaborg said he raised and sold around 200,000 hogs a year across three counties. But when his parents announced to the family that they were done, he said it took about a week to decide he was ready to try something different.

"I had a good job. I got paid well," he said. "But I did it for 25 years. It's really hard on your body, and Tanner just kept talking to me about it."

The Faaborgs began working with Transfarmation in 2021, sold the last herd of hogs a year later and received a $15,000 grant from the program in 2023 to start growing mushrooms and sell products as a yearlong pilot project. The Faaborgs reported that site preparations in one of their outbuildings, supplies, branding and website development cost roughly $35,000.

As the business grows and expands with the new demonstration hub, Tyler Faaborg said they'd like to sell fresh mushrooms to a few companies. Eventually, 1100 Farm could also convert the second hog barn. But Tanner Faaborg said it would be used for something else, possibly microgreens.

Rewilding the farm

The Faaborgs said the transition from CAFO to specialty mushrooms has not always been easy, and they have a long road ahead. But there have been rewards along the way, like the conversion of a manure pit into a freshwater pond.

A Natural Resources Conservation Service grant program, part of the U.S. Department of Agriculture, partially funded the remediation, Tanner Faaborg said. Instead of being an eyesore, he said it's become a haven for frogs, ducks and other wildlife.

"It just shows that if you create the right environment, that rewilding can happen faster than you think," Faaborg said.

Rand Faaborg said the manure pit was a significant source of anxiety when he raised hogs. Sometimes he'd make contact with people who said they would take the manure but not show up, he said.

"That part of my life is gone and in exchange is just this little pond. My grandkids catch frogs," he said. "That's probably been my favorite part of it all."

The Faaborgs also have planted native grasses and flowers to support pollinators. They're expanding their orchard and adding hundreds of trees and shrubs next to the creek that cuts across the farm to support better water quality and wildlife habitat.

Standing next to an empty grain silo that once held pig feed, Tanner Faaborg said he'd like to turn it into a space for visitors to stay overnight and wake up the next morning to sip lion's mane coffee while looking out at the farm.

The list of projects is long enough that they could take the rest of his life to complete. But he hopes the impact of 1100 Farm extends well beyond that.

title: 5 Companies Using NVIDIA AI for Clean Energy
description:
Clean energy isn’t hard to come by, but the pace of large-scale adoption has historically been slow due to bottlenecks — including out-of-date infrastructure, elongated research and development timelines, and upfront cost barriers.

text:
Clean energy isn’t hard to come by, but the pace of large-scale adoption has historically been slow due to bottlenecks — including out-of-date infrastructure, elongated research and development timelines, and upfront cost barriers.

At New York Climate Week, NVIDIA is highlighting five companies pioneering clean energy projects with AI baked into their foundation, accelerating research-to-inception pipelines and ultimately helping build a low carbon grid.

ThinkLabs AI Drives Toward An Autonomous Grid With Digital Twins

ThinkLabs AI is curating digital twins and agents — using the NVIDIA CUDA platform — to speed up interconnection timelines, seamlessly integrate clean energy sources and optimize the grid to handle ongoing variability.

“The grid is getting less and less certain, so the ability to see things not statically, but as a probability — hence all the utility actions — should be risk informed,” said Josh Wong, founder and CEO of ThinkLabs, a member of the NVIDIA Inception program for cutting-edge startups. “That hits not just reliability objectives, but also affordability, so we know how to maximize and optimize investments.”

Southern California Edison used ThinkLabs software to reduce the time required to evaluate each grid interconnection application from 30-45 days to just two minutes.

The speedup came from a ThinkLabs agent that runs grid simulations and identifies solutions to interconnection barriers.

Atomic Canyon’s AI Platform Helps Redefine Operations in the Nuclear Sector

Atomic Canyon, another NVIDIA Inception member, is bringing AI-powered knowledge management and assistance to reactor operators with its NVIDIA accelerated compute-powered Neutron and NIVA platforms to streamline nuclear power plant operations.

Neutron acts as an AI workbench built for nuclear professionals. It turns all of their procedures, regulatory guidance, operating experience, licensing records, design calculations, and structured and unstructured data into a knowledge layer.

NIVA, short for Nuclear Industry Virtual Assistant, was built with the Institute of Nuclear Power Operations, Electric Power Research Institute and the Nuclear Energy Institute as a unified platform bringing AI-powered capabilities to the national nuclear fleet.

“Nuclear is a known technology we’ve been doing for 50 to 60 years, but the way we’ve been doing things simply will not scale to meet the moment that’s in front of us; it needs to be reinvigorated by artificial intelligence,” said Trey Lauderdale, founder and CEO of Atomic Canyon.

Redwood Materials’ Repurposed EV Batteries Power AI Without Waiting on the Grid

Electricity demand from AI is accelerating faster than new grid infrastructure can be built, leading to a bottleneck in the industry’s growth.

Redwood Materials is closing that gap by harnessing its expertise in battery engineering, power electronics and systems design to build large-scale, off-grid power solutions for AI factories — enabling new capacity to come online in months rather than years.

These 100%-recycled electric vehicle batteries are firming up power suppliers by acting as onsite energy storage to create a secure, flexible energy system for AI factories and the national grid at large.

The batteries are integrated into existing clean energy infrastructure with an AI intelligence layer — running on the NVIDIA Blackwell platform — that makes the system hypervigilant and adaptable to the real-time energy needs of the data center it’s supplying power to.

This approach also lowers the cost of power. Redwood’s simplified architecture — built on in-house power electronics — requires far fewer transformers and inverters, eliminates the need for an uninterruptible power supply, and can deploy repurposed or new electric vehicle batteries.

“Using these batteries with our power electronics and systems control software, you can make a highly responsive power source that can deal with the novel fluctuations of AI training,” said Colin Campbell, chief technology officer of Redwood Materials, another NVIDIA Inception member.

TerraPower’s Natrium Reactor Sets New Standard for Safe, Sustainable Nuclear Power

Nuclear energy currently powers 20% of the nation’s electricity. TerraPower is working to make sure that more power is safe, sustainable and quickly harnessable through its emission-free Natrium reactor.

“Twenty years ago, our founders, including Bill Gates, realized that emissions avoidance should also be a part of this energy solution,” said Chris Levesque, president and CEO of TerraPower.

TerraPower is connecting an NVIDIA Omniverse-powered platform to create digital twin software that will support its efforts to accelerate the siting and delivery of future plants from years to months.

Natrium reactors have a unique design that separates them from traditional nuclear power; they’re cooled with liquid metal sodium instead of water — allowing them to operate at a lower pressure, equivalent to atmospheric pressure. This reactor doesn’t require offsite water or electricity to keep it stable — in the event of an emergency, it can keep itself cool without any intervention.

Commonwealth Fusion Systems Creates Fusion Energy Ready for the Grid

Fusion energy is poised to join the clean energy stack in the 2030’s, thanks to Commonwealth Fusion Systems (CFS).

With the help of NVIDIA Omniverse libraries and OpenUSD, CFS is compressing years of experimentation into weeks for its SPARC tokamak demonstration fusion machine, which can successfully replicate the sun’s power source on Earth.

Fusion energy is a carbon-free, safe source of power.

“With fusion, there’s no running out of control,” said Brandon Sorbom, cofounder and chief science officer of CFS. “It is passively safe, since the default mechanism is shutting itself down.”

Using high-temperature superconductors, CFS enables stronger magnetic fields than previous fusion systems.

These magnets allow SPARC’s design to be 40x smaller and, by extension, cheaper to build and operate. The company’s ARC power plant — the first of which will be built in Chesterfield County, Virginia, and will connect to the grid in the 2030s — is more than 10x smaller.

“We will be able to build a first-of-its-kind plant that will be cost-competitive with both renewable and nonrenewable sources of energy,” said Sorbom.

title: Climate Week: Clean Energy Progress Report - New York League of Conservation Voters
description:
As Climate Week gets underway, New York has plenty of clean energy progress to celebrate – and plenty of work still ahead.
[Skip to: Offshore Wind, Solar, Energy Storage, Transmission, Final Word on Planning] Offshore Wind Why Wind Offshore wind is about more than megawatts.
Solar Why Solar Solar energy has been one of the brightest areas of New York’s clean energy transition.
Energy Storage Why Energy Storage New York needs more energy storage – a safe, reliable, affordable solution for a grid already under stress.
Transmission Why Transmission Transmission lines are essentially high-capacity highways for electricity.
text:
As Climate Week gets underway, New York has plenty of clean energy progress to celebrate – and plenty of work still ahead.

From offshore wind and solar to energy storage, projects across the state are already generating clean power, creating jobs, strengthening the grid, and helping protect New Yorkers from volatile energy costs. Here’s where we stand – and where we need to go next.

[Skip to: Offshore Wind, Solar, Energy Storage, Transmission, Final Word on Planning]

Offshore Wind

Why Wind

Offshore wind is about more than megawatts. It’s about energy independence rooted here at home – power that isn’t subject to international conflicts and that can help protect families from the rollercoaster ride of rising energy costs.

New York’s coast is well positioned for offshore wind development, with strong wind conditions and a relatively shallow sea floor that extends for miles offshore.

And for the densely populated downstate region, offshore wind provides something especially important: large-scale generation of clean, locally produced power delivered directly into areas of highest demand.

Where We Are

New York already has one offshore wind farm operating and two major projects under construction. Together, Sunrise Wind and Empire Wind 1 are expected to add another 1,734 megawatts of clean power when completed.

South Fork Wind – Operational

12 wind turbines

132 megawatts

Enough to power 70,000 homes

1,000 workers across five states contributed to the project

Sunrise Wind – In Construction

84 wind turbines

924 megawatts

Enough to power approximately 600,000 homes

Expected to begin operating in 2027

Empire Wind 1 – In Construction

54 wind turbines

810 megawatts

Enough to power approximately 500,000 homes

Expected to begin operating in 2027

Proof It’s Working: Offshore Wind Delivers During the Cold

This winter offered a real-world demonstration of what offshore wind can bring to the grid.

During January’s extreme cold, the nation’s two operating utility-scale offshore wind farms performed as well as gas-fired power plants and better than coal-fired facilities, according to reporting from Canary Media. South Fork Wind posted a 52% capacity factor for the month – putting it on par with New York’s most efficient gas plants.

As Liz Burdock, president and CEO of Oceantic Network, put it, offshore wind is demonstrating that it can provide “reliable power when the grid needs it the most.”

Where We Need to Go

Fund community engagement through the Offshore Wind Predevelopment Support Program.

Ensure state-led support to preserve progress and meet New York’s climate targets.

Support projects that can continue advancing interconnection, state permits, and engineering design while federal permitting and contracting are stalled.

Fight federal efforts to halt this stable, affordable domestic energy source.

Solar

Why Solar

Solar energy has been one of the brightest areas of New York’s clean energy transition. It means a more reliable energy grid, good-paying jobs, lower costs for ratepayers, and fewer harmful emissions.

Where We Are

New York has now installed more than eight gigawatts of distributed solar.

Enough to power more than 1.3 million homes and businesses.

The state is ahead of schedule for its 10-gigawatt goal by 2030.

Generated approximately $12.2 billion in private investment

Supports more than 16,000 jobs statewide.

And solar isn’t just adding clean electricity to the grid. It’s increasingly showing its value when New Yorkers need power most.

Proof It’s Working: Solar Shows Up During Peak Demand

On June 3, New York set a new solar generation record, with solar providing approximately 29% of statewide electricity demand during the noon hour.

And during the first week of July’s heat wave, rooftop and community solar helped New York avoid an estimated $200 million in peak grid costs, according to NYSERDA President and CEO Doreen Harris.

That builds on the estimated $90 million in wholesale electricity costs solar saved New Yorkers last summer by easing pressure on the grid during periods of peak demand.

As Harris recently wrote, those investments are paying dividends by “strengthening the electric grid and reducing costs for New Yorkers during periods of highest demand.”

Where We Need to Go

Advance programs and incentives to achieve 20 gigawatts of distributed solar by 2035 and six gigawatts of energy storage by 2030.

The Governor must sign the SUNNY Act, which would legalize “balcony solar” – small, plug-in panels that families can use to generate renewable energy and lower their energy bills.

The State Legislature must pass Auto Solar Permitting so projects can be completed more efficiently, saving New Yorkers both time and money.

Energy Storage

Why Energy Storage

New York needs more energy storage – a safe, reliable, affordable solution for a grid already under stress.

Energy storage collects electricity and releases it when it’s needed most, including during heat waves, cold snaps, and other periods of extreme demand. That helps stabilize the grid, reduce electricity costs, and decrease reliance on high-polluting peaker plants in surrounding communities.

Energy storage systems are also subject to extensive fire and safety requirements designed to protect communities.

Where We Are

New York now has more than 500 megawatts of energy storage installed, with nearly 1,500 additional megawatts contracted or awarded.

The state has set a goal of reaching six gigawatts of energy storage by 2030 – meaning there is still significant work ahead.

New York has also updated its fire and building codes governing energy storage systems, strengthening the standards that determine how projects are designed and built.

The Case for Storage: Reliability, Affordability and Jobs

In a recent Newsday commentary, Building and Construction Trades Council of Nassau and Suffolk Counties President Matthew Aracich laid out the economic and reliability case for building more storage on Long Island.

“Energy storage is critical infrastructure – which in turn means jobs and investment,” Aracich wrote.

Storage can also make better use of the grid infrastructure New York already has, storing electricity when it is plentiful and returning it to the grid when demand – and prices – rise.

Where We Need to Go

Increase tax incentives for utility-scale energy storage systems.

Lift local moratoriums that are preventing projects from moving forward across New York.

Provide technical assistance and planning support for communities considering energy storage projects.

Identify and develop unused city-owned land in New York City for neighborhood-scale energy storage to protect communities from blackouts and reduce pollution from dirty peaker plants.

Update New York City’s codes to allow for residential solar + storage.

Transmission

Why Transmission

Transmission lines are essentially high-capacity highways for electricity. By providing both energy delivery and grid modernization, projects like CHPE, Smart Path Connect, and Propel NY Energy are essential for transporting clean energy from where it is generated to the communities where it is needed most.

And that need is only growing. New York’s electricity demand is projected to increase significantly over the next two decades. Meeting that demand means not only building new renewable energy capacity, but ensuring our transmission system can keep up.

Projects like these are critical to getting off the expensive roller coaster ride of fossil fuels and providing the stable and affordable clean energy future New Yorkers deserve.

Where We Are

Champlain Hudson Power Express – Operational

The 339-mile, 1,250-megawatt transmission line carries clean hydropower from Canada underground and underwater to the Astoria Energy Complex in Queens, where it enters New York City’s electric grid.

CHPE is expected to deliver 10.4 terawatt-hours of clean energy annually – enough to meet up to 20% of New York City’s electricity needs – while reducing carbon emissions by an estimated 37 million metric tons through 2040.

The project is also expected to generate more than $3.4 billion in economic investment over its 25-year contract.

Smart Path Connect – Operational

Developed by the New York Power Authority and National Grid, Smart Path Connect is a 100-mile project to modernize transmission infrastructure across the North Country and Mohawk Valley – unlocking up to one gigawatt of additional renewable energy.

The project is expected to provide approximately $438 million in benefits annually to New Yorkers by reducing transmission congestion and improving the efficiency and reliability of the grid.

Propel NY Energy – Moving Toward Construction

Last week brought another major transmission milestone.

On September 17, the New York State Public Service Commission granted Propel NY Energy its Certificate of Environmental Compatibility and Public Need – a key approval allowing the project to move forward toward construction.

Led by NYPA and New York Transco, Propel will build approximately 90 miles of new underground transmission lines across Long Island, New York City, and Westchester County, and strengthen connections with the rest of the state and improving the reliability and resiliency of the downstate grid.

Where We Need to Go

Continue upgrading transmission lines and substations across the state

Build the capacity needed to prevent bottlenecks and power curtailment

Continue implementing the RAPID Act to streamline permitting

Ensure that transmission planning keeps pace with growing electricity demand

Wind, solar, and storage must go hand-in-hand with the poles and wires that deliver those clean resources to our homes and businesses – because there is no clean energy transition without transmission.

A Final Word on Planning

If we’re serious about delivering affordable, reliable clean energy, we have to build the grid that makes it possible. But that requires not only adding more new solar panels or wind turbines. It requires thoughtfully and proactively planning the electric grid – with coordination among utilities, power authorities, and state agencies – so we can connect new energy sources, meet growing demand, improve reliability, and keep costs stable and manageable. Importantly, this work needs to happen at a pace that reflects the urgency of climate change.

Ultimately, energy policy is about people. It’s about families being able to afford their energy bills and about kids breathing cleaner air. It’s about making our communities – and the power they rely on – more resilient.

We know that passing laws alone won’t get us there. The next chapter of New York’s environmental leadership must be about execution and delivering tangible results for New Yorkers.

title: Who should pay for lithium-ion battery fire damage? - Resource Recycling
authors: David Daoud, Paul Lane, Javier Castillo
description:
A lithium-ion battery tossed into the wrong bin can travel unnoticed until a compactor, shredder or sorting machine punctures it.
Interviews and other evidence collected by the agency indicated that lithium-ion battery fires were substantially underreported.
SWANA CEO Amy Lestition Burke called lithium-ion battery fires “one of the most urgent safety issues” facing the waste and recycling sector.
Minnesota lawmakers considered another approach after a lithium battery apparently ignited inside a recycling collection truck.
It is whether responsibility for preventing battery fires and responsibility for the losses that result from them should continue to be treated separately.
text:
Editor’s note: Fire safety and electronics recycling will be featured in sessions at the 2026 E-Scrap: The Longevity Conference in New Orleans October 26-28.

A lithium-ion battery tossed into the wrong bin can travel unnoticed until a compactor, shredder or sorting machine punctures it. By then, the person who discarded the battery is gone, the manufacturer is far removed and the recycling operator is left fighting the fire.

The scale of the problem is alarming. The US Environmental Protection Agency identified 245 fires at 64 waste-management facilities between 2013 and 2020 that were caused or likely caused by lithium metal or lithium-ion batteries. The incidents occurred at a number of sites, which include material recovery facilities, landfills, electronics recyclers, scrap yards, waste-to-energy facilities and during transportation. EPA cautioned that its research did not represent a complete accounting. Interviews and other evidence collected by the agency indicated that lithium-ion battery fires were substantially underreported.

European recyclers report similarly serious consequences. Research cited by the European Recycling Industries’ Confederation found that 36% of surveyed waste electrical and electronic equipment recyclers experienced a severe fire between 2016 and 2019. EuRIC reported that severe thermal events could take one to six hours to extinguish and estimated the average cost of more severe incidents at approximately €1.3 million ($1.5 million). The organization warned that such losses can be particularly difficult for a recycling industry composed largely of small and medium-sized companies.

When a fire occurs, the receiving facility faces the immediate operational consequences. Those can include damaged equipment, emergency response, cleanup, interrupted service and lost production. Regardless of how insurance, contracts or subsequent legal claims ultimately distribute the financial loss, the facility must first contend with the fire and the disruption it causes.

The industry has responded by strengthening prevention and emergency procedures. In December 2025, the Solid Waste Association of North America, National Waste & Recycling Association and Recycled Materials Association announced joint guidance covering battery identification, employee training, storage, handling and emergency planning at material recovery facilities. SWANA CEO Amy Lestition Burke called lithium-ion battery fires “one of the most urgent safety issues” facing the waste and recycling sector.

Prevention, however, carries its own costs. Lithium batteries are regulated as hazardous materials during transportation under Parts 171 through 180 of Title 49 of the Code of Federal Regulations. Damaged or defective batteries can require specialized packaging and handling, with additional requirements depending on their condition and how they are transported. Building a collection system capable of identifying, separating, storing and safely moving these batteries therefore requires more than simply placing another collection bin in front of consumers.

States are beginning to move more of these front-end responsibilities upstream. Illinois’ Portable and Medium-Format Battery Stewardship Act requires producers selling covered batteries in the state, beginning January 1, 2026, to participate in an approved stewardship plan providing for collection and end-of-life management. The programs are overseen by the Illinois Environmental Protection Agency. The Environmental Council of the States described the legislation when it was enacted as the country’s 16th battery extended-producer-responsibility law.

Minnesota lawmakers considered another approach after a lithium battery apparently ignited inside a recycling collection truck. House File 3566 proposed a recycling fee equal to 3.2% of the retail price of most covered electronics, with the revenue intended to support a system for collection and recycling of covered electronic devices. The legislation would have allowed retailers to collect the fee from purchasers. Representative Athena Hollins, discussing the truck fire and the broader battery problem, warned that the incident could not be dismissed as a “one-off.”

Illinois’ law and proposals such as Minnesota’s illustrate efforts to move more of the cost and responsibility for collection upstream. Convenient collection systems can give consumers alternatives to throwing batteries and battery-containing products into household recycling or trash, while stewardship programs can make producers participate financially in managing products at the end of their useful lives.

But collection responsibility and catastrophic-loss responsibility are not the same thing. When a battery still reaches the wrong facility and starts a fire, the operator initially confronts the suppression effort, cleanup, damaged equipment and downtime. Existing stewardship programs can shift collection and recycling costs upstream without necessarily assigning responsibility for catastrophic losses caused by improperly discarded batteries.

That distinction has important implications. Producer-funded collection can reduce the likelihood that batteries enter conventional waste and recycling streams, but it does not by itself answer what happens when prevention fails. A manufacturer, retailer, stewardship organization, consumer, municipality, insurer and recycling facility can each occupy a different position in the chain, while the fire occurs at only one of them.

The emerging policy question is therefore broader than who should pay to collect and recycle batteries. It is whether responsibility for preventing battery fires and responsibility for the losses that result from them should continue to be treated separately.

For now, policy is moving more of the prevention cost upstream. The much harder question of how catastrophic fire losses should ultimately be allocated remains largely unresolved.

title: Leveraging Strategic Assets: Attracting Financing in the Developing World in a Post-Aid Era
description:
Context: The Decline of Aid Global development assistance is undergoing a radical transformation.
Low-income countries have a wider choice of sources of development finance at a time when concessional aid is becoming scarce.
